articles.title: Iran claims strike on U.S. ship in Strait of Hormuz as fighting escalates
articles.summary: Iran said Sunday it struck an unmanned U.S. vessel trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz, the latest salvo in a new flare-up of fighting between the two countries.

image.caption: A swimmer remains near the shore as a motorboat passes commercial vessels anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. (Vahid Salemi/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
Iran said Sunday it struck an unmanned U.S. vessel trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz, the latest salvo in a new flare-up of fighting between the two countries.
The U.S. did not immediately confirm the purported attack
The U.S. did not immediately confirm the purported attack, which came a day after the U.S. military said forces struck three Iranian oil tankers in response to a missile attack on Navy warships.

The war began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran on Feb. 28. But since a ceasefire agreement was announced in June, on-and-off fighting has persisted with both sides trying to inflict military and economic pain as negotiations have collapsed.
Strikes come about a week after fighting resumed

The U.S. and Iran resumed attacks last week, following a month of relative calm, with the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian communities along it again being targeted. At least five people were killed earlier in the week during a U.S. bombardment of southern Iran.

The Trump administration appears to have adopted a dual-prong approach to the conflict, responding militarily to attacks on the strait while going after foreign financial institutions that handle Iran's money.

items: U.S. military hits 3 Iranian oil tankers after saying its navy warships were targeted
Iran attacks U.S. bases across Gulf after reports of deadly strike on wedding

blocks.text: But Tehran's hard-line new senior leaders have signaled the willingness to dig in after weathering decades of sanctions.

Iran has found ways over the years to circumvent sanctions, and now the U.S. blockade, and get its oil to buyers to help ease growing economic pressures. That relies in part on a shadow fleet transporting its oil.

Meanwhile, Iran's nuclear program, the issue that contributed to the outbreak of the war, was meant to be addressed in negotiations that fell apart soon after the U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in mid-June.
Diplomats say the U.S., Britain, France and Germany seek to refer Iran to the U.N. Security Council for failure to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations.
Instead, Tehran's new leverage focuses on the Strait of Hormuz that is crucial to global oil and natural gas shipments and was seen as an international waterway before the war began.

articles.title: Clinics for teen moms sought in Congress
articles.summary: Quezon City 5th District Rep. Patrick Michael Vargas has filed a bill seeking to establish Teen Mom Clinics in public hospitals nationwide to provide pregnant teenagers and teen mothers with…

blocks.text: Published September 6, 2026 5:10pm

Quezon City 5th District Rep. Patrick Michael Vargas has filed a bill seeking to establish Teen Mom Clinics in public hospitals nationwide to provide pregnant teenagers and teen mothers with comprehensive healthcare.

Under House Bill No. 3988, or the proposed “Adolescent Pregnancy Prevention Act,” the Department of Health (DOH) would establish specialized Teen Mom Clinics to provide comprehensive prenatal, antenatal, and postnatal care, as well as postpartum counseling to help prevent repeat pregnancies.
The proposed measure also directs the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) to expand its existing residential care facilities for disadvantaged women.

The expansion would include specialized multidisciplinary teams composed of social caseworkers, on-call obstetrician-gynecologists, full-time midwives or nurses, and psychologists, all specifically trained to address the complex needs of pregnant minors.

The DSWD would also be mandated to lead the establishment of strengthened social protection mechanisms against sexual violence, with clear pathways and equipped facilities to protect adolescent victims.
Under the proposed mechanism, expectant and young mothers whose pregnancies resulted from sexual abuse would be provided immediate legal, medical, and psychosocial services.

"By establishing Teen Mom Clinics and strengthening DSWD shelters, we can promote the welfare of our young people and help them overcome the challenges they are facing. They need care and understanding instead of judgment and discrimination,” Vargas said.
Citing official data, the proposed measure noted an increase in live births among girls aged 10 to 14, from 2,320 in 2021 to 3,135 in 2022.
This represented a 35% increase in live births among girls in the age group.

Civil registration records further showed that more than 130,000 of the 180,000 births to minor mothers were fathered by adult men, pointing to cases of statutory rape, incest, and sexual exploitation.

"Adolescent pregnancy is a socioeconomic barrier that often conceals cases of sexual abuse and exploitation. We need safe spaces where young people can seek refuge and heal physically and mentally,” Vargas said.
The proposed measure would also create the Teenage Pregnancy Prevention Council, to be chaired by the DOH secretary and the Commission on Population and Development (POPCOM).

The inter-agency council would include representatives from the DSWD, Department of Education (DepEd), National Youth Commission (NYC), Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), Commission on Higher Education (CHED), and Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) to coordinate healthcare, educational continuity, and legal support.
The bill also requires the establishment of Teen Centers in all municipalities, funded through 10% of the Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) fund.
It would provide automatic PhilHealth coverage for indigent teenage mothers and require schools to include an Adolescent Reproductive Health Curriculum.
The measure also supports sustainable livelihoods through TESDA skills training and prohibits schools from expelling pregnant minors or employers from dismissing them because of their pregnancy.
"When we provide specialized healthcare and safe shelters, we protect young mothers from trauma and give them a fighting chance at a better life," Vargas said.
"We ensure that our young people receive genuine care and protection so they can build a better future for themselves and for the country,' he added.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Shabu worth over P100,000 seized in Bukidnon
articles.summary: CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY — A midnight drug sting led to the capture of an alleged street-level dealer and the seizure of over P100,000 worth of suspected shabu in Malaybalay City, Bukidnon, early Sunday…

blocks.text: CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY — A midnight drug sting led to the capture of an alleged street-level dealer and the seizure of over P100,000 worth of suspected shabu in Malaybalay City, Bukidnon, early Sunday morning, Sept. 6.

Col. Oliver Sotto Navales, Bukidnon Police Provincial Office provincial director, reported the arrest to regional director Brig. Gen. Nestor Babagay Jr. following the operation conducted at around 1:20 a.m.

Operatives from the Malaybalay City Police Station Drug Enforcement Unit and the 1st Provincial Mobile Force Company, working alongside the Provincial Intelligence Unit, entrapped the 48-year-old suspect, identified only as “Magins,” at Purok 6, Barangay Casisang.
Authorities seized eight heat-sealed transparent plastic sachets containing suspected shabu weighing 15.148 grams, with an estimated street value of P103,006.
Also confiscated from the suspect were a P1,000 bill, a black wallet and a gold Isuzu Crosswind SUV (plate number KDU 601).
The seized narcotics were transferred to the Bukidnon Provincial Forensic Unit for qualitative and quantitative analysis.

The suspect remains detained at the Malaybalay City Police Station for documentation and proper disposition. He faces charges for allegedly violating Sections 5 (sale of illegal drugs) and 11 (possession of illegal drugs), Article II of the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002 (RA 9165).

articles.title: 2026 bar exam takers mostly women
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — More than half of the 2026 Bar exam takers are women, consistent with the trend in recent years. As of Sunday morning, Sept. 6, the Supreme Court had logged a total of 11,900…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — More than half of the 2026 Bar exam takers are women, consistent with the trend in recent years.

As of Sunday morning, Sept. 6, the Supreme Court had logged a total of 11,900 examinees, 56 percent or more than 6,000 of whom are women, according to Associate Justice Samuel Gaerlan, this year’s Bar exam chairperson.
Gaerlan also noted that the majority of Bar exam takers appear to be women, based on his inspection of two local testing centers (LTCs) in Metro Manila.
Gaerlan said in a press conference, partly in Filipino, that he was surprised and inspired to see so many women taking the Bar exam.
“While in our time, you could still count women [examinees], but now women make up more than 50 percent,” he also said.
Bar head Cheska Pazziuagan even noted that aspiring women lawyers were taking the exam despite their parental duties.
“If I may share, among the most interesting or the numerous requests that we received this year are moms who would wish to bring breast pumps inside the LTC,” Pazziuagan said.

“So, this also shows that we have so many examinees who just gave birth, who are moms, who are wives, and despite those family circumstances and other struggles in life, they still showed up and went to take the Bar,” she continued.
The second and third days of the Bar exams will be held across 15 LTCs nationwide on Sept. 9 and 13.
Gaerlan said Bar exam results could be released in January.
“Everybody must … enjoy the holiday. I am referring to the Christmas holiday. We will release the result after the holiday season,” the justice said. /mcm

articles.title: Far-right AfD predicted to win big in crucial German state election
articles.summary:
Polling stations open in Saxony-Anhalt with anti-immigration party AfD predicted to gain 41% vote share

German voterswent to the polls on Sunday for a crucial regional election where the…

blocks.text: German voterswent to the polls on Sunday for a crucial regional election where the far-right, anti-immigration and Moscow-friendly Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) is expected to win.
AfD, polling at more than 40% for months in Saxony-Anhalt, even has its sights on winning its first-ever state government, although this is far from assured.
Polls opened at 8am and 1.7 million voters have until 6pm to cast their ballots, with first projections expected shortly after.

The eastern German state is governed by the centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) – the party of Friedrich Merz, the chancellor – in coalition with two smaller parties, and its state premier, Sven Schulze, hopes to rebuild a multiparty coalition to cling to power.

All other major parties have so far maintained a “firewall” of non-cooperation with the AfD, whose Saxony-Anhalt branch is categorised as “right-wing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency.

The AfD’s top candidate Ulrich Siegmund – a 35-year-old who is feted like a rock star at campaign events and has a large social media following – has confidently predicted gaining an absolute majority.
“It was the others who erected the firewalls,” he told Bild. “If no one wants to work with us, then we’ll just have to do it alone.”
Such a scenario would shake Germany, which has so far kept extremist parties in check.
A strong AfD win would also heap pressure on Merz, who has vowed to reboot a stagnant economy and restrict irregular immigration, but has seen his party beaten by the AfD in national surveys too.

“If the AfD wins in Saxony-Anhalt, Merz’s critics will become even more vocal, and calls for better leadership will become impossible to ignore,” said the political scientist Wolfgang Schroeder of the University of Kassel.
Siegmund has promised to lead a political revolution from the state of 2.1 million people and propel the AfD to national victory in 2029.
The AfD’s key campaign promises include a “remigration and deportation offensive”, a ban on LGBTQ rainbow flags at public schools, and an end to new windfarms.
The party has also tapped into a sense of nostalgia for communist East Germany and lingering resentment about an enduring wealth gap with the west, decades after the 1989 fall of the Berlin Wall.
The prospect of an AfD state government has sparked alarm among mainstream parties and minority groups.
Thousands of the AfD’s opponents joined a “festival of democracy” rally in Magdeburg on the eve of the vote.
The German Economic Institute said the AfD’s immigration policy would be “ruinous” for the state, where the population is already ageing, shrinking and highly reliant on foreign-born workers.
Others have voiced fears an AfD-run state security apparatus could leak sensitive information to Russia.
The Kremlin “makes no secret of the fact that the AfD is the most important instrument for destabilising Germany for Putin”, the Thuringia state interior minister, Georg Maier, told the Handelsblatt.
The latest poll, released on Thursday by the public broadcaster ZDF, gave the AfD 41% of the vote.
The CDU was predicted a 23% share, the centre-left Social Democratic party (SPD) 8.5%, and the Greens 6%, while two smaller parties failed to cross the 5% hurdle to reenter parliament.
A similar result may allow a scenario where the CDU and others form a minority government with ad hoc support from the far-left Die Linke, which polled at 11.5%.

articles.title: BI arrests Korean fugitive wanted for fraud in home country
articles.summary: A Korean fugitive wanted for fraud in his home country was arrested by the Bureau of Immigration (BI) during an enforcement operation in Makati City on August 25, 2026.

blocks.text: Published September 6, 2026 4:40pm
A Korean fugitive wanted for fraud in his home country was arrested by the Bureau of Immigration (BI) during an enforcement operation in Makati City on August 25, 2026.
In a press release issued Sunday, the BI identified the fugitive as Son Jongin, 65, who was arrested in a residential area in Barangay Comembo.
The operation was conducted jointly by the BI Fugitive Search Unit and the Korean National Police Agency.
BI records showed that Son was the subject of an arrest warrant issued by the Nonsan Branch of the Daejeon District Court in South Korea in 2020 for fraud, in violation of the country's Criminal Act.
Authorities also determined that Son was an undocumented and overstaying foreign national, making him a fugitive from justice who posed a threat to public safety and security.
During the execution of the warrant, authorities also encountered another Korean national, Song Ung Il, 85.
Song was the subject of a deportation order issued in 2015 for being improperly documented, according to the BI.

BI Commissioner Joel Anthony Viado said the agency would continue to track down foreign fugitives in the country, emphasizing the importance of immigration enforcement in maintaining national and community security.

“Foreign fugitives cannot expect to hide in the Philippines and evade the cases filed against them. We will find them, we will arrest them, and we will enforce our immigration laws,” Viado said in the press release.
The two arrested individuals were turned over to the BI Warden’s Facility, where they will remain while their cases are being processed.

articles.title: ‘Hindi ka biktima’: VP Sara Duterte urged to face accountability amid threats case
articles.summary: Several current and former lawmakers have rejected Vice President Sara Duterte’s portrayal of herself as a victim, saying she must face accountability over the grave threats complaints filed…

blocks.text: September 6, 2026 | 4:33pm

MANILA, Philippines — Several current and former lawmakers have rejected Vice President Sara Duterte’s portrayal of herself as a victim, saying she must face accountability over the grave threats complaints filed against her before a Quezon City court.
Separate statements from current and former lawmakers came after Duterte lashed out at her lawyers in front of the media on September 5, saying that she does not feel safe around law enforcement.
In a statement on Sunday, September 6, Rep. Leila de Lima (Mamamayang Liberal) emphasized that Duterte must face accountability.
“Hindi ka biktima; may pananagutan ka,” De Lima said.
(You are not a victim; you are accountable.)
Former Sen. Antonio Trillanes IV, in a separate statement, also urged the public to “look at Duterte” and choose wisely in the next presidential elections.
“Sana naman maliwanag sa inyo na wala talaga siya (Duterte) sa tamang pag-iisip,” Trillanes said.
(I hope it's clear to you that he/she is really not in her right mind)
“Hindi ito pwedeng maging presidente o manatili bilang bise presidente. Alang-alang sa ating bayan at sa ating mga kapwa Pilipino, pumili naman tayo nang maayos,” he added.
(This person cannot be president or remain as vice president. For the sake of our country and our fellow Filipinos, let's make a better choice.)
Special treatment

On September 4, the Quezon City Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 98 issued a warrant of arrest against Duterte over three counts of grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.

She posted bail on Saturday, September 5, with P120,000 for each count. She appeared personally before the court. One of her lawyers, Paul Lawrence Lim, said that Duterte submitted her mugshots to the court.
For House impeachment prosecutor Rep. Terry Ridon (Bicol-SARO), the said act of Duterte giving her mugshots to the court instead of undergoing booking procedures is a form of “special treatment.”

“The Philippine National Police waived its ordinary booking procedures in the case of Vice President Sara Duterte. It is clearly a case of special treatment that does not speak well of the rule of law and the equality of persons before the law,” Ridon said.
“Dapat pantay ang pagtrato ng batas sa lahat ng mga akusado: ordinaryong tao, senador o pangalawang pangulo. No special treatment,” he added.
(The law must treat all accused individuals equally: whether an ordinary citizen, a senator, or the vice president. No special treatment.)
According to the Department of Justice (DOJ), immunity from suit only applies to the president.

“The DOJ's position is that presidential immunity is lodged solely in the president as chief executive, which is why the DOJ filed the case against the accused,” DOJ spokesperson Polo Martinez told reporters.
For Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla, the Philippine National Police accorded Duterte with “all the respect her position deserves.”
“We have all the body cam footages of her warrants being served. We have all the body cam footages of her arrival to post bail,” Remulla said.
“We knew of her whereabouts the night before but we did not force the warrant of arrest,” he added.
No bearing on the impeachment trial
One of the grounds being challenged by Duterte’s lawyers is the vice president’s alleged immunity from criminal prosecution while being in office, as she is an impeachable officer.
However, for lawyer and former Sen. Franklin Drilon, Duterte’s case before the RTC has no bearing on her ongoing impeachment trial, saying the two proceedings are different in nature.
“As we have said, this impeachment trial is sui generis, a class of its own. It is not a court of law,” Drilon said in a radio interview, according to a OneNews report.

“It is not a criminal case. It is a political process, a process provided for by the Constitution to hold accountable those who should be held accountable… The penalty here, if found guilty, is not imprisonment but removal from public office and perpetual disqualification from public office,” he added.
Impeachment legal spokesperson Benjamin Tolosa also echoed Drilon’s opinion.
He explained that the RTC has made its own judicial determination of probable cause for the issuance of the warrant in connection with Duterte’s case.

“The criminal case and the impeachment proceedings are separate proceedings, with different purposes and consequences. The former determines criminal liability, while the latter concerns the Vice President’s fitness to remain in office,” Tolosa said in a social media post.
The grave threats charge is also being tackled in the impeachment court. It is lodged under Article I of the Articles of Impeachment against Duterte. — with reports from OneNews

articles.title: Sara Duterte’s criminal case no effect on impeachment trial – Gatchalian
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte’s grave threats case before the Quezon City Regional Trial Court (RTC) will have no effect on her ongoing impeachment trial at the Senate Impeachment…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte’s grave threats case before the Quezon City Regional Trial Court (RTC) will have no effect on her ongoing impeachment trial at the Senate Impeachment Court, according to Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian.
He said the two proceedings are separate, with the RTC handling the criminal case and the Senate handling the impeachment case.

“This is my personal opinion, it has no effect on me and on the impeachment trial. The [regional trial] court is different from the impeachment court. How the case goes in court is different from how the impeachment case goes,” he said in an interview with dzBB on Sunday.
“The court had determined that there was probable cause and there will be a hearing. But it doesn’t necessarily mean she’s already guilty and that the court already has a verdict,” he added.
Gatchalian also said that in the impeachment trial, the defense team will still have to present its evidence.
“We’ll see how they will defend [their side], and from there, we’ll make our decision,” he added.

In July, the House prosecution panel rested its case under Article IV, which accuses Duterte of culpable violation of the Constitution and betrayal of public trust over her alleged grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.
Duterte was issued an arrest warrant on Friday, Sept. 4, after a Quezon City court found probable cause to charge her with three counts of grave threats.
The charges stem from Duterte’s public statements in 2024 that she had hired an assassin to kill the president, the first lady, and the former speaker if an alleged plot to kill her succeeded.
Duterte posted P360,000 bail before the Quezon City Regional Trial Court on Saturday.
Gatchalian also called on the police to seriously look into Duterte’s claims that she fears for her life following the issuance of the arrest warrant against her.
“Everyone, including the vice president, should feel safe.” /mcm

articles.title: Sept. 11 was one of many times N.L. residents have opened their homes in a crisis
articles.summary: Newfoundlanders and Labradorians have a long-history of helping those in need, even before the generosity displayed nearly 25 years ago when people opened their homes to stranded airline passengers…

image.caption: George Harvey, his daughter Ann and his son Tom of Isle aux Morts ferried the survivors of the Despatch shipwreck to safety in a small punt, then cared for them for weeks until help arrived. (Illustration by H. B. Goodridge from Sea Stories from Newfoundland, 1958/Memorial Digital Archives Initiativ

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador

Newfoundlanders and Labradorians have a long-history of helping those in need, even before the generosity displayed nearly 25 years ago when people opened their homes to stranded airline passengers during 9/11.
Newfoundlanders and Labradorians have a long history of caring for people in emergencies
It’s been almost twenty-five years since the residents of Gander and other communities in Newfoundland and Labrador took in thousands of stranded airline passengers after the September 11 attacks.
Their generosity inspired books, movies and the musical Come from Away, but it was far from the first time Newfoundlanders and Labradorians had opened their homes to strangers in a crisis.
One evening in July 1828, fisherman George Harvey was walking the lonely beach in Isle aux Morts when he spotted a keg tossing on the waves, a sure sign that a ship had gone down nearby.
At dawn the next morning, he loaded his 17-year-old daughter Ann and 12-year old son Tom into his small punt and set off to locate the wreck.

Hours later, they came upon the Despatch. The ship had struck a rock, but most of its two hundred passengers had managed to cross to a reef, where they were huddled together against the wind and rain “like sea birds.”
Over three days of constant effort, the Harveys hauled the passengers into their punt one by one and ferried them to the safety of the shore.
But their work wasn’t done.
For two to three weeks, while they waited for a relief ship to arrive, the Harvey family cared for the 163 survivors in their home and makeshift shelters.

According to surveyor Joseph Jukes, who stayed with the Harveys a decade later, their food stores “were so completely exhausted, that [they] were compelled to live chiefly on salt fish, with neither bread, flour, butter, nor tea, during the whole of that winter.”

Another shipwreck during World War II had far-reaching impact. When the American destroyer USS Truxtun ran aground on the Burin Peninsula in February 1942, eighteen-year-old Black seaman Lanier Phillips jumped from the deck into freezing waves slick with oil.
He later awoke in the small community of St. Lawrence, where locals had laid the survivors out on tables, stripped off their wet clothes, and were sponging the oil from their skin.
Raised in Georgia in the shadow of the Ku Klux Klan, Phillips said he felt more fear being naked in the presence of white women than he had when he jumped into the water.
“One lady had my hand,” he recalled, “and she said, ‘Gee, this poor fella… the oil is all in his pores.’”
Phillips replied, “That’s the colour of the skin. You can’t get it off.”
The woman, Violet Pike, had never seen a Black man before. She took Phillips to her home, spoon-fed him soup and put him to bed.
“The feeling I had was that all Caucasians were racists and bigots,” Phillips said. “Well, they showed me there were people in the world that were not.”
The experience inspired Phillips to fight segregation and break new ground for Black sailors in the U.S. Navy.

He became the navy’s first Black sonar technician in 1957 and went on to an innovative civilian career as an oceanographer. He was active in the civil rights movement and marched with Martin Luther King Jr. in Selma, Ala.
In later life, Phillips travelled throughout North America speaking about that night in St. Lawrence, his career and his vision for racial equality.
Twenty years after the sinking of the USS Truxtun, thousands of Newfoundlanders were forced to evacuate during fearsome wildfires in 1961.
The town of Terrenceville on the Burin Peninsula was overwhelmed by smoke. While local men stayed to fight the blaze, 450 women and children were ferried in the middle of the night to Bay L’Argent.
Telegraph operators stayed up all night to co-ordinate the rescue, and every car owner in the Marystown area was awakened to drive 60 kilometres and pick the evacuees up.

“Within one hour 40 cars were on the road,” the Evening Telegram reported, “and in less than three hours 200 evacuees were assembled in Marystown’s St. Gabriel’s Hall where hot drinks and sandwiches were distributed.”
Once fed, the evacuees were welcomed into private homes in Marystown, Fortune and Grand Bank.
Then-mayor of Marystown E. P. Reddy said the community’s response was a “spontaneous outburst of charity towards a neighbour in time of dire need.”
Not foreseeing what was to come in 2001, though, Reddy turned out to be mistaken when he reflected that such an act “may never be surpassed in the history of our island.”

Gander’s generosity on 9/11 is getting the Heritage Minute treatment by locals

blocks.text: Is Newfoundland and Labrador really more hospitable than anywhere else?
Most cultures prize hospitality. A moral imperative to help strangers in need is part of what makes human societies adaptive and resilient.

That doesn’t mean all cultures express hospitality the same way. Some societies prefer structured hospitality, where guests are invited and activities planned in advance. Other communities prioritize spontaneous hospitality, welcoming drop-ins and unexpected visitors.

In her book Foreign to Familiar, Sarah A. Lanier suggests structured hospitality is more common in cold climates and spontaneous hospitality in hot climates, because mild weather encourages outdoor mingling and open-door policies.
Harsh environments, where mutual support is critical for survival, can also foster a welcoming attitude.

Hospitality is one of the highest virtues among the Bedouin, who traditionally lived in the desert. Newfoundland and Labrador’s volatile weather and rugged terrain may have promoted hospitality for similar reasons.

Inhabitants of unforgiving surroundings may also get more opportunities to demonstrate hospitality. The turbulent North Atlantic, for better or worse, has supplied Newfoundlanders and Labradorians with many occasions to care for shipwreck survivors.
Whatever the reason, stories of strangers finding a welcome in the worst of circumstances can inspire us all, like Lanier Phillips, to see the best in humanity.

articles.title: Nigel Farage to be quizzed as he battles to contain growing donations scandal – UK politics live
articles.summary:
The Reform UK leader is under pressure after senior aides appeared to plot how to bypass electoral laws on foreign donations

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of UK politics. The…

blocks.text: Nigel Farage to be questioned as he battles to contain growing donations scandal

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of UK politics. The Reform UK party leader, Nigel Farage, is scheduled to appear on Laura Kuenssberg’s Sunday politics programme at 9am, where he will likely be asked more about an undercover investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News which showed two of his senior aides appearing to plot to get around electoral laws on foreign donations.
Accepting donations from a foreign company, including donations in kind such as polling, could constitute a criminal offence and the party has been reported to the police.
Senior aide Dan Jukes and Reform’s head of policy James Orr have both stood down pending the outcome of an internal party investigation.

As my colleagues note in the story, Farage himself remains under pressure over a separate clip in which he was heard saying “it’s all above board” after one of the reporters who was posing as the UK-based son of a wealthy US backer told the Reform leader he had been in discussions with Jukes and Orr for some time.
“I’ll be the registered donor,” the son says. “But then dad will send the money to me, and then as soon as that’s done and all those conversations are had the money is available.”

On Saturday, during the party’s conference in Birmingham, Farage continued to bat away suggestions of impropriety. “I’m not a compliance officer,” he told the BBC. “I frankly wasn’t even listening,” he said in reference to the meeting with the undercover reporters in Clacton.

Farage has framed the investigation, carried out by Verbatim Investigations, which was founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting, as another example of an establishment stitch up, and has denied any wrongdoing, as have Orr and Jukes.
Key events

blocks.text: The Guardian’s city editor, Anna Isaacs, is sitting on the panel on Laura Kuenssbergg’s show alongside broadcaster Jeremy Vine and political scientist Francis Fukuyama.

Her revelation that Nigel Farage received a £5m gift from the Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne shortly before announcing he would stand in the 2024 British general election has dogged the Reform leader ever since she broke the story in April.

Farage, who has given different explanations as to why he accepted the gift, has argued he did not need to declare the money because he received it before he was elected as Clacton MP and it “wasn’t political in any sense at all”.
The parliamentary standards commissioner is investigating whether he broke the rules.

Isaac’s report came before a series of other stories raising questions about Reform’s finances, some of which you can read here. Isaacs was among the journalists who have reported critically on Reform who were banned from the party’s annual conference that concluded yesterday.

articles.title: How Prince Harry and Meghan's return to Britain is setting off 'shockwaves'

image.caption: U.K. newspapers were full of headlines after word broke last month that Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, would be returning to Britain for an extended period. (William J Connolly/Getty Images)

blocks.text: After Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, stepped back as working members of the Royal Family and settled in California in 2020, there was little to suggest they would want to return to the United Kingdom any time soon.
So it came as a considerable surprise when word broke that Harry, Meghan and their two children were on their way back and would settle outside London for an extended period.
"It seems so counterintuitive and so contradictory to everything that they have said since the moment they left," royal historian Justin Vovk said in an interview.

But now they're back, and even though there has been much telegraphing of the idea that Harry and Meghan are not going to be working royals again, the move carries broader implications for both the institution of the monarchy and other members of the Royal Family.
"Regardless of whatever their reasons are, their return creates massive shockwaves," Vovk said.
Harry and Meghan moving back to the U.K.
"What does this mean for Harry and Meghan as a couple? What does this mean for Harry and Meghan and their children as a family unit? How will this impact relations with the rest of the Royals?

"How will the monarchy respond to this? How will the British public respond to this? How will in particular the tabloid and the predatory media respond to this? How will Harry engage with the media in light of his wins and losses in court over the past year regarding media intrusions?"
Harry and Meghan have their supporters and detractors, and as much as they have stepped back from official royal duties, what they do and say continues to draw attention.

"They may not be working royals, but they're still members of the Royal Family," Craig Prescott, a constitutional expert and lecturer in law at Royal Holloway, University of London, said in an interview.
"Harry is the son of the King at the end of the day, and he will never not be the son of the King."
For the monarchy, Harry and Meghan's return could divert attention from day-to-day activities of the House of Windsor.
Londoners react to Prince Harry and Meghan’s move back to U.K.

"Officially, nothing changes," Prescott said. "But clearly, Harry will get attention wherever he goes, whatever he does, and so there is a sort of risk of that being a distraction from the work of the monarchy."
To avert that, Prescott sees a need for "some element" of communication between Buckingham Palace and Harry and Meghan.
Vovk sees their return as potentially a new "crisis point" for the monarchy.

"It all depends on how things are handled on both sides. We know the palace is going to — and they've already taken the position — that [Harry and Meghan are] not working royals, 'we won't be commenting on their lives now that they're back.'
"So a lot will depend on how Harry and Meghan proceed."

How they proceeded over the past few years — in what became a visible estrangement from the wider Royal Family — included several instances of pointed criticism of the monarchy and the family itself, whether through their interview with Oprah Winfrey, a Netflix docuseries or publication of Harry's memoir Spare.
More recently, there has been no public criticism, and with King Charles, there appears to have been some rapprochement.

Harry, Meghan and their children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, visited with the King and Queen Camilla privately when they were in the U.K. last month, prior to word breaking of their return.
"You can imagine at the personal level [King Charles] would want to see his son and the children, as I assume Camilla would at one level," Prescott said.
"But … Harry did single Camilla out for criticism in [Spare] and … that dynamic would be interesting to know more about, how Camilla views all this."

There is, however, no sense that Harry's estrangement from his elder brother, Prince William, has thawed in any way. Much media speculation since the return has focused on how William and his wife, Catherine, Princess of Wales, will be feeling about it.
"We're probably not going to hear a word about anything from them because anything that is said, people will jump on, people will try to read into it," Vovk said.

For William, Prescott suggested, there could be a risk that there would come a point when — particularly if Charles is seen to be a bit more forgiving — that the lack of contact with his brother could start to look "quite surly and sulky."
"At some point, you may have to just let bygones be bygones and just move on and not hold a grudge for forever and a day."

The return also spawns numerous questions around issues that have been at the heart of some of Harry's most vocal grievances, whether over actions of the media — particularly the tabloids — or security for him and his family.
Still, it seems likely that whatever Harry and Meghan do will draw headlines, fuel much conversation on social media and continue to divide opinion.
"Anything that they do creates a public response because whether people like them or people hate them … there is clearly something about them that still activates public opinion," said Vovk.

How will the British press cover Harry and Meghan this time around?

blocks.text: He sees multiple reasons for that, one of the biggest being Harry is the younger son of the late Diana, Princess of Wales.

People who have felt like they connected with Harry after his mother's death in 1997 have continued to feel that connection, said Vovk. He likens Harry to "a reflecting mirror that has a billion different reflecting facets on it, because there are so many millions and millions of people who take an interest in him."
"It says more about us … consuming celebrity culture than it does necessarily about Harry personally."
A new royal face on Canada's $20 bill
Canadians just got their first glimpse of King Charles on the $20 bill. Our CBC friend Natalie Stechyson had this report:
It's official — Canada has a new $20 bill.

Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem unveiled the new, vertical bill featuring a portrait of King Charles on Thursday in Ottawa. It's the first Canadian bank note to feature Charles, whose image replaces that of the late Queen Elizabeth II.

In a news conference, Macklem called the unveiling "historic." It's been more than 70 years since a new monarch appeared on a Canadian bank note. The late Queen Elizabeth first appeared on the bank's inaugural $20 note in 1935 as a young princess, Macklem added.
Two years later, in 1937, the bank's bilingual series featured King George on most of its bills. By 1954, with its landscape series, every note carried the portrait of Queen Elizabeth, until now.
The new bill is also historic because it "features security technologies never before used on a Canadian bank note," Macklem said.
"Our new $20 note is both visually stunning and more secure than ever."
The new note is polymer, predominantly green and vertical in orientation.
The Canadian National Vimy Memorial remains on the back. Charles is centred on the front.
The new note will gradually enter circulation in late February 2027.
In a news release, the bank explained that the portrait of Charles is surrounded by a floral and leafy tapestry "inspired by the King's lifetime dedication to the environment."

Also on the front are provincial and territorial floral emblems representing the 13 provinces and territories. A circular window, which the bank explains is visible from both sides of the note, "features plants that are culturally significant to Indigenous Peoples in Canada."

As for security features, the note has a purple security stripe that includes elements that "spin, transform and pulse" when the note is moved, the bank said. This makes the bill "easy to check and hard to counterfeit."
Bank of Canada governor unveils new $20 bill

"The new $20 note reflects important parts of who we are as Canadians, honouring our Commonwealth roots and our ties with international allies," Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said in the news release.

"It honours our constitutional traditions through the portrait of His Majesty King Charles III and recognizes the service and sacrifice of Canadians through the Vimy Memorial, a symbol that continues to resonate across generations."
The Bank of Canada has previously noted that the $20 bill is its most-circulated currency.

The government announced that King Charles would replace his mother on Canada's currency during his coronation celebration in 2023. The first Canadian coins bearing the image of the King began circulating that December.
Back to royal work
This time of year has a back-to-school, back-to-work, holidays-are-over feel to it, and that seemed to be the case for some senior royals this week, too.
After a traditional summer break at Balmoral in Scotland, King Charles and Queen Camilla had a noticeably busier roster of engagements over the past few days.
They were at the British Museum in London on Wednesday evening to view the historic Bayeux Tapestry.

Other engagements included Charles meeting the Pakistani national cricket team at Clarence House. Camilla was at the Royal Academy of Dance, and had engagements that focused on her literary interests in Liverpool on Friday.
On Thursday evening, Camilla also made a surprise appearance at an event that celebrates "the enduring power of literary correspondence," Buckingham Palace said.
Camilla read out loud a letter that was written by Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother after the death of her husband King George VI in 1952.
The notable uptick in royal engagements early in September is a change from the reign of Queen Elizabeth, who stayed much longer at Balmoral each summer.
"It's a slight modernization of … the royal calendar," said Prescott, who noted that there was a time when it was more based on the ecclesiastical calendar.
"The Queen just followed that rhythm of decades gone past, whereas [now] it's just more typical that September is a fully working month."
There is also, Prescott said, a sense that Charles likes his royal work, "so is perhaps, in a sense, itching to get back."
William to represent Charles at royal funeral in Norway

After the death last week of King Harald V of Norway, King Charles offered condolences and praised the late Scandinavian monarch for his "unwavering dedication," guiding his country "through times of great change with warmth and humility."

Charles also noted "close historical and family ties" between the U.K. and Norway, "with Britain one of the first countries to recognize Norwegian independence and establish diplomatic relations in 1905."

At Harald's funeral on Wednesday in Oslo, Charles will be represented by his son and heir, Prince William, Buckingham Palace announced Saturday. Princess Anne will also attend in a private capacity as godmother to the new Norwegian king, Haakon VII.
Who would represent the Royal Family in Oslo had been a matter of some curiosity.
"Everyone's asking me: 'Who will the Windsors send to the funeral?' because that is quite … significant," Vovk said.
"Over the last … 20 years, the Windsors have not done a great job in terms of participating in the royal community at things like funerals, investitures, those sorts of ceremonials."
One possibility for attending Wednesday's funeral was Prince William. Prescott noted that tradition has held that the British heir to the throne attends such occasions.
Still, there has been some inconsistency around all of this.
"When Elizabeth the Second died, we … sort of just assumed that the kings and queens of everywhere else would come, and so there's a bit of unevenness there in that relationship," Prescott said.

Harald's funeral will be held in Oslo Cathedral. Other royals expected to attend include King Willem-Alexander and Queen Maxima of the Netherlands, King Frederik and Queen Mary of Denmark, King Philippe and Queen Mathilde of Belgium and Crown Prince Akishino and Crown Princess Kiko of Japan.
