blocks.text: Headlines have also focused on the Norwegian royal family since Harald's death, given the presence at a related event earlier this week of his disgraced step-grandson, Marius Borg Hoiby, and the expectation that he will be at the funeral.

Hoiby, who was convicted of rape in June, is the son of Harald's daughter-in-law, now Queen Mette-Marit, from a relationship prior to her marriage to now King Haakon. Hoiby is appealing his conviction and has received permission to attend the funeral.
Royally quotable

"The Bayeux Tapestry — or the Canterbury Embroidery, as it might just have been called — recounts a conflict. Yet here it is today, nearly a thousand years later, as a precious symbol of trust, at a time when trust seems sadly to be in short supply between nations."

— King Charles, during a speech on Wednesday at a viewing of the Bayeux Tapestry Exhibition at the British Museum. The fragile tapestry that depicts the 1066 Norman conquest of England is on loan from France for the 10-month exhibition.
Royal reads
A senior equerry to King Charles and Queen Camilla who captured widespread attention online is to step down from his role supporting the Royal Family. [The Independent]

Sarah Ferguson will return to the U.K. after relocating to a Swiss chalet amid the fallout over the friendship between her and her ex-husband, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, and the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, according to reports. [The Guardian]

Amid family feuds, damaging headlines and questions about its future role, the Royal Family has spent much of the past decade managing its public image. But the importance of good royal PR dates back centuries. [The Conversation]

Princess Ingrid Alexandra has stepped into a historic new role as heir to the Norwegian throne — and appeared to pay a touching tribute to her grandmother as she stood alongside her father at his swearing-in ceremony. [Daily Mail]

articles.title: Nepal flood disaster puts climate justice under spotlight
articles.summary: Days after devastating floods swept through Nepal’s Bhotekoshi-Trisuli river basin, the true scale of the disaster is still emerging. More than 1,250 people have been confirmed dead and almost…

blocks.text: Days after devastating floods swept through Nepal’s Bhotekoshi-Trisuli river basin, the true scale of the disaster is still emerging.
More than 1,250 people have been confirmed dead and almost 4,000 are still missing.

Buildings, bridges, roads and more than a dozen hydropower facilities have been destroyed, causing an estimated $2.6 billion (€2.24 billion) in damage to public and private infrastructure, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).
Search and rescue operations for missing people remain underway, with families still hoping for their safe return.
The exact cause of the glacial collapse remains unclear, but experts say climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.
A global responsibility?
For Nepal, the disaster has raised a question that goes beyond rescue and reconstruction.

It’s about climate justice and who should bear the costs and responsibility for such environmental disasters when the Himalayan nation contributes only a tiny fraction of global greenhouse gas emissions yet faces increasingly severe climate-related risks.
Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah said responding to the catastrophe is a “global responsibility.”

“As we work tirelessly to address the damage caused by this sudden and massive disaster, a deeper question has also emerged: How did this destruction happen to us?” Shah asked while addressing Parliament this week.
“Mitigating and managing its impacts is regarded as a shared responsibility of the international community,” he stressed.
Kathmandu is planning to raise climate justice issues in the upcoming United Nations General Assembly session in New York, where Prime Minister Shah himself is likely to lead the Nepali delegation.

“We will make our case about the impact of climate change and seek global support and moral obligation to tackle it,” Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told DW. “We will also take the initiative of building a coalition of climate-vulnerable countries to raise our collective concerns.”
Highly vulnerable to climate impacts
Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people, has contributed little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming.

The country accounts for just 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions and emits about 0.5 tons of CO₂ per person each year, making it a “negligible contributor to climate change,” according to the World Bank.

But the landlocked Himalayan nation is highly vulnerable to the effects of climate change, with flooding, landslides, glacier-related hazards and other environmental risks threatening lives and livelihoods.
Nepal’s leaders say the country needs long-term international support to adapt to a rapidly changing mountain environment.

The country’s government estimates that implementing adaptation priorities between 2025 and 2035 could require as much as $18 billion to $20 billion. And Kathmandu wants international climate finance to provide most of these funds.
Nepal has spent years arguing in global climate forums that vulnerable mountain countries need greater support for adaptation and resilience.

In December 2009, Nepal held a historic Cabinet meeting at Kala Patthar, near Mount Everest base camp, at an altitude of 17,192 feet, to highlight the threats that climate change and glacial melting pose to Nepal and other mountainous nations.

Bimala Rai Paudyal, a former Nepali foreign minister, said the latest disaster meant “this is an opportune time for us to highlight glacier melting and climate justice issues in international climate forums.”
“Earlier, we were only advocating about climate impacts. Now, we are heavily suffering from it,” she told DW.
Paudyal believes Nepal is well positioned to lead an alliance of vulnerable countries, given its exposure to climate risk as well as its expertise and contribution to the climate justice effort.
An opportunity for global climate action?
Kathmandu has formally approached the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)-backed “Loss and Damage Fund” for assistance over the latest floods.
But the fund, set up by the UN in 2025 to aid the impacts of climate change, has not yet begun distributing its limited cash.

The fund also relies on voluntary contributions and lacks legally binding commitments under current international climate agreements, leaving major emitters such as China, India and the US under no direct obligation to compensate for climate change impacts.
Still, some observers and climate advocates believe Nepal can present a strong case for urgent global climate action.

“Nepal can turn this tragedy into an opportunity for global climate action,” Dinesh Paudel, professor of sustainable development at Appalachian State University in North Carolina, told DW. “For which, Nepal needs to build a consensus among national stakeholders and maneuver cautiously, considering geopolitical factors.”

According to him, Kathmandu can create an ethical movement for climate justice by highlighting the recent flood. This could then lead to creating an effective and legally binding mechanism to deal with climate impacts in the future.
Ashok Swain, professor of peace and conflict research at Uppsala University and also UNESCO Chair on International Water Cooperation, shares a similar view.

“Nepal should not be left to pay for a climate crisis it did little to create or for regional non-cooperation over which it has limited influence,” he said. “This is not a question of charity. It is fundamentally a question of climate justice and a fair distribution of responsibility.” /dl

articles.title: Outrage as Maltese tycoon acquitted in journalist’s murder
articles.summary: “Murderer!” — “Scum!” — “Mafia!” As Yorgen Fenech left the courthouse in Valletta on Wednesday evening, he was confronted by the furious crowd outside. The…

blocks.text: “Murderer!” — “Scum!” — “Mafia!”

As Yorgen Fenech left the courthouse in Valletta on Wednesday evening, he was confronted by the furious crowd outside. The 44-year-old Maltese businessman pushed through, flanked by his security guards. Just minutes earlier, a jury had acquitted him of ordering the murder of the 53-year-old investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.

The verdict came as a shock to her family. Her son, Matthew Caruana Galizia, said it was a “terrible decision by the jurors that our country may never recover from.” He later doubled down on his criticism, describing the verdict in a post on Facebook as “obscene” and saying: “Their decision flies in the face of all evidence, of all logic, of the truth.”

Almost nine years after Caruana Galizia’s murder, Malta is again confronted with the crucial question: Who was responsible for her death on October 16, 2017? The men who procured the bomb, placed it under the driver’s seat and detonated it remotely have already been convicted. But the person who contracted them to do it has still not been legally identified.
A difficult trial

For years, Fenech was considered to be the central figure in the investigations. His arrest on the morning of November 20, 2019, was like something out of a movie. His luxury yacht, Gio, had just left harbor when it was stopped by a Maltese military patrol boat. Fenech was arrested on board and subsequently interrogated by the police.

Fenech’s arrest, and suspicion that people in government circles were involved in the crime, sparked protests all across the country. Joseph Muscat, prime minister at the time, was accused of protecting political allies and stepped down in January 2020. Fenech spent more than five years in detention before being released on bail, under strict conditions, in early 2025.
His trial only began this summer, and the final verdict was decisive. Eight of the nine jurors rejected the prosecution’s argument that it was Fenech who had ordered the journalist’s murder.
Who was responsible?

The prosecution case relied above all on the testimony of Melvin Theuma, who confessed to being the middleman and testified that Fenech had contracted him to organize the murder. Theuma received a pardon in exchange for his cooperation.
But Fenech’s defense called Theuma’s credibility into question, highlighting contradictions in his testimony and false statements he had made previously.

Fenech’s lawyers also sought to prove that evidence pointing to Keith Schembri, chief of staff to Muscat at the time, was not properly followed up. Schembri has denied any involvement in the murder, and the investigators did not charge him as a suspect in this case.

blocks.caption: Investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was killed by a car bomb on October 16, 2017 Image: Rene Rossignaud/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The public prosecutors’ argument was that Caruana Galizia had been investigating Fenech, specifically his company 17 Black and the energy consortium ElectroGas, on suspicion of corruption. This, they said, meant Fenech had a motive for silencing her. She had not, however, been on the point of publishing anything that could have threatened him.
Open questions

Many in Malta are outraged by the not-guilty verdict. But there is no indication to date that Fenech did not receive a fair trial, or that the process was manipulated. For him to be convicted, Fenech’s guilt had to be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

Caruana Galizia’s family are therefore also focusing on institutional failures that they believe facilitated the murder. They complain that these have not been addressed, and necessary reforms not implemented. An official investigation already established, in 2021, that an “atmosphere of impunity” in Malta created conditions that made the murder possible.
Reforms in Malta

Since then, Malta has made progress with a series of reforms, but many say they do not go far enough. This is especially the case with regard to press freedom. In 2021, the committee of inquiry recommended that journalists be better protected against political and economic pressure and their role institutionally strengthened, yet the country is still waiting for comprehensive media reform.

Following years of discussion and a public consultation, the Maltese government brought the relevant bill before parliament in March 2026, but the legislation was not passed before early parliamentary elections in May.

In its latest Rule of Law Report, the European Commission only certifies limited progress made by Malta. It acknowledges that it has introduced some specific protection measures for journalists, but says core recommendations from the investigation into the murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia remain unfulfilled.

blocks.caption: The European Commission has told Malta it needs to do more to strengthen official protections for journalists Image: Sachelle Babbar/Zuma/picture alliance

blocks.text: Government sees progress

But the government paints a different picture. It has highlighted changes to the judiciary and anti-corruption measures, as well as better protection of journalistic sources, and additional measures to protect media professionals. This is what the EU Commission referred to as progress in specific areas.

The case has also shone a spotlight on the slow pace of the Maltese justice system. According to a report by the Daphne Caruana Galizia Foundation, 46% of homicide cases brought to trial between 2010 and 2020 had still not been concluded in mid-2025. The foundation regards this as a structural problem, and warns that when proceedings go on for so long, it compromises the chances of an effective prosecution.
Fresh investigation?

No decision has yet been made as to what will happen now, following Fenech’s acquittal. Judge Edwina Grima has ordered that the evidence presented at trial be passed on to the chief of police, who will decide whether criminal proceedings should be brought against anyone else.
On Thursday, former PM Muscat said that, according to the public prosecutors, further investigations were ongoing.

blocks.caption: Nine years on, the person behind Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder has still not been brought to justice Image: AP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Institute of Maltese Journalists (IGM) has called on the authorities to pursue every line of inquiry that came to light during the trial — including, explicitly, those that lead to former high-ranking politicians. The acquittal must be respected as the outcome of the constitutional process, the IGM said, but it does not close the case.

The demonstrators outside the courthouse in Valletta are in no doubt. Someone must have issued a contract for the murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia. And almost nine years after her death, still no one has been held responsible. /dl

articles.title: Elbows up or down? Why Alberta is diplomacy-first in the trade war
articles.summary: Nathan Cooper, Alberta’s senior representative to the United States, told CBC’s West of Centre that compared to provinces that have taken a more aggressive approach, Alberta has come out ahead.

image.caption: Former speaker of the Alberta legislation Nathan Cooper, right, is now Alberta's top representative in Washington. He says the premier's approach of doubling down on diplomacy is paying off. (Jason Franson/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics
Nathan Cooper, Alberta’s senior representative to the United States, told CBC’s West of Centre that compared to provinces that have taken a more aggressive approach, Alberta has come out ahead.
Alberta's Washington envoy says province's position on alcohol gives it an edge
Alberta’s top U.S. diplomat says playing nice is paying off for his province in the Canada-U.S. trade war.
“I think the premier’s diplomacy-first approach has really not only been helpful for me, but certainly helpful for the province,” Cooper said.
“If we look at the impact of U.S. tariffs on the Alberta economy, we have a disproportionately low impact.”

Experts have said while Alberta’s industries are not immune to the impact of the trade dispute, they are not seeing the direct hit other provinces are. Despite the trade war, the U.S. continues to increase its imports of Canadian oil.
The comments come as Cooper, the former speaker of the Alberta legislature, spent time in Nashville, Tenn., with Premier Danielle Smith last week.
Cooper said American officials have been “significantly more responsive” to his team than some of his provincial counterparts.

Alberta is the only remaining province with no ban or retaliatory levy on U.S. alcohol imports. The province’s position on that is something the Americans have shown “a real appreciation” for, Cooper said.
“I believe that that's actually translated into results for the province of Alberta,” he said.

The premier said her trip to Music City was a personal one, but she took time to meet with business and tourism leaders while there. Ahead of her trip, Smith also appeared on U.S. news networks pushing for a return to the bargaining table.
Honey or vinegar?
Not everyone has been on board with Alberta’s approach.
Following Smith’s trip to Mar-a-Lago last year, she was called out for not being a part of a unified “Team Canada” response.
This summer, Premier Doug Ford pushed for Canadian leaders to take a stronger stance, and called for energy exports to be cut off to the U.S.
Smith’s predecessor, Jason Kenney, has said a modest tax on oil exports should be considered to put extra pressure on the president.
Smith has rejected both ideas and consistently said doubling down on diplomacy is a better approach.
“I think in this scenario, maybe Premier Smith is seen as a dissenting voice or not quite on script,” Evan Menzies, vice-president of Crestview Strategy said in an interview.
But Menzies, who previously worked as a director of communications for Smith’s party, said things look more favourable for Alberta when you zoom out.
“If you're to look at what's bearing good fruit, Alberta's efforts seem to be bearing some good fruit.”
Smith’s too-friendly-to-resist approach contrasts against Ontario Doug Ford’s aggressive advertising and insult slinging.
Cole Hogan, a strategic communications advisor at Alberta Counsel who has worked on Ford and Kenney campaigns, said the divergent tactics make sense considering domestic priorities.
“Ford's approach, while it makes a lot of people feel good … it hasn't garnered the same results that Smith's approach has here in Alberta.”
“They both have different political goals in doing so — they have different industries to serve.”
Separation anxiety
All this comes amid a looming election in Alberta on whether to hold a binding referendum on separation — something U.S. officials are increasingly waking up to.
It's been used by representative Andy Harris to trumpet renewed calls for a 51st state and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick as a sign of disunity and failed trade talks.
On the ground, Cooper said the referendum isn’t frequently raised in his meetings with U.S. officials.
“At the end of the day, one of my key jobs is to try to determine the difference between signal and noise and do what I can to get people focused on the big issues that are impacting our province.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Emily is a reporter and producer with CBC's West of Centre podcast. Previously, she covered Edmonton city hall. She can be reached at emily.williams@cbc.ca.

articles.title: I almost skipped my colon cancer screening, but my bottom and I survived the scope
articles.summary: Despite knowing that delayed screenings lead to late-stage colon cancer diagnoses, Stephen Workman still tried to avoid his own colonoscopy. Eventually, he decided to face the painful procedure with…

image.caption: Despite knowing that delayed screenings lead to late-stage colon cancer diagnoses, Stephen Workman still tried to avoid his own colonoscopy. Eventually, he decided to face the painful procedure with humour. (Jean-Paul Pelissier/Reuters)

blocks.text: Canada·First Person

Despite knowing that delayed screenings lead to late-stage colon cancer diagnoses, Stephen Workman still tried to avoid his own colonoscopy. Eventually, he decided to face the painful procedure with humour.
The colonoscopy gave me peace of mind
· for CBC First Person
· Posted: Sep 06, 2026 4:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 7 hours ago
This First Person column is the experience of Stephen Workman, who lives in Halifax. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ.
At nine a.m., my wife handed me my phone. Somebody wanted to speak with me.
“Hi, Stephen, this is Stephanie. I’m with FIT testing, Nova Scotia.”

FIT stands for fecal immunochemical test. It screens for colon cancer. The test consists of a clear plastic sheet, a tiny garden spade, a sealable container and a stout envelope. I had been avoiding the test for weeks. Finally, I thought, well, it has always been negative. I’ll just get it done.
And then some time after mailing in the test, I usually get a letter. But this time it was a phone call.
Uh-oh.
Stephanie kindly explained that I could have cancer, a polyp, a tumour or nothing, and would I want a colonoscopy?
I pointed out that no one wants a colonoscopy, but I would take the appointment anyway.

She described the steps required to make my colon pristine. As she told me about the pre-procedure diet (bland, colourless and fibre-free, mostly chicken and rice), starting four days before the main event, I started laughing. So much effort, so little reward.

But the thing was, I was thinking: This could really be trouble. I have Parkinson’s disease. I have lived with it for the last six years. If I have cancer, then maybe I get chemo. If I get chemo, then I get chemo brain. I already have Parkinson’s brain. Together, they have got to be a lot worse than either one alone.
When she explained that I might need wet wipes to protect my sensitive bottom from the impending onslaught, I lost it again.
“You only want to do this once,” she said.
“Oh, don’t I know,” I replied.

Did I want the scope at nine in the morning or one in the afternoon? You drink a litre of a laxative called GoLYTELY four hours before the procedure. Or Go Heavily, more accurately. I thought I would be up all night anyway.
“Nine,” I said.
Stephanie was right: get the GoLYTELY icy cold, use a metal straw to the back of your tongue, and it is tolerable.
Barely.
Since I had Parkinson’s disease and constipation, I needed a big old-fashioned double dose.
Let me tell you, this stuff works.
For the first eight to 10 hours, nothing happened.
Then it did.
And then it just kept happening.
At the hospital, little blue footprints led to the colonoscopy suite. It occurred to me this would be an excellent time to get lost, but cancer anxiety had worn me down.
And my wife was with me.
She was empathetic.
“You don’t have cancer,” she said.
Statistically correct. Actually? I wasn’t so sure.

items: Learning I had a rare genetic condition changed how I saw myself as a physician, woman and mom

blocks.text: I could tell who was waiting for a colonoscopy. They had worried looks. They were in blue gowns, sitting on hospital towels. They looked like me.
I have veins like fire hoses but when stabbed with an IV needle, they rolled around like marbles. I apologized for them to the nurse.
Ow. Ow. Ow.
IV in place, the nurse smiled and asked if I was pregnant or breastfeeding.
“Not recently,” I deadpanned.
She laughed and told me I had made her morning.
Mine, too.

items: The butt of jokes: I'm a comedian who is paid to get dozens of rectal exams

blocks.text: In the procedure room the nurse asked if I wanted any drugs.
“Sure!”
My colonoscopist reminded me a bit of an NFL linebacker. In my sensitive state, I was aware of his shoulders. He looked me over.
“You’re a tall, slim guy. There are going to be some sharp angles. Some corners that could be a bit tough to get the colonoscope around.”
If there were corners, they were straightened out.
At first it hurt a little. Then I found myself rocked up off the bed, yelling.
“Ow. Ow. Ow. That really, really hurts.”
I was probably heard in the parkade.
Across the road.
I think the medications lowered my inhibitions. That’s my story, and I am sticking to it.
The nurse put a hand on my shoulder.
“It’s better if you just lie still and relax.”
Sure. Easy to do while a garden hose negotiates a hairpin turn. Inside your abdomen.
The last few minutes of a colonoscopy matter most. Mine were fine. And with the medications it seemed like something that happened to someone else. It ended really well, too.
“Everything looked good,” I was told.
I was so relieved.
Having one chronic progressive disease wears down your resistance to having another. The what-ifs expand geometrically.

Going all PSA for just a moment; In Canada, roughly half of colon cancer cases are diagnosed at Stage 2 or 3. And yet many eligible people still do not complete the FIT test. It takes about five minutes. It comes in a very stout envelope. It can sit on bathroom counters for weeks.
I know.
Mine did, too. Put the garden spade to work.
The day after my colonoscopy, I realized that in my drug-addled state, I forgot one very important thing. So here it is.
A sincere thanks.
I am not sure I would have had the, dare I say, intestinal fortitude to complete a colonoscopy on someone like me. But I am glad my colonoscopist did.
Do you have a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here's more info on how to pitch to us.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Stephen Workman is a physician, writer and patient with Parkinson’s disease. Once a year he writes and performs a short comedic monologue with the Nova Scotia Health Authority Players' Christmas show in Dartmouth, N.S.

articles.title: Etsy seller's 'bruh' T-shirts were removed over a trademark complaint. He says it's trademark squatting
articles.summary: An Etsy seller says the online retailer removed his listings for T-shirts with the word "bruh" after the person who holds a Canadian trademark for it complained. One legal expert worries that the…

image.caption: A computer-generated mockup used by an Etsy seller to advertise their T-shirt design on the online retail platform. The shirt was removed from the site following a complaint from the person who holds a Canadian trademark for the word 'bruh.' (Submitted by Charlene Atkinson)

blocks.text: When Sam Joseph Karam received an email from online retailer Etsy saying 11 of his T-shirt designs bearing the slang term "bruh" had been taken down for a trademark violation, he was immediately suspicious.
"It's usually one or two listings. It's not 11 in a row. So that obviously caught our attention pretty quickly," Karam said.

Karam, who owns the U.S.-based apparel company Customized Designs and sells clothing on sites like Etsy, says the platform also revoked his Star Seller badge — a mark given by the platform that means the seller provides top-tier customer service. Following that, he says he noticed an immediate drop in sales.
In the email, Etsy told Karam the shirt had been reported by someone named Malik Yawar Abbas, who holds a Canadian trademark for the term "bruh."

Karam is one of multiple Etsy sellers who told CBC News they've had items taken down from the platform after their use of the word was reported by the trademark holder. CBC News reviewed multiple emails Etsy sent to Karam and two other sellers that showed the takedowns came in response to complaints by Abbas.

Karam says Abbas, the trademark holder, is "squatting" on the trademark, aiming to make money by licensing the use of the word to others rather than by making a product of his own. Some legal experts say it's up to platforms and the legal system to better prevent trademarks from being used in this way.
No clothes for sale, request for payment

A trademark for the word "bruh" was issued by the Canadian Intellectual Property Office (CIPO) in July 2025 in connection with selling many kinds of clothing, according to the government's trademarks database. Another trademark for the same word was recently granted to Abbas for use in advertising restaurant services.
In an email to CBC News, CIPO did not answer questions about the "bruh" trademark, but said each trademark application the office receives is "examined on a case-by-case basis."

After the listings were removed, Karam found the trademark holder's website and was surprised to find a section detailing how he protects the "bruh" trademark and directing others to license with him in order to get permission to use it.
"We didn't invent the word. the streets did. the internet did. but we realized its power," the site reads.
The site doesn't offer clothes for sale — just mock-ups of clothing and items like energy drinks using the word "bruh."
In an email to CBC News, trademark holder Abbas said those images are there to show "potential commercial applications" of the brand.
When Karam contacted Abbas about the Etsy takedowns to see if he would withdraw his complaint, Abbas said he would if Karam agreed to a number of terms and paid him $1,000.
Karam refused, and says the signs in this case all point toward what he says is "trademark squatting."

"It's quite disheartening," Karam said. "When you have someone immediately turn around and say, 'I want $1,000, simply to go back and retract my complaint,' you know right there that they're acting in bad faith. That's my personal belief."

items: 'Trademark squatting' hurts artists and small businesses and it's coming to Canada

blocks.text: Abbas told CBC News via email that the $1,000 was a proposed settlement that was "part of a negotiated resolution of a disputed trademark matter. It was not paid, and no monetary settlement was concluded."
He also disagrees with the idea that he is squatting on the trademark.
"BRUH is a lawfully registered Canadian trademark being developed as a commercial licensing brand," Abbas wrote.
He has since withdrawn the complaint to Etsy, which he says he did after the 11 designs were removed and those products were no longer being offered to Canadian consumers.
But Karam says the "damage has been done."
He is currently in contact with an intellectual property lawyer and is considering taking legal action to try to invalidate the trademark on the basis of bad faith.
Bad faith trademarks can be taken down

Under a relatively new part of Canada's trademark laws added in 2019, a trademark can be invalidated if it was filed in "bad faith," explains Carys Craig, a professor at York University's Osgoode Hall Law School specializing in intellectual property law.
While cases arguing bad faith have popped up, she says this part of the law is still somewhat untested, so she's not sure what a court might decide in this case.

items: SWAT teams and patent trolls: inside Ottawa's IP plan to promote Canadian innovators

blocks.text: Craig says licensing can be a valid way of using a trademark. Overall, she says the way the "bruh" trademark is being presented on the website, along with the takedown orders that are being sought, might be enough to reach the standard of bad faith.
"We just don't quite know what that looks like yet."

Abbas told CBC News he trademarked the term in order to build a "licensing-only brand at the time when there was no BRUH-named brand in Canada," and disagrees that "protecting, enforcing or commercially developing" the brand should be characterized as bad faith.
"If there is a genuine disagreement about the validity, scope, or infringement of the registration, Canadian law provides mechanisms and forums to determine those issues," he said.
Does a trademark mean you own a word?
Despite broad use, general terms and pop culture phrases can be trademarked — it all depends on the context, according to Craig.

The point of a trademark is to differentiate the products or services of one brand from those of another, she explains. So a word like "apple" can't be trademarked to sell fruit because it's simply describing the product, but to sell computers, it works just fine.

There are some other criteria that are considered during a trademark application, but Craig says that because "bruh" isn't describing the product in this case, the word could reasonably function as a trademark.
But trademarking something doesn't mean you own it outright, and experts say the "bruh" clothes on Etsy might not necessarily be infringing just because they use the word.

Paula Clancy, an intellectual property law partner at Gowling WLG, says for courts to determine if there was infringement, they would look at how the alleged infringer was using the trademark — either as a source of origin, to appear as though it was from a specific brand, or in an ornamental way, as part of a design.
Shirts with phrases like "Bruh, we back," which Karam had taken down, "might well fall within those exceptions," Clancy said — meaning they might not infringe.
Despite that, Karam says Etsy didn't give him a way to appeal its decision to take the products down.

For his part, Abbas said he reported listings to Etsy when he "reasonably believed" the listings might conflict with his trademark rights, and never intended to "prevent people from using the word in ordinary speech or everyday communication."

items: Haus vs. House: Plant store names cause thorny rift

blocks.text: In an email to CBC News, an Etsy spokesperson said the platform assesses and removes items when it receives proper notice of infringement and said sellers are responsible for following all laws and site rules. The spokesperson said sellers should reach out to the person who made the initial complaint if they think their listing shouldn't have been removed.

Clancy says she understands why platforms like Etsy take these trademark takedown requests seriously, but she says a policy that doesn't allow for appeals poses a challenge for sellers who are unlikely to take on the expense of going through the courts.
Testing boundaries of trademark system
Clancy says cases like this are rare in Canada.
"Usually, we see the other way around. We see the infringers using marks without authorization," she said, noting that some people will try to piggyback on the reputation of an established brand.

But Craig worries that because trademark disputes can be so costly, especially for small businesses, cases of trademark squatting or over-enforcement might fly under the radar more often than we think.

She also points out that despite objections from Etsy sellers, the trademark holder in this case has walked a "careful line" that could still be potentially within the bounds of the law, given they were granted the trademark rights and licensing trademarks is allowed.
"This is really testing the sort of boundaries of that trademark system and exploiting some of the … policy weaknesses or loopholes within the system," Craig said.

items: Indigenous intellectual property needs better protections, say advocates

blocks.text: She says tighter rules might be needed to prevent these kinds of situations. More care might be required in the initial stages of issuing trademarks, she says, especially when it comes to zeitgeist-y phrases where there might be more incentive to try to corner them.
Easier processes for challenging possible bad-faith trademarks, and changes to online marketplaces that allow sellers to appeal trademark takedowns, might also help, according to Craig.

She called it a "worst case scenario" to be in a place where everything is protected, nothing is actually litigated and "everything is automatically taken down as soon as a trademark owner claims their rights."

articles.title: B.C. drought forces volunteers to rescue salmon from drying streams
articles.summary: As drought dries B.C. streams, volunteers are moving stranded salmon and other fish to deeper water. But scientists warn rescue efforts are becoming harder to sustain as waterways shrink and extreme…

image.caption: Aivars Liepa Spence, right, a Lake Cowichan High School student, and Dave Friesen, a volunteer from Cobble Hill, use the classic 'pincher' movement to trap fry with nets for rescue at Ashburnham Creek in Honeymoon Bay this summer. (Submitted by Bob Crandall)

blocks.text: Science

As drought dries B.C. streams, volunteers are moving stranded salmon and other fish to deeper water. But scientists warn rescue efforts are becoming harder to sustain as waterways shrink and extreme heat intensifies.
Rescuers move stranded fish to deeper water, but experts warn the effort has limits
· CBC News
· Posted: Sep 06, 2026 4:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 31 minutes ago
Parts of British Columbia have been hit hard by drought this summer.
In Bessette Creek, severe drought conditions recently prompted orders limiting water use in an effort to protect salmon populations from record-low flows.

Temporary protection orders for the Salmon River watershed were also issued at the end of July, rescinded in early August to address increased wildfire risk in the region and then reissued at the end of August.
And those are just the watersheds struggling to the point of government intervention.
Bob Crandall is treasurer of the Cowichan Lake Salmonid Enhancement Society on Vancouver Island.
The society cares for 16 streams connected to Lake Cowichan, and Crandall says they are getting drier each year.
To help, the society does what they call fry salvage — manually rescuing fish from drying rivers and moving them into other waterways.

"I believe if the hand of man has caused these difficulties in the ecosystems, then the hand of man should be out there, trying to make an improvement to the problems," said Crandall, who has been doing this for over 16 years.
While B.C. communities are embracing this intervention as one of the few options available to them, scientists warn this has limits and may not be a good long-term solution.
Efforts to move fish
Together with the Ts'uubaa-asatx Nation and a variety of volunteers, Crandall works to gather fish — mainly salmon, trout and char — and carry them somewhere with more water.

But the work is becoming more difficult as the climate changes. The society has been doing fry salvage since 1984, and Crandall is used to seeing a kilometre or two of rivers and streams dry up over the course of a summer.
But that is no longer the case.
"We have noticed that streams are drying up farther upstream," he said.
"Now, it seems as though we're going five, six and seven kilometers upstream — it's just a lot more effort."

The process involves aerators and bubblers to ensure the fish have enough oxygen, as well as nets to transport them. Crandall says carrying 23 kilograms (50 pounds) of water, fish and equipment across cobbled, dry streambeds can be challenging in hot weather.
He was born in a rainbow trout hatchery, so he has been around fish his whole life, and it is important to him that they remain part of the ecosystem rather than simply dying.
"You can rescue up to 100,000 or 150,000 fish during the course of a drought summer," he said.
Importance of fish
The Ts'uubaa-asatx Nation is also a major part of the fry salvage efforts. Its members help relocate the fish and use drones to determine where streams are drying up.
Crandall called the Nation the best partner the Society has ever had and says much of the work would not happen without it
"It takes an army of people to do it," said Aaron Hamilton, the Nation's operations manager.
Hamilton said that it's been challenging lately because there is no longer a normal pattern to follow. The weather can be extremely hot one month, followed suddenly by heavy rain.

Michelle Corfield, the lands and resource director and negotiator for Ts'uubaa-asatx, said salmon are a keystone resource for the community. The recovery projects are important to the Nation, she said, and it has also invested its own money in the work.
"Salmon are in our DNA," she said. "And it's up to us to ensure that we have salmon for today and into the future."
Corfield says the Nation takes a full life-cycle approach to salmon conservation, including river restoration and conditions in the oceans, rather than focusing only on individual fish.
Challenges to fry salvage
Similar rescue efforts are facing limits elsewhere as drought and extreme heat intensify.
This year's drought has been especially severe in France, and Jean-Pierre Faure of the Fédération de Pêche du Rhône said relocating fish is no longer working for them.
Faure says that there have been multiple weather events that would normally be expected only once every 50 to 100 years.

"The last one this summer is the worst we have ever had," he said. He added that France's management programs are not prepared for the changing conditions because they rely on the past to plan for the future — an approach he says will no longer work.
"It began very early in the end of May and since that time we have had four or five very big heat waves, reaching temperatures we have never seen before."
River flows were so low that fish were forced to gather in very small volumes of water, intensifying competition for food and shelter and causing more deaths.

Faure said fish experience physiological stress and lose energy when water temperatures rise above 18 or 19 C. He said juvenile fish are first to be affected because they have fewer energy reserves, while temperatures above 25 C can be fatal within hours.

"This summer, due to the combined effects of climate change and warm water discharge from the nuclear power plant industry, the average temperature of the Rhône River reached 25 degrees for more than two months," said Faure.
"It's still the case, it's still going on. This has never been seen before."
He said that instead of focusing on short-term interventions such as rescue fishing, the priority should be ecosystem restoration and water-use management.
Moving fish can add stress and cause injuries or spread disease, he said. The work can also cost at least 1,000 to 2,000 euros a day for each kilometre covered.
"When you have thousands of kilometres of rivers that are drying, it's not realistic to go and do this at a large scale."
He also said that when 90 per cent of the watershed is dry, there may simply be nowhere to move the fish.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Bridget Stringer-Holden joined the CBC as a Joan Donaldson News Scholar and is currently working as an associate producer. She graduated from UBC’s Master of Journalism program and is passionate about science and climate reporting. Her work has been featured in The Globe and Mail, Vancouver Magazine, B.C. Business, The Georgia Straight and a variety of student papers, podcasts and radio stations. You can reach her at bridget.stringer-holden@cbc.ca.

articles.title: 'It cannot happen': Why Quebec fans and actors fought to save their own version of The Simpsons
articles.summary: When the beloved Quebec version of the iconic American animated series was cancelled last year, fans rallied to bring it back, not simply because they loved the show, but because they saw Les Simpson…

image.caption: When the Québécois version of The Simpsons was threatened with an uncertain future, fans rallied to save a show they saw as an emblem of Quebec culture. (Bell Media)

blocks.text: LISTEN | How Les Simpson became a part of Quebec culture:
The Sunday Magazine23:15Why Quebec fans and actors fought to save their own version of The Simpsons
Growing up in Quebec, Joshua Biasotto fell in love with watching The Simpsons after discovering the version of the show that's dubbed in the French dialect, Québécois.
He says he not only lived for the long-running American animated sitcom’s quirky characters, irreverent humour and satirical take on life, but he also "developed a big love for Quebec dubbing."
"I've done my research," said Biasotto. "I know which actor is doing the voice of which character."
But last August, after 35 years, Corus Entertainment’s Télétoon, which held the Canadian broadcast rights to the show and oversaw its dubbing, decided not to renew those rights for the 36th season.
This put Les Simpson in jeopardy.
Distraught, Biasotto sprang into action, creating an online petition on Change.org called Sauvons le doublage québécois des Simpsons — “Let's save the Quebec dub of The Simpsons.”
“I was like, it cannot happen,” said Biasotto. “It’s a part of our identity that we lose.”
The Quebec version, he says, was adapted to incorporate local expressions and cultural references that made it feel uniquely theirs.

For example, the characters spoke in regional Quebec accents, including joual, the colloquial dialect associated with working-class Montreal, while U.S. people and places were swapped out for local references.

In one episode, a sketch involving upstate New York — including the cities of Utica and Albany — is replaced in the Québécois version with the Lac-Saint-Jean region and the towns of Jonquière and Alma.

items: Homer leaves Quebec: Petition to save Québécois French dubbing of The Simpsons

blocks.text: Ian Lafrenière, Quebec’s deputy premier and a longtime Simpsons fan, even wrote in a Facebook post that the Quebec version must be saved, describing the cultural and geographical references in the show as "sublime."
And the public outcry to save Les Simpson tapped into something bigger than just nostalgia.
Dubbing is part of a long tradition in Quebec to adapt entertainment from around the world to reflect the province’s language, humour and culture.
Dubbing as Quebec identity

In Quebec, watching American and other English-language shows and films in French has long been part of the culture, says Daniel Béland, director of the McGill Institute for the Study of Canada at McGill University in Montreal.

A dubbing industry emerged in the province after the Second World War, he says, allowing audiences to experience international entertainment in their own language, along with voices, expressions and cultural references that felt familiar.
Although French-language content from France was readily available, Quebec’s distinct culture and language meant that those productions could often feel foreign to local audiences.
“For people to shift from the Quebec version to the French version from France would be really a culture shock,” said Béland.

Dubbing, he says, is also about more than translating dialogue word for word, particularly when it comes to humour. Some jokes simply don’t land when translated directly, so they have to be tweaked or replaced with references that local audiences can relate to.
"It will not be the same experience," he said. "“Humour, like poetry, is really hard to translate."
Quebec, is home to the vast majority of Canada's French speakers, with 84.1 per cent of the province's population speaking French, according to Statistics Canada’s census in 2021.
Keeping the dubbing industry, says Béland, is also a way of preserving the province’s mother tongue.
“There's a sense that Quebec is a French island surrounded by an anglophone sea, so there's this sense of a vulnerability of the French language.”
For the voice actors, it was personal

The possibility that Les Simpson might not return spurred a reaction in Quebec that seemed like “an earthquake,” says Thiéry Dubé, who has voiced Québécois Homer Simpson, the famously bumbling patriarch of the family, since 2017.
“Because for [Quebecers], it's something like poutine, you know? It's so part of our culture and cultural identity here.”
The news had also come during a particularly difficult year for the Quebec dubbing team, says Dubé.
Béatrice Picard, who voiced Homer’s wife, Marge, died in December at 96.
A few months later, in April, Benoît Rousseau, who voiced several prominent characters, including Grampa Simpson, Mr. Burns and Duffman, and served as the show’s main adapter, also died.
Dubé says the uncertainty over the show’s future made an already difficult period even harder.
“We were living day-to-day and waiting, and it was crazy for me, because one day couldn't pass without having somebody just stopping me in the street and saying, ‘Are you guys going to come back?’”
It was the fans’ fierce loyalty that offered some solace.
“[They said] I don't want it to be in French from France, and it was very touching, having all the people cheering for it.”
Bringing Les Simpson back
The campaign worked.

Biasotto’s petition drew more than 35,000 signatures, and Les Simpson was revived in May after Bell Media struck a deal with Disney Entertainment to broadcast the show. The new season is set to premiere Sept. 9 on Noovo.
“It had a bigger impact than I could imagine,” said Biasotto.
The return was also welcome news for difuze, the largest French dubbing facility in Canada, which has studios in Montreal and Toronto, and dubs Les Simpson.
Elizabeth Pélissier, vice-president of dubbing at difuze, says the studio is happy to be a part of bringing back the show in the language Quebec audiences know and love.
“We're just proud to make sure that we can call back all the actors and be part of the art process,” she said.
Les Simpson is returning at a time when Quebec’s dubbing industry is busier than ever.

difuze, founded in 2018, has seen the volume of content it dubs increase, says Pélissier. As streaming platforms such as Disney, Netflix, Amazon and Crave release more television series, the French studio has taken on more work than it once did with films alone.

The studio’s credits include Stranger Things, Moana and Toy Story 5. But the growth, she says, has also brought new challenges. There is more work to dub, but production timelines have become tighter, causing teams to “work really hard on overtime.”
Joey Galimi, president of the National Association of Professional Dubbers, which has represented dubbing professionals across Canada for 50 years, says the industry is “very healthy.”
But he says he’s concerned about the effect AI-generated dubbing could have on human voice actors.
In an emailed statement to CBC, Walt Disney Studios Canada says that under its new agreement, the broadcasting and dubbing of Les Simpson "will continue to be dubbed in Quebec by the local talent."
For Galimi, the revival of Les Simpson is more than a testament to the show’s popularity: it showcases the power of its fans.
“The fact that it was cancelled and it's coming back is also good because it's going to attract more people — new people.”

articles.title: Win Gatchalian: VP Sara threats claim should be taken seriously
articles.summary: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Sunday urged authorities to take Vice President Sara Duterte"s claims of threats and harassment seriously, following the issuance of an arrest warrant against…

blocks.text: Published September 6, 2026 3:50pm

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Sunday urged authorities to take Vice President Sara Duterte’s claims of threats and harassment seriously, following the issuance of an arrest warrant against her.
"Dapat kung meron man banta, kung meron nararamdaman o nakikita ang Bise Presidente na banta sa kanyang buhay at pamilya, dapat seyosohin ito," Gatchalian told Super Radyo dzBB.
(If the Vice President feels or sees any threat to her life or her family, it should be taken seriously.)
"Nanawagan din ako sa ating kapulisan na on their own dapat imbestigahan kung saan nangagaling itong banta dahil hindi maganda ito," he added.
(I also call on the police to conduct their own investigation into where these threats are coming from because this is not a good thing.)
Gatchalian explained that everyone's safety is important, whether a person is a senior public official or an ordinary Filipino.
"Ikaw man ay Bise Presidente o ordinaryong mamayanan, dapt protektahan ang ating pamahalaan sa ganyang banta at hindi magagadang pwede mangyari sa kanilang pamilya," Gatchalian said.
(Whether you are the Vice President or an ordinary citizen, the government should protect you from such threats and any harm that may befall your family.)
On Saturday, Duterte posted bail at a Quezon City court, a day after the issuance of an arrest warrant against her in relation to a grave threats case.
In a statement, the Vice President said she does not feel safe.
"I have documented threats and harassment since 2023. I fear for my children. I do not feel they are safe if I am with them," Duterte said.
"Umalis na nga ako kung nasaan mga anak ko para pumunta sa korte pero pumunta pa rin ang pulis," she added.
(I already left where my children were to go to court, but the police still went there.)
She further said, "I do not feel safe. Pakiramdam ko papatayin nila ako (I feel like they're going to kill me)."
Case won’t affect impeachment
For Gatchalian, Duterte's grave threats case will not affect the ongoing impeachment trial against her.

"Personal opinion ko ito. Walang effect sa akin at sa impeacement dahil iba naman kasi yung sa korte at yung sa imeachment. Na determine ng korte na may probable cause pero di naman ibig sabihin guilty ang hatol na," Gatchalian said in a dzBB Super Radyo interview.

(In my opinion, it will have no effect on me or on the impeachment because the court case and the impeachment are separate. The court may have determined that there is probable cause, but that does not mean the accused is already guilty.)
"Ganun din sa impeachment court. Magkakaroon ng presentation of the defense. Titingnan natin kung ano ‘yung magiging depensa at dun tayo magkakaroon ng decision," he added.
(The same goes for the impeachment court. The defense will present their pieces of evidence. We will assess them and then reach a decision.) —RF, GMA News

articles.title: How climate change and food insecurity could fuel future conflicts
articles.summary: Climate change, conflict, and trade tensions are putting pressure on the global food system. New research suggests the biggest risk is not food shortages, but whether societies can peacefully adapt…

image.caption: El Nino-driven drought has left rice fields in West Java, Indonesia, cracked and dryImage: Donal Husni/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: The world's food system is under growing stress, and new research is pointing to areas where this could lead to conflict.

Severe droughts and extreme weather are damaging harvests in many regions. A developing El Niño event is even threatening to worsen food shortages for millions of people next year. At the same time, wars and geopolitical tensions are disrupting supply chains that keep food and farm supplies moving.
The war in Ukraine has repeatedly shaken grain markets, while the Iran war's impact on the Strait of Hormuz has driven up fuel and fertilizer prices, increasing costs for farmers everywhere.

Experts have long warned that rising food insecurity could fuel instability. When people can no longer feed their families, they argue over land, water, and other resources — or they move. In fragile countries, these pressures can contribute to social unrest and even armed conflict.

Now, new research has suggested where some of these risks are greatest. The Climate-Driven Agricultural Decline Index (CADI), developed by Hannes Mueller and his colleagues, maps how climate change is reshaping agricultural productivity around the world. "The heaviest losses are in the tropical regions," said Mueller, a researcher at the Institute for Economic Analysis and the Barcelona School of Economics.

Climate change is already reducing food production in many parts of the world. Hundreds of millions of people live in areas where harvests are smaller than 30 years ago. Mueller mentioned Cambodia, Bangladesh, Burundi, Nigeria, Paraguayand El Salvador as countries where agricultural losses are already being felt.
"Northern Africa is another region we should pay much more attention to. If you look at the map, it just looks terrible. It really looks horrible," he said.
Burundi's vanishing lakes and the fight to bring them back
And climate change is only one part of the story. Wars, trade disruptions, export bans, and rising fertilizer costs can magnify food insecurity.
Within the next 25 years, nearly half of the world's people could be living in areas where farms are producing less food.
New winners, losers, and conflicts

These pressures can undermine governments, help causemigration, and make it easier for armed groups to recruit fighters. In societies that are already unstable, such factors can push them toward crisis.

Yet CADI's research points to a surprising reality: Gains in agricultural productivity also appear to increase the risk of violence. Mueller said the key issue is not just scarcity, but change. The climate crisis and other shocks do not simply make some regions poorer. They also create new opportunities, changing the value of land and resources.
In some places, land that had been marginal becomes more productive and more valuable. And that attracts investors and produces competition for ownership and access.

So countries that appear to benefit overall may face new tensions. Sudan, for example, is projected to produce more food as the climate changes. But while some areas could become more productive, others may suffer losses, creating new winners and losers within the country and increasing the risk of conflict.

This looming instability, Mueller said, also applies to areas where the change in productivity hasn't even happened yet. "If we know that your land is going to become more productive, maybe I want to grab it from you today. That is exactly where negotiations break down and where we will have violence," he said.

Even in stable, wealthy regions, the climate crisis is creating future problems. It may seem trivial, but the change in grape-growing options in Europe is affecting local farmers. Major producers of sparkling wine have started to buy up land in mountainous regions.

"It is not productive yet, but they already know where future grape harvests will be," Mueller said. "Big agricultural companies are buying land. This is happening all over the world. Locals are displaced because large producers come in, land prices rise, and you start having fights about something that is still 20 or 30 years in the future."
How climate change is reshaping the world's wine map

One of the CADI team's most striking findings is that agricultural change is more likely to lead to conflict in non-democracies. When climate shocks, food insecurity, and competition over resources hit democracies, they tend to have institutions that force competing interests to negotiate rather than fight.

"Democracies may look annoying and cumbersome. Nothing moves as fast as people want. But this is a great thing because it makes people talk to each other," Mueller said. "There is a platform for negotiation. There are institutions that help people negotiate. That process of constantly finding solutions is at the heart of what prevents conflict."
South Asia as a warning sign

"We do not pay enough attention to the threats to the source of our livelihoods," said Abdullah Fahimi of the think tank German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP). "These threats can trigger major crises and displace millions and millions of people. The regions we should watch most closely are South Asia and the Sahel, where climate vulnerability and rapid population growth mean the number of people affected could rise dramatically."

blocks.caption: As India counts its population, researchers warn that climate change could make it harder for parts of the country to produce enough food for a growing number of peopleImage: Diptendu Dutta/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fahimi said South Asia stands out because it depends on both vulnerable water supplies and global food markets. Food prices have already risen significantly over the past decades. "South Asia, with a population of around 2 billion, is highly dependent on imports," he added. Those imports include wheat, maize, and palm oil from countries including Russia, Ukraine, Canada, and Malaysia.
At the same time, local agriculture is increasingly threatened by heat waves, floods, declining land productivity, and saltwater intrusion from rising sea levels.

As well as the immediate human toll, events such as the devastating floods that struck Nepal in August 2026 offer a glimpse of the long-term challenges that could become more common in the future. "The Himalayas and the Hindu Kush mountain ranges supply most of the water for agriculture and drinking water in the region," Fahimi said. "Because of climate change, the glaciers and snow are melting very fast."
In the short term, meltwater could increase water availability. But later in the century, he warned, the region could face "a huge humanitarian crisis that could affect around 2 billion people."

blocks.caption: Farmland was covered in mud after severe flooding along Nepal’s Bhotekoshi River in late AugustImage: Ambir Tolang/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: As food insecurity deepens, the social and political consequences can multiply. "When resource scarcities or the impacts of climate change force people to look for other livelihood opportunities, sometimes they end up being hired by terrorist groups," said Fahimi, who cited examples from Nigeria and Afghanistan.

In other cases, public frustration is directed at governments if they fail to mitigate the effects on people's livelihoods. Their legitimacy is questioned, and this can escalate into violent conflict.

That echoes Mueller's broader conclusion. Climate change, wars, and trade disruptions do not automatically lead to conflict. But climate adaptation cannot just be about growing different crops or using new technologies. People and societies also need to adapt to changes in who has access to land, water and jobs.

The key question is whether societies have institutions that can manage these changes. Where governments, courts, and local institutions can help communities negotiate new realities, shocks may be absorbed. Where those institutions are weak, the pressure on food systems may become a pressure on peace itself.
Graphics: Olof Pock
Will food insecurity spark 'large-scale conflict'?

articles.title: India news: Rahul Gandhi backs student protests in Maharashtra
articles.summary: Opposition Rahul Gandhi has said that students are "tormented" by the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party. The Congress politician has demanded immediate action into the demands of Maharashtra student…

image.caption: Gandhi's remarks come as the Maharashtra government initiated a probe into an alleged paper leak of a state-level recruitment examImage: Ishant Chauhan/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: September 6, 2026
Congress' Rahul Gandhi says Maharashtra student protest reflects 'shattered' trust in system
India's main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi has voiced support for students protesting in Maharashtra against alleged irregularities in a state-level recruitment examination.

"Thousands of students are on the streets, protesting peacefully - the reason isn't just one exam or recruitment, but a trust that's been shattered by the entire system," Gandhi said in a statement on X as he called on the government to listen to the protesters' demands and act.
"Otherwise, this echo of the students will only grow louder until justice is served," the senior Congress party leader said.
Why are the Maharashtra student demonstrations about?

Gandhi's remarks come as the Maharashtra government initiated a probe into an alleged paper leak of the Maharashtra Public Service Commission's (MPSC) Food and Drug Administration examination for Drug Inspector posts.
The offline exam was held on March 22, following which there were complaints that some candidates had allegedly received the question paper or questions beforehand.
Aspirants said that their complaints were not looked into. The recruitment process was completed and the MPSC published a merit list of 488 candidates.

However, the commission later canceled the recruitment process and in a statement cited a police inquiry which prima facie indicated that a candidate had got hold of the question paper before the exam and benefited from it.
On Saturday, the Maharashtra government also constituted a high-level committee to take full stock of the existing recruitment exam system in the country's second-most populous state.
The committee is also tasked with suggesting measures to make the screening process more transparent, secure, reliable and candidate-friendly.
Tribal students' protest

In recent days, several parts of Maharashtra also witnessed a protest by tribal students — including a hunger strike — over poor conditions in student hostels, student safety and recruitment to some 12,500 vacant posts reserved for tribal communities.
The protesters' demands were accepted by the Maharashtra government, leading to the hunger strike being withdrawn.
On Sunday, Rahul Gandhi railed against the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which leads the government in Maharashtra.
"Whether it's the central or state government, every student is tormented by the BJP regime," he alleged.

"Paper leaks, stalled recruitments, the unbearable cost of education, inhumane conditions in hostels, food like poison ...and now, they've seized control of a constitutional body like MPSC and destroyed its credibility," Gandhi, who is the leader of opposition in the lower house of the Indian parliament, said.
Education minister concedes to 'Cockroach' demands, resigns

The protests in Maharashtra come after a massive Gen Z-led protest demanding an overhaul of India's examination system, rocked the country in July. The demonstrations marked one of the biggest public challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's three-term rule and culminated with the resignation of the then education minister.

articles.title: ‘The engine’s on fire’: Qantas flight from Queenstown to Sydney reroutes after flames seen by passengers
articles.summary:
Passenger recalls seeing cabin lights flicker and ‘a lot of screaming’ after suspected engine issue

  • Get our

blocks.text: Liza-Jayne Loch was returning home from a business trip to New Zealand when her Qantas flight ran into trouble.
The plane was climbing above the scenic South Island’s mountain ranges on Saturday afternoon, bound for Sydney, when a bang shook the cabin.
A passenger seated near the left wing soon shouted “the engine’s on fire”, Loch recalled, as the cabin lights began to flicker.
Footage recorded by a passenger and shared with AAP shows flames appearing to issue from the plane’s left engine in a series of rapid bursts.
“I was sitting on the left-hand side of the plane, and the flames were very, very visible,” Loch said.
“There was a lot of screaming at the time.”
As the plane continued to gain altitude, Loch tried to comfort herself by recalling that modern jets could land safely on a single engine.
“That’s what I kept in my head, that we could actually fly on one engine,” she said.
“But the flames kept coming and the noise kept coming.”
Qantas flight QF122 suffered a suspected engine issue shortly after taking off from Queenstown on Saturday afternoon, before making a priority landing at Christchurch.
According to FlightAware, the Boeing 737 landed about 52 minutes after takeoff, touching down shortly before 5pm local time.
The cause of the incident has yet to be determined, but Qantas sent two engineers to Christchurch on Sunday to investigate.
Both engines are thought to have remained in operation for the duration of the flight.
Loch said conditions soon stabilised after the initial shock, while cabin staff sought to comfort passengers.
“The crew were all terribly, terribly calming,” Loch said.
Emergency services were waiting on the tarmac when the flight landed, with passengers allowed to disembark as normal after a short wait.
“There were massive cheers when we landed,” Loch said.
A Qantas spokesperson said the plane was believed to have suffered an engine issue and steps would be taken to support affected customers.
“Our pilots are highly trained to manage situations like this and the aircraft landed safely,” they said.
“We know this would have been a distressing experience for passengers and will be contacting all customers to provide support.”
Affected passengers were put up in a hotel near the Christchurch international airport before being booked on a complimentary flight to Sydney on Sunday.
While the second flight went off without a hitch, Loch said nerves were still high.
“I cried getting off the plane when we landed in Sydney,” Loch said.
“It was quite traumatic.”

articles.title: LTFRB to start accepting Undas special permit applications Sept. 21
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) on Sunday said it will start accepting applications for special permits for public transportation during this…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) on Sunday said it will start accepting applications for special permits for public transportation during this year’s observance of All Saints’ and All Souls’ Days on Sept. 21.
According to LTFRB Acting Chairperson Greg Pua Jr., applications will be accepted from Sept. 21 to Oct. 2, 2026, while the special permits will be effective from Oct. 28 to Nov. 6.
“The goal is to ensure that there will be no stranded passengers by making sure that there will be sufficient passenger buses and other appropriate public transportation,” Pua said.
The board earlier explained that special permits are issued during holidays to allow more public utility vehicles to ply beyond their original routes amid an influx of passengers.

The agency said the following requirements are needed to apply for a special permit: Official Receipt/Certificate of Registration of the unit; valid Personal Passenger Accident Insurance (PPAI); and, for a juridical entity, a Board Resolution and/or Secretary’s Certificate authorizing the application for a Special Permit and designating the authorized representative/s to file the petition.
It then noted the following conditions for the application and approval:

items: Only 50% of the total authorized units per operator per authorized route are allowed;
Units applied for should not be more than 14 years old from the date of manufacture; and
The specific addresses of the terminals at both ends of the applied route must be indicated.

blocks.text: The agency said more than 800 passenger buses were given special permits during the observance of Undas last year. /mcm

articles.title: Serbia: How the funeral of Ratko Mladic is dividing a nation
articles.summary: The body of the former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladic, who died last week in The Hague, where he was serving a life sentence for genocide and other war crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina, has…

blocks.text: The body of the former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladic, who died last week in The Hague, where he was serving a life sentence for genocide and other war crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina, has arrived back in Serbia.
Wrapped in the Serbian flag, Mladic’s coffin was carried by members of the Serbian Armed Forces from the plane to a vehicle that transported his remains to the Military Medical Academy for autopsy.

Several groups of citizens gathered along the route from the airport to the hospital. Standing on overpasses, they greeted the motorcade carrying Mladic’s body, holding banners that read “Thank you, General” and “Heroes never die.”
Pro-government tabloids provided minute-by-minute coverage, referring to Mladic as a “Serbian general” and claiming that he had been “killed in The Hague.”
A funeral with full state honors?

Ratko Mladic was sentenced in 2017 to life imprisonment by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in The Hague for the genocide in Srebrenica, in which more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys were killed, the years-long siege of Sarajevo during the 1992–95 Bosnian War, and other war crimes, including the establishment of detention camps for non-Serb civilians and prisoners of war.

blocks.caption: The body of former Bosnian Serb wartime general Ratko Mladic (in the red van) was transferred to the Military Medical Academy for autopsy after being flown to Belgrade from The Hague Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Belgrade media report that Mladic will be buried in Belgrade on Monday. Justice Minister Nenad Vujic had previously announced that the funeral would be held with the highest state honors.
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, however, says the decision will be left to the family.
Security agencies estimate that tens of thousands of people could attend the funeral.

“We will be there to provide all kinds of logistical and transport support and to maintain public order and security,” said the president, adding, “It is very difficult to ensure and guarantee the safety of everyone.”
Glorification that has continued for decades

For Jasmina Lazovic, executive director of the Belgrade-based Humanitarian Law Center, which has spent decades working on transitional justice and dealing with the past, none of this comes as a surprise.
She points to the long-standing glorification of Ratko Mladic in Serbia and his legacy.

“There is no small town in Serbia without at least one mural glorifying Ratko Mladic. The narrative that he was unjustly convicted has existed for years,” she tells DW. “Now a narrative has emerged that he was killed, despite the fact that he died at the age of 85 after suffering several strokes.”

Lazovic says that these narratives suit the state leadership’s portrayal of Serbia as a country that fought exclusively defensive wars and do not leave enough room for a discussion of the consequences of those wars and the victims they left behind — neither in the media nor in the education system and institutions.

“And there are hundreds of thousands of victims across Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo. Above all, these were crimes committed against civilians, crimes that left the countries of the region — particularly Bosnia and Herzegovina — with a completely transformed ethnic structure,” she said.
Lazovic says that the list of victims also includes those who survived rape and torture, as well as those who were forcibly displaced. “The list is long, and our knowledge is limited,” she adds.
A general without a rank
The announcement that Mladic could be buried with the highest state honors drew swift responses from the international community.

“Glorification of war criminals is contrary to European values. There is no place for it either in EU member states or in candidate countries. I hope the government in Belgrade is aware of that,” said European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos.

Aleksandar Vucic responded by accusing the West and the Hague Tribunal of blaming only Serbs for war crimes and failing to deliver justice for Serbian victims. But for now, he has officially left the decision on whether the deceased general will receive state honors to Mladic’s family.

Jasmina Lazovic believes Vucic will once again take a pragmatic approach and that the final decision will depend on an assessment of what brings the authorities greater political benefit and what could cause greater damage.
She also points out that the issue is not only political, but legal.

“What is being overlooked here is the fact that Ratko Mladic was indeed a general, but he was sentenced to life in prison. Under the Law on the Serbian Armed Forces, anyone sentenced to more than one year in prison for a criminal offense loses their rank and, therefore, all the privileges that come with that rank,” she says.
“If Ratko Mladic were buried with the highest state honors in accordance with the rank he held during the armed conflicts, that would be a direct violation of the law of this country.”
What do Serbs want?

On the question as to how they view Ratko Mladic, Serbian citizens interviewed by DW in several cities across the multi-ethnic autonomous province of Vojvodina expressed sharply differing views, ranging from those who are convinced that Mladic was unjustly convicted to those who accept the genocide designation without reservation.

blocks.caption: Mladic was also convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, where over 8,000 Muslim men and boys were killed in the summer of 1995 Image: Samir Jordamovic/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

blocks.text: “What was he supposed to do, let them kill all the Serbs? Thank you [Mladic], for everything,” one man from Ruma told DW.
“For me, the matter was settled when the genocide verdict was handed down,” said a student from Novi Sad.
But most people simply wave the question away. “I have enough of my own problems,” said Svetlana from Zrenjanin.
Goran, from Novi Sad, believes that it is simply another political issue. “They’ve been making fools of us for years. Nothing is different now,” he told DW.
Lazovic believes that most Serbs are apathetic about the matter.

For her, this is a greater problem than just the pro-government media portraying Serbia as wanting to say goodbye to Mladic as a general. She argues that confronting Mladic’s legacy and the past is essential if Serbian society is to move forward. /dl

articles.title: Pampanga flooding scales down patroness’ 70th anniversary celebration
articles.summary: CITY OF SAN FERNANDO — Widespread and prolonged flooding in Pampanga has prompted the Archdiocese of San Fernando to scale down the celebration of the 70th anniversary of the canonical coronation of…

blocks.text: CITY OF SAN FERNANDO — Widespread and prolonged flooding in Pampanga has prompted the Archdiocese of San Fernando to scale down the celebration of the 70th anniversary of the canonical coronation of the Virgen de los Remedios, the province’s patroness, on Sept. 8.
“Our celebration will be very simple yet meaningful,” Archbishop Florentino Lavarias said in a video message posted online on Saturday.
Lavarias said lamak, or donations given during the event, would be earmarked for food and other essential needs of flood victims.
As of 5 p.m. on Saturday, the Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office reported that 252 barangays in 17 towns had been flooded.

Pampanga, a catch basin for the Pampanga River and its 30 tributaries in Central Luzon, has experienced flooding for 34 days since Aug. 4. The province was placed under a state of calamity on Aug. 12.
The floods have also appeared to deepen devotion to the Virgen de los Remedios, with local processions being held despite inclement weather.
Lavarias said the donations would be handled by the Social Action Center of Pampanga.
A smaller venue, the Repository Chapel at the Arzobizpado de Pampanga, will accommodate representatives from the province’s 12 vicariates during the 3 p.m. Holy Mass.
Hourly Masses beginning at 6 a.m. will also be streamed online.

The image of the Virgen de los Remedios, or the Virgen of Remedies of Pampanga, was canonically crowned on Sept. 8, 1956, just weeks after Pope Pius XII issued a decree on July 15 of that year authorizing its canonical coronation.
Then San Fernando Bishop Cesar Maria Guerrero revived the Marian tradition amid a lack of charity during a period of agrarian unrest in Pampanga.
The image was carved by Victoriano Siongco, the maternal grandfather of Pablo Virgilio Cardinal David.
It has traditionally been paired with the Santo Cristo del Perdon y Caridad, or the Holy Christ of Pardon and Charity.
The two images are brought to parishes across Pampanga as part of a year-round crusade. /mcm
