articles.title: Iloilo City mayor: No quick fix to power woes
articles.summary: ILOILO CITY — The Iloilo City government is working with energy-sector stakeholders on longer-term solutions to continuing power interruptions as residents demand clearer timelines and immediate…

blocks.text: ILOILO CITY — The Iloilo City government is working with energy-sector stakeholders on longer-term solutions to continuing power interruptions as residents demand clearer timelines and immediate measures, Mayor Raisa Treñas said.
In a statement on Sept. 4, Treñas said the city government understood how repeated outages were affecting households, businesses, workers, and everyday activities.
She clarified that the manual load shedding implemented by the National Grid Corp. of the Philippines (NGCP) was not directly under the control of the Iloilo City government.

She also said she recently met with Panay Energy Development Corp. during a meeting of the Iloilo City Business Development Council and learned of efforts to increase power generation capacity in the Visayas.

The mayor cited the expected entry into Iloilo City of LNGPH, described as an integrated liquefied natural gas terminal and power facility, as one development that could help address the region’s power requirements.
Treñas stressed that the supply problem extended beyond Iloilo City and affected the wider Visayas grid.
“There is no instant or overnight solution to this problem. But we are not taking this sitting down,” she said.
The mayor said the city would continue coordinating with power-sector stakeholders to better understand the situation and identify concrete measures to protect consumers. /mcm

articles.title: Palace assures Sara Duterte, allies: PNP won’t harm them
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Palace has assured Vice President Sara Duterte that the Philippine National Police (PNP) under the Marcos administration will not be used to harm her or her supporters,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Palace has assured Vice President Sara Duterte that the Philippine National Police (PNP) under the Marcos administration will not be used to harm her or her supporters, despite her being among the president’s main political nemeses.

The Presidential Communications Office (PCO) on Saturday defended the PNP after Duterte said she feared for her life following the issuance of a warrant of arrest for three counts of grave threats against President Marcos, First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and former Speaker Martin Romualdez.
Duterte also publicly aired her distrust of the police, the courts and even the security team assigned to guard her when she posted bail before the Quezon City Regional Trial Court on Saturday.

“We wish to remind everyone that this administration will not allow the police force to be used as a weapon in any form of violence,” Palace press officer Claire Castro said, quoting the PCO statement.
According to the PCO, the PNP was only carrying out its mandate in accordance with the law, “without bias and without any political considerations, but solely for the benefit of every Filipino.”
“They remain professional in protecting the rights of all people under their care,” it said of the PNP’s 230,000 personnel across the country.
“The administration has full confidence in the PNP leadership and its ranks,” it added.
It urged Duterte to raise any concerns or complaints regarding police actions “through legal channels, rather than through baseless allegations.”
PNP chief Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. on Sunday assured Duterte that the police force would address her security concerns.
Concerned police units were instructed to continue monitoring and assessing threats against Duterte and her immediate family.
To date, the PNP has not identified any verified threat against Duterte or her family.
During the term of Duterte’s father, former President Rodrigo Duterte, the PNP was the main actor in enforcing his anti-drug campaign that led to the deaths of thousands of mostly poor drug suspects.

Investigations by the National Bureau of Investigation and the Commission on Human Rights found that some police personnel were involved in tampering with crime scenes and planting evidence to obstruct probes into the killings of suspects who supposedly resisted arrest, infamously known as “nanlaban” cases.
The cause of death of some drug suspects had also been falsified to show that they died of “natural causes.” /mcm

articles.title: PH Navy seizes P100-M contraband in Western Mindanao
articles.summary: PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur — The Naval Command Western Mindanao (NCWM) confiscated around P100 million worth of alleged contraband in three maritime operations conducted from August 28 to…

blocks.text: PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur — The Naval Command Western Mindanao (NCWM) confiscated around P100 million worth of alleged contraband in three maritime operations conducted from August 28 to September 3.

Authorities reported that the seizures included undocumented diesel fuel valued at P72,172,046; smuggled foreign-brand cigarettes and a motor vessel worth P27,228,969; and illegally transported Lauan lumber valued at P251,999. The combined haul amounted to P99,653,015.
Rear Admiral Constancio Arturo Reyes Jr., NCWM commander, commended the operating units and partner agencies for their vigilance and coordination.

“These operations reflect NCWM’s sustained commitment to securing the maritime domain of Western Mindanao and preventing its use for smuggling and other illegal activities. We will continue working closely with partner agencies to protect our waters and national interests,” Reyes said.
All seized items were turned over to the Bureau of Customs–Port of Zamboanga and other concerned agencies for proper legal disposition.
NCWM emphasized that it will sustain maritime patrols and interagency coordination to curb smuggling, protect legitimate commerce and uphold the country’s maritime laws across Western Mindanao. /mcm

articles.title: Trump’s Iran strategy: Could this become a forever war?
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has given a fairly clear description of what the next phase of the Iran war could look like. The Iranians had tried to rebuild their radar equipment, Trump stated after the…

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has given a fairly clear description of what the next phase of the Iran war could look like. The Iranians had tried to rebuild their radar equipment, Trump stated after the most recent wave of US strikes. “We waited until it was almost built, and then we hit it,” he said.

On Tuesday, American forces once again attacked several targets in Iran. According to US Central Command (CENTCOM), the targets destroyed included “air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites.”
‘Mowing the grass’
Iran responded by firing rockets and drones at US facilities in the region. With this, the war moved on to what CENTCOM had indicated just a few days earlier could be the strategy for the next phase.

According to the news portal Axios, it was considering limited strikes, at regular intervals if necessary, to prevent Iran from reconstituting its military capabilities in the Strait of Hormuz. An American government representative used a concept from Israeli security policy to describe this idea: He called it “mowing the grass.”

The metaphor refers to a strategy that doesn’t even attempt to promise that an opponent will be defeated once and for all. It is enough to regularly reduce the enemy’s military capabilities to the point where the threat remains manageable. When the grass grows back, you “mow” it again.
Applied to the situation in Iran, this would mean the US keeping an eye on which military capabilities the enemy is reconstituting, and attacking once it crosses a certain threshold.
Successes that won’t last

In the past few months, the US has scored some military successes. US forces have significantly reduced Iran’s military capabilities in the Strait of Hormuz, and have begun clearing Iranian sea mines.

However, these successes will not last. Tehran is repairing or procuring new radar installations, anti-aircraft positions and anti-ship missiles. US bombs could certainly destroy important Iranian positions with targeted strikes. But the knowledge and the industrial basis of Iranian military technology would remain.

blocks.caption: This image issued by US CENTCOM shows a precision strike against an Iranian military target in July 2026 Image: US Central Command/AFP

blocks.text: Reconstruction can therefore be delayed, but not prevented. The US will repeatedly be confronted with the same choice: whether to accept that Tehran is regaining its capabilities, or to attack again and destroy them.

Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, warned as early as April that this development could lead to an “enduring low-intensity conflict punctuated by more intensive interventions.”
Trump’s belligerent warnings

The fact that the strategy of “mowing the grass” is reaching its limits is also because it was never designed for a war with a state. Israel developed the strategy to combat non-state actors like Hamas.

However, as Yacoubian pointed out in her article, the Israeli academics who initially coined the term warned that if the opponent had “statist characteristics and/or more powerful capabilities, ‘mowing the grass’ might become an outdated military strategy.” This is clearly the case with the Strait of Hormuz.

The US needs to keep the strait reliably open. Iran, on the other hand, only needs to make people believe that the passage remains dangerous. In this way, even a significantly weakened opponent can impose substantial costs on Washington.

blocks.caption: Keeping the vital shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz open is a priority for the US Image: Atta Kenare/AFP

blocks.text: Another problem for the US is that, while Washington can determine the intensity of its own attacks, it has no control over Tehran’s response. This week, Trump warned Tehran not to launch a retaliatory strike, threatening that Iran would be “totally wiped out as a country” if it did.

Nonetheless, the regime in Tehran immediately fired missiles against American facilities in the region. Jordan alone reported 13 ballistic missiles in its airspace, 10 of which it was able to intercept.
The nuclear question

But Yacoubian believes that repeated American attacks carry a far greater risk. She warns that they may lead Tehran to conclude that “pursuit of a nuclear weapon” is the only way to achieve “lasting deterrence.” This suggests that, by attacking Iran, the US and Israel could actually accelerate the precise development they sought to bring under control.

blocks.caption: The Natanz nuclear facility in Iran was one of the first sites targeted by the US and Israel Image: Planet Labs

blocks.text: From Washington’s perspective, the alternatives available to Trump don’t look much better. If the president accepts Iran rebuilding its military strength around the Strait of Hormuz, he risks renewed attacks on shipping and disruption of one of the world’s most important energy routes.

The consequences for the global economy are well known. In spite of the upheaval and repeated negotiations, a political agreement between Washington and Tehran has so far failed because of apparently insurmountable differences.
America’s next ‘forever war’?

For Trump, “mowing the grass” has domestic appeal, in spite of the uncertainty it brings to foreign policy. The US president would be able to avoid occupation, nation building and deploying large numbers of American ground troops.
At the same time, it allows him to distance himself from the so-called “forever wars” he repeatedly accused his predecessors in the White House of pursuing.

Ultimately, though, this supposed way of avoiding a forever war could become one of its own. Yacoubian describes it as a “Sisyphean attrition strategy without end.” As long as Washington is not prepared at some point to accept the rebuilding of Iran’s capabilities, each successful attack merely creates the justification for the next one. /dl

articles.title: The meltdown of Sara Duterte: From ‘no joke, no joke’ to ‘I do not feel safe’
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte simultaneously faces her grave threats case and impeachment trial — cases which were triggered by one online midnight outburst

blocks.text: Vice President Sara Duterte’s day in court came on Saturday, September 5.

Dressed in black, the second highest official arrived at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court (RTC) with her lawyers Michael Poa and Paul Lawrence Lim to post bail. The court ordered her arrest on September 4 for three counts of grave threats over her alleged assassination treats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and family.
Duterte took her time. She made sure her statements were heard by journalists, with her supporters standing outside the hall.

“I do not feel safe. I do not feel safe anywhere. Pumunta lang ako [rito] kasi sabi ninyo pupunta ako sa court (I only went here because you told me I needed to appear in court),” a visibly upset Duterte said.

blocks.caption: The meltdown of Sara Duterte: From ‘no joke, no joke’ to ‘I do not feel safe’

blocks.text: The Vice President said she worries about her security, repeatedly claiming that she doesn’t trust authorities.

Duterte wanted to bring in people inside the court — the media covering her — while she was processing her bail. Just a few weeks ago, Duterte issued snide remarks against Filipino journalists, claiming, “Philippine journalism falls short of international standards.”
Poa and Lim explained to her that according to the court, journalists may accompany them only up to the court’s staircase. But Duterte continued expressing her qualms.
“Sino’ng nasa likod ko? Naaalala mo ba na si Ninoy Aquino, namatay sa hagdanan (Who’s behind me? Did you forget that Ninoy Aquino Jr. was assassinated while on stairs)?” said the Vice President.
Ninoy Aquino was shot in the back of the head on the tarmac of what was then called the Manila International Airport on August 21, 1983.
After a while, Duterte entered the hall to post her P360,000 bail.
After leaving the court and before entering her vehicle, Duterte hugged two crying women. The supporters were weeping due to supposed concerns about the Vice President’s safety.

blocks.caption: CRYING. Vice President Sara Duterte hugs a supporter outside Quezon City Regional Trial Court on September 5, 2026, after posting bail for her grave threats case. Jire Carreon/Rappler

blocks.text: Duterte then departed, leaving her lawyer to explain to the public what happened inside the court.

“Without prejudice to jurisdictional issues, the Vice President posted bail directly with the RTC Quezon City, [Branch] 98, which was the assigned weekend court. The routine bail procedure was conducted. After receiving all bail requirements, the court issued an order lifting the arrest warrant,” Duterte’s lawyers said in a statement.
Duterte’s warrant was issued on a Friday. The immediate concern was whether she would be arrested for failing to post bail before the court closed.

The lawyers of the Vice President only confirmed on September 4, that a warrant had been issued, but did not disclose whether Duterte would post bail that day. Night came, and still no sighting of Duterte nor her lawyers.

Technically, the Philippine National Police could have arrested her between Friday night and Saturday morning, but it did not. Quezon City Police District chief Police Brigadier General Christopher Olazo told reporters on Friday evening that there was no instruction to arrest anyone, and the police were there at the RTC only to secure the area.

blocks.caption: The meltdown of Sara Duterte: From ‘no joke, no joke’ to ‘I do not feel safe’

blocks.text: “We knew of her whereabouts the night before but we did not force the warrant of arrest,” Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla admitted to Rappler on Saturday.
And yet, Duterte insisted that she does not feel safe, claiming that she fears for her children. She said that despite going to court, the police still went to them.
But Remulla insisted that they accorded Duterte all the respect “that her position deserves.”

“It’s very unfortunate that all the pressure in her life is affecting her perception…. We have all the body cam footages of her warrants being served. We have all the body cam footages of her arrival to post bail,” said the DILG chief.

blocks.caption: The meltdown of Sara Duterte: From ‘no joke, no joke’ to ‘I do not feel safe’

blocks.text: Duterte’s claims about her safety are not new. She has been claiming there are security threats against her.

Her alleged threats against Marcos and family were part of the four articles of impeachment against her at the Senate. To dispute this allegation, her impeachment lawyers said there is supposedly a serious threat against the life of Duterte and family. The threat is called “Operation Romanov,” which takes inspiration from the tragic life of the Romanovs in Russia.
But in July, the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) said they also looked into these alleged threats against Duterte and found none.

blocks.caption: No threats found vs Sara Duterte, says NBI

blocks.text: Duterte said that her lawyers advised her to post bail to avoid detention. She made it appear that she would surely be held under police custody.

“They explained that the civilians who will see and witness my state can give me more protection, compared to staying under detention where I will be secluded and less secure,” said the Vice President in Filipino.
But her grave threats case, again, is bailable. Branch 98’s arrest warrant stated that the bail was set at P120,000 for each count. The Department of Justice (DOJ) also reiterated this on Friday.

Additionally, Duterte was also able to post bail on Saturday because courts allow bail even on weekends. The Supreme Court’s Office of the Court Administrator Circular (OCA) No. 30 series of 2023 made this possible.
There are courts assigned for night and weekend duties for bail purposes, and Duterte availed of this right.

blocks.caption: VEEP. Vice President Sara Duterte, along with legal counsels, arrive on September 5, 2026, at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court, following the issuance of an arrest warrant against her over a grave threats case. Jire Carreon/Rappler

blocks.text: Additionally, Duterte underwent standard court booking procedures, like taking of fingerprints, but because she surrendered to the court’s jurisdiction, she was spared a mugshot. Cops take mugshots of the accused only if they were arrested or surrendered to the police.

Lim said they submitted the Vice President’s photos to the court in lieu of mugshots. OCA Circular No. 204 series of 2022 allows this, but requires the accused’s party to submit “four sets of recently taken black and white 2×2 photographs (front, left and right profiles)…. on all copies of the corresponding bail bond to be issued or posted.”

To some human rights advocates, Duterte was not only accorded respect, she also enjoyed some privileges. Human rights lawyer Maria Sol Taule noted that some of the activists and individuals arrested during the September 21 protests last year were detained for a week “because offices during weekends are closed.”

“The photo here are lawyers, relatives and volunteer paralegals a year ago during the [September] 21 protest—no shortcuts, no special treatment. Everybody gathered to help complete all the requirements needed including bail fund,” said Taule.
Nearly two years ago, on November 23, 2024, the second highest official aired alarming remarks.

In that midnight virtual press conference, Duterte said her supporters should not worry about her safety because she “talked to someone” to ensure that if she gets killed, that person would assassinate Marcos and his family members.

“’Wag kang mag-alala, ma’am, sa security ko. Kasi may kinausap na ako na tao. Sinabi ko sa kanya, ‘Kapag pinatay ako, patayin mo si BBM, si Liza Araneta, at si Martin Romualdez.’ No joke. No joke (Don’t worry about my security, ma’am, because I already talked to a person. I told him, ‘If I am killed, kill BBM, Liza Araneta, and Martin Romualdez),” Duterte said.

blocks.caption: The meltdown of Sara Duterte: From ‘no joke, no joke’ to ‘I do not feel safe’

blocks.text: Few months later, in February 2025, the NBI filed grave threats and inciting to sedition complaints against Duterte over this online outburst. The House of Representatives, in May 2026, also approved the inclusion of grave threats in the articles of impeachment against the Vice President.

By August this year, in the middle of the impeachment trial, the DOJ indicted Duterte for grave threats, but dismissed the inciting to sedition complaint. It said it found enough evidence to prove that the grave threats case could not only stand trial, but also secure a conviction.
Duterte filed a motion to defer her warrant and sought oral hearings as they argued that she can’t face a criminal case because she is the Vice President, an impeachable official.

“If a sitting Vice President may be indicted and prosecuted, then other incumbent impeachable officers such as the Ombudsman, members of the Constitutional Commissions, Supreme Court Justices, and even the President, may also be indicted and prosecuted,” Lim said on August 13.
But Branch 98 denied this motion and proceeded with the issuance of the warrant.

Several legal experts, including one of the framers of the 1987 Constitution, Father Joaquin Bernas SJ, had said in the past that a sitting vice president is not immune from suit. (READ: ‘Vice President does not enjoy immunity’)

“The cases (grave threats, impeachment) can proceed simultaneously. There is no rule that says the impeachment process must be terminated before the criminal case can proceed,” constitutional lawyer Dan Gatmaytan earlier told Rappler.

For now, Duterte enjoys temporary liberty. She is set to face her arraignment in the coming days where she will be read her formal charges, and where the court will ask her to enter either a guilty or not guilty plea.
The Vice President will then have to simultaneously face her grave threats case and impeachment trial — cases which were triggered by one online midnight outburst. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Senate to decide on BSKE reset, 5-year term this week -- Sherwin Gatchalian
articles.summary: The Senate will decide this week on proposed measures seeking to postpone the November 2026 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) and increase the term of office of barangay and SK…

blocks.text: Published September 6, 2026 2:57pm

The Senate will decide this week on proposed measures seeking to postpone the November 2026 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) and increase the term of office of barangay and SK officials from four to five years, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said Sunday.
Speaking to Super Radyo dzBB, Gatchalian said the Senate would discuss the proposed BSKE reset and the fixing of officials' terms this week.

"We will discuss it this week. There should be a decision this week on whether the elections will push through because the filing of candidacies is at the end of the month," Gatchalian said in Filipino.
He said a decision must be made by the end of the week because the measures would still have to undergo a bicameral conference committee, ratification by both chambers, and publication.
Gatchalian said one advantage of postponing the BSKE and fixing the terms at five years would be the savings from eliminating the cost of one election cycle.
The Commission on Elections (Comelec) had said it already spent P8 billion of its P19-billion budget for the BSKE.
Comelec chairperson George Erwin Garcia said some election supplies, including indelible ink, could go unused if the BSKE is postponed.
The BSKE is scheduled for Nov. 2.
Meanwhile, Gatchalian said one disadvantage of extending the term to five years would be that the electorate would have to wait longer to replace an ineffective or frequently absent barangay captain.
According to Gatchalian, the Senate will go on a break on Oct. 8 or 9, so the proposed measures should be approved before then.

Senator Francis Escudero filed Senate Bill No. 2387, which seeks to amend Republic Act No. 12232, or the "Act Setting the Term of Office of Barangay Officials and Members of the Sangguniang Kabataan, and for Other Purposes."
Escudero said the proposed measure seeks to fix, rather than merely extend or postpone, the terms of barangay and SK officials from four to five years.
Meanwhile, Senator Imee Marcos filed Senate Bill No. 2067, which seeks to move the BSKE from November 2026 to October 2027, as the scheduled election date falls on All Souls' Day this year.
In August, a Senate panel approved the proposed measures.
However, the National Citizens’ Movement for Free Elections (NAMFREL) said the BSKE should proceed as scheduled, citing fiscal strain, the Middle East oil crisis, and travel costs.
The Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting (PPCRV) expressed the same view, saying preparations for the BSKE are already underway. — MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Recto: 64% cut in Palace budget won’t hamper operations
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the President (OP) will be able to maintain its operations despite a proposed 64-percent cut in its budget for 2027, Executive Secretary Ralph Recto said in a…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the President (OP) will be able to maintain its operations despite a proposed 64-percent cut in its budget for 2027, Executive Secretary Ralph Recto said in a statement on Sunday.

The House appropriations committee earlier voted 37-5 to swiftly end debate on the OP’s P10.15-billion proposed budget, cutting short discussions after the panel deferred questioning over its spending plan due to parliamentary courtesy.

IRecto said the OP’s proposed budget was “enough for the center to oversee government operations, from responding to emergencies, delivering public services, monitoring economic plans, and protecting the national interests.”
“We are asking for less while remaining fully prepared to do more,” Recto said.
The OP’s 2027 proposed budget is significantly lower than its P28 billion budget this year, the bulk of which, at P17.55 billion, was earmarked for hosting the 2026 Asean Summits.

Recto said the OP’s budget cut was due to the “streamlining of the operations” of the OP’s 49 delivery units and the completion of activities related to the Philippines’ hosting of the 48th and 49th Asean Summits this year.

The funding will support Cabinet meetings, policy consultations, presidential engagements, and the daily operations of Malacañang as the nation’s principal center of executive decision-making and inter-agency coordination.
It will also help deliver timely assistance to vulnerable sectors and enable the government “to mount response to contingencies and challenges.”
“Every day, the president’s schedule is full because the demands of governing do not pause. But activity alone is not our measure of performance,” Recto said.

He assured that every policy, meeting, engagement, and official mission will produce a clear public dividend, whether through jobs and investments, stronger national security, better public services, or greater opportunities for Filipinos.
He likewise stressed that fiscal discipline and accountability remain at the core of the OP’s operations.
He also assured lawmakers that the proposed budget was crafted strictly within the parameters and processes established by the Department of Budget and Management (DBM).
“We sought no special treatment,” Recto said.

Due to the parliamentary courtesy extended by the House to the OP, lawmakers were not able to scrutinize its P4.56 billion confidential and intelligence funds request for 2027, the same amount it had in the 2026 national budget.

The OP also did not need to explain the P1.014 billion it requested for its local and foreign missions and state visits budget for 2027 — slightly lower than its current budget of P1.018 billion for travel expenses.

The OP also has direct oversight authority over the Local Government Support Fund (LGSF), which the Marcos administration is proposing to allocate a record-high P58.32 billion in 2027. Critics warned this might become a tool for political patronage for the upcoming 2028 elections.
The same deference is also expected to be extended by the Senate finance committee once the OP’s 2027 proposed budget reaches the upper chamber.

Budget watchdogs, however, have been calling for an end to stop the traditional practice of extending congressional courtesy to OP, as it violates the system of checks and balances designed by the Constitution. /atm

articles.title: Prince Harry’s surprise UK return renews security row
articles.summary: LONDON — Prince Harry’s return to Britain has reignited debate about whether taxpayers should foot the bill to protect him and his family, with experts warning genuine threats likely…

blocks.text: LONDON — Prince Harry’s return to Britain has reignited debate about whether taxpayers should foot the bill to protect him and his family, with experts warning genuine threats likely exist.
The Duke of Sussex, who arrived in Britain last week with his wife Meghan and their two young children, had previously ruled out returning to his home country, citing security concerns.

The couple left Britain and quit royal duties in 2020 amid a royal family feud and Harry subsequently waged a years-long, ultimately unsuccessful, legal battle to retain UK taxpayer-funded security while living in California.
Now back with their seven-year-old son, Prince Archie, and five-year-old daughter, Princess Lilibet, he has reportedly been pushing for reinstated police protection.
However, when the family landed August 26 at Birmingham Airport, they had private security in place rather than police officers, according to British media.
“It’s very surprising,” Scott Hamer, an ex-protection officer for Harry’s father King Charles III when he was Prince of Wales, told AFP.
“There’s probably people who are being protected now who are at less threat and risk than he is. So the question would be, why does he not receive that protection as well?”
‘Vulnerability’
Harry and Meghan, who are reportedly living in central England’s Cotswolds region, are said to have enrolled their children at private schools there for the coming academic year.
They are thought to have heightened concerns about security around the kids’ daily drop-off and collection, given that these follow predictable patterns.
“The vulnerability aspect needs to be assessed,” said Hamer.
“The fact that he’ll have to take his kids to school at the same time each day, and pick them up at the same time each day, now makes him quite vulnerable.”
Britain’s Royal and VIP Executive Committee (Ravec) — an independent body overseen by the interior ministry — decides which politicians, royals and others get police protection.
Harry battled the ministry in the courts after Ravec downgraded his security following his 2020 North America move.
The prince lost his bid to reverse the decision, branding the 2025 dismissal of his appeal a “good old-fashioned Establishment stitch-up”.
With his return, Ravec’s risk management board will likely be re-evaluating the threat level he faces.
“It’s very real,” explained Hamer, noting it could range from international terrorism to extreme right-wing actors opposed to his marriage to mixed-race Meghan.
‘Threat’
The Sunday Times reported last week that Harry’s lawyers wrote to interior minister Shabana Mahmood in August requesting she intervene.
The paper said he had lost faith in Ravec’s ability to rule fairly on his security needs, citing sources close to him.
A government spokesperson said the protection system was “rigorous and proportionate” while noting its long-standing policy not to provide details of arrangements.
“Doing so could compromise their integrity and affect individuals security,” the spokesperson added.
Harry is thought to be pushing for police protection in part because private security in the UK cannot be armed.

“That’s what his argument is: that the threat against him is so great that it can only be dealt with [through] an official police protection team,” another former royal protection officer, Simon Morgan, told AFP. “He feels that he should get it.”
However, the British public appear to think otherwise.
Just six percent say the prince’s security should be fully taxpayer-funded while 63 percent believe the couple should pay for it, according to a poll last week for The i Paper.
“He’s paid for security in the States. I can’t see why he can’t pay for security here — it’s a lot less dangerous,” royal expert Andrew Lownie told AFP.
‘Lot of money’
Hamer said whether Harry was a working royal or not “shouldn’t be part of it,” noting ex-PMs get protected despite leaving office.
Lownie predicted Harry would succeed in getting some taxpayer-funded protection reinstated for the same reason.
But he noted the bill for such services has ballooned over the last decade, which has seen six prime ministers leave office — compared to just two in the prior 10 years.
“If we’re doing it for all these prime ministers, then I think we’re going to have to do it for Harry and his family. But that is going to cost a lot of money.”
Harry has consistently argued he and his family are at increased risk given he is the king’s son and due to his UK military service.
The prince completed two tours of Afghanistan and claimed in his explosive 2023 memoir “Spare” to have killed 25 Taliban fighters.
Choosing to make the high-profile admission prompted criticism at the time from some British veterans, who noted it could increase his personal security risk. /dl

articles.title: Maria Ressa: Journalists must build, own technology to protect information integrity
articles.summary: Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa says journalists must have a say in the systems that increasingly determine how news is distributed

blocks.text: TRUTH. Rappler CEO and Nobel laureate Maria Ressa speaks at the Nobel Peace Conference 2026 about restoring information integrity.
Screenshot from Nobel Peace Center
Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa says journalists must have a say in the systems that increasingly determine how news is distributed

items: Maria Ressa emphasized the need for journalists to take control of technology to ensure information integrity, advocating for them to become tech builders.
She warned that news organizations face imminent threats due to outdated business models and the changing landscape influenced by AI, which reduces the need for users to visit original news sources.

Ressa described the current information crisis as an 'information armageddon,' highlighting the dangers posed by technology that prioritizes profit over public good, and called for a collective effort to build alternative infrastructures for journalism.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa urged journalists to take control of the technology that increasingly determines how news reaches the public in the face of artificial intelligence.

“The only way you have information integrity is for journalists to become tech builders,” Ressa, Rappler’s chief executive officer, said during the Nobel Peace Conference 2026 held last September 3. “We must build, we own our data, we own the technology.”

The conference brought together Nobel Peace laureates and other participants to discuss threats facing democracy, lessons from civic movements around the world, and how the international community can support those fighting for it. This year’s discussions also included the growing influence of big tech on democratic societies.

blocks.caption: Maria Ressa: Journalists must build, own technology to protect information integrity

blocks.text: Ressa warned that news organizations could “die in the next five to eight months” because the existing business model is no longer viable. Adapting to new tools is no longer enough. News organizations also need a say in the systems that determine how their journalism reaches their audience.

For years, publishers have relied on Google and other social media platforms to drive readers to their websites. AI-powered search is now changing that relationship by giving users direct answers to their questions.
This results in a reduced need to visit the original source. Fewer referrals mean fewer opportunities for publishers to build audiences and generate revenue from their journalism.

Ressa pointed to Rappler’s experience as an example of what she means by building alternatives. After years of dealing with online attacks, Rappler developed an application using the Matrix protocol, a project eventually expanded to other media groups.
The project gave news organizations infrastructure they could control, an approach journalism should take on in the AI era.
“Build your own technology,” she said. “Build your multilateral organization.”

blocks.caption: LIVESTREAM: UN launches preliminary report by the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI

blocks.text: Ressa described the wider problem as an “information armageddon.” The erosion of shared facts makes it harder for societies to establish a common understanding of reality.
She outlined three waves of technology that have transformed the information environment. These include social media, large language models and generative AI, and increasingly autonomous AI agents.
“Every one of these stages are built to hack our biology,” Ressa said. “They’re designed not for you, they’re designed for profit.”
Social media is designed to keep people engaged, she pointed out. Chatbots can simulate human intimacy, while AI agents are increasingly capable of carrying out tasks on a user’s behalf.
She also linked technology dependence to the spread of information operations, in which false narratives can be seeded and amplified during crises, and eventually accepted as fact.
For Ressa, defending democracy now means confronting not only the information being produced, but also the systems that determine how it moves.
“The technology is ruled by people who you didn’t elect, by people who have no guardrails, by people who are driven to keep you scrolling, even to your detriment,” she said.
Ressa co-chairs the UN’s Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence, a 40-member body tasked with assessing the risks, capabilities, and broader impacts of AI.

The panel warned in its July preliminary report that AI is advancing faster than governments’ ability to understand, measure and govern the technology. It said the rapid deployment of AI brings risks not only to societies and economies, but also to human rights and security.

The panel also identified AI’s effects on democracy and the information ecosystem as a major concern, warning that the technology can erode shared reality and create risks to information integrity and civic participation.
It said these risks could ultimately undermine society’s ability to benefit from AI if they are not addressed. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Adiong hits Sara Duterte’s safety fear remark: How ironic
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — House prosecution panel spokesperson and Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong on Sunday criticized Vice President Sara Duterte who expressed fears for her safety, saying it was…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — House prosecution panel spokesperson and Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong on Sunday criticized Vice President Sara Duterte who expressed fears for her safety, saying it was “ironic” as she was facing a grave threats case.
Duterte on Saturday posted a P360,000 bail for three counts of grave threats before a Quezon City court a day after an arrest warrant was issued against her.

Her cases stemmed from an online press conference in November 2023 where she said she had spoken to someone about having President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez assassinated, if she herself is killed.
“How ironic na the reason why she was there ay para magpiyansa, mag-post bail on an allegation of a grave threat. Accused siya na siya yung nagbabanta,” Adiong said in an interview with dzRH.
(How ironic is that the reason why she was there to post bail was for an allegation of a grave threat. She was accused of making those threats.)
“So mukhang ito lang ata yung nakita natin na kung sino pa yung nagbanta, siya pa rin yung biktima,” Adiong added.
(So it seems that whoever made the threats was made to look like the victim.)
Before entering the QC Hall of Justice, Duterte said she does not trust the police and that she fears for her safety and that of her family.
She also said she had felt unsafe since 2023 as a result of harassment ther family was facing.
Adiong pointed out Duterte’s demeanor when she made the remarks on Saturday, saying that it was not the look of someone who seemed scared for her life, noting that “it’s the other way around.”

“Pero if you’re looking at the way, the demeanor and the manner by which she was telling this to her lawyers, hindi yun yung nakikita natin na takot na takot. Palaban pa rin siya. Mas matapang pa nga siya doon kaysa doon sa mga pulis,” Adiong said.

(But if you’re looking at that way, the demeanor and the manner by which she was telling this to her lawyers, it does not show fear. She is still feisty. She is braver than the police officers there.)
The lawmaker also criticized Duterte’s claim that she has been receiving threats since 2023, saying that she was the one who threatened Marcos.
He added that “it’s not an indication of someone who’s been receiving threats.”
Adiong, however, said the supposed threats against Duterte should still be investigated.
The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Saturday said it has not received any information regarding any threats against Duterte and her family.
Even so, PNP Chief PGen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said they are monitoring and assessing the situation to ensure Duterte’s safety. /gsg

articles.title: Sara Duterte’s claim of fearing for her life ‘pure drama’ – Castro
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte’s remarks that she fears for her life were “pure drama,” former ACT Teachers Rep. France Castro said on Sunday. Castro, a staunch critic of the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte’s remarks that she fears for her life were “pure drama,” former ACT Teachers Rep. France Castro said on Sunday.

Castro, a staunch critic of the Dutertes, said the vice president was in no position to cast herself as a victim after a warrant was issued for her arrest over charges that she threatened President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
She also said Duterte’s remarks on Saturday were an attempt to control the narrative and portray herself as a victim.
“This bratinella’s just full of drama,” Castro said, using the Filipino slang for a female brat.
“She only wants to flip the narrative and make herself the victim,” the former lawmaker added.

On Saturday, Duterte posted P360,000 bail for charges that she made grave threats against Marcos, First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former Speaker Ferdinand Martin Romualdez. Before entering the Quezon City Hall of Justice, she said she did not trust the police or the court.
“I do not feel safe, I really do not feel safe. I don’t trust the court, I don’t trust the police,” she said.
Duterte said she had felt unsafe since 2023 due to harassment of her family by certain authorities, whom she did not name.

“The irony is striking: this is the same family that once threatened political opponents, those who exposed their misdeeds, and enforced tokhang and extrajudicial killings — now she claims to be the one under threat,” Castro said. /mcm

articles.title: 2 PWDs among 2026 Bar examinees
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — A blind person and an amputee were among the tens of thousands who took the Bar exam this year, Associate Justice Samuel Gaerlan said on Sunday. READ: First day of 2026 Bar…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — A blind person and an amputee were among the tens of thousands who took the Bar exam this year, Associate Justice Samuel Gaerlan said on Sunday.
Gaerlan, the Bar exam chairperson, said the two persons with disabilities were among those assigned an encoder to assist them in navigating the exam.
“We also have examinees who were allowed to take exams with the assistance of an encoder,” Gaerlan said in a press conference. “One lost sight to a rare form of meningitis … and one lost both arms.”
The Supreme Court (SC) justice also said one person deprived of liberty (PDL) took the Bar exam.
The male examinee, he said, was not required to take the exam behind bars.
“We allowed him to go to the local testing centers, but of course, with the implementation of security protocols,” he said.
Meanwhile, the Bar exam this year was conducted through laptops, but three examinees were allowed to take handwritten examinations.

Those granted the exemption were a 69-year-old “with a limited exposure to computers throughout their life,” a 64-year-old with a chronic eye condition, and a 49-year-old who “lost their laptop before their exam.”
As of Sunday morning, the SC logged a total of 11,900 exam applicants out of the 13,441 officially admitted to take the licensure test.
“There was an increase in the number of examinees this year as compared to other years,” Gaerlan said. “I think we have the highest number.”
The second and third days of the Bar exams will be held across 15 local testing centers nationwide on Sept. 9 and 13. /mcm

articles.title: Ebola: Why children are last to be treated in medical crises
articles.summary: In the latest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, children are more likely to die than adults. But it's not always due to the disease. Specific medicines for younger people are often…

image.caption: Children have been badly affected in the current Ebola epidemic, and treatment options for them remain limitedImage: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/REUTERS

blocks.text: The current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been devastating. Since the outbreak began in mid-May, more than 3,000 people have died.

Almost half of people infected with Ebola are expected to die, and the mortality rate is particularly high for young children. According to a commentary by Doctors Without Borders recently published in medical journal The Lancet, the mortality rate for children under the age of 5 is over 60%.
But often, it's because of a lack of medication and information on how to use it with young patients, rather than then disease itself.
"Children must be centered in Ebola treatment and prevention research," the aid organization wrote in early September.

At the heart of the debate is the EBO-PEP study, which began mid-July. The study looks at an experimental antiviral drug called obeldesivir, which is being studied for its ability to protect people exposed to the Bundibugyo Ebola virus, the strain responsible for the current deadly outbreak.

But children weighing less than 30 kilograms (about 66 pounds) and around 12 years old or younger, were not included in the original study. But that could change soon with protocols to include children weighing over 20 kilograms.

blocks.caption: Children under the age of 5 are significantly more likely to die from Ebola fever than adultsImage: Benediction Murhabazi/AFP

blocks.text: Children weighing less than 20 kilograms — that is, roughly 6 years old or younger — won't be included in the treatment. There is an alternative treatment for them: Another antiviral drug, remdesivir, given intravenously. But as Doctors Without Borders argued, a 10-day course of infusions is difficult to administer during an outbreak, especially for young children.

According to Neal Russell, a pediatric doctor based in London who consults for Doctors Without Borders and who was also the lead author of the Lancet commentary, young children are at particularly high risk from Ebola. This could be due to their weakened immune systems, underlying health conditions, or the fact that treating them for Ebola is especially challenging in an outbreak.

For example, children are often harder to diagnose than adults because early symptoms resemble other illnesses, and young children often find it difficult to describe their symptoms accurately. Other issues include the fact that children cannot always be accompanied into an Ebola treatment center by their parents or caregivers, something that is especially important in their recovery. Younger Ebola patients also require closer monitoring and specially trained staff.
Ebola outbreak in DR Congo outpaces efforts to contain it
Ebola in Berlin

In May, an American doctor was treated at Berlin's Charite hospital after contracting the Bundibugyo Ebola virus while caring for patients. His wife and their four children were also considered at high risk. The medical team in Germany decided to treat the family prophylactically with an experimental antibody drug called MBP134.
"Of course, a careful risk benefit assessment had to be carried out," said Han Ngoc Le, a doctor at the hospital who was involved in the treatments.
The available data about the drug's impact on children was very limited. But at the same time, the children were at high risk of catching Ebola after close contact with their sick father.

In the end, all the family remained healthy and no apparent side effects were seen. It's unclear whether the experimental treatment prevented infection in the children. Such a small sample can't be mapped onto the larger population either.

But the test was valuable nonetheless. "The mere fact that the antibody was so well tolerated even in 1-year-olds and children under 12 is a valuable finding upon which future studies can build," Le said.
Why do such gaps in knowledge exist?
Le explained that, from a medical perspective, children cannot simply be thought of as "small adults."

Their metabolisms function differently, they react differently to medications, their pharmacokinetics — what a body does with a drug — are simply different. The same sort of cautions also apply to pregnant women.

That's why dosages of medication can't simply be transferred from adults to children. It's also why any new medications require separate studies so that specific dosages can be determined and potentially special formulations can be developed. Children might require kid-friendly syrups instead of adult-size tablets, for example.
DR Congo launches Ebola trial for high-risk contacts

"All of this creates extra costs," said Marc Biot, access coordinator for Europe at Doctors Without Borders, who works to ensure people in need can get affordable, good-quality medical products. He said research institutions and pharmaceutical companies often see investing extra in pediatric studies as a lower priority.

"It is faster and it can be cheaper if you only focus on adults," said Biot — which is why treating children and pregnant women usually only becomes part of the research at a later stage of drug development. "That is our plea — a plea not only to the scientists, to the pharmaceutical companies, but also to those who fund and allow trials to happen — to allow that to happen on the same speed for adults as for children and pregnant women."
Biot said it's sad to see that pressure is needed to make it happen. "Whenever you start a clinical trial, you also should include pregnant woman or children," he argued.
A difficult balance

None of this is new. In 2020, the Global Accelerator for Pediatric Formulations network was founded — supported by the World Health Organization(WHO) — to accelerate the development and availability of child-friendly medicine worldwide.
This isn't an issue limited to Ebola. Russell pointed to the 2024 mpox epidemic in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where children made up a large proportion of those infected or killed.

Although a vaccine existed for mpox, it wasn't made for children. The WHO advised it be used "off label" for minors, but they tended to get it a lot later than adults anyway. Experts say they've observed similar patterns with other diseases including HIV, tuberculosis, and during the COVID-19 pandemic.

blocks.caption: When it comes to the development of medicines and vaccines, the first samples are often made for adult patientsImage: Thomas Lohnes/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: "When you're doing a research study, which is not in an emergency, [it makes sense] to protect children and pregnant women from any potential harm of an investigational product," said Russell. "But when you're in an emergency, the balance between protecting those people from any potential harm from research, and protecting them from the very fatal disease, changes."

Berlin-based doctor Le believes children and pregnant women should be considered right from the beginning of any new clinical trials. "They shouldn't be excluded from participation just like that," she said. "Instead, sub-studies or parallel studies should be set up from the outset."

Russell calls for a similar approach. He wants to see all people benefit equally from scientific progress during a health crisis — especially in a health emergency, when the most vulnerable should not be the last to benefit from that progress.
"No matter who you are, you should have the same opportunity to have access to these medical products," he said.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Martin Romualdez camp seeks due process amid possible new allegations
articles.summary: The camp of former House Speaker Martin Romualdez on Sunday appealed to the Office of the Ombudsman for fairness as it sought an opportunity to respond to any new allegations against him.

blocks.text: Published September 6, 2026 2:12pm
The camp of former House Speaker Martin Romualdez on Sunday appealed to the Office of the Ombudsman for fairness as it sought an opportunity to respond to any new allegations against him.

Ade Fajardo, Romualdez’s legal counsel and spokesperson, made the appeal following reports that former Public Works Secretary Manuel Bonoan may be pressured to link Romualdez to the flood control scandal.
“We are requesting the Ombudsman to inform us if there is any allegation from Secretary Bonoan against former Speaker Romualdez and to give us ample time to comment on it,” Fajardo said.

“Fair play and due process require that such information and opportunity be accorded to us at this point in the process, the preliminary investigation stage, not if and when the Ombudsman decides to file charges in court,” he added.
Romualdez’s legal counsel also requested information on the reported 28 new witnesses before the Ombudsman, including any statements they may have made against their client.

“There is also the report that the Ombudsman has 28 new witnesses. We would like to know if there is any statement from them against our client, and we would like as well to have the opportunity to respond,” he said.
GMA News Online has reached out to the Office of the Ombudsman for comment.
The Sandiganbayan Fifth Division earlier granted the Ombudsman’s motion to drop Bonoan from the plunder and graft charges involving former Senator Jinggoy Estrada.
Bonoan was among Estrada’s four co-accused whom the Ombudsman charged in May with allegedly conspiring to collect more than P500 million in kickbacks from flood control projects.
On August 20, Romualdez filed a supplemental affidavit asking the Ombudsman to stop the preliminary investigation against him.
This came after former Marines, including security aide Orly Guteza, withdrew their allegations against Romualdez.

In his new affidavit, Guteza claimed that Sen. Rodante Marcoleta and former House lawmaker Mike Defensor had tapped him to fabricate accusations against Romualdez in exchange for money and scholarships for his children.
Guteza said he regretted what he did and asked for forgiveness, saying he had been swayed by promises from Marcoleta and Defensor.
With the retraction by Guteza and other former Marines, Fajardo said there was no more “credible evidence” against Romualdez.

“There has been no accusation from any of them since this controversy erupted more than a year ago. Of course, it would surprise us, to say the least, if an allegation surfaces now or in the future,” he said. — MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Falklands row shows urgent need to commit to 3% target, says Labour defence committee chair
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Tan Dhesi says Argentinian threats make it more crucial than ever that PM increase defence spending

Javier Milei’s threats to the Falkland Islands make it even more important that…

blocks.text: Javier Milei’s threats to the Falkland Islands make it even more important that Andy Burnham increase defence spending immediately, according to the Labour chair of the defence committee.

Tan Dhesi said the comments by the Argentinian president this week show why the government should raise military spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. But he said Burnham’s plans remain mired in confusion after the prime minister appeared to reassure him that the 2030 target would be hit, only for Downing Street to later retreat.

“It’s important the prime minister and the chancellor don’t defer those decisions to next year,” Dhesi told the Guardian. “We’ve seen Germany publicly expose Russia for the drone incident [in Leipzig]. Now we’ve got a threat from Argentina saying they are looking to take over the Falklands. We owe it to the Falklands – they say it’s their right to self-determination. It’s important that we also defend them from this threat.”

Dhesi was speaking after a turbulent week in geopolitics and defence policy. The Labour MP appeared to have secured a promise by the prime minister on Wednesday that the UK would spend 3% of its economic output on defence by 2030, at an estimated additional cost of £10bn a year.
During Burnham’s first prime minister’s questions since taking office in July, Dhesi asked him whether he backed the 2030 commitment, warning “vibes alone just isn’t going to be enough”.

He was speaking soon after the chancellor, John Healey, declined to sign up to the 2030 target, even though he resigned from Keir Starmer’s government over the issue. Burnham replied that he had “made that commitment”, only for No 10 to say the prime minister was not making a firm commitment.
The government instead has signed up to a longer-term Nato target of spending 3.5% on defence by 2035.

blocks.caption: Tan Dhesi asked Andy Burnham whether he backed the 2030 commitment to defence spending at Wednesday’s PMQs. Photograph: House of Commons/PA

blocks.text: “There was no clarity [on the government’s defence policy], that’s why I asked the question,” Dhesi said. “There was a clarification post-PMQs that there isn’t an agreement to reach 3% by 2030. I wasn’t aware of [any] clarity [on this question], and that’s what was reconfirmed afterwards. We’re still in a similar situation. My question is valid and important for the country.”

Later in the week, Donald Trump appeared to call American support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falklands into question. The US has traditionally remained neutral on the islands’ ownership, while accepting Britain’s de facto control, but the president suggested this could be changed in retaliation for the UK’s lack of support for his war in Iran.
“Don’t forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the strait of Hormuz, and you weren’t there to help me,” he told GB News. “Your country was not there to help me.”
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Javier Milei threatened oil sanctions against firms planning to exploit oil close to the islands.  Photograph: Mariana Nedelcu/Reuters

blocks.text: His comments about the islands have emboldened Milei, who said on Thursday night “winds of change” favourable to his country’s claim to the islands were “blowing around the world”.

He added: “The US is considering this change of position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come.”
He also said companies developing oil “behind the back of the Argentine government” would be barred from doing business in Argentina.
Ministers in the UK condemned Milei’s comments on Friday, saying the Falklands would remain British for as long as the people who live there wanted them to.
