Taraneh Rahimi was told prison guards would rape her sister, Romina, if she did not sign a confession

The twins were 19 and still in high school when they were taken from their beds in the…

blocks.text: The twins were 19 and still in high school when they were taken from their beds in the dead of night by masked men later identified as being sent by the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.

After four months of desperately seeking news from hospitals and state institutions, their mother, Marzieh Nourmohammadi, finally learned their fate. Taraneh and Romina Rahimi had been seized over their decision to join millions on the streets of Iranian cities during the January protests against the regime. The twins were unrecognisable by the time of their mother’s prison visit in May.

The women’s scalps were patchy from being dragged around by their hair, and their faces were bruised, according to their US-based cousin. It is claimed that Taraneh, who dreams of running her own horse stable one day, had been told the prison guards would rape Romina in front of her unless a confession was signed.

blocks.caption: Taraneh Rahimi, who has a love of horses. Photograph: Taraneh Rahimi

blocks.text: The visit by their mother to Dowlatabad prison, in Isfahan, the main city in central Iran, was five months ago. It has now emerged from the Iranian courts that Taraneh has been sentenced to death for her participation in the January protests, and that Romina has been given a 25-year prison sentence. Neither of the women have been seen by their family since the sentencing.

blocks.caption: Romina Rahimi. Photograph: Romina

blocks.text: The difference in the sentences remains a mystery, but the twins’ cousin, Masoud Nourmohammadi, who lives in the US state of Utah, said he struggled to understand anything done by the regime.

“They do not follow their own law,” said Nourmohammadi. “There is an 18-day period that lawyers can go and appeal but in a lot of [execution] cases recently that has not happened. They just sentence and take the kids and execute them and hang them. So I mean, nothing, nothing really makes sense.”

Nourmohammadi, 43, said he believed Taraneh was sentenced to death by hanging because of her obvious innocence. “You can see her eyes and you know right away that she is a kind person,” he said. “My sense is like they’re looking to put fear within the people, to say: ‘Look, no matter how fine you are, no matter how innocent you are, we can get you, and don’t come to the streets any more.’”

Despite the logistical difficulties presented by the war with the US and Israel that began in February, Iran has executed more than 500 people this year, including at least 29 people in connection with the anti-government protests in January.

At least 16 women have been among those executed. Hundreds more protesters have either been sentenced to death or are facing charges which could carry the death penalty, including more than 70 in Isfahan.
Last month, the UK and 30 other countries signed a joint statement condemning the executions of the January protesters and describing them as an attempt to silence dissent.

Nourmohammadi, a healthcare IT specialist who arrived in the US from Iran 22 years ago, is speaking out despite receiving death threats via text messages and social media from people who say they know his home address. His cousins’ case, he said, should instil a determination to end the Islamic regime.

blocks.caption: A screengrab from footage of anti-government protests in Tehran in early January. Photograph: Social Media/Reuters

blocks.text: The two women joined the protests on 8 and 9 January in Istafan, along with 18 million others. The men who came for them a month later dragged them out with bags over their heads and offered no explanation. “The family didn’t know where they were,” Nourmohammadi said. “They had no idea. They were searching for them everywhere, different courts, hospitals. Then my aunt received a call saying: ‘We have your girls, come to see them at the prison.’”

Seeing her daughters was heartbreaking for his aunt, Nourmohammadi said. “She did not recognise her own children: they were beaten up, badly swollen faces, bruises all over their body, broken elbows, knuckles, feet, and they basically had no hair because they would pull their hair and drag them from one cell to another cell. She found out that they had been in solitary confinement.”

Marzieh Nourmohammadi, who raised her daughters, now 20, on her own, was not allowed to attend their trial. Their lawyers said Taraneh told the court that any admissions had been secured through torture. No evidence of the sisters’ involvement in violence was provided, it is claimed. They had never been involved in protests before.
“My mum lives with me,” he said. “There’s not a single second that I pass her and she’s not crying.”

articles.title: Nepal’s flood-displaced mothers struggle for privacy and care
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Pariyar, who likes to be identified by only her last name, is a breastfeeding mother who is three months into caring for a newborn who does not stop crying. On the morning of August…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Pariyar, who likes to be identified by only her last name, is a breastfeeding mother who is three months into caring for a newborn who does not stop crying.

On the morning of August 26, Pariyar fled her home in Trishuli when the floods came and is now staying with dozens of strangers under one roof, where men smoke cigarettes near where she nurses her baby and where sleep, food and privacy all arrive on somebody else’s schedule.

“We are all in the same place, so it is difficult,” she says. “There is cigarette smoke, the smell of alcohol, and the baby cannot sleep.” Pariyar says her breast milk supply has decreased since the floods, leading her to try formula. However, it seems to upset the baby’s stomach, causing her to cry even more after feeding.
“If there was a safe place, and the baby could get her vaccinations here, that would be better,” Pariyar says. “We are not getting food on time either. We are not getting enough to eat.”

Pariyar’s account is part of a much larger and unfinished crisis unfolding in the flood-hit districts along the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli corridor northwest of Kathmandu. With roads and bridges damaged by landslides, pregnant women and new mothers are among those struggling hardest to get what they specifically need—a female-friendly space to breastfeed, food timed to nursing schedule, and a way to reach emergency care if labour turns dangerous.

The United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), estimates that around 4,430 pregnant women are living in the areas across the 15 municipalities in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, the districts hardest hit by last week’s devastating floods.

The figure is a humanitarian planning estimate based on an affected population of about 310,000 people, rather than a headcount of individually identified pregnant women. Based on the estimate, around 492 births could be expected in the following month, with roughly 74 women potentially requiring emergency obstetric care.

Aid workers say the problem is not only the scale of it. It is that these women are being folded into a relief system built around a single, generic idea of what a displaced person needs which rarely is for a breastfeeding or postpartum mother, their privacy, or an infant’s need for anything softer than the staple dal bhat.

Pariyar’s experience is not unique. In another shelter along the same corridor, Sharmila Shrestha, 33, sleeps on a classroom floor with two children: her own 14-month-old daughter, carried back to her over a six-hour walk through the hills after the flood separated them for two or three days, and her sister-in-law’s 18-month-old son. Both the infants eat what the adults eat, because nobody has brought food that suits them.

“They aren’t giving any special food for babies,” Shrestha told the Post over phone. “We are forced to feed that same heavy adult food to the small child.” What would help most, Shrestha says, is simple: “If only we had a decent, proper place to stay. That would bring some peace of mind.”
The concern is not only how many women are pregnant, but whether they can access care when they need it.

At Trishuli Hospital, the district-level hospital serving the area, the maternity ward has become an improvised outpost of crisis medicine. Basanti Pancha, who runs the department, says the hospital has performed nine deliveries since the floods but was struggling to keep pace with everything else. Women have kept arriving for fever, reduced fetal movement and urinary tract infections in pregnancy.
“Because of the floods, our service delivery has become very difficult,” Pancha says.

Electricity is unreliable enough that staff run a generator for surgeries and now sterilise instruments in small batches by hand. Four maternity patients have been referred out in recent days—two by military helicopter, two by ambulance, including a woman with a severe wound infection after delivery.

“Previously, Kathmandu was just a two-hour road trip away,” Pancha says. “Now, by road, nobody knows how many hours it will take because of the landslides.” What used to be routine, she adds, has become “a lot of stress” for staff who have no advanced neonatal unit to fall back on if a case turns critical.
“Pregnancy itself brings a lot of natural anxiety, stress and doubt about what will happen,” Pancha says. “But the floods have added a layer of extra stress on these women.”

blocks.caption: Sexual violence and trafficking have become quiet, urgent risks, worsened by the number of families now scattering toward Kathmandu in search of help that never arrived locally. Post Photo

blocks.text: Rekha Shrestha, executive director of women’s rights organisation WOREC, says her team members are finding the same pattern across every holding centre they visit: women, men, children, the sick and healthy all are sharing one undivided space. The holding centre at Chandrawati Secondary School, for instance, houses more than 1,000 people, including over 500 women, among them pregnant women and new mothers.

“Everyone is in the same place,” Rekha says. Her organisation has begun setting up female friendly spaces in affected areas, where women and adolescents can talk privately and raise concerns they would not otherwise voice in a crowded hall.
Relief distribution, she says, has often assumed everyone in a shelter needs the same things.

Menstruating adolescents are not given sufficient sanitary pads. In one distribution, she says, women were handed a single pad and told it should last three or four days. Sexual violence and trafficking have become quiet, urgent risks, worsened by the number of families now scattering toward Kathmandu in search of help that never arrived locally.

“Pregnant women and postpartum mothers have special needs,” she says. “There is no private space to bathe, to dry clothes, to breastfeed. That privacy is not an extra service in a disaster response,” she adds. “It’s a necessity.”

Rekha says her organisation is pressing officials to separate vulnerable groups within shelters, disaggregate population data by gender and age, and ensure nutrition and medicine reach women who are otherwise kept into a single, undifferentiated relief effort. “It is extremely necessary to look at the diversity within the group,” she says.

UNFPA, too, describes its 4,430 figure as only an initial estimate, one it is refining with the Ministry of Health and Population and the Health Cluster. The number is modelled, not counted door to door, derived from a pre-flood population of roughly 310,000 across the affected municipalities. “We’ve used a standard demographic ratio for how many women in a given population are likely to be pregnant at any time,” says Sriram Haridass, UNFPA’s representative in Nepal. Teams are now working to identify and reach those women individually, a process he says will take weeks. For now, the priority is keeping maternity services running while the referral system is rebuilt.

“Babies do not wait for roads to reopen,” Haridass says. UNFPA is supporting mobile health teams offering antenatal and postnatal care and psychosocial support, and has dispatched 2,000 dignity kits, 800 Kishori kits and 300 shelter tarpaulins, with 32 reproductive health kits ready for deployment. But locating a woman, Haridass says, is only half the task. “She must know where to seek care and have a functioning referral pathway if she needs urgent assistance,” he says.

That gap, between being counted and being cared for, is what women like Pariyar and Sharmila Shrestha are still living inside. Neither of the nursing mothers is asking for much: a place that treats them as something other than one more body in a crowded hall. “This is very difficult for us,” Pariyar says. “We need a separate space.” /dl

articles.title: Floods revive questions over an abandoned Nepal mountain airstrip
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — When devastating floods tore through the river basins lying at Rasuwa and Nuwakot last week, reaching the affected areas by air became a challenge of its own. The landscape had been…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — When devastating floods tore through the river basins lying at Rasuwa and Nuwakot last week, reaching the affected areas by air became a challenge of its own.

The landscape had been altered by landslides and flooding, while there was no air traffic control tower to coordinate the dozens of military and civilian helicopters involved in the rescue effort. During the emergency, helicopters had to operate under military supervision from an open area at the Nepal Army’s training center in Trishuli.
The disruption has revived memories among veteran aviation officials and pilots of an airstrip that has been largely forgotten by a younger generation: Langtang airport.

For those who came of age after Nepal’s political transition in 1990, the airport is little more than a name in official records. But for older aviation professionals, its short, rough runway in the mountains of Rasuwa represents something that could have been valuable during the latest disaster.
The crisis has revived debate over whether an operational Langtang airport could have eased the pressure on helicopter rescue operations.

Five helicopter trips carrying people or relief supplies could potentially have been replaced by a single small aircraft flight, while an operational airport with communications and air traffic management infrastructure could also have helped organize helicopter movements more efficiently.

“If the Langtang airport had been operational, it could have provided significant support for relief and rescue operations,” said Gyanendra Bhul, an information officer for the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal and an air traffic controller.

The scale of the aviation operation during the disaster illustrates the potential value of such an alternative. Military and civilian flight records show nearly 1,000 take-offs and landings in Trishuli and surrounding areas over the course of a week.

With an airstrip capable of handling small, 19-seat aircraft and equipped with communications facilities, authorities might have reduced some of their dependence on helicopters to search for hundreds of missing people, transport relief supplies and carry out charter flights.
It could also have created room for more helicopter operations by taking some of the transport burden off them.

That makes the story of Langtang more than the history of a closed airport. It raises a broader question about how governments assess infrastructure in a country repeatedly exposed to earthquakes, floods and landslides.
Lalit Bikram Shah, a former director general of the aviation department, said the value of an airport should not be judged only by the revenue it generates during normal operations.
The lives it can help save during a disaster also have to be considered, he said, even though such a value cannot be measured in cash.
Several decades ago, single-engine Pilatus Porters operated from the airstrip, carrying tourists, project supplies and charter passengers into a part of Rasuwa that had no road access.
At the time, the airport itself was major infrastructure.

Today, Langtang remains listed in the official records of the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal, including with an International Civil Aviation Organization airport code, merely as “airport not in operation”.
The airport sits at an elevation of 3,658 meters, or about 12,000 feet, above sea level. Its runway is 420 meters long and 30 meters wide and has an unpaved surface.
There is no fuel facility, rescue service or fire-fighting service, according to the authority’s current airport records.
On paper, the airport still exists. In an emergency, however, it cannot be used as an operational air link.
That distinction has become particularly stark after the latest floods.
Langtang’s aviation history began not with large aircraft but with the small, single-engine Pilatus Porter, a rugged aircraft capable of operating from short mountain runways.
Shah, 81, who became the first Nepali to serve as a regional director of the International Civil Aviation Organization, remembers the airport before it fell into disuse.
Regular scheduled passenger services were not necessarily its most important function. Charter flights, development projects and flights operated for various organizations were central to its role.
“Passenger charter flights were also operated,” Shah told Kantipur on Friday, recalling the period before 1990.
Foreign development projects used the airstrip to transport equipment and supplies. Essential goods, including food, could also be flown into the remote mountain region.

Shah remembers four Pilatus Porters operated by then Royal Nepal Airlines, as well as aircraft operated by the United Nations Development Program and the US government, conducting specialized operations from Langtang.
The aircraft were suited to the short runway and difficult terrain.
Former Nepal Airlines pilot Kundan Giri remembers a similarly active airstrip, with flights carrying tourists as well as local charter passengers, project supplies and relief material.
“If the airport had remained operational, this disaster would have been easier to manage,” said Giri, a senior captain. “An airport from which aircraft can operate is a lifeline.”
Giri said the runway could be approached from either direction and that there had been potential to extend it if necessary.
A larger aircraft was once considered
There had even been attempts to determine whether Langtang could accommodate a larger aircraft.
Veteran pilot Phizo Nath Nepali said studies were carried out in the late 1980s on the possibility of operating Twin Otters from Langtang and other mountain airstrips, including Syangboche.
Nepali himself landed a Pilatus at Langtang as part of efforts related to the proposal.
The transition to Twin Otter operations never materialized. After the political changes of 1990, Nepal Airlines did not have enough aircraft to start the service, Nepali said.

According to his recollection, the airport had begun operating in the 1970s, initially with foreign pilots flying the Pilatus Porter. As those pilots left Nepal, the pool of Nepali pilots willing to fly single-engine aircraft became smaller.
“The end of the Pilatus Porter in Nepal was not simply a runway issue,” Nepali said. “The generation of aircraft and pilots was also changing.”
Nepali said other pilots, including Bishal Dewan and Manoj “Juju” Shrestha, later flew Pilatus aircraft from Langtang and other short mountain airstrips.
A study around 1988 examined whether relatively modest improvements could allow Twin Otters to operate from Langtang.
According to Nepali, the conclusion was that the runway could accommodate the aircraft with some extension and improvements.
“If the runway had been extended a little, a Twin Otter could have operated there quite comfortably,” he recalled.

Local residents supported the idea, unlike in Syangboche, where some tourism operators opposed it. They feared that allowing tourists to fly directly into Syangboche would reduce the two-day trek and hurt local hotels and other businesses.
Langtang did not face the same resistance, Nepali said. /dl

articles.title: DBM to auto-release funds for gov’t salary deficiencies by Q4
articles.summary: MANILA – Government employees who are promoted or whose positions are reclassified may soon receive salary adjustments faster as the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) moves to automatically…

blocks.text: MANILA – Government employees who are promoted or whose positions are reclassified may soon receive salary adjustments faster as the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) moves to automatically release funds for personnel services (PS) deficiencies without requiring agencies to submit separate requests.

Acting Budget Secretary Kim Robert De Leon said the DBM is drafting a policy that would allow the department to identify salary funding gaps through updated agency plantilla records and release the necessary funds even without a formal request.
The policy is targeted for signing by the end of September, with live testing across government agencies scheduled in the fourth quarter of 2026.

Under the current system, agencies must inform the DBM of personnel who have been promoted or whose positions have been reclassified, including their new salary levels, before the department can determine and release additional funding.
“Hindi na kailangan pang i-request (There is no longer a need to request it),” De Leon said in a radio interview Saturday.

“Kailangan lang i-update ng ahensya yung master list na tinatawag namin ng kanilang plantilla, at ‘pag nakita namin na may kulang, kahit walang request, kailangan i-download namin sa kanila yung kakulangan nung pambayad ng pondo (The agency only needs to update its plantilla master list, and once we see that there is a deficiency, even without a request, we need to release the funds needed to pay for it),” he added.

De Leon said the reform will initially be tested in the fourth quarter, when agencies typically submit requests for PS deficiencies or additional funding to cover salaries and other personnel requirements.
The proposed mechanism could particularly benefit public school personnel whose positions are upgraded under the Department of Education’s (DepEd) Expanded Career Progression (ECP) System.
The DBM recently approved the release of PHP8.68 billion to cover salary differentials for 93,344 reclassified public school positions for fiscal years 2025 and 2026.
Under the proposed 2027 National Budget, PHP12.09 billion is also earmarked for the continued implementation of the ECP System.

The proposed DepEd budget for 2027 is PHP975.963 billion, including funding for salaries, the PHP10,000 annual teaching allowance, career progression, training, medical allowance, and other personnel benefits.
De Leon said the proposed automatic mechanism would apply not only to DepEd but also to other national government agencies with PS funding deficiencies.
The DBM will use the fourth-quarter test to assess the mechanism’s effectiveness before considering its broader institutionalization.

articles.title: Haze emergency grips Malaysian Borneo town
articles.summary: SERIAN, Malaysia — Acrid smoke hung heavily over the Malaysian town of Serian, seeping into homes and cloaking roadside stalls, as residents navigated an air‑quality emergency fueled by…

blocks.text: SERIAN, Malaysia — Acrid smoke hung heavily over the Malaysian town of Serian, seeping into homes and cloaking roadside stalls, as residents navigated an air‑quality emergency fueled by transboundary haze from Indonesia’s raging fires.
Malaysia declared a state of emergency in Sarawak state’s Serian district on Borneo island on Friday, after air pollution readings reached critical levels.

Toxic haze has shrouded parts of Indonesia and Malaysia for weeks as Jakarta struggles to contain fires that have scorched large tracts of Borneo and Sumatra, with the plumes drifting into neighboring Malaysia, Singapore and Brunei.

In Serian, about 65 kilometers (40 miles) southeast of Sarawak’s capital Kuching, residents tried to carry on with weekend routines but said the thick haze forced them to plan shorter trips to avoid the worst of the smoke.
“I rarely leave the house when it’s like this (the haze). I only come out to buy food and groceries, then I’ll immediately head home,” said Ajen Anak Kunok, 64, a local retired technician.
Ajen told AFP he had spent the past week battling shortness of breath and a sore throat due to the ongoing haze, before going to the hospital Saturday for treatment.
But the smoke was difficult to escape even at home, a mere 10 kilometers (six miles) from Indonesia’s Kalimantan province where the fires were raging.
“Even when I turn on the air conditioner, I can still smell the smoke in my house,” Ajen said.
Hazardous levels
Sarawak, which shares a border with Kalimantan, has borne the brunt of pollution in Malaysia.
On Friday, Serian became the first district in the country this year to declare an emergency over the worsening air quality when API levels passed 500 and peaked at 512.
Under Malaysian guidelines, API levels above 300 are classified as hazardous, while readings beyond 500 usually trigger consideration of a local emergency.
At the town’s markets, the usual bustling throng dwindled, while roadside sellers of Serian’s famous durians waited in vain beside their piles of fruit for customers that came in diminished numbers.
The district’s scenic Ranchan Waterfall — usually popular with locals and tourists alike — was unusually quiet, with just a few visitors dotted around.
Roadside durian seller Siaw Thien Ha, 53, said the emergency has already hit his livelihood hard.
He struggled to earn even half of his usual income of 400 ringgit ($98) for the weekend.
“I’m worried that my income will be affected… But during the durian season, there is money to be made,” he told AFP.
“So I don’t have a choice but to bring the durians here to sell to support my family,” he said.
Friday’s emergency declaration will also keep some 647 schools closed until at least the end of the week in Serian district, which has a population of around 154,000 people.
Sister Irmina Peter, 64, who teaches at the St Joseph’s Private Primary School in Kuching, told AFP she was worried that the emergency could drag on and spill over to other districts in Sarawak.
Rain in Serian on Friday night and Saturday morning, believed to have been the result of ongoing cloud seeding operations, brought some respite, with API levels dropping to 219.
Serian’s state of emergency however remained in place.
Sister Peter said “we don’t want the schools to be like during Covid-19 lockdown, where we couldn’t do much.”
“We can’t go on with our normal routine… we have to go to work, children have to go to school. It affects us very much.” /dl

articles.title: [Tech Thoughts] The tightrope walk between online safety and draconian laws
articles.summary: Balancing public safety interests with overreaching laws needs to be intensely scrutinized by the public, unless they want to lose out in all the ways that matter

blocks.text: The Philippines’ Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT), under its secretary, Henry Aguda, wants Meta Platforms to integrate the country’s national ID into the account verification process for its social media platforms, namely Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and WhatsApp.

Details on the request aren’t all there quite yet, but the current reasoning suggests users will be asked to provide specific data from their national ID to confirm that they are of age to use Meta’s suite of social media platforms and prove they’re the person actually using it.
Either that, or it may perhaps ask users to provide another form of identifying data, like their passport or driver’s license, to get through the verification process.

From a logistical standpoint, it may feel like a no-brainer to get people on board with such a move in the interests of public safety, but I do feel the DICT and the Philippine government need to be clear with what they plan to do before they go and push a plan through for consideration.
Balancing public safety interests with overreaching, potentially draconian laws needs to be intensely scrutinized by the public, unless they want to lose out in all the ways that matter.

Specifically, I’m curious about what Meta will want to ask from a user to verify their age. Current age estimation hinges on facial recognition, but that can be circumvented by stubborn teens with uninterested parents giving away their selfies.

Asking users to provide an ID makes the process of circumvention harder, but then we also deal with data privacy and data security concerns. Instead of just dealing with the government as a point of failure, you’re now also dealing with a corporation handling portions of a country’s data.

All Meta might need is the name and birthdate on your national ID, and nothing else, but that’d also depend on the arrangement between the Philippine government and whatever Philippine arm of Meta they’re planning to bring in.

According to a TechWatch PH report, TraXion Tech founder and CEO Ann Cuisia suggested using a “Yes” or “No” approach to the verification — where a yes means you’re old enough, no extra information needed — but we would still need to integrate with Meta and have the systems in place to tell them that Person A should get access to social media and not Person B.
One consideration that needs to be taken into account is the fact that the rollout of the national ID system hasn’t gotten to everyone yet.

According to Worldometer, there are nearly 118 million Filipinos now, and PhilSys said in a December 2025 release that it has gotten to about 90 million Filipinos so far into the project as of October 2025.

That’s about 28 million Filipinos who might not get access to a common form of socialization online, assuming they even have a smartphone or are knowledgeable enough about technology to want to use social media to begin with.

Whether not having social media access is good or bad might be beside the point, though. What’s important to note here is that under this potential plan, not every eligible Filipino who wants access to social media will be able to get to use it if they’re completely without any form of identification — a problem that’s noticeable seeing as we have a physical national ID card backlog.

I would prefer my personal details to be kept with me, so I’m inclined to want some kind of measured approach where everyone can have a stake in the process of instituting it. It might take longer to implement, but there’s less chance of it being haphazard if everyone has eyes on it.I wonder if it’d be possible for the Philippine Statistics Authority to align with social media companies to develop a system that determines who’s old enough to get access to Facebook, Instagram, X, and the like, without them giving the data out.
Moreover, I would want the system to not be opaque so cybersecurity experts and the Filipino public can scrutinize the plans and implementation accordingly.
The DICT unilaterally saying, “Hey, this is OKAY!” does not sit right with me. As always, checks and balances are needed.
If the Philippines is to walk a tightrope between online safety and draconian overreach, everyone should be watching to make sure we don’t fall into the deep end.

articles.title: Hungary begins hunt for corrupt regime's billions
articles.summary: Hungary's new prime minister promised he would recover billions stolen or diverted by the previous administration. A new "super authority" is about to begin that work. Its success or failure will…

image.caption: In his election campaign, Peter Magyar promised to recover government funds that were stolen or diverted by the Orban administrationImage: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP

blocks.text: Asset recovery — it sounds bureaucratic but behind this phrase is one of the most important campaign promises made by Hungary's new government.

Hungary's new prime minister, Peter Magyar, and his Tisza party want to retrieve funds and assets that went — in some dubious ways — to the family of ousted Hungarian leader Viktor Orban or his allies, various oligarchs, or frontmen. The new government wants those funds back for state use, and it also plans to hold the beneficiaries accountable under law.

Billions of euros were stolen or diverted and, if social media is to be believed, many Hungarians want to see the individuals responsible behind bars. Magyar has talked of a sum of around €60 billion ($70 billion), though other estimates suggest the real amount could be three times that much.
Orban, allies lived lives of luxury
Observers say the success or failure of the asset recovery will almost certainly influence the future of Magyar and the Tisza party.

The huge sums of money are linked to images of decadent luxury under Orban. The former Hungarian prime minister's family, party members, and friendly oligarchs lived on luxury estates, flew in luxury jets, vacationed on luxury yachts, and repeatedly won billions worth of public contracts.

Orban-affiliated entrepreneurs, artists, academics, and journalists were also generously supported with public funds for years. Often their main qualification was loyalty to the former prime minister.

blocks.caption: Former Prime Minister Viktor Orban has alleged that his successor has 'dismantled the rule of law' since coming to powerImage: Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Those lifestyles contrasted with the lives led by Hungarians in poverty, the image of neglected public infrastructure, poor conditions in schools and hospitals, and the exodus of many young Hungarians from the country, as well as a huge deficit in the state budget, some 7.5% of Hungary's national income. These contrasts explain why there is such a popular desire for justice.
It's been almost four months since the new Magyar government took office and anti-corruption actions have officially started.
At the end of July, the new government established the National Asset Recovery Authority, or NVVH — a sort of "super institution" with very broad powers and independence.

Hungary hasn't had an authority like this in its modern history. The way state assets were privatized in the 1990s after communist rule was problematic, as it often was elsewhere in the former Soviet bloc. When Orban first came to power in 2010, there was a half-hearted attempt to address the corruption of the previous government under Ferenc Gyurcsany, but it came to nothing.
Hungary new PM lifts lid on Orban-era government luxury
This time, things are meant to be different.

The NVVH will investigate where public funds flowed and how assets like real estate were used. Although no specific date has been set, the investigations will primarily focus on the Orban government's time in power, so dating back to 2010. The authority is also meant to make sure this cannot happen again, and will look into how public funds and assets are to be used in future.
The NVVH has both policing and prosecutorial powers, so it can investigate cases and bring charges. The authority is accountable to Hungary's parliament.
Controversy around new anti-corruption body
But the creation of the NVVH has not been without controversy.

Late last week, parliament appointed Anna Unger, 46, a political scientist at Eotvos Lorand University in Budapest, to head the new anti-corruption and asset recovery body. Unger is an expert on political systems, democratic institutions, and party financing and was chosen out of almost 100 other applicants in a process with several stages.

Some were surprised at Unger's appointment, as she wasn't really a public figure. Her research has included political corruption but she's not a recognized expert on the topic, nor is she a lawyer. Observers had expected a lawyer or an anti-corruption expert to get the job, somebody like Miklos Ligeti, head of legal affairs at Transparency International Hungary since 2012.

blocks.caption: Anna Unger was named head of the new accountability organization in late AugustImage: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP

blocks.text: Ligeti also applied for the job but is reportedly being considered for a position as a deputy director. Unger will have four deputies with different duties and responsibilities. Katalin Tasnady, a well-known prosecutor with around two decades of criminal law experience, was made the NVVH's deputy chief of investigations.

Government representatives said Unger had presented a comprehensive political vision for the agency's work. During her parliamentary hearing, she said that under Orban, Hungary saw more than just what one might call classic corruption. An almost feudal system had prevailed, she argued. That was why in addition to restitution and asset recovery, the system had to be thoroughly investigated and exposed so that it would never happen again, Unger said.
No justice in next 6 years?
Unger caused the biggest upset when she said it would be folly to expect legally binding verdicts in any major corruption cases during the NVVH's first six-year term.

Robert Puzser, a popular commentator and personality on social media, called Unger's statement "devastating." Voters had given Magyar "unprecedented power to hold the country's plunderers to account," he said on Facebook, and if Hungarians had to wait more than six years, it could cause the collapse of this new government.
The new prime minister himself reacted angrily to critics who said the NVVH should have had a lawyer at its head.

"Nobody promised people they could vote for the leader of the NVVH as if it was a [reality TV] casting show," he wrote on Facebook. Plenty of experts thought Unger was absolutely suitable for the job.

In a podcast on the 24.hu media outlet, political science Gabor Torok surmised that the way that the NVVH had been established indicated that it would be a "strong political institution" that aimed to come to terms with the recent past.

Torok said the public expects the Tisza party to thoroughly reckon with the old system, and the new government will only be able to maintain the public's trust if it doesn't look like the "culprits of the previous order" are getting away with their past crimes, he said.
This article was originally written in German.
New Hungarian Prime Minister Magyar takes on Orban's legacy

articles.title: Brisbane expected to swelter under hottest September day in years as east coast faces unseasonably warm weather
articles.summary:
Queensland capital forecast to hit 34C with local fire bans issued for Ipswich and Lockyer Valley, while Sydney sees reprieve from record heat

  • Get our

blocks.text: Early spring fire bans have been put in place as Australia’s eastern states reckon with unseasonably hot conditions for the start of the season.
The Bureau of Meteorology (BoM) warned of unseasonal heat in the low to mid-30s in north-eastern New South Wales and south-east Queensland.
Brisbane had a forecast top of 34C, while Sydney had some respite from the recent record temperatures, with a forecast top of 23C, as that heat moved north.

If Brisbane reaches its predicted temperature peak, it would be the hottest September day in the city since 2019. Brisbane recorded a temperature of 31.6C in the late morning, the weather bureau said, while the Ipswich suburb of Amberley recorded a peak of 35.7C in the early afternoon.
“It’s a bit of an ‘all eyes on the temperatures this afternoon’ type [of] thing until that south-easterly change gets in, which is probably about 6 or 7pm tonight,” the BoM’s Steve Hadley said.
The Queensland fire department issued local fire bans for Ipswich and the Lockyer Valley as the state came close to shattering records for the highest temperatures seen in early September.
Areas from Gladstone to the Gold Coast were likely to come a few degrees shy of breaking the record for the state’s highest recorded temperatures for the start of spring.
The state had experienced its third-warmest winter on record with temperatures 1.8C above the long-term average.
BoM meteorologist Jonathan How said over the past 24 hours, a cold front swept across south-eastern Australia, bringing damaging winds, rain and storms.
“At the same time, parts of eastern NSW saw their warmest early spring day on record,” he said.
But a dry cool change was moving up the east coast, bringing milder temperatures from Monday. Western Australia is set to get more rain this week, while Tasmania and Victoria can expect some showers.
South-east Queensland’s fire bans came a day after a similar ban was issued for the greater Sydney region, with early spring temperatures climbing to 33C on Saturday in the NSW capital.
after newsletter promotion
Maximum temperatures across the city during the first days of September matched the midsummer average of 26.4C, warmer than any other start to spring since observations began.
Severe weather warnings were in place for south-eastern Australia over the weekend as damaging winds fuelled the hot conditions.
Jumping castles were picked up by strong winds in two separate incidents in NSW and Victoria on Saturday.
Two children were treated for head injuries at a scene in Banksia, in Sydney’s south, before being transported to hospital.
An infant with minor injuries was also hospitalised, while a woman was treated at the scene.
Two children in Mount Duneed, near Geelong in Victoria’s south-west, were hospitalised after the jumping castle they were using was lifted into the air.
Temperatures are expected to drop in the coming days across both NSW and Queensland.

articles.title: SolGen asks Pasig court to resolve motions on wage hike freeze order
articles.summary: The Office of the Solicitor General asked a Pasig City court to immediately resolve its pending motion for reconsideration seeking to lift the freeze order on Metro Manila's P85 daily minimum wage…

blocks.text: September 6, 2026 | 1:48pm
This undated photo shows an individual counting Philippine peso bills.
The Philippine STAR / Walter Bollozos

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) asked a Pasig City court to immediately resolve its pending motion for reconsideration seeking to lift the freeze order on Metro Manila's P85 daily minimum wage increase.

In a motion to resolve the OSG's motion filed on September 3, state lawyers urged Pasig City Regional Trial Court Branch 152 to rule on the government's “Urgent Motion for Reconsideration Ad Cautelam” filed on August 17, seeking to dismiss the cases filed by construction firms and set aside the court's August 13 order that issued a writ of preliminary injunction against the wage hike order.
According to the OSG, the motions filed by the government are now “ripe for resolution.”

“Moreover, the issues raised in the Motion concern the continued implementation of Wage Order No. NCR-27 and directly affect minimum wage earners, employers, and other stakeholders throughout the National Capital Region, which issues plainly pertain to the unreleased daily increase in workers' wages that this Honorable Court enjoined,” the OSG said.
“Its early resolution would therefore serve the interests of justice, fairness, and public welfare by removing uncertainty on a matter imbued with significant public interest,” it added.

The government's primary legal defense counsel stressed that a prompt ruling is necessary because the OSG's motion raises a threshold objection regarding the RTC's jurisdiction over wage board decisions.

"Questions of jurisdiction are not deferred to the end of a case; they are resolved at the earliest opportunity, precisely so that neither the parties nor the Honorable Court expend further time and resources on proceedings that may ultimately be void," the motion read.
The controversy stems from a Department of Labor and Employment wage order that granted a two-tranche P85 daily minimum wage increase for over 1.1 million workers in the National Capital Region.
The first tranche—a P60 increase—was slated to take effect on July 25, followed by the remaining P25 in January 2027.

However, petitioners, construction firms Readycon and R-II Builders, filed a petition for declaratory relief, alleging that the wage board failed to properly consider employer capacity to pay under the Labor Code amid rising fuel and operational costs.
Branch 152 granted a temporary restraining order on July 30, followed by a writ of preliminary injunction on August 13 after requiring the petitioners to post a P10-billion bond.

The government and various labor groups have challenged the injunction, citing Article 126 of the Labor Code, which explicitly prohibits courts from issuing injunctions or restraining orders against wage board proceedings.
Lawyer Sonny Matula, president of the Federation of Free Workers (FFW), backed the OSG’s motion, urging the court to immediately address jurisdiction before taking any further steps.
He argued that if the court lacks authority, there is no reason to stall the proceedings while workers suffer financially on the sidelines.

“We are one with the OSG on this. Jurisdiction is not an issue you save for dessert—it belongs at the beginning of the meal. If the court has no jurisdiction, there is no reason to keep dribbling the ball while workers wait with empty pockets on the sidelines. Resolve it now,” Matula said.

Matula stressed that both the government and labor are aligned in their appeal, adding that alongside the OSG's stance and labor's pleas, the immediate financial strain on workers every payday should serve as a clear signal for the court to resolve the matter.

“The OSG has spoken. Labor has spoken—even if labor is still waiting to be allowed inside. Most importantly, workers’ empty pockets speak every payday. We respectfully hope the Court hears all three,” Matula said.

articles.title: Kremlin says Ukraine talks with US envoys were useful; no sign of breakthrough
articles.summary: President Vladimir Putin tells US envoys that Russia was making 'real progress' on the battlefield and was confident of achieving its goals

blocks.text: TALK. Russian President Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, as US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff stands nearby during a meeting at the Kremlin in Moscow, Russia, September 5, 2026.
Sputnik/Mikhail Metzel/Pool via Reuters
President Vladimir Putin tells US envoys that Russia was making 'real progress' on the battlefield and was confident of achieving its goals

items: Russian President Vladimir Putin engaged in over three hours of talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, discussing potential avenues for a settlement to the Ukraine war, but no breakthroughs were reported.
Putin expressed confidence in Russia's military progress and emphasized the need to address the root causes of the conflict, while the US officials described the talks as substantive and beneficial.
Despite discussions, significant differences remain between Russia and Ukraine regarding territorial claims and the terms for ending the war, with both sides preparing for continued military actions.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MOSCOW, Russia – Russian President Vladimir Putin held more than three hours of “highly useful” talks on Saturday, September 5, with two US envoys seeking a deal to end the Ukraine war, a Kremlin aide said, but he gave no indication of any breakthrough.
The aide, Yuri Ushakov, said Americans Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner “outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement.” Ushakov did not say what these ideas were.

He said Putin had told the pair that Russia was making “real progress” on the battlefield and was confident of achieving its goals, while stressing the necessity of addressing “all the root causes of the conflict.”

These are statements that Moscow has made repeatedly since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Russia’s smaller neighbor in February 2022. Both sides have intensified long-range air strikes in recent weeks while the front lines remain largely static.
A White House official told Reuters the talks had been “substantive” and that next steps would be announced in the coming weeks.

There was no comment from Witkoff and Kushner, who were visiting Moscow for the first time since January on behalf of President Donald Trump. They flew out of Moscow soon after the talks and are due to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in Kyiv on Sunday, September 6.

“The talks went beyond a mere exchange of views on resolving the Ukrainian crisis. Economic issues and potential major, mutually beneficial Russian-American projects were discussed in some detail,” Ushakov said. “Overall, one can say that the negotiations were timely and highly useful for both sides.”
Putin’s investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, posted on X that the meeting had been an “important peacemaking visit.” He and Ushakov were both present at the meeting.
The Russian president praised Trump’s efforts to end the war.

“Understanding that he is entering a difficult situation, he nevertheless does not stop his efforts to help bring about a settlement and to make his contribution to resolving the Russian-Ukrainian conflict,” Putin said in televised remarks at the start of the talks.
Trump suggested on Friday, September 4, that the US had a fresh proposal aimed at ending the war but did not elaborate.

Putin promised to ensure the safety of the US negotiators. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said earlier that Putin had ordered the Russian military not to strike Kyiv for three days because of their trip.
Over the previous 10 days, Russia pounded the Ukrainian capital day and night with missiles and drones, including an attack on Friday on the headquarters of the SBU security service.

Ukraine has inflicted damaging hits throughout the summer on Russian refineries, oil terminals and warehouses of online retailer Wildberries, in an attempt to raise the cost to Moscow of continuing the war. Zelenskiy said Kyiv was prepared to refrain from strikes on Moscow through Monday.
Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on how to end the war, the deadliest in Europe since World War Two.
A person close to the Kremlin, speaking before reports emerged of the trip by Trump’s envoys, said Putin was still intent on capturing more territory.

“There is no chance of reaching an agreement regarding the front line until Putin finishes securing the remaining part of the Donetsk region,” this person told Reuters, adding that the Kremlin leader was confident — based on reports from his commanders — that this would happen by the end of the year.

Western military analysts see such a possibility as remote, given Moscow’s slow rate of progress. Ukraine has refused to surrender land it has successfully defended at huge cost, and rejects such terms as tantamount to surrender.

The Kremlin said on Friday the position that Putin set out in a speech two years ago — that Ukraine should cede the entire territory of four regions claimed by Russia and abandon its plan to join NATO — was “unshakeable.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: PNP vows to address VP Sara Duterte’s trust, safety issues
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines—The Philippine National Police (PNP) assured Vice President Sara Duterte that it would address her security concerns, monitor threats, and rebuild trust, following her statement…

image.caption: PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. (left) and Vice President Sara Duterte (right) (Photos from Office of the Chief PNP/Facebook and INQUIRER FILE)

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines—The Philippine National Police (PNP) assured Vice President Sara Duterte that it would address her security concerns, monitor threats, and rebuild trust, following her statement that she no longer feels safe.
On Saturday, Duterte said she fears for her life after an arrest warrant was issued against her for three counts of grave threats.
Ahead of her arrival at the Quezon City Hall of Justice, Duterte said she does not trust the police, the courts, and even the security team assigned to guard her.
“Rebuilding trust is a continuous process of demonstrating our integrity through our actions,” said PNP chief Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. in a statement on Sunday.
“We assure the public and our leaders that the PNP stands ready to protect every Filipino fairly and professionally,” Nartatez added.
Concerned police units were instructed to continue monitoring and assessing threats against Duterte and her immediate family.
The PNP also urged the vice president or her representatives to submit any documents or reports related to the alleged threats for verification and proper assessment.
To date, the PNP has not identified any verified threat against Duterte or her family.
On Saturday, the PNP provided security during her appearance before the Quezon City Regional Trial Court and confirmed she arrived at and left the court safely.
While assessing Duterte’s safety concerns, the PNP stated it “enforces court orders lawfully, protects all citizens without political bias, and maintains professionalism in its operations.”
The PNP said their “operations are conducted with utmost professionalism, impartiality, and absolute respect for individual rights without fear or favor.”
A day after an arrest warrant was issued, Duterte posted P360,000 bail before a Quezon City court, securing her provisional liberty.
The warrant stemmed from allegations that she made grave threats against President Ferdinand R. Marcos, First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former Speaker Martin Romualdez. /gsg

articles.title: Volcano eruption triggers flight suspensions at Indonesia's main airport
articles.summary: More than 20,000 passengers are stranded after ash was detected in airspace near Jakarta following volcanic eruptions.

blocks.text: A volcanic eruption has halted hundreds of flights at Indonesia's main international airport, stranding tens of thousands of passengers.
Authorities said 209 flights were suspended after ash from Mount Anak Krakatoa was detected in airspace near Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport on Sunday morning.

The volcano had started erupting late on Friday night, generating continuous seismic activity, lava fountains, and booming sounds across surrounding regions. Two more eruptions happened early on Sunday, authorities said.
More than 22,000 people have been impacted by the suspension of flights, which has been extended until 13:30 (0630 GMT).
The transport ministry said the pause in operations mainly affected flights to and from Singapore, also other international routes including Doha, Sydney and Kuala Lumpur.
Authorities have confirmed there is no tsunami warning linked to the recent activity of the volcano, which is in the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra.
The health minister has urged residents in affected areas to stay indoors and wear face masks to protect against respiratory, eye, and skin risks.

Anak Krakatoa, which means Child of Krakatoa, has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa.
Indonesia sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where there is high volcanic and seismic activity.

articles.title: When the lost Mindoro bleeding-heart was finally photographed
articles.summary: The detection of the elusive Mindoro bleeding-heart twenty years later inspires hope and forebodes changing habitats

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The team set up nine camera traps in the forests of Mindoro last August. They determined the locations of the camera traps based on knowledge of the Mindoro bleeding-heart’s habitat, behavior, and as well as what the Iraya Mangyan knew about the endemic bird’s previous whereabouts.

“We combined historical data and then the biophysical and bioclimatic layers of Mindoro Island to create a [species distribution] model,” John Bibar, a researcher from the Center for Conservation Innovation (CCIPH) who was part of the field team, explained.
“When we got the result and zoomed in, the area was an ancestral domain in the northern part,” Bibar said.
Bibar and the rest of the team spent around two days scouring the forests of Mindoro to install the camera traps. They conducted transect walks and used bioacoustic devices.

On the last day of their week-long fieldwork, the team, composed of Manila-based conservationists and Iraya Mangyan patrollers, checked the recorded footage. They had moderate hopes. It was the first time they had deployed the camera traps.

Yet, there it was. In the footage from the last camera they checked. The Mindoro bleeding-heart, raising its right wing. A hello to the community of birders and conservationists it had inspired to wonder for 20 years.
“We said, ‘It looks like it’s saying hello to us,’” said Jennica Masigan, conservation program director of CCIPH. For Masigan, the search for the Mindoro bleeding-heart was personal.
Masigan is a wildlife biologist whose curiosity about the bird began when she started doing field research. She would often hear from others how elusive and rare the Mindoro bleeding-heart was.
“But it wasn’t until I started leading field expeditions that I developed a passion for looking for this bird,” said Masigan.

The last confirmed sighting of the bird was in 2005, inside the Siburan Forest Reserve in Occidental Mindoro. The ground-dwelling pigeon is critically endangered. Its name comes from the distinct red patch on its chest.

Sightings of rare species are a cause for celebration for a community that has built a cause around them. More so among birders, a community of enthusiasts who travel long distances for the chance, however uncertain, to glimpse a rare bird. Birdwatchers help monitor the status of birds by sharing sightings within the community and documenting the species they spot.

blocks.caption: CAPTURED. The endemic Mindoro bleeding-heart (right) photographed twenty years since its last documentation. It was detected upland which was unusual as it was more known to have resided in lower elevations. Photo courtesy of Center for Conservation Innovation
CAUGHT. Photos of the Mindoro bleeding-heart at the Sablayan Prison and Penal Farm in 2005, taken by Don Roberson. Courtesy of ebird

blocks.text: Conservationists have launched a global effort listing “lost” birds in a bid to find and document them.

The global initiative Search for Lost Birds defines a lost species as one “not confirmed alive by photographic, audio or genetic information for over 10 years in the wild and has no ex situ population under human care.”
Before CCIPH was able to record the Mindoro bleeding-heart last August, the bird was among those considered lost.

“Every year that passed without a trace of the Mindoro bleeding-heart pushed the conversation closer to that edge, whether continuing to search was still justified or whether it was time to let go,” the organization’s researchers wrote. “The bird, it turns out, was not ready to let go.”

blocks.caption: LOST. A screenshot from Search for Lost Birds, a platform that lists down lost birds across the world. Listed among them are the Mindoro bleeding-heart (Gallicolumba platenae) and the Sulu bleeding-heart (Gallicolumba menagei).

blocks.text: Researchers say the pigeon’s reemergence should be understood in the context of changing habitats. The bird was traditionally known as a lowland species. But this particular Mindoro bleeding-heart appeared in front of a camera trap installed 900 meters above sea level.
CCIPH takes note of the “warning.” Species don’t leave their habitats, researchers said, “unless something about that habitat has stopped working for them.”
In 2020, CCIPH created the Mindoro Forest and Biodiversity Conservation Program. The conservation work involves the Indigenous Iraya Mangyan, as much of it covers their ancestral domain.

“The Mindoro bleeding-heart, it’s part of a forest that also supports people,” said Masigan. She mentioned that a protected forest is “shared value” between conservationists and the indigenous people who live in these lands.
“When we protect that bleeding heart, we are also protecting the ecological system that supports human well-being.”

articles.title: Supreme Court: 11,900 out of 13,441 Bar aspirants took first-day exams
articles.summary: This number is out of the 13,441 applicants which was cleared by the High Court to take the examination for admission to the practice of law.

blocks.text: September 6, 2026 | 1:10pm
Examinees arrive at the gate of the University of Santo Tomas in Manila for the first day of the 2026 Bar Examinations on Sept. 6, 2026.
The STAR / Edd Gumban

MANILA, Philippines — There are 11,900 aspirants who have taken the 2026 Bar Examinations on the first day of the examinations, on Sunday, September 6, Supreme Court Associate Justice and 2026 Bar Exams Chairperson Samuel Gaerlan said.
This number is out of the 13,441 applicants which was cleared by the high court to take the examination for admission to the practice of law.
The number of takers was higher than last year’s first-day takers of 11,437 candidates.
“I think we have the highest number of applicants and examiners as compared to the previous years,” Gaerlan said.
“They are inspired to take the bar exam, and maybe they were thinking that I am reasonable and fair, so they did not postpone taking the Bar Exam,” he added.
On the first day, bar aspirants will take political and public international law in the morning and commercial and taxation laws in the afternoon.
For the second day of the Bar Exams on September 9, bar aspirants will take Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds and Labor Law and Social Legislation.
On the last day of the exams, September 13, examinees will take Criminal Law and Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics, with Practical Exercises.
No barriers
According to Gaerlan, there are Bar examinees who face predicaments and disabilities yet choose to push through the examinations.
Since the 2020/2021 Bar Examinations, popularly known as the “Best Bar Ever,” the Supreme Court has implemented digitized Bar Examinations through the Examplify software.
However, in this year's examination, according to Gaerlan, there are three individuals who were permitted to take the examination in written form due to their conditions.
One examinee, 64, has a chronic eye condition. Another examinee, 49, is undergoing therapy for a shoulder injury, and another examinee, 69, had limited exposure to computers.
Four examinees were also allowed the assistance of a coder.
“One lost sight through a rare form of meningitis. Another 75-year-old who struggles with computer literacy and a third one who lost both arms,” Gaerlan said.
There is also one person deprived of liberty who was allowed to take the Bar Examinations in one of the 15 local testing centers.
“Of course, with (the) implementation of our security protocols in coordination with the Office of the Judiciary Marshals,” Gaerlan said.
