articles.title: Drone attack blamed on guerrillas kills at least three soldiers in Colombia
articles.summary:
Officials accuse National Liberation Army of launching strike followed by clash inside military compound

An attack involving explosives dropped from drones followed by a clash inside a…

blocks.text: An attack involving explosives dropped from drones followed by a clash inside a military compound in north-eastern Colombia has killed at least three soldiers and wounded four, Colombia’s army said on Saturday.
Local authorities blamed the attack – which took place late on Friday – on the rebel National Liberation Army (ELN).

It targeted a military unit in the municipality of Ocaña, in the Norte de Santander department, which borders Venezuela. Two soldiers died at the site and a third after receiving medical attention, Colombia’s military said on X.

Colombia’s president, Abelardo de la Espriella, condemned the attack. “For every police officer or soldier murdered, we will bring the full weight and legitimate force of the state down upon the criminals,” he said.

Much of ELN, an armed group active since 1964, is based in the Catatumbo region, which includes parts of the Norte de Santander and Cesar departments. ELN also harbours dissident factions of the now defunct Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) that did not join the peace agreement a decade ago.
Both groups are vying for control of the strategic region, which connects to the porous border with Venezuela and is one of Colombia’s primary coca-producing areas.
In August, an explosion outside a police station in Cucuta injured 11 police officers and killed a police dog. Officials also blamed that attack on the ELN.
Earlier this week, at least one civilian was killed and 11 other people were injured after a car bomb exploded outside a police station in north-eastern Colombia.

articles.title: More voters identifying as Democrats and not calling themselves Republican
articles.summary:
Latest data from Gallup, showing 49% leaning Democrat and 39% Republican, marks sharp reversal from 2024

More voters are identifying as Democrats and shying away from calling themselves…

blocks.text: More voters are identifying as Democrats and shying away from calling themselves Republican, according to the latest quarterly data published by Gallup.
Some 49%of voters surveyed leaned Democrat, including independent voters asked to pick one party or the other. Only 39% of respondents leaned Republican.

That 10-point spread marks a sharp reversal from the four-point advantage that Republicans held over Democrats in the fourth quarter of 2024, when voters sent Donald Trump back to the White House and Republicans swept both houses of Congress. Democrats are seeing their most sizable advantage since 2008, when Barack Obama was elected president, according to the New York Times.
The data offers the latest evidence that Trump’s second term has proved unpopular with voters, driving a potential backlash.
Trump’s approval rating stood at 52% at the time of his second inauguration in January of 2025, according to an average of polls published by the New York Times.

But his popularity dwindled immediately, as he cleaved the federal workforce, imposed price-inflating tariffs, passed a profligate spending bill and launched a rudderless war with Iran. Some 58% of voters now disapprove of his performance, with only 38% approving, according to the Times.

Democrats are hoping to take advantage of Trump’s tanking popularity. Liberals are likely to retake the US House of Representatives in midterm elections this November. The party is much less certain to retake the US Senate, though polling is giving Democrats reasons to feel optimistic.

A growing share of American voters have not identified with either party in recent years. Back in 2002, roughly a third of voters surveyed by Gallup identified as either Republican, Democrat or independent. By last year, 45% of respondents called themselves independents, with only 27% identifying as either Democrat or Republican.

articles.title: Sara Duterte posts bail: ‘I don’t trust the court’
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte on Saturday posted a P360,000 bail before a Quezon City court, securing her provisional liberty a day after a warrant was issued for her arrest on…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte on Saturday posted a P360,000 bail before a Quezon City court, securing her provisional liberty a day after a warrant was issued for her arrest on charges that she issued grave threats against President Marcos, first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and former Speaker Martin Romualdez.

Duterte appeared before Branch 98 of the Quezon City Regional Trial Court (RTC) shortly before 11 a.m., accompanied by lawyers Michael Poa and Paul Lawrence Lim. Bail was set at P120,000 for each of the three counts of the charge.
But what was supposed to be a routine legal proceeding saw the accused—who was haled to court for what she said in a fit of rage—becoming the one expressing fears for her safety.
‘I do not feel safe’

The case stems from Duterte’s remarks during an online press conference on Nov. 23, 2024, when she said she had spoken to someone about killing Marcos, the first lady and Romualdez if she herself were killed.
Duterte has denied the allegations.
The same remarks form part of the impeachment case now pending before the Senate.
Before entering the Hall of Justice, Duterte repeatedly said she did not trust the police, the courts or even the security personnel assigned to protect her.
“I do not feel safe, I really do not feel safe. I don’t trust the court, I don’t trust the police,” she told reporters and her lawyers.
Duterte said she had felt unsafe since 2023 due to the harassment of her family by certain authorities, whom she did not name.
She asked: “Who will answer for it if I die later tonight? Who will be held accountable?”
Duterte initially refused to enter the building, laying out several scenarios she feared could put her life at risk.
She worried that she could be placed in a small elevator with police officers, leaving her vulnerable.

She also pointed to firearms carried by the officers posted at the building and said she could no longer trust even her own security detail because, in her view, they were picked for the job by the Marcos administration.
The Vice President remained hesitant even when assured by her lawyers that they would stay by her side.
Standing near the staircase at the Hall of Justice, she recalled the 1983 assassination of former Sen. Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino Jr.
“Do you remember that Ninoy Aquino died on the (airplane) staircase?” she asked her lawyers in Filipino.
Duterte then asked journalists to accompany her to the fifth floor, where she would post bail.
“I want a lot of people to see it. I really don’t know what will happen to me in there,” she said.
Her appeal effectively asked the media to serve as witnesses to whatever might happen to her inside the building.
The discussion between Duterte and her lawyers, held in front of reporters and police officers, went on for about 40 minutes before Poa finally persuaded her to go inside.
Duterte later said her lawyers advised her to post bail rather than be in police custody.

“They explained that I would be better protected by civilians who could see and notice my situation, compared to remaining in detention where I would be isolated and have less protection,” she said in a statement released by the Office of the Vice President.
Duterte also expressed concern for the safety of her mother and children.

Lim said Duterte’s lawyers were considering possible legal action over the implementation of the warrant, particularly after she alleged that authorities had gone to places where her mother and children were staying.
Duterte said government pressure and harassment against her family had continued since 2023.
Her allegations have not been independently verified, and Philippine National Police chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said Duterte had not reported any threats to the police.
“To date, however, the Vice President has not reported to the PNP any threat to her life or to the safety of her family, including the threats she said date back to 2023,” Nartatez said.
He added that the PNP had not monitored any incident posing danger to Duterte or her family.
Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said authorities “knew of her whereabouts the night before but we did not force the warrant of arrest.”
Remulla said the PNP had body-camera footage of the serving of the warrant and of Duterte’s arrival at the Hall of Justice.
Historic arrest, routine bail
“The PNP accorded her all the respect her position deserves,” he said, adding that the pressure surrounding Duterte’s situation appeared to be affecting her perception.
As the Vice President left the Hall of Justice after posting bail, her supporters gathered outside chanted “Duterte! Duterte!”
She hugged one of them, who was weeping, before proceeding to her vehicle.

Duterte’s lawyers stressed that she was not given special treatment. Lim said his client voluntarily appeared before the court that issued the warrant, so there was no need for her to be physically arrested and have her mug shot taken.
“She had to go through the same process,” Lim said.

As part of the process, the court received the photos provided by Duterte, an affidavit of undertaking, a barangay certification of her Davao City residence, a sketch of her Davao home and a government-issued ID.

But Lim explained that posting bail did not mean Duterte had already surrendered to the court’s jurisdiction. He said her legal team continued to assert that an impeachable officer like the Vice President could not be criminally charged while in office.
Constitutional law professor Paolo Emmanuel Tamase of the University of the Philippines College of Law disputed that view.
“There’s no basis in Philippine constitutional law for the immunity of a vice president from any type of suit, including a criminal suit,” Tamase said.
Unlike the president, who enjoys immunity from suit while in office, the vice president does not have the same constitutional protection, he said.
Tamase also distinguished impeachment from criminal liability.
Impeachment concerns the removal of an impeachable public official, he said, while a criminal case seeks to hold an official accountable for an alleged criminal act.
“If that argument were to be respected or to be given weight, you would have … at least 30 officers who are impeachable and therefore cannot be sued,” Tamase said.
Such an interpretation would create a major gap in the system for holding public officials accountable, he added.

Tamase called Duterte’s arrest proceedings historically significant because she is the highest-ranking sitting public official in Philippine history to have been subjected to criminal prosecution and arrest proceedings.
The bail process itself, however, was routine because the charges are bailable, he said.
Tamase said the criminal case before the RTC and Senate impeachment proceedings are separate, although the arrest warrant could influence public opinion.

It could reinforce the view that Duterte’s statements constituted criminal threats, he said, but could also strengthen among her supporters the narrative that government institutions were being weaponized against her.
Duterte’s request for media to accompany her inside the Hall of Justice came amid that broader dispute over public trust in the institutions handling her cases.

blocks.caption: FEELING UNSAFE Vice President Sara Duterte tells the media on Saturday she distrusts even her own security escorts and asks them to accompany her to the fifth floor of the Quezon City Hall of Justice, where she later posted bail on three counts of grave threats filed against her. —Grig C. Montegr…

blocks.text: Not the first
Duterte is not the first Philippine vice president to face criminal complaints while in office.
During the presidency of her father, Rodrigo Duterte, then Vice President Leni Robredo was among opposition figures charged in 2019 in connection with the “Ang Totoong Narcolist” videos.

Robredo faced complaints for sedition, inciting to sedition, libel, cyberlibel, estafa, harboring a criminal and obstruction of justice. The complaints were based largely on allegations by Peter Joemel Advincula, the self-described narrator of the videos known as “Bikoy.”
The PNP-Criminal Investigation and Detection Group filed the complaints against Robredo and other opposition figures in July 2019.

The Department of Justice dismissed the complaints against Robredo in February 2020 for lack of evidence and probable cause, before the cases reached trial. —WITH REPORTS FROM GILLIAN VILLANUEVA, AND ISABELLE PECHAY

articles.title: B.C. man lost for 5 nights in mountains near Squamish shares survival story

image.caption: Stanislav Volo speaks about his five night ordeal in the backcountry. (CBC News)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New
A Squamish man who survived a grueling five nights in British Columbia's Coast Mountains is sharing more about his experience.
Stanislav Volo says he survived on gummy bears and wildflowers as he sheltered in a cave
A man who survived a grueling five nights in British Columbia's Coast Mountains is sharing more about his experience.
Stanislav Volo became the subject of a massive search after he failed to return from a hike on Sunday after riding up the Sea-to-Sky Gondola, just south of Squamish.
Search and rescue crews found him Friday evening on the Indian Arm Forest Service Road after he'd descended the mountain injured, but under his own power.
B.C. man who went missing in mountains found alive
In an interview with CBC News on Saturday after being discharged from the hospital, the 43-year-old father of two was in good spirits, despite bruises and a black eye.
“I basically relied too much on technology in this situation, and technology unfortunately sometimes fails," Volo said.
Volo had intended to hike the Mount Habrich Loop, an area search and rescue crews decribed as technical, exposed alpine terrain.
He said his phone died when he got to the top of the mountain, and he was unable to find his way down.
“I was panicking," he explained.
Volo heard what he thought was the highway, and with about four hours until the Gondola shut down for the day, decided to start descending in that direction.
It turned out to be the wrong direction — what he actually heard was pipeline construction.
But he slipped and fell in a drainage, injuring his heel and his wrist. That's when he realized he wasn't able to retrace his steps.
“I guess I have no option but to keep going down and down, slowly but surely," he explained.
Volo said he spent several nights sheltering in a small cave near a waterfall, where he focused on recovering, trying to stay warm.
He said he rationed a few packages of gummy bears before he discovered a sweet-tasting wildflower to eat.
Search teams looking for missing hiker in Sea-to-Sky region
“Maybe it's not that sweet right now if I try it, but back then it felt so sweet," he said.
“I was like OK, if I have the plants, and I know where to stay, I have my little hut where I am hiding from the rain, I think I can wait here a few more days to get my heel back in a working state."
He described seeing several helicopters, but was unable to get their attention.
Eventually, he said he made the decision to climb down the mountain.
“You have two options basically, you wait for the helicopters to come and rescue you … or you have to do something about it," he said. "Basically I decided to take a chance and get out of there.”
Despite his injured foot, he slowly and painstakingly worked his way down the mountainside, eventually intersecting first with a river, then a road.
He ran into a construction worker who connected him with the search and rescue crews who were already in the area.

items: More stories from Vancouver-South Coast

blocks.text: “It was such a joy and such an amazing feeling of being there, and just tears of happiness were running down my face," he said.
On Friday, Squamish Search and Rescue search manager Tyler Duncan said was is "remarkable" Volo survived.
He said Volo descended the back side of the mountain, a route that involved steep, technical terrain.
"I would absolutely love to sit down with Stas and have a good conversation about what he has been up to for the last six days," Duncan said. "It's got to be a remarkable story."
Now back in Squamish and recovering with his family, Volo was effusive in his thanks to search crews and everyone that helped look for him.
He added that he's learned plenty of lessons and hopes sharing his story will help others.
"It can happen to anyone," he said. "You never know what is going to happen."
With files from Natasha Fatah and Alanna Kelly

articles.title: TV presenter among 11 sentenced to death in Egypt drugs case
articles.summary: Sarah Khalifa is best known for her TV programme Mission Impossible which dealt with crime issues.

blocks.text: Egyptian television presenter Sarah Khalifa and 11 other people have been sentenced to death by hanging after being convicted of drugs charges.
According to state-owned al-Akhram newspaper, they were part of a criminal gang which imported ingredients used to make drugs with the intent of selling them.
They also had illegal firearms and munitions.
Khalifa, 39, is best known for her TV programme Mission Impossible which dealt with crime issues. She has denied the charges.
The verdict - which can be appealed against - was first announced last month.
However, it was only confirmed a month later after the court obtained a religious opinion from the grand mufti of Egypt - a legal requirement in death sentence cases.
During the trial, the court heard that authorities had seized more than 750kg (1,653lbs) of narcotics and the imported raw materials to make them.
Twenty witnesses had given statements to the prosecutors, al-Akhram said, in addition to electronic evidence that included conversations and video clips.

According to the state-run Akhbar al-Youm newspaper, when asked by the judge about her alleged role during a court appearance last September, Khalifa said she had never seen any drugs until she was photographed with them inside the anti-narcotics authority offices.
According to a 2025 Amnesty International report, there were 492 death sentences in the course of the year, 23 of whom were executed, external.

The defendants were found guilty of drug trafficking and rape, "crimes that did not amount to 'intentional killing' to which the use of the death penalty must be restricted under international law and standards", the report said.

articles.title: Prince William to attend King Harald's funeral in Norway
articles.summary: The Prince of Wales will represent the King at the funeral of Harald V in Oslo next week.

blocks.text: The Prince of Wales will attend the funeral of King Harald V of Norway on Wednesday in Oslo, Buckingham Palace has announced.
Also going to the funeral, in a personal capacity, is Princess Anne, who is godmother to Norway's new monarch, King Haakon VIII.
The late King Harald, a popular, modernising figure who had been on the Norwegian throne for 35 years, died last month at the age of 89.
Royal sources say Prince William's attendance, representing his father King Charles, follows the convention that the monarch does not usually go to the funeral of another head of state.
Large crowds are expected for the farewell to King Harald on 9 September, with a funeral procession to be followed by a service at Oslo Cathedral.
Thousands have queued to pay their respects to the late king, during his lying in state in the chapel of the Royal Palace in the Norwegian capital.
At the funeral, alongside Prince William, will be the widowed Queen Sonja, members of the Norwegian royal family including new King Haakon VIII, and other European royals.
The service will be followed by a private burial in Norway's royal mausoleum in the Akershus Fortress.

articles.title: Woman injured in bear attack in Whistler backcountry
articles.summary: A woman was taken to hospital on Friday after a bear attack in the backcountry near Whistler.

image.caption: Conservation officers are investigating a bear attack in the backcountry near Whistler. (Dan McGarvey)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New
A woman was taken to hospital on Friday after a bear attack in the backcountry near Whistler.
Trails closed in Callaghan Conservancy following attack Friday evening
The B.C. Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS) said a group of three hikers ran into two bears near Conflict Lake in the Callaghan Conservancy around 5 p.m. PT on Friday.
The service said one of the bears attacked a woman before disengaging.

items: More stories from Vancouver-South Coast

blocks.text: Whistler Search and Rescue president Brad Sills said it helped transport conservation officers to the scene, and to evacuate the woman by helicopter.
He said the woman had a severely lacerated leg. B.C. Emergency Health Services said the victim was transported to hospital in stable condition.
BCCOS swept the area and killed an adult male black bear at the attack site due to safety concerns, it added.
However, the service said it has not been able to confirm if a black bear or grizzly bear was responsible for the attack.
Sills said the area is known grizzly habitat, and hikers in the area need to take precautions including making plenty of noise.
“It’s not enough to call out intermittently when you’re hiking, when you’re in known grizzly bear terrain, you need to be calling out all the time,” he said.
The BCCOS said officers were returning to the site on Saturday.
B.C. Parks has closed trail access in the area and is urging people to stay away.

articles.title: Why many Syrians feel Assad death sentence isn't enough
articles.summary: In July, a Syrian court sentenced former dictator Bashar Assad to death for crimes against his own people. But after 14 years of civil war, many survivors are demanding more when it comes to…

image.caption: Despite terrible memories of death during the war, including that of her brother, Huda Khayti now often returns to her hometown of DoumaImage: privat

blocks.text: Huda Khayti often finds herself returning to the place where she lost almost everything. Khayti, a Syrian women's rights activist, survived a 2013 chemical weapons attack on the east Ghouta region by forces of the former Syrian dictator Bashar Assad.

Her brother was killed by the bombs of the Assad regime and its allies. Her women's center was destroyed along with her home and in 2018, she had to leave her hometown of Douma — a major city in Ghouta — and flee to Idlib, a rebel stronghold in northern Syria.

Today, Khayti regularly visits her hometown, which is about 10 kilometers (about 6 miles) northeast of the country's capital, Damascus. Since the Assad regime was overthrown in late 2024, Khayti has traveled regularly between Idlib and Douma, where she's even working on opening a new women's center.

"Ghouta means so much to me emotionally," she told DW. But every time she returns there, she is also confronted with remnants of the civil war. "When I'm traveling through the country I see traces of war everywhere, so many houses and so much infrastructure destroyed. So much suffering. So much trauma."

blocks.caption: In Douma, Huda Khayti visits the grave of her murdered brotherImage: privat

blocks.text: Almost two years since the overthrow of the Assad regime, Syria has started a process to examine the crimes of the regime in court. In mid-August a Damascus court sentenced Bashar Assad and other high-ranking members of his regime to death in absentia. Assad is currently living in Russia, where he fled after his government was overthrown. Many senior officials are also there or hiding elsewhere.
Among other things, Assad was found guilty of premeditated murder, torture and depriving individuals of their liberty. The court said these were war crimes and crimes against humanity.

"Of course, this conviction of Assad is a good thing," Khayti said. "Even if it's only on paper. Bashar Assad may have been convicted but he just continues to live his life in Russia — like so many other Syrian criminals who fled to Russia."
Justice served in Syria?

The court's conviction had a big impact in Syria anyway. "The verdict had a lot of echoes by people, they were so happy," said Lina Chawaf, a Syrian journalist, media expert and researcher at Harvard University's Center for Middle Eastern Studies. "Many media celebrated the verdict on the statement day as a victory and consider it as part of transitional justice."

Still, it remains unclear whether there will be any actual punishment following the conviction. Although Russia and Syria agreed on an extradition treaty in 2023, observers say it's unlikely Russia would send Assad, a long-time ally, back to Syria. Additionally, according to the treaty, if the death penalty is likely, that could prevent extradition too.

In August, Syria's Deputy Justice Minister Mustafa al-Qassem said the country had established a commission to cooperate with Interpol and that cooperation with other countries in extraditing fugitive suspects would speed up legal proceedings.
Syria still scarred after 14-year civil war

Rana Sheikh-Ali, founder of Daret Salam (Peace Circuit in English), which uses technology to build peace and empower women, believes the Assad trial in August should be seen as largely symbolic. From a human rights perspective, she opposes the death penalty, but at the same time she says many locals saw the death sentences as just.
But the prosecution of high-ranking regime members is only one aspect of the transitional justice process.

Transitional justice isn't just about criminal trials. Other aspects include searching for missing people, investigating crimes, deciding on reparations and formulating institutional reforms. With all that, the focus should be on victims and survivors.

Numbers supplied by the Syrian Network for Human Rights indicate just how big the task is. In an article, the advocacy network reports that over 234,805 civilians were killed during the civil war, at least 202,000 of them by the Assad regime and its allies.

In addition, there are also at least 181,312 cases of arbitrary arrest and enforced disappearance to investigate as well as 45,339 deaths resulting from torture. It's thought that the actual numbers are likely far higher. The network has also documented 217 chemical weapons attacks by the Assad regime.
Victim-centered process needed

Women's rights activist Khayti was just a few kilometers from the epicenter of one of those attacks in eastern Ghouta in 2013. "I remember it like it was yesterday," she recounted. "I can't forget the screams of the victims. I kept thinking we were next. I felt that scratchiness in my throat, that burning in my eyes."

For a system of transitional justice that is truly victim-centered, it's not enough to just have survivors act as witnesses in court. "Victims must also participate in every detail related to the transitional justice process," she explained.

Additionally, those who were impacted by the crimes must be able to participate voluntarily and be protected as they do, Sheikh-Ali added. They should be able to talk about their experiences and should also be heard on topics like compensation, financial support and public recognition.
For survivors like Khayti, this means not just making Assad and a few top regime officials the primary targets of justice.

"I also want to see convictions for individuals who wrote reports that led to people ending up in the Saydnaya torture prison," Khayti said. "These individuals are just as guilty as the torturers themselves."

blocks.caption: Huda Khayti also runs a women's center in Idlib and works with people in refugee camps on the Turkish borderImage: privat

blocks.text: At the moment, though, it's unclear exactly how thoroughly Syria will confront its past.

"Convictions in absentia against Assad and other officials send an important signal after decades of impunity," said Sophie Bischoff, managing director of Adopt a Revolution, a German-Syrian human rights organization that supports civil society initiatives. "But for survivors like Huda Khayti, these sentences remain symbolic as long as those convicted are not actually held accountable — and it's also still not transparent exactly who is to be held accountable and on what legal basis, and who would be granted immunity."
Bischoff also noted that the new Syrian state has yet to fully and comprehensively investigate crimes against humanity and war crimes committed in Syria.

"So far it's primarily been Syrian civil society organizations and human rights activists who have been researching and documenting these cases for years," she told DW. "Systematic state documentation of violent crimes committed during the Assad regime era is only just beginning."

The new Syrian government has created two commissions to work on issues of transitional justice. In late August, one of these — the National Commission for Missing Persons — launched a platform called Athar, where families of the missing can submit information.

The other organization, the National Commission for Transitional Justice, was established in May 2025 but has so far dealt only with crimes committed by the Assad regime. It has not dealt with crimes committed by militias fighting the war or the extremist group known as the "Islamic State".
Return to Syria: Rebuilding and seeking justice in Yarmouk
Investigating all war crimes
"This falls far short," said Bischoff. "For a comprehensive reckoning and a new beginning in a Syria for all, the war crimes of all warring parties must be included."

For Khayti, the requirement to place victims at the center of the process of transitional justice also has another difficult aspect. Her testimony is being heard, but at the same time she is forced to return to the original trauma.
"It's difficult for me to talk about it and I often feel like I'm reliving it," Khayti explained.
Sheikh-Ali said centering the victims means those impacted play a meaningful role in the process. But as they do so, she added, they should also be protected.

It's also important to remember these events, Khayti added. In Douma, she is working on ways to preserve recollections of the war. "We need to inform younger people about it so that the memory doesn't fade," she said.
In Syria, she said now it's about finding the missing, holding all perpetrators to account, fully investigating all crimes and giving survivors a voice.
"We will continue to be loud," Khayti said. "And we will continue to demand justice."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Robin Morgan, child star who became feminist, poet and editor, dies aged 85
articles.summary:
Leading second-wave feminist co-founded Women’s Media Center with Jane Fonda and Gloria Steinem

Robin Morgan, a child star of the 1940s and 50s who grew up to become an all-American radical…

blocks.text: Robin Morgan, a child star of the 1940s and 50s who grew up to become an all-American radical as a poet, essayist, editor and second-wave feminist, has died. She was 85.
Morgan’s death was confirmed Saturday by the Women’s Media Center, an organization she co-founded with Jane Fonda and the celebrated author and activist Gloria Steinem, who died Wednesday.

During the 1960s and 70s, Morgan embodied and inspired historic changes in how women lived and thought. As she was happy to point out, the one-time “ideal American girl” and adored “little Robin Morgan” was a rule breaker and justice seeker with a notable list of achievements, along with a prison record and an FBI file.

Julie Burton, president of the Women’s Media Center, called Morgan “one of the architects of the contemporary women’s movement”, hailing her writing and “global leadership for justice and equality”. The statement didn’t specify the location, date or cause of Morgan’s death.

Morgan was at the center of some of the defining moments of what came to be called second-wave feminism, expanding upon the achievements of the suffragists a half-century earlier. In 1968, she was among the organizers of the first protest against the Miss America pageant, joining fellow activists in tossing their bras (soon mythologized as burning) into a “freedom trash can”. The 1970 essay anthology she edited, Sisterhood Is Powerful, is considered one of the essential texts of the modern women’s movement.

Her legacy was one of deeds, words and images. Morgan is widely credited with coining the term “herstory”, the feminist reworking of “history”, and popularizing the clenched fist/female symbol icon of the liberation movement. Her poem Monster, with such lines as “I want a women’s revolution like a lover/I lust for it” was quoted at feminist rallies and beyond. Her poem Arraignment helped capture the movement’s embrace of the late Sylvia Plath and condemnation of her husband, poet Ted Hughes, whom Morgan and others blamed for Plath’s suicide in 1963. Morgan’s rhyming couplet “I accuse/Ted Hughes” inspired the title for Sonic Youth’s song J’Accuse Ted Hughes.

Labeled an “anarchist housewife” in one government report, Morgan confronted the establishment, left and right. In 1970, she and fellow protesters were arrested and jailed after occupying the offices of the avant garde Grove Press, whose owner, Barney Rosset, was fighting employees’ efforts to unionize. In the widely reprinted 1970 essay Goodbye to All That, she called out activists and libertines from Abbie Hoffman and Hugh Hefner to Dave Dellinger and the music group the Fugs.

blocks.caption: Morgan, then the editor-in-chief of Ms, celebrates the magazine’s spring comeback in her New York office on 28 February 1990. Photograph: Susan Ragan/AP

blocks.text: In her personal life, Morgan had male and female lovers and was married for more than 20 years to the gay poet Kenneth Pitchford, with whom she had a son, the musician, activist and record company executive Blake Morgan. She once described her marriage as a “two-member commune” and was so resistant to labels that she remembered being “straight-baited” by feminists who thought she should be a lesbian and chastised by conservatives who assumed she was a lesbian.
In her 2001 memoir Saturday’s Child, she expressed joy and amazement at how her life had turned out and how she was able to retain “a threadbare, somewhat surreal sense of humor”.
“Put that in your apple pie and smoke it,” she wrote.

Besides Saturday’s Child, she completed more than 20 books, including The Word of a Woman: Feminists Dispatches and the poetry collections Monster and Dark Matter. She followed Sisterhood Is Powerful with Sisterhood Is Global (1984) and Sisterhood Is Forever (2002), featuring such contributors as Steinem, Simone de Beauvoir and Eve Ensler. For several years, she was editor-in-chief of Ms magazine.

In 1984, she was a founder of an early feminist thinktank, the Sisterhood Is Global Institute. In 2005, she, Steinem and Fonda launched the Women’s Media Center, which has a mission to support “the visibility, viability and decision-making power of women and girls in media”.

blocks.caption: Morgan at age five, in New York on 8 August 1947. Photograph: Robert Kradin/AP

blocks.text: More recently, she hosted a syndicated radio show and remained active despite being diagnosed with Parkinson’s, which inspired several poems and a TEDWomen talk in 2015.

In a different era, she might have been just another forgotten child star. Born in 1941 in Lake Worth, Florida, and raised in New York, she never saw her father while growing up and was told – falsely – by her mother that he was dead. Her mother also shaved a year off her age, claiming she was born in 1942, to make her early public career seem even more impressive.

She would meet some of the era’s biggest stars, from Abbott and Costello to Sal Mineo, and was popular enough to inspire such commercial tie-ins as Robin Morgan dolls. Magazines described her as “unspoiled” and “courteous” and “the ideal girl-next-door”, immune from “violent outbursts of antagonism against established society”.

As she recalled in Saturday’s Child, producer Dan Ehrenreich squeezed her shoulder so hard that Morgan could feel his fingernails. He turned her microphone away and eventually placed his hand over her mouth.
“I realized that I loved and respected that child who fought back in what was the first political act I recall ever daring to make,” Morgan wrote.

articles.title: Egyptian TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death for drug crime
articles.summary:
Sarah Khalifa, 39, charged with forming organised criminal gang to manufacture and traffick drugs

An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for…

blocks.text: An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for manufacturing and trafficking narcotics in a sprawling drug case, official media reported on Saturday.
The presenter, Sarah Khalifa, 39, is best known for her programme Mission Impossible, which dealt with issues concerning security and crime.

The state-linked Al-Ahram newspaper said a Cairo court sentenced “Khalifa and 11 other defendants to death by hanging on charges of forming an organised criminal gang specialising in procuring materials used in manufacturing narcotics, with the intent to traffic them, and possessing and carrying unlicensed firearms and ammunition”.
The verdict came after the court consulted the Grand Mufti of Egypt for his religious opinion, a procedure required by Egyptian law in capital cases.
The verdict is subject to appeal.
Khalifa also owns a cosmetic surgery clinic and a production company that specialises in organising parties and events.

According to the state-run Akhbar el-Yom newspaper, the defendants were charged with “manufacturing synthetic drugs with the intent to traffic them, by importing the materials used in manufacturing from abroad”.
Al-Ahram reported that authorities seized more than 750kg of narcotics and raw materials, and found two apartments used as laboratories as well as unlicensed firearms and ammunition.
The court also sentenced Khalifa and others to five years in prison over a separate case involving the kidnapping and assault of a young man.
Egypt applies the death penalty for premeditated murder, terrorism, some rape offences and drug trafficking.
According to the Egyptian Commission for Rights and Freedoms, 541 death sentences were issued in Egypt in 2025.

articles.title: Croatia: Toxic waste protest draws tens of thousands
articles.summary: The Zagreb demonstrators demanded that the government come up with a plan to clear illegal toxic waste in 20 days. Prime Minister Plenkovic has promised to tackle the issue.

image.caption: Tens of thousands of people attended the protest in ZagrebImage: AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A protest in Zagreb against Croatia's government drew tens of thousands of people who blamed the government for its lack of action over the illegal storage of toxic waste.

A landfill near the town of Gospic, located some 200 kilometers (124.2 miles) to Zagreb's southwest, is being used to hold toxic waste from several countries, including Germanyand Italy, according to reports.
The demonstration saw signs such as "ecocide equals slow genocide" and "halt waste import," with many of the people in attendance also holding Croatian flags.

The protesters called for all illegal landfills to be cleared due to them polluting groundwater, as well as a new waste management plan across the country within the next 20 days. They also demanded that the government put a temporary ban on waste imports in place.

blocks.caption: Protesters waved Croatian flags and demanded better waste managementImage: AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Investigation underway

An investigation in relation to illegal waste dumps has been ongoing since the arrests of 13 people in February 2025, with Europol cooperating with Croatian authorities in the investigation. Four companies are also under investigation.

According to Europol, most of the 35,000 tons of waste had come from Italy, but also from Slovenia and Germany, and consisted of plastic refuse and toxic hospital waste, bringing about a profit of some €4 million ($4.6 million) for the suspects, who had also likely forged documents falsely declaring plastic waste as suitable for recycling.
Local environmental activists dispute the number of waste tons and say 37,000 tons had been illegally dumped in Gospic alone.
Prosecutors also published a report in August that confirmed the Gospic soil contamination, also saying it had spread beyond the site itself.
This presents a "significant risk for the environmentand people's health," the report said, despite the drinking water in Gospic remaining so far unaffected, health authorities said.
Conservative Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic promised the toxic waste site in Gospic would be covered by mid-October before the waste gets removed from it.

articles.title: Pulong Duterte insists Davao City got no congressional district budget
articles.summary: Davao City Representative Paolo “Pulong” Duterte on Saturday insisted that his hometown did not receive any congressional district allocation, disputing Palace Press Officer Claire Castro"s earlier…

blocks.text: Published September 6, 2026 12:17am

Davao City Representative Paolo “Pulong” Duterte on Saturday insisted that his hometown did not receive any congressional district allocation, disputing Palace Press Officer Claire Castro’s earlier statement that the government had provided funding to the city.
On Friday, Castro said Davao City received P52.80 billion in national tax allotment (NTA). Duterte, however, said this was different from the funding he was referring to.

“Ang NTA ay automatic appropriation para sa mga LGU (local government unit). Alam naman nating lahat iyan. Hindi ko sinabi na walang NTA ang Davao City…pero ang tinutukoy ko ay budget allocation para sa congressional districts,” Duterte said in a Facebook post.

(The NTA is an automatic appropriation for local government units. We all know that. I did not say that Davao City does not have an NTA. What I am referring to is the budget allocation for the congressional districts.)
Castro had cited the P52.80 billion NTA in response to Duterte’s allegation that Davao City had received no government funding.
“Sa sinasabing walang government funding na nilaan sa Davao City, ayon kay Cong. Pulong [Duterte], ito ang totoo,” Castro said.
(Regarding Cong. Pulong Duterte’s claim that no government funding was allocated to Davao City, this is the truth.)
Duterte said it would be best for the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) to show the records.

In a message to GMA News Online, Castro clarified that she had only been specifically asked about the NTA allotment, her assessment of the claim that Davao City had received no funds from the national government, and whether there were pertinent records to support the claim.

“It is better for the media to ask Pulong Duterte for those ‘proposed projects and their feasibility studies’ to see if the alleged denial of the congressional allocation was justified or not,” Castro said.
GMA News Online has also reached out to the DBM for comment and will update this story once it responds. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: VALORANT: Xavi8k on GE advancing to VCT Pacific grand finals — ‘We’re not done yet’

articles.title: PDP-Laban denounces Sara arrest warrant
articles.summary: The Partido Demokratiko Pilipino-Laban has denounced the issuance of a warrant of arrest against Vice President Sara Duterte, calling it an “assault” on the legitimate political…

blocks.text: September 6, 2026 | 12:00am
Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Quezon City Hall of Justice on September 5, 2026.
Michael Varcas / The Philippine STAR

MANILA, Philippines — The Partido Demokratiko Pilipino (PDP)-Laban has denounced the issuance of a warrant of arrest against Vice President Sara Duterte, calling it an “assault” on the legitimate political opposition.
It pointed to the fact that the arrest warrant was issued by a regional trial court judge recently appointed by President Marcos.

“The blatant attempt to decimate the political opposition is disingenuous yet obvious: appoint people beholden to the present administration to key positions in government agencies and use these agencies as weapons of mass harassment against those who dare oppose the prevailing corruption masterminded by the Palace,” PDP-Laban national spokesman Ferdinand Topacio said.
He urged the people to maintain their support “to the leaders of their choice” and resist the imposition of those that have been repudiated and “stand fast against the forces of dictatorship.”
However, House Deputy Speaker Paolo Ortega V said the issuance of the arrest warrant only means that Duterte should now confront the charges through the judicial process available to every accused.
Ortega said Duterte will have every opportunity to dispute the charges, question the prosecution’s evidence and avail herself of the remedies provided under the Rules of Court.

He said the development should therefore be allowed to proceed according to law, with the court ultimately determining criminal liability after hearing the evidence of both the prosecution and the defense.

For his part, Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon told Duterte to stop portraying her arrest as a threat to her safety and instead address the grave threats charges against her through the proper legal process.
Ridon made the statement after Duterte repeatedly expressed fears for her life after arriving at the Quezon City Hall of Justice yesterday to post bail.
Meanwhile, former press secretary Trixie Cruz-Angeles said Duterte’s supporters will remember the warrant of arrest against Duterte as oppression.
In a short video uploaded by Bilyonaryo News Channel, Angeles said, “History might not be a very kind judge because we will remember.”

“We will remember this, it is all on record and there will be people who would attest, there will be people who will stand with this, to all of these events and we’ll interpret them as oppression. So good luck in 2028,” she added. — Evelyn Macairan

articles.title: JV hopes reforms will boost Senate ratings
articles.summary: The Senate’s trust ratings will likely improve following reforms put in place by the new leadership, according to finance committee chairman Sen. JV Ejercito.

blocks.text: September 6, 2026 | 12:00am
Senator JV Ejercito on March 4, 2026.
STAR / Ryan Baldemor
MANILA, Philippines — The Senate’s trust ratings will likely improve following reforms put in place by the new leadership, according to finance committee chairman Sen. JV Ejercito.
The senior deputy majority leader said the reforms include transparency measures in scrutinizing the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027.
Ejercito vowed to ensure that confidential funds are limited to government agencies with law enforcement and military mandate, including national security and the Office of the President.
“To avoid controversies, we will not give (confidential funds) to civilian agencies,” Ejercito said.
Agencies with lump sum budget items would be required to submit programs of work to ensure the funding goes to implemented projects and not lost to corruption.
“We will ask for all the details so we know how the funds will be used,” Ejercito said.
He hoped the Senate could redeem the public’s trust through reforms and prevent a repeat of the previous years’ budget insertions, which led to the flood control scandal.
Ejercito noted that the Senate ratings dropped while the House of Representatives improved.
He attributed the dip to the chaos that preceded the current leadership of Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian.
“It’s the first time in history that the Senate’s trust ratings are lower than the House. But hopefully, with the reforms in place, the Senate can regain the trust of the people,” Ejercito said.
He was reacting to the OCTA Research Group’s survey where the Senate’s ratings dropped to 41 percent in a survey conducted from July 4 to 11 from 44 percent in March.
Twenty-seven percent said they distrust the upper chamber, up from 24 percent, while undecided respondents remained at 32 percent.
The Senate’s performance ratings also dropped from 42 percent to 38 percent, with those dissatisfied with its performance increasing from 27 percent to 32 percent.
Undecided respondents hardly moved, from 31 percent to 30 percent.
The latest OCTA poll coincided with the start of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on July 6.

It captured the tumultuous Senate presidency dispute between Alan Peter Cayetano and Gatchalian, the May 13 shooting incident at the Senate and Sen. Ronald Dela Rosa’s escape, and the arrest of Sens. Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta on non-bailable plunder charges.
The House of Representatives’ trust ratings improved in the second quarter.
Thirty-eight percent said they trust the House, up from 36 percent, while 28 percent said they distrust it, down from 33 percent.
Undecided respondents increased from 30 percent to 33 percent.

In terms of performance, 37 percent said they were satisfied with the Lower House, up from 35 percent, while 32 percent were undecided, down from 35 percent. Those who were undecided hardly moved, from 30 percent to 31 percent.
OCTA’s second quarter survey had 1,200 respondents and a margin of error of plus/minus three percent. — Janvic Mateo

articles.title: DPWH working on detailed flood master plan
articles.summary: After the massive floods in Metro Manila and other provinces, the Department of Public Works and Highways is eyeing to create a science-backed flood management infrastructure plan to strengthen…

blocks.text: September 6, 2026 | 12:00am
Residents wade through floodwaters while others use paddle boats in a village in Lingayen, Pangasinan on August 30, 2026.
Cesar Ramirez / The Philippine STAR

MANILA, Philippines — After the massive floods in Metro Manila and other provinces, the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) is eyeing to create a science-backed flood management infrastructure plan to strengthen long-term disaster preparedness in the country.
DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon has ordered the updating of all flood management master plans in the wake of the floods brought by tropical cyclones and the enhanced southwest monsoon.
He said they are laying the technical foundation for future flood control projects that are based on science.

The DPWH is collaborating with the University of the Philippines-Project Nationwide Operational Assessment of Hazards (NOAH), local governments and key partner agencies in the integration of hazard mapping and scientific data before the projects are implemented.
The DPWH is also working with NLEX Corp. for long-term solutions to ease the flooding at the North Luzon Expressway-San Simon Interchange in Pampanga.

Meanwhile, the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) has directed its regional offices to coordinate with expressway managements for the timely dissemination on the status of the expressways within their respective areas of responsibility.
The directive covers Metro Manila, Ilocos Region where the TPLEX is located, Central Luzon where the SCTEX and NLEX is located and CALABARZON where SLEX, STAR Toll, CALAX and MCLEX are located.

Acting LTFRB Chairman Greg Pua Jr. said they also instructed all regional franchising and regulatory offices in the three regions to coordinate with the local government units in identifying alternative routes from the expressways in cases of emergency and other unexpected incidents similar to what happened at the San Simon area of NLEX.

“The incident that happened in NLEX is a wake-up call for us in the LTFRB and other agencies to do our part in coming up with measures to maximize the assistance to the public,” Pua said. — Josiah Antonio

articles.title: US military says it struck three Iranian tankers after American warships came under missile attack
articles.summary:
Officials said US aircraft carrier and destroyer avoided attacks before three Iranian tankers were struck by the US

The US…

blocks.text: The US military said Saturday it struck three Iranian oil tankers after US navy warships came under missile attack, further escalating tensions in the region and warning it would “if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet”.
According to the military, a US aircraft carrier and destroyer avoided “multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks” while patrolling the region. No US personnel were injured.
Two of the Iranian oil carriers were “permanently disabled”, the Pentagon said, while a third tanker, which was unladen, was destroyed.
The US said the vessels were part of a shadow network that helped finance Iran’s powerful Revolutionary Guards and armed proxy groups operating across the region.
“We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet,” the head of US Central Command, Adm Brad Cooper, said in the statement.

The announcement followed an earlier report from Iran that the US had attacked an Iranian tanker near Kharg Island in the Gulf. Tasnim, a semiofficial news outlet affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, reported the strike happened on Saturday morning. It said the tanker’s crew survived and was being evacuated.

The US said one tanker was struck off Kharg Island, while another was hit near Jask. The unladen tanker was struck in the Gulf of Oman. The US statement also shared what it described as video footage of the strikes.

The latest attacks came nearly a week after the US and Iran resumed strikes after about a month of relative calm in the on-again, off-again war that began with US and Israeli attacks in February. Attempts at negotiations have collapsed.
One of the strikes hit a wedding in southern Iran on Tuesday, killing four people, including a child, and injuring dozens, according to Iranian officials.
The US vice-president, JD Vance, said “sometimes things happen” when asked on Thursday whether an US strike was responsible for killing people at the wedding celebration.
after newsletter promotion
The renewed strikes have also brought fresh scrutiny to a 28 February US attack in Minab that struck a school compound and killed at least 156 people, most of them schoolchildren.

A preliminary US military inquiry reportedly found that the attack resulted from a targeting error after outdated coordinates identified the school as part of a nearby Revolutionary Guards naval base. The Pentagon said at the time that it was investigating. A full report has not been made public.
Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: US hits three Iranian oil tankers after saying its warships were targeted
articles.summary: US Central Command says the attacks came after Iran launched ballistic missiles at two of its Navy warships.

blocks.text: The US military says it has hit three Iran-linked oil tankers after ballistic missiles were launched towards two of its warships in the region.
US Central Command (Centcom) said on Saturday it had "permanently disabled" a tanker near Kharg Island and another near the Strait of Hormuz, and "completely destroyed" a third in the Gulf of Oman.

Centcom said it "successfully evaded" multiple attacks from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeting a US aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer. No American troops were harmed, it said in a statement.
Iranian state media earlier reported that one of its oil tankers had been struck by US missiles off the coast of Kharg Island.
"Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost - taking out three of yours," said Admiral Brad Cooper, Centcom's commander.
"We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet."
The strikes come nearly a week after renewed attacks between the US and Iran, which followed a month of relative calm between the warring sides.

The US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran on 28 February, with Iran responding by attacking Israel, US bases and allied states in the Gulf, and effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz to marine traffic.

articles.title: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner land in Moscow aiming to revive Ukraine talks
articles.summary:
US envoys expected to meet Vladimir Putin before going to Kyiv, after peace efforts floundered in recent months

The US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have arrived in Moscow to try to…

blocks.text: The US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have arrived in Moscow to try to resuscitate a deal to end Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, as both sides said they would halt airstrikes for the visit.

The envoys were met at the airport on Saturday by the Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev, a key interlocutor for the Trump administration’s efforts to end the Ukraine-Russia war. The US outlet Axios reported that they were expected to meet the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, later in the day.

The visit came as Trump suggested on Friday a new proposal to end the war, without providing any details on what his new plan might be. Trump made ending the war a priority early in his second term, but his efforts have so far yielded little results.

“I sent Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, two great negotiators. They’ve done a great job, and we sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done. And there may be a good chance that we’ll do it,” Trump said.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said Kyiv would stop its airstrikes during the US officials’ visit and asked Moscow do the same. The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said on Saturday that Putin had ordered a 72-hour pause in strikes on Kyiv.

Large gaps remain between Russia and Ukraine on how to end the war. On Friday, the Kremlin said it was sticking by the position Putin set out two years earlier – that Ukraine should give up four regions claimed by Russia and not join Nato. That position is intolerable to Ukraine.

Witkoff and Kushner were expected to visit Kyiv on Sunday, which would be the first time the two envoys have visited the Ukrainian capital. Both have visited Moscow before, their latest visit in January when they met Putin in the Kremlin.

As peace efforts floundered in recent months, with US attention turned to its war with Iran, the conflict has intensified. Ground troops have been locked in a grinding stalemate along the 775-mile (1,250km) frontline with little advances on either side. Both sides have intensified their aerial attacks in recent weeks, hitting increasingly distant targets.

Ukraine has carried out long-range strikes on Russian military facilities, oil refineries and e-commerce warehouses, to try to degrade Russia’s war-effort and economy. Its strikes on Russian oil refineries have led to fuel shortages and rising prices at the pump.

On Friday, a Russian drone hit the headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), one of the agencies which are responsible for carrying out deep-strike operations in Russia. Zelenskyy has vowed to retaliate. Russia has also increased its attacks on Kyiv and other cities with waves of bombardments, stretching Ukraine’s air defence systems.

Zelenskyy accused Russia of trying to disrupt the envoys’ visit to Ukraine with strikes on Kyiv’s two airports overnight. “Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine,” Zelensky said in a post on X.
Officials visiting Ukraine have largely done so by train, as Ukrainian airspace has been closed since 2022 due to the war.

On Friday, Russia carried out overnight strikes, killing five people and wounding five more at a factory in the southern Dnipropetrovsk region, according to thje local military administration head, Oleksandr Hanzha. He said those killed were employees working at the factory who were “doing their job when enemy missiles cut off their lives.”
A 62-year-old man was wounded and several homes and a building were damaged in an another attack on the region’s Nikopol district, Hanzha said.

Russia also struck a shopping centre in the southern Mykolaiv region with drones overnight, damaging the building and wounding a 72-year-old man and a 17-year-old girl. Emergency services said they were repeatedly forced to withdraw because of the threat of more strikes.
Ukraine’s air force said Russia launched ballistic missiles and 167 drones overnight, including jet-powered UAVs. Ukrainian air defences disabled 128 of the drones, the air force said.
Russia’s defence ministry said it had shot down 53 Ukrainian drones overnight.

articles.title: Cut the cameras: Flock surveillance cameras spur rare bipartisan backlash
articles.summary:
Politicians on the right and left are pushing back against Flock as more Americans voice opposition to the tech

Growing factions from both sides of the political aisle in the US are pushing…

blocks.text: Growing factions from both sides of the political aisle in the US are pushing back against surveillance cameras made by a single company, a rare response in a sharply divided country with a president pushing an unwaveringly pro-tech agenda.

The bipartisan backlash against Flock Safety cameras resembles nationwide rage toward the construction of large datacenters that power artificial intelligence. Polling shows roughly 75% of Americans oppose new datacenter construction in their areas.

Flock’s cameras are automated license plate readers (ALPRs), which take pictures of vehicle license plates so police and security companies can log the movement of cars in a given area. There are about 120,000 Flock cameras across the US, which conduct roughly 2bn scans per month. The company is staring down controversy after reports of abuses of its cameras by police officers in multiple states, who have used them to stalk ex-lovers and track people seeking abortions. The network the cameras feed into is also frequently utilized by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Data and polling from the Washington Post show that social media posts about Flock have increased since July, and about 46% of Americans oppose ALPRs being used in their community – up 13 points from the previous year. Vigilantes are posting videos of themselves destroying the cameras to digital applause. According to privacy and surveillance experts, hatred of Flock cameras has become bipartisan.

“In my 20-plus years at the ACLU, I’ve never really seen such a grassroots uprising against surveillance technology like this,” said Jay Stanley, a senior policy analyst at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). “On the left, there’s a historical memory of law enforcement spying on and interfering with advocates for social change … On the right, there’s a long tradition of ‘don’t tread on me’ – keep the government out of my life, keep it from looking over my shoulder.”

Both liberal and conservative politicians are pushing back against Flock cameras. Greg Abbott, Texas’s Republican governor, blocked state agencies from procuring Flock products. On the other side of the political spectrum, Bernie Sanders, the progressive US senator, is promising to introduce legislation to restrict the use of Flock cameras. Republican senator Josh Hawley has launched an investigation into potential Flock privacy abuses, and Democratic congressman Ro Khanna is cosponsoring a bill with Republican congressman Thomas Massie to prevent federal funds from being used to purchase Flock cameras.

Municipal leaders of all political stripes are dropping contracts with Flock, though sometimes they replace the license plate readers with another brand of camera and continue the surveillance. We reached out to Flock Safety for a statement and did not receive a response before publishing.

Surveillance hasn’t always been a unifying topic in US politics. Debates over the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (Fisa), the Patriot Act and other surveillance issues have often been divisive. This appears to be an unusual case where politicians are getting on the same side of a hot-button issue.

“Privacy, to some extent, is bipartisan,” said Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. “When you put up these cameras, they last longer than the current administration. You might trust the people in power now who put them up – but are you going to trust the next people who get access to that equipment?”

Americans have been showing up at town hall meetings by the dozen over the past six months or so, and there have been numerous protests to show opposition to Flock surveillance cameras around the country. More than 100 jurisdictions have canceled their contracts so far, according to data from the non-profit Institute for Justice. An organization called DeFlock, founded in 2024, hopes to increase the numbers by compiling a map of the cameras’ locations.

While ALPRs aren’t new, Flock, founded in 2017, has made them far more prevalent than they used to be. The company’s software allows disparate law enforcement agencies to share data with one another, meaning a license plate scan by a police department in one state could easily and quickly be used in another.
after newsletter promotion

“Flock represents tech companies in bed with governments, doing the exact stuff people have become distrustful of and resentful about for the past few decades. It feels like it’s finally hit the boiling-over point,” said Woodrow Hartzog, a professor of law and computer science at Boston University.

Hartzog predicts the actions against Flock Safety will continue at the state and local level amid this growing popular outrage. He expects people are going to stay angry about the issue, and politicians will have to respond.

“The pushback we’re seeing against Flock cameras is one of the most vivid illustrations I can think of that surveillance is not inevitable – that these tools aren’t inevitable,” Hartzog says. “It’s up to all of us to stop them.”

articles.title: Masked anti-migrant protesters block UK's Dover terminal
articles.summary: Chanting "stop the boats" and wearing balaclavas, the demonstrators blocked traffic at the UK's busiest international ferry port.

image.caption: Police said they eventually moved the masked protesters onto trains out of Dover portImage: Oscar Rihll/PA Wire/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Hundreds of masked people blocked traffic at England's port of Dover on Saturday as part of an anti-migrant protest, halting ferry traffic between France and the UK.
Video footage showed demonstrators in balaclavas chanting "stop the boats," in a reference to refugees and migrants who attempt the dangerous English channel crossing in a bid to reach Great Britain.

This came despite the fact that crossing dropped 40% between January and August 2026 compared to the previous year. However, the perceived threat of migrant boats has become a rallying cry for the far-right Reform UK party.
Police said that they were "engaging" with protesters and that normal traffic had resumed at the port after several hours.
Government condemns 'travel disruption'

"The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behavior in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused," said a spokesman for the government of Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Under Burnham and his predecessor Keir Starmer, migrant crossings have been greatly reduced in part due to closer cooperation with French authorities.
Dover is the UK's biggest international ferry port, handling some 15,000 passengers a day during the summer and welcoming more than a third of the UK's trade goods with the European Union.

articles.title: Fact check: Germany's postal voting system isn't rigged
articles.summary: As Germany heads into three elections in September, rumors are circulating on social media claiming that postal voting is not secure — claims that have also been made about other elections. Here's…

image.caption: Postal voting has become a target for fraud allegations in Germany, as it has in other democracies, including the USImage: Revierfoto/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Stakes are high in Germany's three September state elections. In Saxony-Anhalt, where voters go to the ballot boxes on Sunday, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) could make history in by winning an outright majority.

The AfD's Saxony-Anhalt branch, which has been classified by the domestic intelligence agency as a "confirmed right-wing extremist organization", could become Germany's first far-right state government since World War II.

Mail-in voting, or "Briefwahl," has become an increasingly common feature of German elections. But the rise in mail-in ballots has been followed by a renewed wave of speculation and claims questioning the security and integrity of postal vote.
DW Fact check examined a sample of claims circulating online and assessed what the available evidence shows.
Does postal voting manipulate election results?
Claim: Cases of fraud involving postal ballots prove that postal voting is unreliable.
This claim recurrently appeared in posts about postal voting that DW Fact check reviewed on social media platforms including TikTok, X and Facebook.

Some posts point to individual cases of electoral fraud involving postal ballots and present them as evidence that the system as a whole is flawed. One verified account on X using the AfD logo, for example, cited two cases — a mail-in vote being cast on behalf of an elderly woman with dementia, and hundreds of voters in Magdeburg receiving multiple ballots — before calling postal voting defective and demanding immediate reforms.

blocks.caption: Social media is rife with posts like this one on X, which cited individual problems with mail-in ballots as evidence that postal voting is fundamentally unreliableImage: X/AfD

blocks.text: DW Fact check: Misleading. Individual cases of fraud, errors or violations do not demonstrate that the entire postal voting system is unreliable or that it has affected the outcome of an election.

The post by the X account with the AfD logo refers to two real incidents, but does so in a misleading way. The claim about an elderly woman may refer to a case in Dessau, where police recently investigated an alleged vote cast on behalf of a 95-year-old woman with "severe dementia" but found no evidence of manipulation. The other incident occurred in Magdeburg, where 440 voters did receive duplicate ballots for the September 6 election ; however, the duplicates were invalidated and could not be used to cast additional valid votes.

Cases of electoral misconduct involving postal ballots have occurred in postal voting, as they have with voting at polling stations. In one case in Dresden, a man manipulated absentee ballots during the 2024 local and state elections, primarily in favor of the far-right Free Saxons party as well as the AfD. And in Bavaria, a former mayor was accused of manipulating postal voting documents in a March 2026 local election.

There have also been documented mistakes, administrative problems and delays in the handling of postal ballots in previous German elections. A 2021 study examining postal voting in German federal elections between 1998 and 2017 found that these weaknesses were primarily related to organization and logistics. Researcher Daniel Hellmann of the Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg said, however, that the research was still ongoing.
But such problems are not evidence of widespread fraud or of postal ballots being manipulated on a scale capable of changing an election result.
The 2021 study concluded that postal voting in Germany was secure overall. It found that none of the incidents examined could have changed an election result by even a single seat.

"If problems have occurred, they have generally been reviewed through legal channels and proportionate consequences have been imposed," Lukas Stötzer, an election researcher at the University of Witten/Herdecke in western Germany, told DW. "The postal voting system works and is secure, and that's why it is becoming more popular."

blocks.caption: In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund has called for postal voting to be restricted to justified exceptional cases. But officials have defended postal voting as a secure and established procedureImage: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: Postal voting easy to manipulate?
Claim: Postal votes are easily manipulated during counting.

"It can be assumed that postal voting in Saxony-Anhalt will massively distort the election result, This is also relatively easy to do, and the checks on postal voting are laughable," wrote one user on X with about 130,000 followers on August 14.

blocks.caption: Some posts have argued that postal votes are easier to manipulate during the counting processImage: X

blocks.text: This claim was also a recurring theme among the posts reviewed by DW Fact check, with some of the content presented in satirical, AI-generated cartoons. The AI-generated video depicted here on TikTok and labelled satire, for example, shows a man involved in counting ballots simply altering the votes from AfD to the center-right CDU party, and then calling a man named "Friedrich" — presumably Chancellor Friedrich Merz — to say that he had "everything under control."

DW Fact check: False. Germany has detailed procedures governing the handling and counting of postal ballots. Postal votes are transported, stored and opened according to established rules, and their counting takes place publicly.

Members of the public are generally allowed to observe the election process, including the counting of votes, without having to demonstrate a particular interest or affiliation. This applies to postal ballot counting as well.

That means election officials do not simply open postal ballots and count them behind closed doors. The process is conducted by election boards, whose work can be observed by members of the public and each parties' representatives.

blocks.caption: In Germany, eligible voters can be called upon by local authorities to serve as election workers and are generally required by law to accept the roleImage: ABBfoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: In an interview with German public broadcaster ARD Christa Dieckmann, Saxony-Anhalt's state election commissioner, pointed to public observation as an important safeguard. "The best way to ensure the fairness of the election is to come to the polling station as an observer for elections as the basis for choosing a legitimate government," she said.

DW Fact check also encountered numerous claims promoting what has been dubbed the "nursing home theory," which alleges that elderly people who are unable to vote in person may not be casting their ballots freely, but could instead be pressured or influenced by certain political parties or caregivers.

DW Fact check has investigated similar claims in the past, many of which have been promoted by AfD politicians. It has found no substantial evidence to support the broader allegation that postal voting in nursing homes is systematically manipulated or that elderly voters are routinely pressured into voting for particular parties.
A familiar claim beyond Germany

The doubts surrounding postal voting are not unique to Germany. Similar claims have surfaced during elections in other democracies, often becoming entangled with broader political battles over the legitimacy of elections.

During the 2020 US presidential election, President Donald Trump repeatedly claimed that expanded mail-in voting would lead to widespread fraud. Fact-checkers documented and debunked repeated false and exaggerated claims about the security of mail ballots. Ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, the Trump administration is again seeking to impose new restrictions on mail-in ballots, measures that have faced repeated legal challenges.
Fact-check: The truth on burned votes
Election researcher Stötzer said such claims can become part of a broader political strategy to undermine trust in democratic institutions.
"Right-wing populist parties strategically fuel these doubts," Stötzer said, adding that such claims can later be used to justify electoral law changes that benefit those parties.
He said the immediate impact of such allegations may be limited. But if they are repeated election after election, the longer-term consequences could be more serious.
"Public trust in electoral institutions could suffer," Stötzer said. Election results that are considered undesirable could then routinely be attributed to alleged irregularities in postal voting.
This is a collaborative project between ARD-faktenfinder, and DW Fact check.
