articles.title: Civilians among at least 60 killed in Yemen as ground fighting escalates
articles.summary:
Houthi rebel offensive against government forces on west coast leads to some of deadliest clashes in years

Clashes between Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-aligned Houthi…

blocks.text: Clashes between Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-aligned Houthi rebel movement have killed more than 60 people, including civilians, as the Houthis pushed forward with a military offensive on Yemen’s western coast.

Twenty-six government troops and 31 Houthi fighters were killed during several hours of fighting in the country’s south-west on Saturday, medical and military sources told Agence France-Presse (AFP). A missile strike also killed six civilians and injured seven others travelling by bus in the city of Taiz.

The killings were the latest in a series of bloody clashes in recent days as the Houthis continued an offensive in western Taiz and southern Hodeidah along the Red Sea coast. On Friday, 129 were killed in fighting between rebel and government forces, according to an AFP tally.

The fighting is some of the deadliest in years, after the collapse in July of the 2022 ceasefire. The truce fell apart after an Iranian plane attempted to land in Houthi-controlled Sana’a, triggering attacks by the Yemeni government on the airport.

The Houthis are trying to beat back governmental troops to capture strategic hills overlooking Bab al-Mandeb in order to advance towards port cities on the coast. So far, they have managed to capture areas in western Taiz.

In Taiz, a government military officer said the “coming hours will be decisive” as the Houthis had taken positions near the city a day before. They added that reinforcements had been arriving from Aden to try to stem the Houthi advance.
On Friday, government forces said that they had recaptured the al-Khazan and al-Makahna hills west of Taiz, two strategically important areas for controlling the region.
The Houthis had previously controlled the port city of al-Makha overlooking Bab al-Mandeb, before being pushed out by government forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition.

The Bab al-Mandeb strait is a crucial maritime chokepoint for ships heading to the Suez canal. About 10% of global maritime trade passes through the strait. Saudi Arabia has been using the strait to export oil for months after the start of the US-Iran war.
If shipping is disrupted in Bab al-Mandeb, it will only further raise the cost of global goods, which has already rocketed as a result of the virtual closure of the strait of Hormuz since March 2026.

If the Houthis manage to recapture the port city and take key areas along the Red Sea coast, it will help them control naval traffic in the Red Sea. In July, the Houthis declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, and they have repeatedly disrupted traffic in solidarity with Gaza since the start of the war there in October 2023.

Yemen has been embroiled in a civil war since 2014, when the Houthis and allied forces took the capital city of Sana’a and pushed the then government out of power. A Saudi-led coalition then began a military intervention to support the Yemeni government and fight the Houthis, a strategic ally of Iran.

At least 150,000 people in Yemen have been killed in the fighting, and hundreds of thousands more have died from related causes such as hunger and diseases. About 4.5 million people have been displaced by the fighting and more than 18.2 million are in dire need of humanitarian assistance, according to the UN.

Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Saturday called on the Supreme Court to act on a complaint filed last year by former Ombudsman Samuel Martires against seven Court of Appeals (CA) justices for alleged gross ignorance of the law.
In a radio program on Saturday, Remulla said his office was responding to the Supreme Court’s challenge to file complaints over alleged misconduct in the judiciary.
“Ang ginagawa namin ngayon, iniipon namin lahat ‘yung graveyard namin ng mga reversed cases and TROs issued. Sa admin ito. So iniipon namin ‘yan, ipa-publish namin ‘yan,” he said.
(What we are doing now is collecting all the reversed cases and TROs issued in administrative cases. We are compiling them and will publish them.)
GMA News Online sought the side of the Supreme Court for comment and will update this story once a response is received.

Remulla recalled that Martires filed the complaint on March 21, 2025, against Associate Justices Louis Acosta, Marlene Gonzales-Sison, Rex Bernardo Pascual, Mary Charlene Hernandez-Azura, Roberto Quiroz, Rafael Antonio Santos, and Ferdinand Baylon.
The former Ombudsman accused the CA justices of alleged gross ignorance of the law and conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service.
The complaint stemmed from the justices’ issuance of a temporary restraining order (TRO) against a preventive suspension order involving eight members of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Antique.
“To date, there appears to be no public record of the Judicial Integrity Board or the Supreme Court having acted on or resolved the complaint,” Remulla said.
Remulla underscored his office’s mandate to inform the public about such cases.

“We will also inform them of everything, but we will also inform the public. Since you're inviting us to file the complaints, we will also inform the public. It's our duty to inform the public of these things that have happened,” he said. — MCG, GMA News

articles.title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong
articles.summary: As the UN adopts a new world map to reflect Africa's true size, let's take a closer look at what different maps get right and wrong.

blocks.text: The now widely used Mercator map was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.
Its main purpose was to help European sailors navigate the oceans, as cartography Professor James Cheshire at University London College explained.

"He wanted a straight line to be drawn on a map to look like a straight line in reality if you followed a compass bearing," he told the BBC. "That was what it was intended to do, and that's what it does brilliantly well."
To keep those angles correct on a flat map, Mercator had to stretch the grid lines wider as they moved away from the equator toward the poles.
His map accommodates for the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem much smaller than they are, with countries nearer the poles appearing stretched.
The distortion is a result of it being impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart.
More than 450 years on, Mercator's creation is still the basis for many of the maps we see in classrooms, on TV and online, including Google Maps.

But critics of the Mercator map say there is a psychological effect to viewing some places as smaller than they actually are and others as larger, as we instinctively view bigger things as more important.
For Kenyan geographer Kioko Muendo, this has implicitly downplayed Africa's vast resources, population and investment opportunities.
"Maps are more than just guides for travellers - they shape how regions are perceived politically and economically," he told the BBC.

articles.title: PNP: VP Sara has not reported threats, harassment
articles.summary: Philippine National Police chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said Vice President Sara Duterte has yet to report to the PNP any threat against her and her family. Nartatez said this in a…

blocks.text: Published September 5, 2026 9:31pm
Philippine National Police chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said Vice President Sara Duterte has yet to report to the PNP any threat against her and her family.
Nartatez said this in a statement hours after Duterte said that she had been receiving threats and harassment since 2023, the year she broke away from the Marcos administration.
She added that she feared for her children.
Nartatez said the PNP said it has taken note of the concerns raised by the vice president, vowing that it would monitor the situation.
"To date, however, the Vice President has not reported to the PNP any threat to her life or to the safety of her family, including the threats she said date back to 2023," Nartatez said.
"Likewise, the PNP has not monitored any verified threat against the Vice President or her family," he added.
Nartatez also said the police provided security to Duterte when she posted bail. She was able to safely arrive and leave the court.
"The PNP remains open to receiving any document, report, or statement concerning the reported threats," Nartatez said.
Duterte on Saturday posted bail at a Quezon City court, a day after the issuance of an arrest warrant against her over her grave threats case.
The QC Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 98 set the bail at P120,000 per count. It found that there is probable cause to hold Duterte for trial, prompting it to issue an arrest warrant against her.
Shortly before she posted bail, Poa told reporters that Duterte was considered "surrendered."
GMA News' Jonathan Andal quoted Duterte's counsel Paul Lawrence Lim as saying the vice president did not have her mugshot taken inside the courtroom.
She took the stairs to and from the QC RTC-Branch 98 inside the Hall of Justice, saying she wanted to be seen by the media amid her security concerns.
In a statement, Duterte said she does not feel safe.
"I have documented threats and harassment since 2023. I fear for my children. I do not feel they are safe if I am with them," she said.
"Umalis na nga ako kung nasaan mga anak ko para pumunta sa korte pero pumunta pa rin ang pulis," Duterte added.
"I do not feel safe. Pakiramdam ko papatayin nila ako," the vice president said.

Duterte did not appear before the Quezon City court on Friday, the day that the warrant was issued. Additional police forces had been deployed at the Hall of Justice, with cops bringing inside the building a backdrop used for taking mugshots.
Policemen were securing the area on Saturday as well. Poa and Lim arrived at the Hall of Justice ahead of the vice president.

To recall, the DOJ filed three counts of grave threats against the vice president over her remarks that she hired an individual to kill President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former speaker Martin Romualdez, should an alleged plot against her succeed.

Following this, Duterte filed a motion to quash on the ground of jurisdiction, arguing that she and other impeachable officers have limited procedural immunity while in office under the 1987 Constitution.
The court held the oral arguments on Duterte’s motion in late August.
For her part, Duterte previously said her remarks were "maliciously taken out of logical context."
The vice president's alleged grave threats against Marcos is also the basis of one of the Articles of Impeachment against her in the ongoing trial before the Senate impeachment court. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: US envoys meet with Putin, leave Russia for Kyiv
articles.summary: Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow to try to revive the Ukraine peace talks. They are also scheduled to visit Kyiv on Sunday.
articles.byline: Zac Crellin, Nik Martin, Sean Sinico

image.caption: US special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow on SaturdayImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: The US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday evening.
"The situation is of course not simple," Putin told the US officials in footage aired on Russian state media.
Putin and US envoys held "useful" talks on a range of ideas to end the war in Ukraine, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters.
According to Russian state news agency TASS, US envoys left Moscow after the meeting.

Earlier, US President Donald Trump did not provide any details on the potential peace plan, including whether it involved Ukraine giving territory to Russia as he has previously suggested. Instead, he said, "We have an idea for peace."
Russia, Ukraine pause strikes for three days
Russia will pause strikes against Kyiv for three days, the Kremlin said earlier on Saturday, coinciding with peace negotiations led by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Putin "has ordered that no strikes be carried out against Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight today," Kremlin spokesperson Dmirty Peskov told state media.
It comes after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy already committed to pausing airstrikes for the talks.

"As with previous diplomatic visits by the American side, we will ensure the normal functioning of Russian airspace so that the negotiators can arrive safely. We are concerned about their safety, not about Russia," Zelenskyy said.
US envoys to visit Kyiv next
Zelenskyy announced on Friday that Kushner and Witkoff would visit Ukraine on Sunday following talks in Moscow.

Recent media reports have questioned whether the pair would indeed travel to Ukraine. Despite trips to Moscow to meet with Russian officials, the US envoys have not visited Kyiv since Trump's reelection last year.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy said he had been in contact with Kushner and Witkoff.
"I ⁠have ​just spoken ​with the US president’s ​envoys," Zelenskyy said ‌on Telegram.
"From the moment of this conversation, ​we ⁠are ready to observe a ⁠ceasefire ​in airstrikes against the cities involved in the negotiation process."

Trump had promised to end the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, on his first day back in office, but has more recently said that the feat was more complicated than expected. In the past, he has blamed Ukraine for the Russian invasion and a "personality problem" between the countries' leaders for the continued fighting.

blocks.caption: Kushner and Witkoff met with Russia's Putin (left) in January; they have not been to KyivImage: Alexander Kazakov/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool Photo via AP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Drone strikes continue
Meanwhile, a Russian drone hit the headquarters of Ukraine's domestic security service (SBU) in Kyiv on Friday.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the strike "a major escalation" of the war.
"Moscow launched this strike during a renewed push for peace — laying bare its true rejection of diplomacy," he wrote on X.
Zelenskyy said he ordered "an appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike."
Ukraine has also launched repeated drone strikes on Russian oil infrastructure and the retail giant Wildberries.

articles.title: Critics, Dutertes react to arrest order in VP Sara's grave threats case
articles.summary: After Vice President Sara Duterte asked who would be held accountable if something happened to her following the issuance of an arrest warrant in her grave threats case, Bicol Saro party-list…

blocks.text: Published September 5, 2026 8:24pm

After Vice President Sara Duterte asked who would be held accountable if something happened to her following the issuance of an arrest warrant in her grave threats case, Bicol Saro party-list Representative Terry Ridon on Saturday said she should answer for the allegations against her.
A Quezon City court issued an arrest warrant for Duterte over alleged grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.
In front of the Quezon City Hall of Justice on Saturday, before posting bail, Duterte said she did not feel safe.
“I do not feel safe at all. Sinong sasagot kapag namatay ako mamayang gabi? Sinong mananagot?” she said.
(Who will be accountable if I die tonight? Who will be liable?)

“‘Sinong mananagot?’ Kayo po, Madam Vice President, ang kailangang managot at sumagot sa mga alegasyong kinakaharap ninyo. Tama na po ang drama. Wala naman pong grave threats case ngayon kung hindi dahil sa mga pahayag na naging batayan ng kasong isinampa laban sa inyo,” Ridon said in a statement.

(“Who will be accountable?” You, Madam Vice President, need to be accountable and answer for the allegations you are facing. Enough drama. There would be no grave threats case now if not for the statements that became the basis for the case filed against you.)
“Harapin po ninyo ang proseso at ilahad po ninyo ang inyong depensa sa korte,” he added.
(Face the process and present your defense in court.)

Meanwhile, ML Party-list Representative Leila de Lima, who spent five years in detention during former President Rodrigo Duterte’s administration on drug-related charges, said the issuance of the arrest warrant means the court found sufficient basis to examine the evidence against the Vice President.

“VP Sara may not be used to being held accountable, but now she must answer the accusations against her in a criminal court. Hindi na nga dapat tumagal ito (This shouldn’t have taken this long), but at least, it's finally happening,” De Lima said on Friday.
In a separate Facebook post, De Lima asked, “Bakit sila umiiwas at natatakot sa due process?”
(Why are they evading and afraid of due process?)
'Political harassment'
Duterte’s relatives in the House of Representatives defended her and criticized the arrest warrant.
“I am with VP Inday. I am a Filipino, and I don’t feel safe,” Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo “Pulong” Duterte said in a Facebook post after his sister posted bail.
In a separate statement, Pulong’s son, Davao City 2nd District Representative Omar Duterte, called the arrest warrant “a clear act of political harassment.”

Omar Duterte likened the case to what was done to former President Rodrigo Duterte, who is currently detained at the International Criminal Court and awaiting trial on crimes against humanity charges in connection with his administration’s war on drugs.
“To the Filipino people, I ask you with all sincerity: please wake up and see what the current administration is doing,” Omar Duterte said. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Rescuers in Nepal pull 2 people alive from the debris 10 days after devastating floods
articles.summary: Rescuers in Nepal pulled out a Chinese man and a woman in separate operations Saturday, 10 days after devastating floods hit the country, as teams continued searching for thousands of missing people.

image.caption: A Chinese national is shown after being rescued by soldiers during an ongoing operation at the Trishuli-3A hydropower project, in Nepal's Rasuwa district, on Saturday. (Nepal Army/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
Rescuers in Nepal pulled out a Chinese man and a woman in separate operations Saturday, 10 days after devastating floods hit the country, as teams continued searching for thousands of missing people.
900 workers still missing, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in various tunnels

Rescuers in Nepal pulled out a Chinese man and a woman in separate operations on Saturday, 10 days after devastating floods hit the country, as teams continued searching for thousands of missing people.

The man was rescued from a hydropower tunnel, according to a social media post by the country's prime minister's office, bringing the total to three workers pulled alive from the Trishuli hydropower project. Two Nepalese workers were rescued on Friday.

Nepal's army said a joint rescue team of Nepalese military personnel and South Korean disaster experts rescued the man from a 225-metre tunnel and that he was undergoing a health assessment. Images showed him being evacuated by helicopter, with an army medic checking on him during the flight.
A photo released by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV showed two rescuers carrying the man out of the tunnel.
CCTV shared audio of the man talking to an officer, saying how he repeatedly shouted whenever he saw the rescue crews' lights, but they could not hear him.

items: 2 trapped workers rescued from hydropower tunnel 9 days after Nepal floods

blocks.text: "When they rescued me today, when they shone [the light] before my eyes, I couldn't believe it," he said.
The man was taken to hospital and was in stable condition, according to CCTV.

Rescue efforts have increasingly focused on 12 hydropower projects across Nepal, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said. Specialized rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects, hoping to find survivors.
2 workers rescued from buried Nepal tunnel
In flood-hit Nuwakot town, a woman was rescued alive from a house, Nepal's army spokesperson said Saturday. Officials said she was airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment.
Images released by Nepal's army showed rescuers finding the woman covered in mud inside the damaged house. They gave her bottled water before pulling her to safety, wrapped in a grey blanket.
At least 1,300 people were killed in the Aug. 26 floods, which were likely caused by a glacier collapse, and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to Nepal's disaster management agency.

articles.title: Rescuers in Nepal find two more people alive after flood disaster
articles.summary:
Chinese man at Trishuli hydropower project and Nepali woman in Nuwakot found 10 days into rescue operation

Emergency responders rescued a Chinese man and a Nepali woman in two separate…

blocks.text: Emergency responders rescued a Chinese man and a Nepali woman in two separate operations on Saturday, as authorities continued to search for thousands of people missing 10 days after massive floods hit Nepal.

The Nepali military said a joint team comprising personnel from its army and South Korean disaster experts rescued the man from a 225-metre (740ft) tunnel in the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, and that he was undergoing a health assessment. Pictures showed him being evacuated by helicopter after being carried out of the tunnel.

Rescue efforts have focused on a dozen hydropower projects across Nepal, where about 900 workers are missing, 500 of whom are thought to be trapped in huge tunnels. International rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the US have been searching through debris and damaged structures at the projects to try to find survivors.
Two Nepali workers were rescued from another tunnel in a hydro-station on the Trishuli River on Friday.
Experts have said that as time passes, the possibility of finding missing people alive in the tunnels is diminishing.

The Nepali woman, 64, was rescued from a damaged house in the devastated town of Nuwakot. Photos published by the Nepali army showed rescuers discovering the woman submerged in mud before she was pulled to safety and airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment.
Members of Nepal’s police force cheered as she was pulled from the home, the lower half of which was buried in thick sludge.

Emergency responders have been working to find survivors from the devastating floods in Nepal, which were triggered by a glacial and rock collapse on 26 August. Their work has been complicated by the massive infrastructural damage caused by the floods, with more than 40 bridges having collapsed and rivers swelling unpredictably.
At least 1,375 people have been killed in the floods, with more than 5,000 missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

articles.title: How haze from Indonesian fires impacts Southeast Asia
articles.summary: JAKARTA, Indonesia—Thick smog has blanketed parts of Indonesia as the vast archipelago for weeks battles to contain fires that have burned large swathes of Borneo and Sumatra. The hazardous smoke has…

blocks.text: JAKARTA, Indonesia—Thick smog has blanketed parts of Indonesia as the vast archipelago for weeks battles to contain fires that have burned large swathes of Borneo and Sumatra.
The hazardous smoke has led to an increase in respiratory problems, forced schools to close, and has been drifting to neighboring countries including Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines.
Here’s what to know:
Where are the fires?
Most of the fires are concentrated on Borneo island, home to vast tropical jungle that Indonesia shares with Brunei and Malaysia, as well as Sumatra.
So far this year, nearly 300,000 hectares of land have burned in Indonesia, according to an independent estimate from the Nusantara Atlas portal.
Indonesia saw an uptick in carbon emissions since late July.
By the end of last month, the levels were comparable to previous El Nino years of 2015 and 2019, Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) senior scientist Mark Parrington told AFP.

“We’re seeing already now… really extreme fire emissions comparable to those previous strong El Niño years, and also the extent of the smoke and the haze and the air quality impacts,” Parrington said.
Fires in the archipelago have released more than 23 million metric tons of carbon emissions between August 28 and September 3, according to CAMS’ Fire Emission Watch portal.
It was higher than 20.7 million metric tons of emissions from fires over the same period in 2015, which was a strong El Niño year.
What causes the fires?

Analysts said that the El Niño weather phenomenon, which the United Nations said this week could turn out to be the strongest in four decades, has contributed to creating drier conditions in Indonesia and made it easier for fires to spread.
But slash-and-burn land-clearing practices also contributed to the damage, said David Gaveau, founder of the Nusantara Atlas.
“El Niño does not ignite fires. It creates the dry conditions that allow human-started fires to escape and become very large,” he told AFP.
The fires are difficult to extinguish because many occurred on peatlands, a wetland ecosystem with layers of partially decomposed organic materials that become flammable when dry.
Between January and August this year, more than 210,000 hotspots were detected in peatland areas across the country, according to NGO Pantau Gambut.
“Peat is a naturally wet ecosystem and stores large amounts of organic material. When peat is drained, this organic material is converted into fuel,” Pantau Gambut spokesman Wahyu Perdana said.
What is the impact?
More than five million people across Borneo and Sumatra are directly exposed to the health risks from haze, deputy health minister Dante Saksono Harbuwono said last month.
Over 1.4 million students were attending classes remotely, with many schools closed due to worsening air quality, an education ministry official said this week.
In Malaysia, soaring pollution levels prompted the government on Friday to declare an emergency in a region of the Sarawak state in Borneo, with nearly 650 schools closed next week.

In the Philippines, air quality was slowly returning to normal after a week of reaching “very unhealthy” and “severely unhealthy” PM 2.5 levels that saw officials shutter schools in cities and provinces citing the drifting haze.
The haze also drove air quality in Singapore’s central region to an “unhealthy” level on Friday, the country’s National Environment Agency data showed. /apl

articles.title: Nepal tunnel rescue revives hopes 10 days after flood
articles.summary: KATHMANDU, Nepal—Rescuers in Nepal pulled a Chinese alive on Saturday from a tunnel buried by debris, as emergency response teams dug with new vigor in the search for missing people 10 days after…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU, Nepal—Rescuers in Nepal pulled a Chinese alive on Saturday from a tunnel buried by debris, as emergency response teams dug with new vigor in the search for missing people 10 days after catastrophic flooding.

A joint rescue team comprising personnel from the Nepal Army and foreign experts rescued the man from 225 meters (738 feet) inside the tunnel of the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project in Rasuwa district, a military statement said.
A picture of the rescue published on the army’s Facebook page shows the man, identified only as Luhaitao, with his arms around the shoulders of two camouflage-clad rescuers.
He looked alert but his hands were covered in thick, slimy mud.
“His health is currently being assessed and further search and rescue operations are continuing,” the army said.

The survivor was among hundreds of hydropower workers who went missing since a tsunami-like wall of water and mud swept through the China-Nepal border following a vast glacial and rock collapse on August 26.
Two Nepali hydropower workers were rescued on Friday at the Trishuli 3A tunnel, where searches continued alongside multiple other sites, with at least 12 hydropower projects destroyed by the floods.
So far, 1,344 bodies have been recovered in Nepal, according to the national disaster agency, with around 5,000 people missing.
In China, state media said 31 people had been killed and 531 were missing. That takes the overall death toll to 1,375 people, and more than 5,500 missing.
Thousands in relief camps
Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP that “work is underway at the tunnels” to locate any survivors.
The government initially said it believed more than 100 workers could be alive inside multiple tunnels.
Rescuers called it a “miracle” after the two Nepali men, caked in mud, were pulled out alive on Friday, nine days after being trapped by the flood.
They were taken to hospital and are said to be in a stable condition.
Experts from India, China, Australia and South Korea have been aiding Nepali rescuers in their search of survivors inside blocked tunnels.
With morgues overflowing, some 1,030 bodies hade been buried in mass graves after taking DNA samples for future identification, Nepal Police said Saturday.
Prime Minister Balendra Shah promised to provide “safe and comfortable accommodation” for thousands of people displaced by the diaster and currently living in temporary relief camps.
“We know that staying there (in camps) is not easy for you,” he said in a Friday post on social media.
But he promised to “once again create an environment where you can dream about and build your future.” /apl

articles.title: ‘It cost me many friendships’: former Brazil military chief reveals inside struggle to stop Bolsonaro’s coup
articles.summary:
Carlos de Almeida Baptista Júnior describes 2022 meeting in new book as ex-leader’s son vies with Lula for presidency

The far-right populist Jair Bolsonaro was in his final days as Brazil’s…
articles.byline: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: The far-right populist Jair Bolsonaro was in his final days as Brazil’s president when, six weeks after losing the election and still refusing to recognise the result, he summoned the heads of the armed forces to a meeting.
The defence minister, Gen Paulo Sérgio Nogueira de Oliveira, took out a document from a plastic folder and handed copies to the commanders of the navy, army and air force.
It was a draft decree proposing to invalidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s election in October 2022 and keep Bolsonaro in power.

“The draft coup decree – which some people still insist to this day never existed – was there, awaiting approval or rejection; consensus or a majority,” writes the then head of the air force, Lt Brig Carlos de Almeida Baptista Júnior, in a new book coming out this month.

After learning that the document would prevent Lula from taking office, Baptista Júnior told the defence minister he refused even to receive it: “The air force will not take part in this.” He then stood up and left the room.

blocks.caption: Carlos de Almeida Baptista Júnior.   Photograph: Personal archive, courtesy of Carlos de Almeida Baptista Júnior

blocks.text: The extensive investigation and trial that convicted Bolsonaro of attempting a coup concluded that the plot failed to move forward mainly because the heads of two of the three armed forces – Baptista Júnior and the army commander, Gen Marco Antônio Freire Gomes – refused to take part.
The navy commander, Adm Almir Garnier Santos, was convicted, as was Nogueira. Both are serving their sentences at military facilities, while Bolsonaro is under house arrest.
Freire Gomes has kept a low profile, but Baptista Júnior, speaking to the Guardian by video call, said he had decided to write a book to help prevent history from repeating itself.
In the book, the 65-year-old former fighter pilot gives a detailed, first-hand account of the various ways in which Bolsonaro tried to cling to power.

Baptista Júnior said he was motivated by the fact that, despite the abundance of evidence presented during the former president’s trial, opinion polls still showed that about a third of the population did not believe there had been an attempted coup.

“Keeping in power someone who lost an election is a coup d’état,” he said, speaking from his home in Brasília, where he was dressed in civilian clothes – having recently retired – and about to pick up his grandson from school.

The book, the Portuguese title of which translates as I Said No! – An Anti-Coup Bulwark, is due to be published on 15 September, about two weeks before the first round of the presidential election, in which Lula will face one of Bolsonaro’s sons, the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro.

Some Bolsonaro supporters have accused Baptista Júnior of trying to influence the vote, although he makes clear that he will vote for neither Lula nor Flávio, and criticises both in the book. He said the timing of the book was simply the result of the writing and editing process.

blocks.caption: President Lula addressing supporters at a campaign rally in São Bernardo do Campo this month. Photograph: Miguel Schincariol/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Despite writing that he voted for the far-right populist in the 2018 and 2022 elections, and even recounting a lighthearted moment at a barbecue when he saw the first lady reprimand the president for drinking beer, Baptista Júnior is critical of Bolsonaro, a former army captain who spent 30 largely undistinguished years as a city councillor and then congressman before reaching the presidency.

He describes his former boss as someone with “significant limitations in political, institutional and administrative experience” and an “almost total imperviousness to outside opinions or information that did not conform to the ‘truths’ he had already established as his own” – citing his refusal to accept facts such as the scientific evidence supporting Covid-19 vaccination.

During the election, Bolsonaro became “entirely consumed by his own efforts to remain in office”, writes Baptista Júnior. After repeatedly casting doubt on the vote, the president ordered the armed forces to investigate the electronic voting system, but refused to accept their reports when they found no irregularities.
“He may still not believe the election result even today. Whether that is a matter of character, personality or something pathological, I don’t know,” said Baptista Júnior.

The book touches on, but does not go into detail about, one of the most shocking revelations from the coup investigation: a plan drawn up by army special forces to kidnap or assassinate Lula, the newly elected vice-president and a supreme court justice. Baptista Júnior writes that he was not summoned to those meetings and only learned about them through the press.

He does, however, recount more than a dozen meetings in which Bolsonaro summoned the heads of the armed forces to discuss ways to remain in power. At one of them, he witnessed the army chief tell the president, after hearing a proposal for an institutional rupture: “If you do that, I’ll have to arrest you.”

Baptista Júnior had already given that account in testimony, and during the trial both Freire Gomes and Bolsonaro denied it. But he stands by his account in the book, writing that it was not something anyone present would forget.

Saying no to the coup cost the pilot “many friendships”, he said. Even some military personnel still call him a “traitor” or a “watermelon”, a slur for soldiers seen as green on the outside because of their uniforms, but communist red within.

The attacks started soon after the air force chief refused to join the plot, when the army general Walter Souza Braga Netto, whom Baptista Júnior considered a friend, ordered other military officers to attack him on social media and “make his life and his family’s hell”. Braga Netto, Bolsonaro’s running mate, was also convicted over the attempted coup.

Most of Baptista Júnior’s revelations in the book initially emerged in 2024, when he was summoned to testify to federal police and only then, more than a year after leaving office, revealed that he had witnessed an attempted coup.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Jair Bolsonaro face off with police Brasília in January 2023 in a demonstration calling for the overthrow of President Lula. Photograph: André Borges/EPA

blocks.text: Juliano da Silva Cortinhas, who worked on the civilian side of the defence ministry between 2013 and 2016, before the Bolsonaro administration, said: “It’s positive that he [Baptista Júnior] and the army chief said no to the coup, but as a matter of duty they should have reported it to the police as soon as it happened.”

Cortinhas, who heads a security research group at the University of Brasília, said the armed forces could not present themselves as the “saviours” of democracy because that would be like “tripping society up and then holding out a hand to help it back to its feet”.

“It was the commanders who allowed active-duty officers to take part in politics,” he said, noting that the Bolsonaro administration had by far the largest number of military personnel serving in civilian posts since the end of the brutal 1964–85 military dictatorship.

Cortinhas sees as positive the fact that high-ranking officers were convicted of an attempted coup for the first time, but noted that others involved in the plot escaped justice, and many were not even identified.
“The risk of a new coup is even greater today,” he said.

The new factor, he said, was the US president, Donald Trump, who has sought to influence elections across Latin America in support of far-right candidates such as Flávio Bolsonaro. In 2022, when Joe Biden was in the White House, Bolsonaro’s vice-president acknowledged that attempting a coup would leave Brazil in a “difficult position before the international community”.

Cortinhas said he feared that if Lula was re-elected and Trump refused to recognise the result, some members of Brazil’s military could feel emboldened. “Coup-supporting groups remain within the armed forces,” he said.
Baptista Júnior confirmed that, although it was difficult to know how many, there remained active-duty military personnel who believed a coup d’état would be justified under certain circumstances.
“That’s why eternal vigilance is the best path,” he said.

articles.title: Gaza refugee says sister-in-law ‘would be alive’ if Home Office had let her come to UK
articles.summary:
Anwar, who lives in Glasgow, says Home Office refused visa application despite Maryam having cancer

A man living in the UK has said he believes his sister-in-law who died from cancer in Gaza…

blocks.text: A man living in the UK has said he believes his sister-in-law who died from cancer in Gaza would still be alive today if the Home Office had agreed to bring her and her family to Britain.

Anwar, who lives in Glasgow, fled Gaza in 2020 and was granted refugee status in the UK in 2021. After the destruction of large areas of Gaza by Israeli forces following the Hamas attacks on Israel in October 2023, he applied to bring his brother Hassan, Hassan’s wife, Maryam, their two young children and other family members to the UK in October 2025. He said the Home Office rejected their application.

The process required them to travel to a visa application centre (VAC) for biometric checks, but there was not, and still is not, a VAC in Gaza. It is difficult for Palestinians to leave the territory to access a VAC elsewhere.
In April this year the family asked the Home Office to waive this requirement and grant permission for “predetermination” of their application and “biometric excusal”.
The Home Office is understood to have rejected this request, so the family launched a legal challenge. The Home Office agreed to reconsider its decision but issued a new refusal in July.

Prior to the second Home Office refusal, and shortly after Maryam gave birth to Ismail, who is now seven months old, she was diagnosed with renal cell carcinoma, which had spread to her lungs. Doctors in Gaza said they did not have the facilities to treat her.

The family provided the Home Office with medical evidence concerning Maryam’s condition, including cancer test results and medical referral reports. They also provided evidence of their living conditions in Gaza, which involved sleeping in tents and shortages of food, medicine and clean water.
Anwar said the Home Office again refused the family’s request for predetermination and biometric excusal but that it accepted the evidence of Maryam’s cancer.
In the Home Office’s letter refusing the visa application on 31 July, seen by the Guardian, officials stated: “Given the current situation in Gaza, reliable healthcare may not be accessible.”

They accepted that Maryam was facing a significant risk of harm because she was in a conflict zone and could not travel to a VAC. Although the Home Office officials found the circumstances relating to travel to a VAC “somewhat compelling”, they concluded that owing to the difficulty in travelling to the VAC, it was “in the best interests of the children to stay with their parents and delay travel to the UK” for the time being.

They concluded the family’s situation did not meet the threshold for “compelling circumstances” and said that pre-entry checks needed to be carried out because the family came from “a territory where terrorists operate”.
In the legal challenge, the family’s lawyers stated: “It is difficult to understand what circumstances would ever qualify as compelling if the present circumstances do not.”
Maryam died from cancer on 28 August.

Gordon McKee, the Labour MP for Glasgow South, raised the family’s case with ministers in June. He warned about Maryam’s deteriorating health and the consequences of the collapse of reliable healthcare in Gaza.
In his letter to Mike Tapp, then a Home Office minister, McKee said the case involved “exceptional humanitarian circumstances”. He asked Tapp to consider reviewing the case personally.

Anwar said: “We believe Maryam’s case raises serious questions about how the UK government deals with Palestinian families in Gaza who are trying to reunite with their families in Britain, particularly when a family member becomes seriously ill while trapped in a conflict zone and unable to safely reach a VAC.
“I believe that if the Home Office had agreed to bring Maryam and her family from Gaza to the UK when we first applied last October, Maryam would still be alive today.

“Maryam is now gone, but her family remains in Gaza. We are now urgently asking the UK government to intervene to protect Maryam’s surviving family members and to find a way to bring them to safety and reunite them with their family in the UK.”
Speaking from Gaza, Maryam’s husband, Hassan, said: “I am struggling to come to terms with losing my wife while I remain trapped in Gaza with our children, including our seven-month-old baby.

“Throughout Maryam’s illness, we were trying to find a way for our family to overcome the biometric requirement and move forward with our applications. The Home Office accepted that Maryam had cancer and acknowledged the evidence, but decided that our circumstances were still not compelling enough to justify biometric deferral or predetermination.
“Now I have lost my wife, and I am left trying to protect our children and find a way to get them out of Gaza and to safety.”
Home Office sources said they did not routinely comment on individual cases.

articles.title: Trump signs order to remove endangered species protection for grey wolves
articles.summary: The US president says the move will help ranchers, but conservationists say it could derail efforts to recover populations.

blocks.text: Donald Trump has signed an executive order to remove endangered species protection for the grey wolf and a subspecies, the Mexican wolf.

The US president's decision could pave the way for pastoral farmers to kill the canines to protect their livestock. His order said ranchers played a "vital role" in the food supply chain and American cultural heritage.
But conservation groups have criticised the move, saying it could derail long-term efforts to recover the endangered wolf populations.
There were 319 Mexican wolves in the wild in the US in 2025, up from just four when they were reintroduced in 1998, US Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) figures show.
Meanwhile, there are roughly 18,000 grey wolves across the US, though they are still considered endangered as most of their habitat has been destroyed by humans.

An attempt to de-list them at a federal level in 2022 became tied up in litigation, and some campaigners have indicated they intend to do the same of the US Department of Interior acts on Trump's order.

The executive order does not give ranchers immediate license to shoot wolves preying on livestock, but instead gives Interior Secretary Doug Burgum 90 days to determine whether the grey and Mexican wolf populations had recovered enough to warrant being taken off the endangered species list.
Noting that US livestock herds were at a 75-year low while demand for beef had risen by 10% in the past decade, the order added: "More can and should be done to support this critical industry."
However, environmental groups pointed to studies that suggested wolf attacks on livestock were rare and had little impact on ranchers' income.

"This is a huge distraction to placate a handful of ranchers and make them believe that wolves are a greater threat than President Trump's own policies," said Greta Anderson, deputy director of Western Watersheds Project, which works to conserve wildlife in western US states.

The Wolf Conservation Center noted that ranchers were entitled to up to 100% compensation for any livestock losses caused by wolves under the current system, with individual states providing funding for programmes to deter attacks.

"The Mexican grey wolf is not recovered simply because the population has grown," said Claire Musser, executive director of the Grand Canyon Wolf Recovery Project. "Weakening federal protections now would put decades of recovery work at risk."
The executive order comes as the Trump administration is seeking to lower record-high beef prices for consumers, driven by drought and an outbreak of parasites in US beef stocks.
Ranchers have been frustrated by Trump's decision to loosen restrictions on beef imports to address price rises, putting pressure on their already tight margins.

The US government launched a campaign to systematically exterminate wolves towards the end of the 19th Century. This, along with farmers and landowners trapping and killing wolves, pushed them to the brink of eradication.
Ranchers still view them as a nuisance, which tackling lethally constitutes a federal crime.

articles.title: Snowbirds take their final flight over Toronto until the 2030s at this weekend’s air show
articles.summary: The 77th Canadian International Air Show is roaring back into the city this Labour Day weekend, with high-flying demonstrations at Toronto’s lakeshore.

blocks.text: Toronto
The 77th Canadian International Air Show is roaring back into the city this Labour Day weekend, with high-flying demonstrations at Toronto’s lakeshore.
An array of aircraft will zoom over city’s lakeshore over Labour Day weekend
Snowbirds take their final flight over Toronto until the 2030s at annual air show
The 77th Canadian International Air Show is roaring back into the city this Labour Day weekend, with high-flying demonstrations at Toronto's lakeshore.
This year's air show marks the final Toronto appearance of the Snowbirds, a nine-jet aerobatics team, until their fleet is replaced in the 2030s at the earliest.
The significance of this weekend's performances isn't lost on Maj. Maciej Hatta, the pilot tasked with leading the Snowbirds as they fly in tight formations around the city.
"It's on our minds," he told CBC Radio's Metro Morning.
"[But] obviously I can't be thinking about that the whole time, because we've got a nine-plane formation to worry about leading around the city safely."
CBC News Network's David Common speaks to Retired LCol Dan Dempsey about the Snowbirds
The team's signature CT-114 Tutor jets were ordered by the military as training aircraft in 1961 and have been used for performances for more than five decades.
Hatta, who grew up outside Toronto, says seeing the Snowbirds fly as a child is part of what inspired him to become a pilot in the first place.

"It is touching to hear that everybody's got a slightly different Snowbird story, whether it was watching from a condo in downtown Toronto, or… somebody's dad or or mom working on the team as a technician or pilot,” he said.
Replacements coming ‘as quickly’ as possible: Ottawa
Military officials have been warning for decades that the Tutors have gone far past their intended lifespan and needed to be replaced.
In May, Defence Minister David McGuinty announced that the planes would be grounded after a busy summer performance schedule, ending with a final appearance at the Grey Cup in Calgary.
The Swiss-made, turbo-prop CT-157 Siskin II has been chosen to replace the Snowbird squadron.
"Negotiations are underway with the manufacturer and we intend to procure those aircraft as quickly as we possibly can," McGuinty said at the time.
On Friday, Canadian veterans gathered to watch the Snowbirds during their final rehearsal before the air show.
"This is a wonderful day," said retired air force pilot Mort Lightstone as aircraft zoomed overhead, "These aircrew men and women are a national treasure."
A 77-year Labour Day weekend tradition

This year's air show will also have demonstrations by a Royal Canadian Air Force CF-18 and an RCMP Black Hawk helicopter — though a last-minute schedule change saw the United States' F-16 demonstration team drop out.
The daily performances run from noon to 3:40 p.m. every day from Saturday through to Monday.
The Canadian International Air Show, now in its 77th year, is an end-of-summer fixture — though not one everyone enjoys equally.
PHOTOS | Canadian Snowbirds, RCMP Black Hawk Helicopter, Pink Jet part of this year's lineup:
The noise associated with the event is routinely criticized for being disruptive for people and pets alike, and for upsetting Torontonians who are struggling with PTSD or memories of war.

Hatta says he understands those concerns, but encourages Torontonians to think of the show as a way to inspire future pilots and technicians who may one day help save lives, for example as a part of a search-and-rescue mission.
"There's a little more to it than meets the eye," he said.
On its website FAQ, the air show writes that the show complies with "all regulations, including those published by Transport Canada relating to noise."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kate McGillivray is a writer and newsreader in Toronto. She's worked for the CBC in Montreal, Sherbrooke and St. John's, and she always wants to hear your feedback and story ideas. Get in touch here: kate.mcgillivray@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Germany: From emigration to immigration destination
articles.summary: Migration is a sensitive topic in Germany, with public debate dominated by the fear of uncontrolled immigration. But over two centuries, millions of Germans emigrated in search of a better life.

image.caption: A statue in the port of Bremerhaven commemorates the millions of Germans who emigrated abroadImage: S. Ziese/blickwinkel/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Why should [they] be suffered to swarm into our Settlements, and by herding together establish their Language and Manners to the Exclusion of ours? [...] [They] will shortly be so numerous [...] and will never adopt our Language or Customs."

These defamatory comments about refugees and asylum-seekers sound as if they might have been made today by the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany party (AfD). Yet in this instance, the people vilified and accused of refusing to integrate are Germans — and the harsh judgement was made in the 18th century by none other than Benjamin Franklin, one of the Founding Fathers of the United States.

The pursuit of happiness and a better life are mentioned in the American Declaration of Independence, which Franklin helped write. Over the centuries, they have been the motivation for countless people to turn their backs on their respective homelands.

blocks.caption: Benjamin Franklin, one of the Founding Fathers of the United States, warned against accepting German immigrantsImage: Public Domain

blocks.text: The Germans who emigrated to America in Franklin's lifetime were actually fairly limited in number. By 1820, only about 150,000 had successfully made the journey. Often, they were persuaded by compatriots who told tales of their tremendous success in their new homeland and celebrated the prosperity they had supposedly attained in a very short space of time. What most people back home didn't know was that these recruiters received a commission for every migrant.

"The crossing on a sailing ship cost about what a tradesman would earn in a year," said Simone Blaschka of the German Emigration Center in Bremerhaven. "To be able to afford that, families had to sell all their worldly goods."
A journey into the unknown

They would have had no idea what awaited them on board the ship. During the crossing, which took several weeks, they were packed together below deck in a very confined space, plagued by bedbugs, fleas and rats. Many fell sick with dysentery, typhoid, smallpox or scurvy.

In his book "Journey to Pennsylvania in the Year 1750," the schoolmaster and organist Gottlieb Mittelberger described what he had experienced on the voyage: "Many people whimper, sigh and cry piteously for their homes; most of them get home-sick. Many hundred people necessarily die and perish in such misery, and must be cast into the sea."

blocks.caption: Many European immigrants who came to the US in the 20th century arrived by boat in New YorkImage: Raimund Franken/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: On arrival in America, Mittelberger wrote, the majority of his fellow passengers were effectively auctioned off. These were people without means who were granted free passage after undertaking to work for years as bonded laborers in exchange. In the US, their contracts were sold off. Mittelberger saw families torn apart and parents forced to sell their children.
An invitation from Russia

As these early migrants were traveling to America, there was simultaneously a big wave of emigration from Germany to the east. People followed the call of the Russian czarina, Catherine the Great, herself a German princess by birth.

On July 22, 1763, she issued a manifesto inviting people to come to Russia, with the aim of cultivating uninhabited regions for arable farming. She promised the new arrivals free transport to their chosen place of residence, land, also free of charge, the first year tax-free, schooling, exemption from military service, and a special political status that would allow them to maintain the German language and, for the most part, govern themselves.

blocks.caption: Catherine the Great officially invited Germans to immigrate to Russia in the late 18th centuryImage: akg-images/picture-alliance

blocks.text: However, in the 19th century the American continent once again became the dream destination. "The German population almost doubled in the 19th century, so you can imagine what the job market was like," said Blaschka from the German Emigration Center. The situation was exacerbated by failed harvests and famines.
"People didn't see any future for themselves or their children, and decided to emigrate," she said. In this way, around 6 million Germans were drawn to the New World.
Migration: A burden or an asset?
Germans were far from the only ones who left their homeland.

"Between the beginning of the 19th century and the World War I, there were probably around 60 million Europeans who left their homes," said Jochen Oltmer, a professor at the Institute for Migration Research and Intercultural Studies in Osnabrück. Then, in the mid-20th century, this trend reversed and Europe went from being a continent of emigration to one of immigration.

blocks.caption: Migration researcher Jochen Oltmer has studied the immigration waves to and from Europe in the 19th and 20th centuriesImage: Michael Gründel/NOZ

blocks.text: In the 1950s and '60s, the future looked rosy for postwar West Germany and its "economic miracle." From 1956 onward, so-called "guest worker trains" arrived in stations like Stuttgart, Dortmund and Cologne, carrying Italians, Greeks, Spaniards, Portuguese, Yugoslavs and Turks, attracted by the promise of well-paid jobs in the new Federal Republic.
By the time the ban on recruiting foreign labor came into force in 1973, around 14 million people had come to West Germany as "guest workers." Around 3 million stayed permanently.

Yet Germany still did not consider itself an immigration country. "For a very long time, we were dealing with the mindset: It doesn't matter why people came to the Federal Republic; they don't belong, because in any case they'll leave the country again and disappear," said Oltmer.

blocks.caption: Between 1956 and 1973, around 14 million 'guest workers' came to Germany from other European countriesImage: Hans Heckmann/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In 2025, according to Germany's Federal Statistical Office, more than 30% of Germany's total population had a migrant background. Yet many third- and fourth-generation citizens still don't feel they belong, which has to do with the perspective of the society in which they live.
Who's welcome – and who isn't?
These days, Germany is keen to attract skilled workers, but refugees are only granted asylum if they are politically persecuted in their homeland, or are fleeing war.

As a migration researcher, Oltmer is constantly examining the reasons why some migrants are accepted and others are not. This question was especially relevant in 2015, when refugees came to Germany in very large numbers.

"The attitude was: 'OK, you people from Syria, in light of the Syrian civil war, you are entitled to protection.' But at the same time this society says of people from Afghanistan, 'In your case, we're a bit more sceptical,'" he said.

blocks.caption: Germany took in hundreds of thousands of refugees in 2015, above all people fleeing the civil war in SyriaImage: Johannes Simon/Getty Images

blocks.text: Yet asylum accounts for barely 10% of immigration to Germany, Oltmer explained. The majority of immigrants are not people fleeing their country. "This means that when it comes to scandalization and the creation of certain negative images, we are seeing a massive distortion of the debate." And the descendants of the German emigrants Benjamin Franklin once reviled as "Palatine boors" have long since perfectly integrated into American society.

In Germany, however, integration is taking much longer. "Many people have no possibility of regularizing their status and obtaining a stable residence permit, even though everyone involved knows they can stay, and will stay," said Oltmer. He believes people urgently need to sit down and clarify how they want German society to look in future.
"It may be a very hard, even hurtful discussion. But it's the only way."
Berlin initiative helps immigrant moms find their feet

articles.title: As Canada-U.S. relations sour, border towns of upstate New York fear damage will be permanent
articles.summary: As U.S. President Donald Trump fights with Canada on tariffs and his decision to rename Lake Ontario, Americans along the border in upstate New York fear the heightened fight could spell the end of…

image.caption: People watch the sun set over Lake Ontario in Olcott, N.Y., on Aug. 25. (AP Photo/Adrian Kraus)

blocks.text: At his marina in Sackets Harbor, N.Y., on a cloudy Wednesday afternoon, Mayor Alex Morgia looks toward the water and paints a vivid picture of the beauty he often sees, even on an overcast day.

"Sometimes those are the best sunsets because the sun will peek through underneath and then you get all of the cascading colours on the underside of the clouds," Morgia says, looking out over what has recently become North America's most controversial lake.
"We get sunsets over the lake year-round," Morgia says, before clarifying: "Over Lake Ontario, not to be vague."

Sackets Harbor, located on the lake's eastern shore around a 40-minute drive from the Canadian border, finds itself caught up in a war of words and wares, as the United States and Canada feud over tariffs and U.S. President Donald Trump's decision to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America."

items: Ontario premier unveils Lake Ontario sign in Hamilton as tensions with U.S. escalate

blocks.text: The harbour, Morgia points out, was even mentioned in Trump's executive order.
It's not the first time the quaint village has been at the front lines of a fight between these two nations: Sackets Harbor was the site of two major battles during the War of 1812, Morgia says.
"People find cannonballs in their yard all the time," he said. "People use them as doorstops."

While Morgia downplayed how much support Trump has for renaming the lake, he — along with other U.S. residents and officials living near the border in upstate New York — is concerned this heightened fight could spell the end of close Canadian ties, to the detriment of their communities.

"We had a brief period of time where I thought he was distracted with other problems and was going to leave the Canadians alone and we could be friends again. Obviously, that ship has sailed," Morgia said.
'It hits in the heart'

About a half-hour drive north of Sackets Harbor, on the U.S. side of the Thousand Islands Bridge over the St. Lawrence River, Corey Fram is fretting that the already difficult situation he faces is about to get much worse.

As director of the Thousand Islands Regional Tourism Development Corporation, Fram is responsible for marketing on both sides of the border. But after Trump got elected for a second time, there was a substantial decline in Canadian spending and border crossing, he said.
"It hurts to lose that economic impact of Canadian visitors on the New York side. But in a border community, it hits in the heart," Fram added.
Decline in Canadian cross-border travel continues

While he understands there may be a strategy Washington and Ottawa are each pursuing that buoys their countries' economic standpoints, those efforts have the opposite effect on border communities, he said.
"There's almost a sense that those of us along the border are having to pay the price for what is a supposed economic benefit for the greater good of each of the respective countries," Fram said.

items: U.S. border city residents put their 'Elbows Up' for Canada amid trade war

blocks.text: Anthony Adamczyk is facing the same issue in Ogdensburg, N.Y., about 45-minute drive northeast. He's the executive director of the Ogdensburg Bridge and Port Authority, which owns and manages the local bridge spanning the St. Lawrence.
Despite a slight uptick in border crossings from Canada in January 2025 compared to the previous year, they declined the following month and have never recovered, Adamczyk said.

Overall, traffic volume decreased 23 per cent in 2025 compared to 2024, equating to about 136,000 vehicles. The bridge's toll revenue went down 35 per cent, representing about $536,000 in lost revenue.

Fram's longer-term concern is that the number of Canadian tourists will permanently remain lower. He told CBC's The House that each time a major crisis affects border crossings — like the COVID-19 pandemic or the 9/11 terrorist attacks — the numbers fall and never return.
"My concern is this is yet another step, a big jump down that we're not going to get back to where we were in 2024 anytime soon, and maybe not ever."
Residents divided over Trump's tactics

The ongoing fight over tariffs and Lake Ontario's name puts residents of Ogdensburg and Sackets Harbor in a complicated position. The two areas fall within St. Lawrence County and Jefferson County, respectively — both of which Trump has won by more than 10 points in previous presidential elections.

Outside a Walmart in Ogdensburg, Greg Barr told The House he visits Canada all the time and has never had any issues with Canadians. But when asked about the trade war, he said he thinks the U.S. has been "way too generous."

items: Carney dismisses 'unelected' Trump officials' explanation for why trade talks fell apart

blocks.text: "Not [just] to Canada but to other countries," Barr said. "[Trump's] getting things more even, to me. Maybe he has a different way of doing it, but he does get results."
Jim Rupert, who runs a taxi service that takes clients back and forth from Canada all the time, echoed Barr's view that Trump's tactics are a means of equalizing the playing field.
"I hate to listen to [Trump] half the time because he rambles, he rants, he does this and that, but the policies are solid."
But Carol and Gary Davis, who say they've noticed how much more their groceries cost nowadays, say they can't make sense of Trump's actions.
"When he got elected, gas was going to be cheap, food was going to be cheap," Gary said. "It's just the opposite."
Carol, who voted for Trump in the last election, said she's disappointed with the president — though she felt there weren't better options when she cast her ballot.
"So, yeah, I guess I do have regrets now."
Local Republican lawmaker weighs in

Scott Gray, a Republican assemblyman who represents Ogdensburg and Sackets Harbor, is aware of residents' concerns. He told The House he's not opposed to tariffs, but doesn't want them to harm either his residents or Canadians.
"We have enjoyed a long-time exchange in our economy and our trade, and I think we should try to maintain that," Gray said.
He said he hopes some key irritants, like U.S. access to the Canadian dairy market, can be corrected through trade negotiations. But tariffs, he added, can be disruptive — as are counter-tariffs.
Gray pushed back on behaviour from the White House, including Trump repeatedly calling Canada the 51st state and U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth belittling two female Canadian cadets.
Hegseth's comments on Canadian military 'stupid,' says U.S. Democratic senator
But he also placed some blame at Canada's feet, like when Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Trump could "kiss my ass" in response to tariff threats.

"We need to make sure there's a fair trade deal, and we need to do it without creating animosity and friction, which is largely caused by whatever antics that you want to describe out there," Gray said.

Back at the marina in Sackets Harbor, Morgia questions whether the U.S. government will stop antagonizing its northern neighbour. He's sympathetic to Canadians' calls for Americans to step up and pressure their leaders to back off on punishing their country.

"I guess not until [midterm elections in] November. People are trying, but right now the Republicans control most of the government. And until that changes, I don't think he's going to be held to account."

articles.title: Tate brothers officially indicted with trafficking and sex crimes in Romania
articles.summary: Andrew and Tristan Tate are currently in a Miami jail fighting extradition to the UK over separate charges and deny all the allegations.

blocks.text: The brothers - former kickboxers with dual US and British citizenship - have been under criminal investigation in Romania since December 2022.
They have been mainly based there since 2017, drawing a large social media audience - many of them young men - through misogynistic messages and images of a luxury lifestyle.
Romanian prosecutors described a case as centring on a vulnerable female who was 15 at the time of the alleged offence, in information released on Friday.

She is alleged to have been recruited by Andrew and housed in a building in Luton, Bedfordshire, so he could sexually exploit her. Tristan is alleged to have been an accessory, prosecutors say, using physical aggression to coerce the victim.
DIICOT investigators allege Andrew controlled her through surveillance and physical aggression, and coerced her to perform sex acts on video chats for his financial gain.
Andrew is also accused of moving her to Romania to carry on exploiting her in two of his homes.
He is separately charged with having sex with a minor, who was 15, in Romania.
Prosecutors have also requested four of the brothers' luxury cars worth £710,000 be confiscated. They believe money was laundered through their purchase.
The two brothers were previously indicted in Romania on trafficking charges, but in 2024 an appeals court in Bucharest sent the case back to prosecutors after deeming some evidence inadmissible.
It is not yet clear if DIICOT will seek their extradition from the US and the indictment has to be examined by a judge before any trial can begin.
The Tates have denied all the allegations and say their online personas are not their real personalities.

Their lawyer in Romania, Eugen Constantin Vidineac, said: "Today's decision by DIICOT does not determine guilt and it should not be presented as though it does. It represents the prosecution's latest attempt to bring this case before a court following the failure of its previous indictment to proceed to trial.

"The history of these proceedings matters. The previous indictment was subjected to judicial scrutiny and the court identified significant irregularities which prevented the case from moving forward to trial.

"DIICOT has now chosen to file a new indictment. We will examine every aspect of it with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process.

"Our clients continue to reject the allegations against them. They have the right to the presumption of innocence, the right to properly examine the evidence relied upon against them and the right to mount an effective defence."

Correction 5 September: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated that the Tate brothers were charged with further offences. The article has been updated to make clear they have been officially indicted with offences of which they had already been accused. It has also been updated to reflect that Andrew, not Tristan, was alleged to have recruited the 15-year-old.
