The latest request by Duterte’s lawyers comes after they also urged the TC III to order the prosecution to amend the scope of the charges in terms of counts for a “more defined scope” of the crimes under the jurisdiction of the ICC.

They also asked for an exhaustive list of “underpinning acts which represent the entirety of the charges against the accused.” Duterte, who is detained in the Scheveningen prison complex in The Hague, is accused of three counts of murder as a crime against humanity in connection with the deaths of 76 people from 2013 to 2018. /cb

articles.title: Rome pushing back vs golf cart ‘invasion’
articles.summary: ROME, Italy — Beneath its splendor of monuments and ruins, the Eternal City is taking aim at a modern-day chariot: the golf cart. Even rolling along at a moderate speed, these golf carts have so far…

blocks.text: ROME, Italy — Beneath its splendor of monuments and ruins, the Eternal City is taking aim at a modern-day chariot: the golf cart.
Even rolling along at a moderate speed, these golf carts have so far outpaced regulation—with hundreds of them carrying tourists through Rome’s historic center. But the city is mounting a crackdown.
For critics, the carts are running amok, parking illegally, worsening congestion and unlocking another level of overtourism.
Some local media invoke sensational language, calling it an “invasion” and saying Rome is being “held hostage by golf carts.”
But advocates argue the carts are silent, occupy less space than tourist vans and buses, and don’t choke the air with exhaust that also stains historic monuments.
Enmity on the road
The Associated Press (AP) got a taste of the enmity during a late August ride when a black, eight-seater van pulled up alongside.
“You’re in the middle of the road!” its driver barked. “Move it!”
“Always the same! The road isn’t yours!” the golf cart driver shouted back. Both gesticulated angrily with their free hands, following a time-honored Roman traffic tradition.
Carts like this zip through Rome’s cobblestone alleys, past tourists eating spaghetti carbonara from checkered tablecloths and shops hawking tote bags stamped with clichés (“Ciao Bella!”).
“We don’t have a proper stop for golf carts, so we park where we can—as legal as possible,” driver Martin Halili said.
Little room for parking

Even before the golf cart boom, parking was a pain. Cars, vans, Vespas and motorcycles are stationed atop curbs, crosswalks and medians. Trucks double-park while unloading. Plus, an average 50,000 vehicles enter daily.

Unsurprisingly, some residents are unhappy. “This was the last straw because, unfortunately, there has already been traffic here for a long time, since there are too many categories of vehicles authorized,” Luigi la Licata, head of the Monti neighborhood association, told AP. “The golf cart is the most obvious one—and the latest—but there are many others.”
Golf cart bookings this summer grew 147 percent from 2024, according to TripAdvisor, whose subsidiary Viator is the biggest source of passengers.
Rome has as many as 500 carts, with one-fifth belonging to the Metur association of tour operators, established last December to seek common ground with locals and the city.

“Overtourism is a real problem, and we’re not denying it. And maybe we’re also part of it in a way. But if we’re part of it, then at least be part of it in a smart way,” Pascal van Duijnhoven, the association’s president, said. “We believe, especially for Rome, that it’s a solution. And we really hope that people start looking at it like this.”
EVs, carts of all types
Eugenio Patanè, Rome’s deputy mayor for sustainable mobility and transport, is striving to restore order and reduce traffic—not just golf carts.
In July, electric vehicles (EVs) started paying for admission to the historic center—a strategic shift from cutting emissions to tackling congestion.
The number of authorized vehicles is now down about one-quarter, to 350,000, and Patanè still aims to halve the number of daily entrants.
But it hasn’t been so simple to put the brakes on golf carts. For one thing, not all carts are created equal—technical specifications mean some fall under existing rules while others can roam freely.
Patanè aims to present regulation that would establish fixed tour routes, cap the number of carts of all types and create a system to select operators.
“Cities where this golf cart phenomenon is expanding truly have very few weapons,” he said, adding that “this phenomenon that has now become rampant and, in some cases, even worrisome.” /cb

articles.title: Trump’s ‘retribution’ could now include Falklands as favor to Milei – and revenge on the UK
articles.summary:
US president suggests he might support his Argentinian acolyte’s drive to reclaim sovereignty of disputed islands

Donald Trump…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has long embraced vengeance. “I am your retribution,” he declared to an admiring audience at the 2023 Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) as he commenced his march back to the White House.
It is unlikely Argentina, and far-flung holdovers of the former British empire, were on the US president’s mind at the time.
But the tide of international events in the past three and a half years have turned Trump’s vindictive mindset to the advantage of Javier Milei, the boisterous rightwing Argentinian president.

Trump’s notorious fixation with payback was almost entirely the trigger for Milei’s televised address to his fellow Argentinians on Thursday, as he stated his intention to reopen his country’s claim to a set of windswept islands in the south Atlantic – known to Britain as the Falklands, and to Argentina as the Malvinas.

The centuries-old dispute over the islands’ sovereignty has lain dormant since 1982, when the two countries fought a brief, but bloody, conflict that began after Argentina’s ruling military dictatorship invaded the territory.

Britain reclaimed them after troops in a naval taskforce dispatched by the then prime minister, Margaret Thatcher – ironically lionized by Milei as a political exemplar and inspiration – stormed the territory and eventually forced Argentina’s surrender.

An uneasy peace has reined in the generation since, although Argentina, which returned to democracy the year after the conflict, has never renounced its claim to the isles – despite the adamant insistence of their less than 2,000 inhabitants that they remain British.

This week, however, Trump suggested he is reconsidering US support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falkland Islands. Why would the president go out on a limb to threaten this fragile peace? And why now?
Milei jumped on Trump’s comment that he was “reviewing” the US’s longstanding neutral stance on the territory’s sovereignty, which amounts to a de facto recognition of Britain’s control.

Fueling Trump’s animus is grievance that Britain, under former prime minister Keir Starmer, declined to support the US president’s decision to go to war on Iran, another irony given that country’s deep-rooted suspicions of Britain and its imperial past.

The president’s obsession that allies declined to help him in a war he never consulted them on runs deep and wide – from Westminster to Seoul – and has the potential to upend US relationships around the globe, if unchecked.
And Milei’s attempt to capitalize on Trump’s vengeance underlines the potential for ripple effects of this war to reach waters far beyond the Gulf.
In what has become a repetitive refrain, Trump laid bare his sense of wounded affront in an interview with a rightwing British cable channel on Thursday.

“Your country was not there to help me,” he told GB News. “We didn’t need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader, ‘Why don’t you send a couple of ships?’ He said, ‘We don’t have any.’ It was pretty sad, the whole thing.”

Milei’s opportunism could also be used by Trump as a bargaining chip – to lever more money from the cash-strapped UK treasury for defense spending and Nato contributions, after the new British chancellor of the exchequer, John Healey, recently suggested that it might not reach increased spending targets.

It is a sorry pass for the “special relationship”, fostered through alliances in two worlds wars and deepened during the cold war and subsequent conflicts. Yet Britain is hardly alone in feeling the heat of a wrathful Trump.
Vengeance has been targeted in recent months at numerous other allies, now regarded with more hostility by the White House than traditional adversaries such as Russia and China.

Annual joint military exercises with South Korea – a vital ally of Washington since the Korean war broke out in 1950 – were suddenly scaled down and cut short by six days last month, on Trump’s orders, because of his irritation that the Seoul government declined to join the fight against Iran.

He has repeatedly threatened to bomb or “blow up” the tiny Gulf kingdom of Oman, which has had friendly ties with the US for 200 years, if it impedes his efforts to reopen the strait of Hormuz, which Iran has closed to most commercial shipping.

The White House also announced the withdrawal of 5,000 US troops from Germany after the country’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, rebuffed pressure to get involved in the Iran conflict and said Trump had been “humiliated” in the conflict.
Threats of retribution have also been aimed at Spain, which has resisted pressure to boost defense spending, and Italy, whose prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, was a former Trump ally.
Turbulence under Trump

But Milei, a self-styled “anarcho-capitalist” who has paraded with a chainsaw to signify his attitude to public spending and attended Trump’s 2025 inauguration, remains on the US president’s good side.

Last year, the administration extended his troubled government a $20bn loan guarantee to stabilize the infamously shaky Argentinian economy – but premised the money on Milei’s party defeating the leftist opposition in forthcoming congressional elections, which it duly did.

This time there are no guarantees, other than that of never-ending turbulence at the hands of Trump. Such rough currents may be the “winds of change” Milei referenced in Thursday’s speech, delivered – Trump-style – with his cabinet members flanking him.

But he may have been aware the phrase had other, historical connotations – evoking the words of a famous speech in 1960 by then British prime minister Harold Macmillan in Cape Town, heralding independence for Britain’s former colonial possession in Africa.
“The wind of change is blowing through this continent,” Macmillan said then. “Whether we like it or not, this growth of national consciousness is a political fact.”

In his address, Milei suggested the sun was setting on Britain, just as it once did on its empire, citing multiple crises of a migratory, demographic and economic nature that are unlikely to be resolved. “It is clear that they are on a path of decline,” he pronounced.

He did not mention his own falling political popularity – a factor which may also have played a key role in the former military junta’s decision to seize the islands in 1982, as opposition grew against the backdrop of mass disappearances of political dissidents and multiple human rights abuses.

Then, too, Britain was grappling with tensions over immigration and race riots, soaring unemployment and long-term economic decline that Thatcher had been elected pledging to reverse. In the late winter of 1982, there was little sign that she was capable of doing so – until the Falklands conflict sparked a sudden upturn in her political fortunes.

But she had the solid backing of the special relationship, and her ideological soulmate, Ronald Reagan, in the White House. Andy Burnham, Britain’s newly installed Labour prime minister, must contend with the chill wind emanating from the menacing and destabilizing presence of Trump.

articles.title: Outrage as Maltese tycoon acquitted in journalist's murder
articles.summary: Maltese businessman Yorgen Fenech has been found not guilty of complicity to murder journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia. Almost nine years after the attack, the question of who ordered her death…

image.caption: Protesters gathered outside the Maltese Parliament following the verdict in the Caruana Galizia murder trial on WednesdayImage: Darrin Zammit Lupi/REUTERS

blocks.text: "Murderer!" — "Scum!" — "Mafia!"

As Yorgen Fenech left the courthouse in Valletta on Wednesday evening, he was confronted by the furious crowd outside. The 44-year-old Maltese businessman pushed through, flanked by his security guards. Just minutes earlier, a jury had acquitted him of ordering the murder of the 53-year-old investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.

The verdict came as a shock to her family. Her son, Matthew Caruana Galizia, said it was a "terrible decision by the jurors that our country may never recover from." He later doubled down on his criticism, describing the verdict in a post on Facebook as "obscene" and saying: "Their decision flies in the face of all evidence, of all logic, of the truth."

Almost nine years after Caruana Galizia's murder, Malta is again confronted with the crucial question: Who was responsible for her death on October 16, 2017? The men who procured the bomb, placed it under the driver's seat and detonated it remotely have already been convicted. But the person who contracted them to do it has still not been legally identified.

blocks.caption: Maltese businessman Yorgen Fenech was acquitted on Wednesday of conspiracy and complicity to murderImage: Kevin Schembri Orland/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A difficult trial

For years, Fenech was considered to be the central figure in the investigations. His arrest on the morning of November 20, 2019, was like something out of a movie. His luxury yacht, Gio, had just left harbor when it was stopped by a Maltese military patrol boat. Fenech was arrested on board and subsequently interrogated by the police.

Fenech's arrest, and suspicion that people in government circles were involved in the crime, sparked protests all across the country. Joseph Muscat, prime minister at the time, was accused of protecting political allies and stepped down in January 2020. Fenech spent more than five years in detention before being released on bail, under strict conditions, in early 2025.
His trial only began this summer, and the final verdict was decisive. Eight of the nine jurors rejected the prosecution's argument that it was Fenech who had ordered the journalist's murder.
Who was responsible?

The prosecution case relied above all on the testimony of Melvin Theuma, who confessed to being the middleman and testified that Fenech had contracted him to organize the murder. Theuma received a pardon in exchange for his cooperation.
But Fenech's defense called Theuma's credibility into question, highlighting contradictions in his testimony and false statements he had made previously.

Fenech's lawyers also sought to prove that evidence pointing to Keith Schembri, chief of staff to Muscat at the time, was not properly followed up. Schembri has denied any involvement in the murder, and the investigators did not charge him as a suspect in this case.

blocks.caption: Investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was killed by a car bomb on October 16, 2017Image: Rene Rossignaud/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The public prosecutors' argument was that Caruana Galizia had been investigating Fenech, specifically his company 17 Black and the energy consortium ElectroGas, on suspicion of corruption. This, they said, meant Fenech had a motive for silencing her. She had not, however, been on the point of publishing anything that could have threatened him.
Open questions

Many in Malta are outraged by the not-guilty verdict. But there is no indication to date that Fenech did not receive a fair trial, or that the process was manipulated. For him to be convicted, Fenech's guilt had to be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

Caruana Galizia's family are therefore also focusing on institutional failures that they believe facilitated the murder. They complain that these have not been addressed, and necessary reforms not implemented. An official investigation already established, in 2021, that an "atmosphere of impunity" in Malta created conditions that made the murder possible.
Reforms in Malta

Since then, Malta has made progress with a series of reforms, but many say they do not go far enough. This is especially the case with regard to press freedom. In 2021, the committee of inquiry recommended that journalists be better protected against political and economic pressure and their role institutionally strengthened, yet the country is still waiting for comprehensive media reform.

Following years of discussion and a public consultation, the Maltese government brought the relevant bill before parliament in March 2026, but the legislation was not passed before early parliamentary elections in May.

In its latest Rule of Law Report, the European Commission only certifies limited progress made by Malta. It acknowledges that it has introduced some specific protection measures for journalists, but says core recommendations from the investigation into the murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia remain unfulfilled.

blocks.caption: The European Commission has told Malta it needs to do more to strengthen official protections for journalists  Image: Sachelle Babbar/Zuma/picture alliance

blocks.text: Government sees progress

But the government paints a different picture. It has highlighted changes to the judiciary and anti-corruption measures, as well as better protection of journalistic sources, and additional measures to protect media professionals. This is what the EU Commission referred to as progress in specific areas.

The case has also shone a spotlight on the slow pace of the Maltese justice system. According to a report by the Daphne Caruana Galizia Foundation, 46% of homicide cases brought to trial between 2010 and 2020 had still not been concluded in mid-2025. The foundation regards this as a structural problem, and warns that when proceedings go on for so long, it compromises the chances of an effective prosecution.
Fresh investigation?

No decision has yet been made as to what will happen now, following Fenech's acquittal. Judge Edwina Grima has ordered that the evidence presented at trial be passed on to the chief of police, who will decide whether criminal proceedings should be brought against anyone else.
On Thursday, former PM Muscat said that, according to the public prosecutors, further investigations were ongoing.

blocks.caption: Nine years on, the person behind Daphne Caruana Galizia's murder has still not been brought to justice Image: AP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Institute of Maltese Journalists (IGM) has called on the authorities to pursue every line of inquiry that came to light during the trial — including, explicitly, those that lead to former high-ranking politicians. The acquittal must be respected as the outcome of the constitutional process, the IGM said, but it does not close the case.

The demonstrators outside the courthouse in Valletta are in no doubt. Someone must have issued a contract for the murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia. And almost nine years after her death, still no one has been held responsible.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: In Saxony-Anhalt election, small parties will be kingmakers
articles.summary: The far-right AfD has good odds of winning an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt's parliament this state election, enabling them to govern alone. It all depends on whether other parties make the cut.

image.caption: Saxony-Anhalt is governed from the state parliament in MagdeburgImage: ArTo/Zoonar/IMAGO

blocks.text: It's rare that a state parliament election in Germany attracts as much media interest as this one in Saxony-Anhalt. On September 6, 2026, the 1.7 million eligible voters in the eastern German state will decide whether the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party can form a state government for the first time.

So far, there has not been a head of government who belonged to a proven far-right party in post-World War II Germany — at neither federal nor state level. That would change if AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund were to be elected to this position, since the Office for the Protection of the Constitution in Saxony Anhalt already classified the AfD as such in 2023.
Siegmund's chances of a historical triumph are high: For months the AfD has been comfortably leading the polls with well over 40% of the vote.
AfD, CDU and Left Party will get into parliament

Aside from the AfD, there are only two other parties who can count on being included in the next state parliament: The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of current State Premier Sven Schulze and the socialist Left Party, which is traditionally strong in eastern Germany, the former socialist GDR.
All other parties have cause for concern they could fail to reach the 5% threshold of votes necessary for entry into parliaments in Germany.
This even applies to the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), who currently form part of the federal government coalition with the CDU and its Bavarian counterpart, the Christian Social Union (CSU).
SPD, Greens, FDP, BSW might not make the 5% mark
The SPD is losing popularity nationwide. In Saxony-Anhalt, they are polling below the 8% they won five years ago.

The third party in Saxony-Anhalt's current governing coalition, formed in 2021, has even fewer hopes: The neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP) are polling only about 3%. Following the FDP's failure in the Bundestag general election of 2025 and multiple defeats at the state level, supporters are bracing themselves for the next setback.

The environmentalist Greens are also concerned about returning to the state parliament. The party, whose core voter base is in wealthy western German cities, is vehemently rejected by many voters in rural areas because of its climate policies and multicultural vision of society.
Concern over Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW)

And then there is the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), founded in 2024 by its namesake, a former Left Party co-leader. The party is economically left-leaning, but socially right-wing conservative and populist. This is its first time participating in a state election in Saxony-Anhalt.

After the BSW gained 6.2% of the vote in the European parliament elections in 2024 and won results of between about 12% and 16% in the eastern German states of Brandenburg, Saxony and Thuringia during its first year, it failed by only a few thousand votes to reach the 5% hurdle to enter German parliament in the 2025 general election.

The BSW never really recovered from this setback. They went on to be defeated in three further state parliament elections. The party also has cause for concern in Saxony-Anhalt, where it has been polling under 5%.

Should it win representation after all, Sahra Wagenknecht has already announced that her party's lawmakers would not vote an AfD premier into office, but abstain from the vote paving the way for him to win a majority in parliament and take office.
Considering the poor polling numbers for the BSW in Saxony-Anhalt, political scientist Oliver Lembcke speaks of an "endgame" for the party as a whole.
What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt?
Small parties could prevent absolute majority for the AfD
The fact is: The more parties fail to reach the threshold, the higher the likelihood of the Alternative for Germany will be able to govern alone.

On the other hand, if aside from the AfD, the CDU, Left Party and SPD win representation in the next Saxony-Anhalt parliament, and those three parties together hold more seats than the AfD, the situation is complicated. This is because in 2018 the CDU adopted a so-called "resolution of incompatibility," which rejects cooperation with both the AfD and the Left Party.
If the CDU sticks to this, forming even a minority government would be very difficult, perhaps impossible.
Could the CDU form a minority government?

Political scientist Lembcke from Ruhr University Bochum in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia argues that the CDU should have adapted its incompatibility resolution to the changed conditions of the party systems and political landscape. Because it has failed to do so, this issue could now escalate drastically in Saxony-Anhalt.
The Left Party is prepared to support Premier Sven Schulze of the CDU to secure a second term.

"In recent years, we, the Left Party, have shown that we take responsibility for this country. Especially when it comes to inhibiting the AfD," Left Party co-leader Luigi Pantisano told television broadcaster ZDF.
He pointed to the states of Thuringia and Saxony, where the CDU leads coalition governments without a parliamentary majority and depends on the support of the Left Party.

Given the foreseeably complicated situation, one thing is clear ahead of the September 6 election: either Saxony-Anhalt faces an incredibly difficult coalition-building process, or the state will be governed by the AfD — if the party profits from the failure of many small parties and thereby receives an absolute majority in the state parliament.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Germany's civil society alliance takes on the far right
articles.summary: Trade unions, churches and human rights activists are worried about the rise of the far-right AfD. How can civil society protect people who are threatened by far-right extremism?

image.caption: In 2024, hundreds of thousands across the country rallied in protest against right-wing extremismImage: Stefan Boness/IPON/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fighting for democracy and human rights in Germany today means mustering up a lot of courage.

For Felix Pankonin, locking and checking all doors and windows around the house has become practically second nature. Sometimes, a hot-tempered lawmaker from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party shows up on his property. Pankonin's bicycles have been vandalized, and he has received threats that something will happen to his animals. Most recently, his partner was physically assaulted.
Pankonin is the project director of educational programs on political issues, Jewish history and antisemitism at the Hillersche Villa in Zittau, in the eastern German state of Saxony.

The situation is similar for Keerthana Kuperan, who works as a political adviser at DaMOst, the umbrella organization for migrant groups in eastern Germany. Kuperan, whose parents are from Sri Lanka, said right-wing extremism has had a major impact on her work over the past three years.

"We have completely different security protocols now. After 6 p.m. no one is left alone in the office, and when putting up posters in rural areas, security measures are put in place beforehand," she said.

Kuperan's work is primarily focused on ensuring the safety of activists. Another aspect of her work involves dealing with challenges from the AfD, which files parliamentary information requests, often on migration, in order to delay political proceedings and highlight issues that should not really be controversial.

blocks.caption: Ahead of the state election in Saxony-Anhalt, numerous business owners with a background of migration went on strike against racism and fascism, and in support of a free and democratic societyImage: Peter Gercke/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In Saxony-Anhalt, a federal state with a very low proportion of foreigners, state legislative elections will be held on September 6. DaMOst observes that the political landscape has shifted to the right. This has led to the discrediting of democratic networks, which has affected their funding and job opportunities.
Green Party politician becomes target of hostilities

Miriam Zeller, a city councilor in Stendal, a city of 37,000 in northern Saxony-Anhalt, is a member of the environmentalist Green Party and is running in the election. Zeller told DW that the hostility against her was even more intense when the Greens were in power.

Her daughter stopped being invited to birthday parties, and she herself was viciously accused of being a warmonger. From the very beginning, the Greens had declared their solidarity with Ukraine after it had come under attack from Russia.
"It can't get any worse than this," said Zeller.

blocks.caption: Miriam Zeller, a Green Party candidate, has also felt the impact of the shift to the right in her private lifeImage: Miriam Zeller

blocks.text: However, she pointed out that, fortunately, as a teacher, she is a civil servant and therefore cannot lose her job.
For others, the specter of losing one's job — should the AfD come to power — is very real.
Alliance for Democracy: Educating people on how to defend themselves
The Together for Democracy alliance aims to support individuals or institutions that are being attacked or threatened by far-right extremists — people like Pankonin, Kuperan and Zeller.

The aim of the group's Solidarity Agreement — which over 80 groups have signed, including labor unions, the major Christian churches, sports organizations, human rights groups as well as social and environmental organizations — is to ensure that anyone who is targeted for their commitment to democracy will not be left alone. The groups joined forces in 2024 to form an alliance against the far right when it became clear that attacks on democracy were intensifying.

Now, alliance members want to also offer help and support in the event of attacks on youth or cultural centers, hate campaigns against people who speak out publicly, or when volunteers are threatened — whether through public expressions of solidarity or by providing legal or financial support. The alliance includes powerful actors such as the German Trade Union Federation (DGB) and environmental organizations like Greenpeace.

Yasmin Fahimi, the head of the DGB, which has over 5 million members, took the opportunity to present the new agreement in Berlin. When asked by DW whether the AfD, in the event of an election victory, could actually fire all public employees, Fahimi was clear.

"This fantasy of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt — to carry out a complete personnel shake-up in government agencies, ministries, courts and the police — is completely unlawful," Fahimi said. "We are making it clear to our members that they can fight back against this. It is also a manifestation of an authoritarian mindset to believe that one can simply issue a decree and do as one pleases. That's not how our democracy works."

That is why the DGB is training its members both in constitutional law and civil service law so they can defend themselves, Fahimi said. The trade union leader has called for more commitment from politicians.

"We must ensure — especially in regional areas, but also within our institutions — that people cannot simply be forced to comply with unlawful orders. I believe it would be good for the Conference of Interior Ministers to discuss how to provide clear information, seminars and workshops on these issues, so that public servants, ministry employees and staff at institutions governed by the rule of law are not left to fend for themselves," she said.
Threats, abuse to German mayors hurting local government
Teaming up to hlep 'bring this injustice to light'

"Of course, this alliance can mean more protection for queer people who are active on the ground," said Andre Lehmann, from the Queer Diversity Association(LSVD+) — a civil rights organization that has represented the interests and concerns of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans* and intersex queer people (LGBTQ+) since 1990.

"Right now, we're seeing a lot of attacks on Pride events all over Germany. In some cases, local organizers don't even know what to do in such situations. That's where an alliance like this can step in," Lehmann told DW.
The Islamist attack on the Pride event in Berlin has deeply unsettled the queer community, said Lehmann. On top of that, many democracy projects are being financially bled dry right now.

The alliance will hardly be able to make up for the lack of funding for democracy projects that has resulted from the federal government's cuts and restructuring. However, teaming up with other organizations helps build strength, said Sophie Lampl, who works for Greenpeace.

"That is certainly one of the strengths we can bring as an environmental organization: our ability to campaign. To provide support when civil society organizations or individuals are attacked, to publicly stand up for them and to bring this injustice to light," Lampl said.
Will the alliance also be able to help in rural areas?

Pankonin has often helped the Together for Democracy alliance — by providing legal advice, funding for security and moral support. Pankonin would like to see more involvement from major organizations in rural areas.

Green Party politician Zeller reports that she has also received aid from small local networks. She believes that a large network, with its newfound solidarity, can make a big difference and could be a vital source of support, even in rural areas.
For his part, Lehmann is determined. "We will defend our democracy and, if necessary, guide our local people through this valley," he said.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: UN votes to adopt new world map to reflect Africa's true size
articles.summary: The Togo-sponsored resolution was backed by 164 nations - the US the only nation to vote against it.

blocks.text: The Mercator map was designed in 1569 by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to help European explorers navigate across the world.
The distortion of his map is a result of the fact that it is impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart.
Whenever a map of the world is drawn, compromises need to be made.
The Mercator map shows the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem smaller than they are, with countries nearer the poles appearing bigger.
In an effort to correct this, a team of cartographers in 2018 created an equal area map they called the Equal Earth projection.
In February, the AU's 54 member states adopted it, saying it "more accurately represents the sizes of all continents, particularly Africa".
Ahead of Friday's vote, Togolese Foreign Minister Robert Dussey told the Reuters news agency: "A fair world begins with a fair map."
Earlier he had told a UN briefing: "A map is never neutral. It shapes perceptions, influences how the place of peoples and continents in the world is understood."
The UN vote is non-binding but will see changes to the maps used by institutions around the world.

articles.title: Russia hits Ukrainian security headquarters in drone attack, Zelensky says
articles.summary: The unmanned aerial vehicle struck without warning in the heart of the Ukrainian capital.

blocks.text: Russia hits Ukrainian security headquarters in drone attack, Zelensky says
Image source, Reuters
A Russian drone has hit the headquarters of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) during a strike in the heart of Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
The unmanned aerial vehicle crashed into the SBU headquarters on Friday afternoon, targeting a room used by security chief Oleksandr Poklad.
It is not clear whether Poklad was in the building, but Zelensky said he had since spoken to him to order an "appropriate, tangible response".

"The drone was aimed directly at the office of the Head of the Security Service in that building," Zelensky confirmed. It suggests Russia's new drones are growing in accuracy and signals Moscow could step up strikes before possible US mediation talks this weekend.
"All emergency services are on the scene. Everyone affected will receive the necessary assistance," Zelensky added in a message on Telegram.

"I instructed Poklad to deliver an appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike, to the Russians once everything is ready. Our military will support this response."
Images of the office widely shared online showed black smoke pouring from two windows on the front of the building.
Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said the attack was a "major escalation that demands resolute responses".
"Moscow launched this strike during a renewed push for peace - laying bare its true rejection of diplomacy," he added.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said five people had been hurt in the SBU attack, but did not elaborate on whether they were inside the offices.
The Russian defence ministry also said on Friday it had struck a cargo vessel in the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk and a tanker near Odesa.
In recent weeks Russia has escalated its daytime strikes on Ukrainian targets.
In many instances it has employed jet-powered drones which are faster and harder to intercept. It is not yet known which type of munition was used in this latest attack.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Firefighters work to put out fires in the building following the Russian drone strike

blocks.text: Firefighters work to put out fires in the building following the Russian drone strike
The strike on the SBU building is a rare example of Russia successfully hitting a government building.
Previously Ukrainian offices have remained unscathed despite attempts from the Kremlin to stifle defences to its advances.
The SBU - which is just over the road from the St Sophia cathedral, the oldest building in Kyiv - is a key part of Ukraine's war efforts as it conducts deep strikes to damage Russian infrastructure.
The drone came during yet another air raid alert. There was a brief whine before an explosion echoed across the roof tops and smoke rose into the sky.
Despite the ongoing exchanges, US mediators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Russia and Ukraine this weekend, reports say, as efforts to end the war continue.
The envoys will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin on Saturday in Moscow, and then will hold talks with Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday in Kyiv, Axios said, citing US officials.
Witkoff and Kushner have led US President Donald Trump's efforts to broker a peace deal, without a breakthrough so far.

articles.title: How vulnerable is Germany's infrastructure?
articles.summary: The growing number of attacks on substations and railway lines in Germany is raising concern. Experts say that people will have to get used to the likelihood that such incidents will continue.

image.caption: Germany is registering an increasing number of attempted sabotage attempts on its critical infrastructureImage: Thilo Schmuelgen/REUTERS

blocks.text: On Tuesday morning, unknown perpetrators attempted to attack the power supply near the coal-fired power plant at Jänschwalde in the eastern state of Brandenburg, partly succeeding in their objective. Then, later the same evening, a substation near Cologne suffered a disruption in what is believed to have been an act of sabotage.
On Wednesday, an explosion occurred near the railway station in the Bavarian city of Augsburg, caused by a hand grenade, according to investigators.

In the early hours of Thursday, several incendiary devices were thrown onto a construction site in Munich, close to a number of defense companies. Then, on Thursday evening, a suspicious object was discovered at a power substation in Dormagen, between Cologne and Düsseldorf. Investigators say a claim of responsibility has since been received.
While it remains entirely unclear who was behind the attacks in Jänschwalde, Cologne and Augsburg, investigators in Munich have arrested at least two suspects, reportedly Bulgarian nationals.
Already 160 attacks on critical infrastructure this year

What all these incidents have in common is that they appear to have targeted so-called critical infrastructure: energy facilities, the rail network, companies of strategic importance to national security and defense contractors.

Taken together, these sites can hardly be protected in their entirety. According to media reports citing an internal document, the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) has recorded 160 potential acts of sabotage and more than 700 suspicious drone sightings so far this year.
People in Berlin express concern over Russia

Even if the exact circumstances of each incident remain unclear, their rapid succession has created a growing sense of constant threat among the public. To find out how people are reacting, DW spoke to residents on the streets of Berlin.

One woman described her immediate reaction: "Fear. I was just talking about it with a colleague. It makes me feel very uneasy. I think about it a lot, and yet no one really talks about it. Maybe it's because people are afraid and would rather push it out of their minds?"

One man added: "We first need to recognize that something is happening, that we are under attack. I have very close ties to Russia and very close Russian friends, and it is very, very painful to see what is happening."
Is Germany's civil defense prepared for crisis?
A freeze in German-Russian relations

The fact that Russia is the first thing that comes to many people's minds when they hear about the recent wave of attacks is hardly surprising. On Tuesday, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of Bavaria's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), both members of the governing alliance with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), appeared before the press. They announced that the German government is convinced Russian actors were behind the attempted drone attack on Halle/Leipzig Airport on August 4.

The government responded by closing Russia's consulate general in Bonn and ending the lease on the Russian House in Berlin. Moscow, in turn, retaliated by shutting down the Goethe-Institut in Moscow. Relations between Germany and Russia are now at their lowest point in years.
"We are no longer at peace, but neither are we at war," Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) remarked last year.

The reality is that since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in the spring of 2022, Germany has been among Ukraine's strongest supporters, both financially and militarily. That holds true even though successive German governments, including the current one, have consistently maintained that the country is not itself a party to the war.
Germany's support for Ukraine as a motive?
Since then, the Bundeswehr, after years of continuous downsizing, has undergone rapid rearmament, driven in part by concerns that Russia could pose a threat even to central Europe.

Neither at war nor at peace: Sönke Marahrens, a colonel in the German armed forces and a security expert at Kiel University, believes Germans would be well advised to prepare for this new form of confrontation, whoever may be responsible for it.

He told DW: "Hybrid warfare and hybrid activities are, in my view, essentially the same thing because they rely on the same methods. Foreign states or organizations pursue their strategic interests without resorting to diplomacy. This can take the form of sabotage, disinformation or attacks on critical infrastructure."
At the same time, the researcher stresses that it would be difficult to describe the situation as a state of war.
Private firms urged to strengthen infrastructure security

But it would be too simplistic to attribute every such incident immediately and unequivocally to Russia. Earlier this year, for example, an attack on a cable bridge in southwest Berlin caused a power outage that lasted several days. Hundreds of thousands of people were affected in freezing temperatures. In that case, which remains unsolved, suspicion has fallen on far-left extremists.

A debate has long been underway in Germany over how best to prepare for such attacks in the future. This spring, the government passed legislation known as "KRITIS" aimed at strengthening the protection of critical infrastructure, although the law has yet to enter into force.

Herbert Reul (CDU), the interior minister of the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, noted in an interview with public broadcaster ZDF that critical facilities, including those operated by private companies, can already be monitored through video surveillance. Responsibility for securing the surrounding areas, however, lies with authorities such as the police. As Reul put it: "In Germany, we are sensitive when it comes to video surveillance and, more generally, to measures that affect civil liberties or data protection."

Reul argued that companies themselves need to invest more in protecting their facilities. The German Police Union (DPolG) takes a similar view. Its chairman, Heiko Teggatz, said that safeguarding critical infrastructure is not primarily the responsibility of the police, but first and foremost of the operators themselves: "Those responsible for the security of their facilities must also invest in their protection," Teggatz said. What is lacking, he argued, is not technical capability but a consistent willingness to invest.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: 'We expect our sons to be killed,' father of teen shot dead in West Bank tells BBC
articles.summary: Palestinian teenagers Omar al-Naasan and Khalil Abu Alia were shot dead when Israeli settlers and soldiers entered a village in the occupied West Bank.

blocks.text: Funerals have taken place for two Palestinian teenagers who were shot dead this week when settlers and soldiers entered a Palestinian village in the occupied West Bank.
The killing of Omar al-Naasan and Khalil Abu Alia comes amid near-daily attacks by Jewish settlers in the village of al-Mughayyir, south of Nablus.
"We expect that when our sons walk in the street, they are likely to return to you injured or killed," Mohammed Al-Naasan, Omar's father, told the BBC.
Israel's military says it fired on "instigators of a violent riot" and that the incident is under review.
The United Nations says more than 80 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the territory since the beginning of the year.

articles.title: Nepal rescuers try to reach dozens trapped in tunnel after two found alive
articles.summary: More than 1,300 people have died and thousands are missing, but rescuers' hopes have risen after finding survivors in a tunnel.

blocks.text: The full impact of the flood in Tibet is unclear. China has released information through state media outlets showing the devastation around the border, but has given few details about the victims or the impact on local villagers.
In Nepal, however, rescue operations are taking place at seven hydropower tunnels in which more than 150 people are feared trapped - as well as in 19 other areas.
In the early hours of Friday morning, rescuers heard what they thought could be voices at the Trishuli 3A hydropower site.
According to local reports, they called out "don't worry, we're here to rescue you" - and heard back a faint "okay".

Crews clambered in to find Sanjaya Shah and Kabir Maharjan - both had injuries on their hands and legs, "possibly" from crawling through the tunnel. Both were airlifted to the Army Hospital in the capital, Kathmandu.
Maharjan, who was rescued second, is in a critical condition, the prime minister's office said. Shah was also undergoing medical tests.
The body of a third person was found in the same tunnel later. A local official said it was swollen and could not be immediately identified.
Officials believe another 39 people are in the Trishuli 3A tunnel, although it is not clear if all are alive.
Col Jhabindra Reshmi said that his teams had rescued more than 400 Nepali nationals and 270 foreign citizens following the flash flooding on 26 August.
He has said mud and rocks have made entering tunnels difficult and rescuers were having to dig access holes to get underground.
Engineers have been pumping air into the tunnels.
Last week's floodwaters washed away a lot of heavy machinery, making it harder for rescuers to unblock tunnels, says a representative for Nepalese power companies.
Uttam Bhlon Lama, vice president at Independent Power Producers of Nepal, told the BBC's Newsday programme that the rescue of the two men on Friday would "motivate the rescuers to do more".
"The flood level is still very high," Lama added.
Nepalese authorities have warned that rainfall may cause additional flooding in the region.
At least 1,287 people are known to have died in Nepal, with 5,083 still missing.
On the Tibetan side, the death toll reported by Chinese media on Friday was 31, with 531 people unaccounted for.
Emergency teams in Tibet appear to be focusing on helping the living rather than holding out hope for more survivors.

articles.title: Bystanders rescue SUV occupants who crashed into Rideau River in Ottawa
articles.summary: Two occupants of an SUV that crashed into the river near Mooney's Bay on Friday morning had to be pulled from the water to safety. The rescue shows how important it is to have basic swimming skills,…

image.caption: Emergency crews respond to Friday morning's single-vehicle crash at the corner of Riverside Drive and Walkley Road. Thanks to the quick efforts of several bystanders, two people inside an SUV that crashed into the Rideau River were able to safely make it to shore. (Gabrielle Huston/CBC)

blocks.text: Ottawa·Updated

Two occupants of an SUV that crashed into the river near Mooney's Bay on Friday morning had to be pulled from the water to safety. The rescue shows how important it is to have basic swimming skills, according to one of the women who rushed to help.
Shows how important it is to have basic swimming skills, says one rescuer
Two people whose SUV crashed into the Rideau River on Friday morning are safe after several others who were in the area rushed into action to rescue them.
Emergency services responded to the single-vehicle collision around 5:50 a.m. at the corner of Riverside Drive and Walkley Road near Mooney's Bay, according to Ottawa paramedics.
They said an SUV went into the water and that two people inside had made it back to shore. They were assessed by paramedics and released at the scene.
CBC News saw a long silver pole on the road and boats labeled "Ottawa Fire" on the water around 6 a.m. on Friday.
Lesley Tomlinson had been out for a run that morning and was near the intersection when she heard the sound of a car braking and skidding.
She told CBC the SUV had skidded through the intersection, hit the light pole, went over the embankment and crashed into the water.
"I was dumbfounded," she said.
'He can't swim!'
"There was definitely a moment of panic as to, how do I help these people?" Tomlinson said.

Two other people emerged on the scene to help, she said. One woman came out of a house nearby and called 911, while another woman who'd been in a car behind the SUV pulled over and jumped into the water.
Tomlinson said she watched her help the driver out of the car and then go around to the passenger's side, yelling: "He can't swim!"
A former lifeguard, Tomlinson dove into the water. When she reached the car, it was mostly submerged and the passenger was holding onto it.
"I was very assertive and I told him that he was not to touch me, he was not to put his arms around me, that that would mean we would both drown," Tomlinson recalled.
"I told him that he is going to lie on his back and I am going to hold his head and I'm going to bring him in. ... We got him into that position just as the car completely submerged."
'You really need basic swimming skills'
Tomlinson said she swam with him to shore while supporting his head.
Speaking to CBC News afterwards, she said it didn't hit her how extraordinary the situation was in the moment.

items: Do you know what to do if someone is drowning?
How to know when someone is in trouble in the water

blocks.text: Tomlinson emphasized that it was a group effort to help, saying the woman who had pulled over and jumped in first was "the real superstar."
Later that day, Tomlinson went to work as a teacher and told her students about what happened.

"I felt it was so important to impress upon them the ability to swim. The driver was not a strong swimmer but he could keep his head up ... the other person couldn't swim and didn't know what to do," she said.
"I really think the takeaway from this whole thing is that you really need basic swimming skills because you never know what situation you're going to be in."
Police told CBC on Saturday that the SUV had been recovered from the Rideau River.

Gabrielle is a journalist for CBC News in Ottawa and Sudbury who loves to learn new things. She has a bachelor's degree in the humanities and journalism from Carleton University and has previously written for tech outlets like TheGamer and MobileSyrup. articles.title: PVL: PLDT stays focused amid noise as title defense hits rough patch
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines— Defending champion PLDT got the brunt of criticism on social media after absorbing back-to-back losses in the PVL Invitational Conference. After sweeping 13 games en route to…

blocks.text: Savi Davison and the PLDT High Speed Hitters during a game vs Farm Fresh Foxies in the 2026 PVL Invitational Conference. –MARLO CUETO/INQUIRER.net
MANILA, Philippines— Defending champion PLDT got the brunt of criticism on social media after absorbing back-to-back losses in the PVL Invitational Conference.
After sweeping 13 games en route to back-to-back titles in the PVL on Tour and Invitational last year, PLDT lost two of its first three games in its title defense.

Savi Davison, however, came to the rescue, dropping 32 points as the High Speed Hitters revived their title hopes with a 25-16, 25-22, 23-25, 25-20 win over Farm Fresh on Friday at Smart Araneta Coliseum.
Aware of the outside noise, coach Rald Ricafort is trying to ease the pressure by focusing on one game at a time rather than defending their title.

“The defending champion tag isn’t really relevant to us this conference because it just adds hype and becomes a distraction,” said PLDT coach Rald Ricafort in Filipino. “What’s more important for us is how we responded after the losses to Nxled and Vietnam, which were really tough for us, especially because we didn’t have much time to recover mentally.”

“I told them before the game that if that’s the lesson we’re going to get from this conference, then we have to maximize it. There are so many distractions outside of the game, but this is our job, so we really have to stay focused,” he added.

blocks.caption: PLDT High Speed Hitters' Savi Davison during a game vs Farm Fresh Foxies in the 2026 PVL Invitational Conference.

blocks.text: PLDT High Speed Hitters’ Savi Davison during a game vs Farm Fresh Foxies in the 2026 PVL Invitational Conference. –MARLO CUETO/INQUIRER.net
Team captain Kath Arado, who had 24 digs, said the High Speed Hitters have also learned to lean on one another amid the criticism.

“Honestly, you can’t really avoid it because social media is huge now and fans are really invested in volleyball. Personally, I’m not really active on social media, so that helps me avoid the noise,” said Arado in Filipino.
“It also helps that we have our coaches handling the technical side. We check on each other whenever we see each other and ask, ‘How are you?’ From there, we can tell if everyone is doing okay.”

“But what we really want to build is our relationship as a team. Whatever we hear outside or whatever happens within the team, we need to stay together. We’ll just listen to what the coaches tell us because that’s what will help us grow as a team,” she added.
Ricafort also credited the squad’s growth after three seasons together, particularly in handling adversity.
Kath Arado and Savi Davison on PLDT’s final elimination game against Creamline. #PVL2026 @inquirersports pic.twitter.com/H4bdXo4WT8 — Lance Agcaoili (@LanceAgcaoilINQ) September 4, 2026

“The team is definitely growing, and credit to all the teams because the games have been really tough. I think the biggest growth I’ve seen from us is that we’re now able to pinpoint the technical things we need to fix. Before, there were still a lot of differences among the players, but now we’re more solid even when we lose,” the PLDT coach said.

“We’re already at the point where we need to focus on growing as volleyball players. We really want this conference, but because of what happened, we weren’t able to get the games and results we wanted. It’s not over yet, though. We still have to fight until Tuesday,” he added.
PLDT hopes to stay in finals contention against Creamline on Sunday.

“They’re champions, they’ve been together for a long time, and they know each other really well. They’re a tough team to play against, but that’s our job. If we want to win, we have to work harder and stay focused,” Arado said.

“Creamline won’t give us an easy win. It’s not going to be like previous conferences where we could just expect to win. We have to think that we’re back to zero. We won today, but now we’re back to zero. We have to keep working and study them.”

articles.title: VP Sara's 2 ex-security officers, alleged bagman dropped as witnesses
articles.summary: MANILA- The House prosecution has dropped plans to present two of Vice President Sara Duterte’s former security officers and alleged former bagman Ramil Madriaga as witnesses in her impeachment…

blocks.text: MANILA- The House prosecution has dropped plans to present two of Vice President Sara Duterte’s former security officers and alleged former bagman Ramil Madriaga as witnesses in her impeachment trial, saying evidence already presented is sufficient to support allegations of misuse, misappropriation and irregular liquidation of P612.5 million in confidential funds.

House impeachment team adviser and spokesperson Ace Barbers identified the two former security officers as Col. Raymund Dante Lachica and Col. Dennis Nolasco, who have both figured in testimonies on the handling of Duterte’s confidential funds at the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and Department of Education (DepEd).

“The three allegations in this article have already been substantiated by the previous witnesses na iniharap, ‘yun nga ’yung sinasabi natin sa misuse, misappropriation, at saka irregular liquidation (presented on the misuse, misappropriation and irregular liquidation of confidential funds),” Barbers said during an online press briefing Friday.

“Sa prosecution panel, with the witnesses na iniharap, napatunayan na po natin ’yan (The prosecution panel had already proven that with the witnesses already presented) … So there is no need for additional witnesses like Col. Lachica, Col. Nolasco, and Madriaga,” he added.
Acosta testified as a hostile prosecution witness that Duterte instructed her to turn over four PHP125-million tranches, or a total of PHP500 million in OVP confidential funds, to Lachica.
She also disclaimed personal knowledge of how the money was ultimately distributed after turning it over to him.
Nolasco, meanwhile, was linked to DepEd’s confidential funds through the earlier House testimony of former DepEd SDO Edward Fajarda.

Fajarda testified during House proceedings that he turned over three PHP37.5-million confidential fund releases, totaling PHP112.5 million, to Nolasco upon Duterte’s instruction when she was education secretary.
Madriaga had been considered a potentially significant prosecution witness after identifying himself during House impeachment proceedings as Duterte’s former aide and alleged bagman.

In a sworn testimony before the House Committee on Justice in April, Madriaga claimed that he personally handled and distributed the first PHP125 million in OVP confidential funds released in December 2022 and disposed of the entire amount in less than 24 hours.

He alleged that he delivered bags containing millions of pesos to several locations upon Duterte’s instruction and implicated Lachica and Nolasco in the alleged movement of the money. Duterte has denied Madriaga’s allegations.

Despite Madriaga’s earlier inclusion among prospective witnesses, Barbers said the prosecution now believes his testimony, along with those of Lachica and Nolasco, would no longer be necessary given the evidence already on record.
The prosecution will instead proceed with its remaining witnesses as it seeks to complete its presentation of evidence on the confidential fund charge.

The witnesses are Fajarda and his wife, DepEd Assistant Secretary Sunshine Charry Fajarda; Philippine Statistics Authority Assistant National Statistician Marizza Grande; Police Maj. Jovelyn Magay; and Commission on Audit official Bresilio Sabaldan.
The Senate impeachment court has issued subpoenas for the five to appear as prosecution witnesses in the Sept. 7 to 9 trial proceedings.

Edward Fajarda’s personal appearance, however, could still be dispensed with because of his medical condition if the prosecution and defense agree to stipulate on the matters his testimony is intended to establish.

The prosecution is targeting Sept. 9 to finish presenting evidence on Article I, which covers the alleged misuse, misappropriation and irregular liquidation of PHP612.5 million in confidential funds. (PNA)

articles.title: Nick Kyrgios gets month ban for cocaine, enters treatment program
articles.summary: SYDNEY–Australia’s Nick Kyrgios was cleared Friday to return to tennis after accepting a one-month ban for using cocaine and entering a treatment program. The 31-year-old, who reached the final…

blocks.text: FILE–Australia’s Nick Kyrgios reacts during the Australian Open first-round (AO1) singles match at Rod Laver Arena in Melbourne on January 14, 2026. (Photo by DAVID GRAY / AFP)
SYDNEY–Australia’s Nick Kyrgios was cleared Friday to return to tennis after accepting a one-month ban for using cocaine and entering a treatment program.
The 31-year-old, who reached the final at Wimbledon in 2022, failed a doping test during an ATP event in Mallorca on June 22.
He was provisionally suspended on August 4 by the International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA), admitting he made “a huge mistake”.
In a statement Friday, the doping agency said Kyrgios had explained his use of the drug occurred socially during a night out before he was due to play in Mallorca.
The ITIA consulted an independent scientific expert at a World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)-accredited laboratory, who found his explanation was consistent with the level of cocaine found in his sample.
“As a result, the ITIA accepted that Kyrgios’ use of cocaine was outside of competition,” the ITIA said.
Under WADA rules, the default suspension for a breach of this type is three months, which can be reduced to one month if an individual commits to a treatment program.
“Kyrgios has entered into a treatment programme,” the ITIA added.
“As such, the player’s suspension will end on September 3, 2026, subject to completion of the program. Prize-money and ranking points from the Mallorca event will be forfeited.”
Boasting a big serve and booming ground strokes, Kyrgios has won seven singles titles on the ATP Tour and rose to a high of 13 in the world in 2016. He is now ranked 918.
His finest performance was on the grass at Wimbledon in 2022, when he reached the championship match, losing in four sets to Novak Djokovic.
Despite his natural talents that is as good as it got, with a series of injuries taking their toll.
He has had numerous surgeries, the most serious a complete reconstruction of his right wrist in 2024.
The Australian last played as a wildcard entry in the men’s doubles at Wimbledon in July this year, when he and partner Alexander Bublik lost in the first round.
Kyrgios was contrite when the news of his cocaine use emerged last month.
“I recently failed a drug test in Mallorca after testing positive for cocaine,” he posted on Instagram at the time. “I made a huge mistake and I take full responsibility for it.
“I’m sorry to my fans, my family, my sponsors and everyone close to me. Above all, I’m sorry to the kids who follow me.
“I know the example this sets and I’m deeply disappointed in myself.”
