Some argue that the map has subtly shaped international power dynamics by minimising the physical presence of the global south and visually inflating northern hemisphere nations while shrinking equatorial regions. This, they say, has reinforced systemic biases in international trade, development priorities and educational frameworks.

One of the Mercator projection’s most prominent critics was Arno Peters, a German historian, who launched the Peters world map based on the Gall–Peters projection in 1973. It has often been used as an alternative to the Mercator map.

blocks.caption: The 2018 Equal Earth Map. Photograph: equal-earth.com

blocks.text: Togo’s #CorrectTheMap campaign is promoting the use of the more accurate 2018 Equal Earth design, which was developed by an international team of cartographers. Supporters say it will help to reverse perceptions of Africa and decolonise global curriculums.

Some analysts agree too. JJ Enoch, a London-based senior associate at JS Held, a geopolitical risk advisory firm, said the Mercator projection visually diminished Africa’s true scale. He linked the campaign to a quest by African nations for “greater influence in global institutions and greater control over how the continent is represented”.

He added: “Adopting an equal-area map … would provide a more accurate basis for education and public understanding, while signalling that Africa’s demographic, economic and geopolitical importance should no longer be viewed through inherited and distorted conventions.”

blocks.caption: A map of Africa from Mercator's atlas dating between 1595-1602. Photograph: Royal Geographical Society/Getty Images

blocks.text: Togolese authorities hope the vote will go the same way as another African Union-backed decision at the UN this year. In March a Ghana-sponsored resolution to describe the slave trade as “gravest crime against humanity” passed, with 123 states voting in favour. Three states voted no and 52 abstained.

Ghana’s success has given supporters of the map cause to believe in a favourable outcome. Togo’s government is planning an event in Lomé, the Togolese capital, with Unesco, the African Union and tech brands such as Google Maps during the first quarter of next year to map out the implementation of the resolution.
Dussey said: “To those who say why now, I say, why not? When we look at the world map … it is time for us to change the narrative.”
He added: “It’s time for us in Africa to take responsibility to change what we can change ourselves.”

articles.title: DMW: 2 Filipinos dead in Strait of Hormuz attack
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) has reported the death of two Filipino seafarers on board the Saudi-flagged crude oil tanker SIDR which was hit by unidentified…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) has reported the death of two Filipino seafarers on board the Saudi-flagged crude oil tanker SIDR which was hit by unidentified projectiles as it was about to cross the Strait of Hormuz.

Migrant Workers Secretary Hans Cacdac said in a press briefing on Wednesday that the victims were among 16 Filipino seafarers on the vessel when it was attacked on Aug. 31. The rest were unharmed with the vessel now off the coast of Oman.
“Unfortunately, we have two crew members who died as a result of the attack,” Cacdac told reporters, adding that a fire broke out on the tanker but it was contained by the crew.
“We are already working on the immediate repatriation of all the crew members, including the two fatalities,” he said.
According to the DMW chief, he would personally visit the families of the victims although he did not disclose where they reside, citing privacy concerns.

The DMW and the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration will also provide assistance to the families while government agencies coordinate with authorities in Oman on the repatriation of the Filipino seafarers, Cacdac said.
President Marcos has likewise ordered that assistance be given to the victims’ families, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said on Thursday.

“First and foremost, the President and the administration extend their condolences to the families of the two seafarers from Cabuyao, Laguna, and Daanbantayan, Cebu. The President has also ordered immediate assistance for the families of our two fellow citizens who perished, as well as the provision of all necessary support—including the benefits, compensation and insurance proceeds—rightfully due to them,” Castro said in a briefing at the Malancañang.
“The government will not neglect the families left behind by our two fellow citizens. Once again, we extend our condolences to the families of our two seafarers,” she added.

The DMW, meanwhile, remains on red alert amid continuing security risks in the Strait of Hormuz, Cacdac said. According to him, they were coordinating with the Department of National Defense and the Department of Foreign Affairs on the security situation involving Filipino seafarers in the region.
About 3,000 Filipino seafarers remain aboard vessels in the wider Persian Gulf, although they are not necessarily all within the Strait of Hormuz, Cacdac said.
High-risk area

Since Feb. 28, when the United States and Israel launched an attack on Iran, triggering the Middle East conflict, about 31 ships carrying 421 Filipino seafarers have been attacked while entering or leaving the strait.
Cacdac said that 268 of those seafarers have since returned to the Philippines. Of the 421, 406 were unharmed, 10 were injured but had recovered, three had died and one remains officially missing.

The DMW, however, is not imposing a blanket deployment ban on Filipino seafarers passing through the Strait of Hormuz unlike its policy covering the Northern Black Sea, because of the strategic importance of the waterway and the principle of freedom of navigation, he added.

Instead, shipowners must conduct risk assessments before voyages and ensure that adequate security measures are in place, including security protocols, possible escorts, armed guards and reporting mechanisms, he said.
“We are disallowing deployment to the extent that there is a refusal of sailing by the seafarer,” Cacdac stressed.
He said that the right of Filipino seafarers to refuse sailing in high-risk areas must be respected.
The DMW will investigate the incident, including whether the appropriate safety and risk-assessment measures were followed.

Cacdac said the SIDR appeared to have been heading toward the Strait of Hormuz after coming from the eastern coast of the United Arab Emirates and sailing northward off Oman, but the vessel’s exact route remains subject to further determination.
For now, it is still too early to provide details on how the two Filipino seafarers died, he noted.
“It is not yet clear how exactly that happened. Usually, when we are still 24 to 48 hours removed from the event, we will find out the details as we go along,” Cacdac said.

He added that the DMW remains in contact with Bahri, the Saudi shipping company in charge of the vessel, and would meet with its top management to discuss the incident and the safety of Filipino crew members. /das

articles.title: Iran war is not a war, US VP Vance says
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, United States — U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Thursday he would not categorize the Iran war as a war, despite continuing clashes with Tehran six months after the start of the…

blocks.text: WASHINGTON, United States — U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Thursday he would not categorize the Iran war as a war, despite continuing clashes with Tehran six months after the start of the conflict.
Vance’s comments came amid growing signs that President Donald Trump is trying to draw a line under the conflict that has bogged down his administration.
“I wouldn’t call it a war. Right now, there is no active shooting,” Vance told a White House briefing when asked if the war would be over by the U.S. midterm elections in November.
Vance added that “I recognize there have been places where this has flared up,” but said major combat operations only lasted for six weeks after the U.S.-Israel war started on Feb. 28.

“But when you ask when will this end, you’re asking me a question like when will the Iranians stop shooting at ships? I think the reality is I don’t know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians,” he said.
After several weeks of calm, fresh clashes began with U.S. raids on Sunday, deepening the impasse in the six-month war, as Iran maintains a stranglehold on the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
Vance insisted that the United States would not reopen talks with Iran until it ended attacks on commercial shipping.

But with fuel prices threatening to cost Trump’s Republicans their control of Congress at the ballot box, his administration has begun pushing the message that oil flows through the waterway are now returning to pre-war levels.
Wedding strike probe
“Their control over the Strait of Hormuz is effectively gone,” Vance said of Iran.

“If you go back three months ago, how much oil and gas was coming out of the strait under Iranian threats? It was virtually nothing. Now, it’s almost back to where it was before the conflict even started,” Vance said.
Trump’s approval ratings are near record lows as the president who vowed to keep the United States out of any more foreign wars finds himself in a quagmire with the Islamic Republic.
Eighteen U.S. troops and thousands of people in Iran and Lebanon have died in the conflict since February.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump was now discussing with senior aides whether to declare the Iran war over. He posted a photo of a banner saying “Mission Accomplished” last week.
Iran pressed on with fresh attacks on Thursday, saying it hit U.S. military bases in Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates to avenge a strike on a wedding that it blamed on Washington.
Vance said the United States was probing the wedding strike but cast doubt on Iranian reporting of the incident.

“I know that we’re investigating,” Vance said. “I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good source of information about what’s happened in the conflict thus far. So I’m extremely skeptical of this.”
The Iranian Red Crescent said the missile attack on the wedding in the Iranian coastal town of Kuhestak killed four people late Tuesday, including a child, and wounded more than 50. /das

articles.title: ‘Friend-for-hire’ services gain traction in Thailand
articles.summary: “Friend-for-hire” services have started taking off in Thailand as the country’s social landscape changes with an aging population and a rise in the number of unmarried people. The service is a new…

blocks.text: “Friend-for-hire” services have started taking off in Thailand as the country’s social landscape changes with an aging population and a rise in the number of unmarried people.
The service is a new type of gig work in which people are paid to act as companions, for instance accompanying someone on a trip to take photos or even joining them in indoor rock climbing.

Although no official figures are available, industry players say demand for professional companions has increased in recent years due to the rise in people living alone, changing lifestyles and the influence of social media.
According to global market research company Euromonitor International, 29.5 percent of Thai households were single-person households in 2025, exceeding the global average of 21.9 percent.
And that growing segment has created rising demand for products and services designed for independent living, such as single-seat restaurant tables and solo travel.
For many clients, however, the motivation for hiring a companion is convenience rather than loneliness.

Ainthuon Rattanawaraporn, a university student and content creator from Bangkok, said she initially used the service out of curiosity but soon found it solved a problem—friends were sometimes too busy to come with her on trips but she was not yet comfortable traveling alone.
“I also wanted someone to take pictures for me,” she said.
Unlike asking friends for favors, hiring a companion allowed her to freely request specific photo angles and compositions because photography was part of the service.
“I don’t want to bother my friends by asking them to take hundreds of photos during a trip,” she said. “With a hired companion, I can tell them exactly what kind of pictures I want.”
Growing demand
The growing demand has created new income opportunities for people like Thanaporn Charoenchuea, a 20-year-old university student who started her “Snap Like a Bestie” service.
Within about two months, she had served more than 50 clients. She said her customers are not simply looking for someone to take photographs.
“They want someone who can make them feel comfortable while capturing natural-looking photos,” she said.
Apart from taking photos, Thanaporn spends much of her time chatting with clients, helping shy or introverted people relax before posing for pictures.

“The biggest challenge is making sure every client enjoys both the experience and the final photos,” she said. “I love photography and meeting new people, so I find the job both enjoyable and rewarding.”
On busy days, she accepts up to three appointments, each lasting between one and three hours. She only accepts bookings in public places after screening clients through their social media accounts.
For another companion service provider, Penkawin Wangniwetkul, known as Ice, the business has evolved well beyond photography.

After leaving her full-time job as a television coproducer, Ice spent several years working as a presenter, master of ceremonies, and online marketing host before entering the companionship business about three months ago.
The opportunity came unexpectedly after relatives suggested she accompany two elderly women on shopping trips and outings.
“I realized there was genuine demand for someone who could simply accompany people,” she said, adding that she later began posting about the experience on social media, leading to more referrals.

Today, clients hire her for activities, including running, gym workouts, aerobics, shopping, spa visits, cafe hopping, and even indoor rock climbing. A typical booking lasts two to three hours, and she charges 1,000 baht ($30) per hour.
Ice has served more than 10 clients and intentionally limits bookings because she continues to work as an MC and presenter. She also screens every client before accepting an assignment.

Her clients have included public figures, including an actress she accompanied to a veterinary clinic. She has also received requests to attend wedding receptions as a companion, although she was too busy to accept.

Despite growing demand, Ice is selective. She turns down requests that could compromise her safety or make her feel uncomfortable, including accompanying male clients to late-night entertainment venues.
Outside city trips
The service has also expanded to trips outside the city. Company employee Sasiprapa Nookong is among those who hired a companion during a trip to Chiang Mai.

Sasiprapa said that while traveling with a friend, they decided to spend one day pursuing different interests. Her friend planned to go hiking, while she preferred visiting cafes around the city, so she contacted a university student offering the service after seeing reviews on TikTok.

“I believe this service meets the needs of people who occasionally want company, not long-term companionship,” she said, echoing others in stressing that safety should always come first when hiring strangers.

Sociologist Narupon Duangwises of the Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn Anthropology Centre wrote in a report that interacting with hired companions may provide emotional comfort for people who find it difficult to make friends in everyday life.

But he noted that one feature distinguishing “friends for hire” from traditional friendship is the ability to choose a companion based on physical appearance, unlike friendships that develop naturally.
He therefore suggested that service providers establish clear rules and boundaries to protect themselves and prevent situations, such as sexual harassment or other forms of violence. /das

articles.title: El Niño could be strongest in decades, UN warns
articles.summary: GENEVA, Switzerland — El Niño is forecast to be the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago, the United Nations’ climate agency warned Thursday, with the UN chief saying the world…

blocks.text: GENEVA, Switzerland — El Niño is forecast to be the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago, the United Nations’ climate agency warned Thursday, with the UN chief saying the world was in the “danger zone of extreme weather.”
The weather phenomenon is set to become “very strong” in the months ahead and is almost certain to persist through February, the World Meteorological Organization said.
“If this trajectory continues, it may be stronger than anything since our monitoring began,” WMO chief Celeste Saulo told reporters in Geneva.
El Niño will peak toward the end of this year — though its knock-on effects on the climate will continue well into 2027, said the WMO.
El Niño warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall.
Heat in the oceans is released more slowly into the atmosphere, pushing up global temperatures the year after it develops.
The powerful 2023-24 El Niño contributed to 2024 being the warmest year on record, and “we should not be surprised if this record is broken,” Saulo added.

“El Niño is firmly established and will intensify into a very strong event in the coming months, with big impacts on rainfall and temperature patterns and associated risks of floods, drought and extreme heat,” the WMO said.
Highway to the danger zone
El Niño is a naturally occurring phenomenon and is not caused by climate change.
But scientists expect it will exacerbate the heat of a planet already warming from burning fossil fuels, while amplifying weather extremes.
“El Niño is being supersized before our eyes,” said UN chief Antonio Guterres.

“The science leaves no room for doubt: The planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up. Sea surface temperatures are rising, temperatures keep climbing, and the world is in the danger zone of extreme weather.”
WMO chief Saulo urged disaster management authorities and climate-sensitive sectors like agriculture, fisheries, health, energy and water to prepare themselves.
“This exceptional El Niño … has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world,” she said.
“We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods, and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies.”
El Niño typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months.
Conditions oscillate between El Niño and its opposite, La Niña, with neutral conditions in between.
El Niño can reshape weather and climate patterns thousands of kilometers away from the tropical Pacific.
Pacific Ocean heating up

Wilfran Moufouma-Okia, the WMO’s climate prediction chief, said some places would be affected before, some during and some after the peak later this year — though the strength of the peak is not an indicator of the severity of the impact.
For September-November, WMO forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of above-normal temperatures “across almost all land areas.”
The index, which measures sea surface temperature anomalies in the central eastern equatorial Pacific, has strengthened from an average 1.5°C above normal between May and July.
Weekly values between late July and mid-August ranged from around 2.2°C to 2.6°C above average, indicating continued El Niño intensification.
The UN agency classifies El Niño events as weak, moderate, strong or very strong — meaning this one is set to reach the highest level out of four.
Moufouma-Okia said the classification meant a sea surface temperature anomaly of more than 2°C.
“That category is open: We know where it starts; we don’t know where it ends,” he told AFP.
The average forecast is pointing toward an anomaly peaking at 3.6°C — way higher than the last two very strong El Niños in 1997-98 and 2015-16.
In some areas, subsurface ocean temperatures were more than 8°C above average during July and early August.
Saulo called this a huge reservoir of “very warm ocean waters that will fuel the intensity of El Niño.”
The UN’s International Organization for Migration agency appealed Thursday for $110 million to protect 4.9 million people from the potentially severe impacts of the phenomenon. /das

articles.title: Spacecraft bound for Mercury begins ‘tricky’ arrival
articles.summary: PARIS, France — After an eight-year journey, a spacecraft carrying European and Japanese probes began the months-long, high-risk approach to Mercury on Thursday to study the Sun-scorched planet. The…

blocks.text: PARIS, France — After an eight-year journey, a spacecraft carrying European and Japanese probes began the months-long, high-risk approach to Mercury on Thursday to study the Sun-scorched planet.
The BepiColombo mission set off from Earth in 2018 on a winding path to study the smallest and least understood planet in our solar system, with the aim of releasing the two probes into its orbit.
On Thursday, it began its arrival phase, described by the European Space Agency (ESA) as its “most operationally challenging planetary arrival sequence ever attempted.”

Mercury’s relatively tiny mass — it is only slightly bigger than the moon — means its gravitational pull is extremely weak compared with the Sun’s, making it complicated for spacecraft to approach the planet without ending up incinerated or lost in space.
“It’s a very ambitious mission,” Santa Martinez, the mission manager at ESA, told a press conference ahead of its arrival.
The spacecraft had to travel more than 10 billion kilometers (miles), executing a series of nine flybys, to speed up, slow down and perfect its trajectory.
The two probes, which are attached to each other, finally separated on Thursday from the transfer module that has propelled them — a crucial first step in the final approach.

It was the equivalent of “launching a new spacecraft. Only this spacecraft happens to be around a different planet,” explained Ignacio Tanco, ESA’s head of inner solar system mission operations, before the separation began.
All went to plan
On Thursday, Mercury was some 63 million km from the Sun and 200 million km from Earth.

“At these distances … any real-time operation becomes impossible,” Tanco said, explaining there was about a 30-minute delay between checks being performed and commands being executed from the ground to the spacecraft.
It meant the spacecraft had to check and execute the separation autonomously — a “tricky business,” Tanco said.
But all went to plan.
The spacecraft autonomously cut the four mechanical struts connecting the orbiters to the module.
Spring mechanisms then gently pushed them away.
The separation took place at a speed of 40 centimeters (16 inches) per second, leaving the two entities relatively close given the vastness of space.

Due to the distance between the probes and Earth, the signal confirming the operation’s success reached the control center in Darmstadt, Germany, nearly two hours later — at 1353 GMT — sparking rounds of applause and cheers.
“This is the best-case scenario, that the telemetry comes exactly at the moment we expect it,” said Elsa Montagnon, in charge of module operations at ESA.
“The spacecraft has completed its reconfiguration as expected,” she said with relief.
The probes are due to enter Mercury’s orbit on Nov. 21.
The next tricky phase will come on Dec. 9 and 10, when the two probes separate into their respective orbits.
From April, the ESA’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) will begin studying the planet closest to the Sun with unprecedented precision, passing just 480 km from its surface.
The Japanese Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio) will focus on its space environment and magnetic field, following an elliptical orbit that will carry it as far as 11,000 km away.
New chapter
Mercury is the least studied of the four rocky, innermost planets in our solar system, which include Venus, Earth and Mars.
NASA’s Mariner 10 was the first probe to capture a close image of its lunar-looking surface in 1974.
The MESSENGER probe then orbited the planet in 2011.
But many mysteries remain about its magnetic field, iron core and surface marked by hollows.

With its 16 instruments and 1.7-billion-euro ($2.0-billion) budget, BepiColombo “is going to bring to humanity and to the scientific community unprecedented views of Mercury … and it’s going to open a new chapter in our understanding of the solar system,” Martinez said. /das

articles.title: Spain’s PM says no evidence ‘whatsoever’ Morocco behind Ceuta border breach
articles.summary: Pedro Sánchez continues to defend Rabat after police report claiming border forces helped 70,000 cross border

blocks.text: Spain has seen no evidence “whatsoever” that Morocco planned or facilitated a mass border breach into its north African territory of Ceuta, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has told parliament.

The address on Thursday followed the emergence of a police report, commissioned by a judge and widely quoted in the media, claiming Moroccan border forces had actively aided about 70,000 people to cross the border in late July.

“I ‌can assure you ‌that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, ‌nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever,” Sánchez told parliament.

Speaking the morning after about 50,000 people marched in Madrid to protest his handling of the Ceuta crisis, the socialist prime minister also denied the government had received any warning of the mass breach, saying no reports to authorities had anticipated “the scale or probability of what eventually happened”.

blocks.caption: A protest against the Spanish government’s handling of the recent border breach at Ceuta. Photograph: Francesco Militello Mirto/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Sánchez has repeatedly defended Morocco during the crisis, highlighting Rabat’s cooperation in returning most of the migrants in the days after the surge.

But he said on Thursday that Spain had summoned Morocco’s ambassador on 21 August because of “unacceptable statements” made by two ministers over Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish north African territory. Last month, Morocco’s justice minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi, publicly reiterated Rabat’s sovereignty claims over the cities.
Sánchez said he had “for now” ruled out Moroccan government involvement but conceded that Moroccan forces had allowed crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on 30 July.
Many of those who crossed said in interviews they had been actively encouraged to do so. Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, called on Sánchez to resign for his “incompetence and complicity”.

In response to Sánchez summoning the Moroccan ambassador to discuss the crisis, Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, said: “Morocco doesn’t need an ambassador in Spain – you are its ambassador.”

blocks.caption: People who entered Ceuta from Morocco in late July on hunger strike last month to demand asylum.  Photograph: Laura Rincon/EPA

blocks.text: As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter Ceuta at the end of July. The influx unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.

On Thursday, Sánchez appealed for European solidarity over the crisis. He did not single out any countries by name but, in a pointed passage apparently aimed at Italy and Denmark, the two countries that had led public criticism of Spain, said the principle of solidarity should apply to Ceuta as much as it applies to Greenland and Lampedusa.
Although 90% of the people had returned to Morocco within 24 hours, several thousand, including at least 500 minors, are thought to remain, either living on the street or in makeshift shelters.

Amid calls from Vox to return them to Morocco, Sánchez reminded parliament that under Spanish, European and international law, migrants had a right to be treated as individuals. “You can’t just grab someone by the arm and drag them across the frontier as though they were a sack of dirt,” he told MPs.

In reference to the hundreds of destitute minors, Aina Vidal of the leftwing group Sumar, said: “They’re children, not invaders, not soldiers. They didn’t come carrying bombs, they arrived wearing water wings, in tears.”

It seems likely the government will invest in facilities in Ceuta to accommodate the remaining migrants rather than risk the political backlash both in Spain and across Europe were they to bring them to the mainland.
There is also evidence that, faced with hunger as well as hostility from many local people, some migrants have already begun going back to Morocco.

However, as Sánchez told parliament, the per capita income of Ceuta is eight times that of Morocco and “even if we build a wall 100 metres high there will still be people prepared to throw themselves into the sea to get across”.
“We will not stop working until Ceuta emerges from this difficult situation: stronger, more prosperous, and more integrated with the rest of Spain and the EU,” he added.
Additional reporting by Jakub Krupa

articles.title: Yen soars as Bank of Japan tipped to raise interest rates
articles.summary: Jump lifts currency to highest level against dollar in a month, while global markets remain jittery

blocks.text: The Japanese yen has soared by more than 1.7% against the dollar amid speculation the Bank of Japan is set to raise interest rates.
The latest jump on Thursday lifted the yen to its highest level against the dollar in a month, at 155.85, and followed a 0.9% move the previous day.
Global markets remain jittery after this week’s dramatic government bond sell-off – caused by fears of a fresh inflation increase as a result of higher oil prices.
Investors have been reassessing their expectations for the future path of interest rates, in Japan and across other major economies.
Remarks by a Bank of Japan policymaker, Hajime Takata, suggesting it needs to move more “nimbly”, appeared to have heightened the prospects of a decisive move.

The chief executive of the financial adviser deVere, Nigel Green, said the scale of the yen appreciation over such a short time period underlined the febrile state of markets. “Markets this jumpy don’t need a shock to move hard, a rumour is enough,” he said.
Citi said in a note to clients: “(The) remarks are the strongest messaging we’ve heard from the board and reintroduces the idea of an expedited rate hike trajectory.”

The Bank of Japan has been incrementally raising rates for the past two years, after the economy finally shrugged off decades of deflation, or falling prices – but its main policy rate was left unchanged at 1% in July.
Markets now believe there is a 77% chance of a rate rise at the BoJ’s next meeting, which starts on 17 September.

Commenting on the latest market moves, Japan’s vice-finance minister for international affairs, Atsushi Mimura, said he was “neither satisfied nor reassured”, and policymakers “remain on a state of heightened alert”.
after newsletter promotion

The global bond market sell-off – pushing up the yield, or interest rate, on government borrowing – intensified earlier this week after the US Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, used a speech last Friday to indicate that he was determined to bring inflation back to target.

Warsh had previously baffled some investors by withdrawing the Fed’s approach of signalling future rate moves, known as “forward guidance” – but in Friday’s speech at the central bankers’ conference in Jackson Hole, he said that if inflation did not move towards the 2% target the Fed would have “more to do”.

The bond sell-off appeared to have eased on Thursday, with yields on 10-year UK government bonds, known as gilts, hovering at about 5.1% in morning trading – having touched the highest level since 2008, close to 5.3%, earlier this week.

articles.title: Dozens of trapped hydropower tunnel workers in Nepal could still be alive, official says
articles.summary: About 46 people believed to be trapped in ‘room-like’ structure inside hydro plant tunnel on Nepal-Tibet border
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Gaurav Pokharel in Kathmandu

blocks.text: Nepal authorities have said they are “confident” that dozens of workers in Nepal’s Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant are still alive, more than a week after deadly flash floods left them trapped in an underground chamber.
Authorities said that at least 639 workers were still missing from hydropower plants built along Nepal’s Bhote Koshi and Triushuli rivers.

Most of the projects were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the river valley last week, triggered by ‌the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.
The deadly flash floods reached up to 100mph (160km/h), according to scientists, and travelled more than 60 miles down the river valley, wiping away whole villages, bridges, and hydropower dams.
At least 1,252 people have been confirmed dead from the floods. More than 4,200 remain missing.

According to a preliminary estimate by the UN Development Programme, the disaster created at least 2.2m tonnes of debris, including parts of buildings, rocks and sediment. Large boulders and flood waters deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud.

Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on these tunnels, where authorities believe workers may ⁠have survived for more than a week due to air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued from the hydropower projects.

blocks.caption: A turquoise-green house stands tall amid sludge near Trishuli River in the aftermath of flash floods.  Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Speaking on Wednesday, officials said they believed 46 people were still alive in an underground room in Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, and efforts were ongoing to locate them using excavators and other heavy equipment.

“We are very confident that they must be alive after one week because … they have food and water over there in the building,” Amhsu Kiran Shahi, a board member of the Nepal ⁠electricity authority, told Reuters.

Durga Gurung, 60, said his brother Jhappad Bhujel was among those trapped in a hydropower tunnel. “Right now, we are just relying on God,” he told the Guardian. “We have not been given any information about whether the people inside are alive or not.

“Neither the army nor the people from the electricity authority are telling us anything. So many days have passed that we have reached a point where it feels like all we can do is hope for a miracle.”
“Our relatives are sitting inside a dark tunnel,” he added. “How long can they possibly survive?”

blocks.caption: The area around Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant before the flash flood.  Photograph: Maxar/DigitalGlobe/Getty Images

blocks.text: Major rescue operations were under way or planned at four hydropower projects. Two sites – the Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project and the Upper Trishuli 3A facility – where about 90 people are missing, offered the strongest prospect of finding survivors because of the presence of air inside the tunnels, Shahi said.

The Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project is located in Rasuwa district, about three miles away from the border with Tibet, which was one of the areas of Nepal hardest hit by the floods, and remains almost inaccessible except by helicopter. “This is the only project where it’s possible to walk through ‌the tunnel,” Shahi said. “The army tried doing that three days ago, but they didn’t find the room. We are going in again.”

At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, another project hit by the floods, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels ⁠because of the thick mud. The authorities believe about 30 to 40 people may still be alive in the tunnel. “We are expecting [survivors] in there because we ​are told there is a ​dry space inside. We are ​trying to break into the tunnel now,” said the Nepali army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet on Wednesday.

The army said the search and rescue operation would go on for as long as there was hope for survivors, but that efforts would also continue to recover the dead bodies. “We are using every technology ​available in Nepal ‌right now, and we ​are taking help ​from the Indians, Chinese, Koreans. We have experts from Australia too,” added Basnet.

Families of those still trapped in the projects have returned to the Nepal electricity office for the past eight days, in the hope for information. Laxmi Adhikari’s brother Jeevanlal Adhikari had gone to the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project to test the machines, when the floods hit.

She accused the authorities of withholding information from the families, and of not acting fast enough to save their relatives. “We have been running from one ministry to another and from disaster management authority to another government office, trying to find my brother,” she said. “We keep going from place to place, but the rescue operation has not been accelerated.”

She said the lack of answers made the wait even more painful: “When the water came rushing in, where did he go? Did he manage to get to safety? They haven’t even given us definite information about whether our people are alive or not.”

Nepal has invested more than $9bn (£6.7bn) in building hydropower dams across the mountains, huge sums given the country’s small economy. According to preliminary surveys, the floods debilitated or destroyed 11 hydropower plants and knocked out about 10% of Nepal’s total electricity-generation capacity.
According to the authorities, more than 20,000 houses will have to be rebuilt in the aftermath of the flood. Nepal has put the cost of recovery at more than $5bn (£3.7bn).

articles.title: DOJ careful in evaluating US extradition bid for Apollo Quiboloy
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines—The Department of Justice (DOJ) said it continues to assess the request by the United States to extradite jailed evangelist and alleged sex offender Apollo Quiboloy, as it does…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines—The Department of Justice (DOJ) said it continues to assess the request by the United States to extradite jailed evangelist and alleged sex offender Apollo Quiboloy, as it does not want to take the matter to the court “half-baked.”

Justice Undersecretary Ian Dato said in a news briefing on Thursday that the main factor in determining whether the DOJ should proceed with filing a petition for extradition in a local court is whether the request is “thorough enough” to stand in court.

“The department is conscious of the fact that it should not be filing anything half baked,” Dato stressed. “It will not bound itself to a timeline, but it will make sure that whatever case or petition it will file in court will stand scrutiny by the judge.”

The DOJ received on Aug. 7 the vast amount of documents from the US to boost its request for extradition of Quiboloy, who is facing charges of sex trafficking, visa fraud and cash smuggling in the US.

Chief state counsel Dennis Chan had noted that once the DOJ completes its evaluation and finds that the extradition request was in compliance with the 1994 treaty between the Philippines and the US, a petition would be formally filed before a regional trial court.
However, this could still be challenged by Quiboloy, but only up to the level of the Court of Appeals, based on the Supreme Court’s new extradition rules.
The DOJ also earlier maintained that it is serious in its commitment to international law as well as to a fair judgment of the case. /mr

articles.title: Victims sue South African government over 1961 Sharpeville massacre that left 91 dead
articles.summary:
Claim relating to infamous apartheid-era shooting of protesters part of wave of litigation for apartheid-era crimes

The day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South…

blocks.text: The day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South African township of Sharpeville gathered to protest against pass laws, which forced “Black, Indian and Coloured” South Africans to carry documents at all times specifying where they were allowed to be.

Abraham Mofokeng joined the march, one of dozens organised nationwide by the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), a breakaway group from the African National Congress. “The weather was very nice, the sun was out. You could not have suspected that the day would go so horribly,” said Mofokeng, who was then a 20-year-old factory worker.

blocks.caption: Abraham Mofokeng, who was shot in the foot and back while protesting against South Africa’s apartheid pass laws during the Sharpeville massacre on 21 March 1960.  Photograph: Rachel Savage/The Guardian

blocks.text: Mofokeng, now 86, was among the thousands gathered peacefully outside the police station in Sharpeville, which is about 40 miles south of Johannesburg in a heavily industrialised region known as the Vaal Triangle.
The crowd was singing, he said, when officers opened fire without warning. At least 91 people were killed and 238 injured, in what became known as the Sharpeville massacre.

As Mofokeng fled, a bullet grazed the inside of his right foot, ripping his shoe off. A woman fell to the ground before him; he jumped over her and kept running. Only later, when he noticed blood running down his legs, did he realise he had been shot in the back, where a bullet remains lodged in his spine.
Mofokeng is among three claimants suing the South Africa government, in a case filed on Thursday, for compensation for the massacre. If the case is successful, dozens more could file claims.

The case is part of a wave of litigation demanding justice for apartheid-era crimes, amid widespread disillusionment with ANC-led governments that have failed to rectify South Africa’s huge racial inequality and poverty since the end of apartheid over three decades ago.

blocks.caption: Dead and wounded South Africans lie outside the Sharpeville police station. Photograph: PN2

blocks.text: In January 2025, 25 survivors and relatives of victims of apartheid state violence sued South Africa’s government for failing to prosecute cases referred to it by the post-apartheid Truth and Reconciliation Commission. That May, the president, Cyril Ramaphosa, announced a judicial inquiry into potential political interference, which is still ongoing.
Spokespeople for South Africa’s justice department did not respond to a request for comment on the Sharpeville compensation case.

In the immediate aftermath of the Sharpeville massacre, police claimed that protesters had been throwing rocks at them. “I don’t know how many we shot,” said Colonel J Pienaar, the local police commander, according to a story published by the Guardian the following day. “It all started when hordes of natives surrounded the police station. My car was struck with a stone. If they do these things they must learn their lesson the hard way.”

In July 1961, in response to victims filing compensation claims, the white minority regime passed a law indemnifying the government and anyone acting under its authority for any actions taken “in good faith for the prevention or suppression of internal disorder, the maintenance or restoration of good order, public safety or essential services, or the preservation of life or property”.

blocks.caption: Members of a choir perform during the commemorations of the massacre, at the Phelindaba cemetery in Sharpeville, on 21 March 2026.  Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The law, which was made effective retrospectively from the date of the massacre, is still in force today. The claimants’ legal team is arguing that the law is unconstitutional.

The claimants are hoping to get compensation of about 500,000 rand (£23,000), said Daniel Leader, a partner with UK law firm Leigh Day, which is advising the South African legal team, led by Lawyers For Human Rights, an NGO.
Mafokeng was awarded 30,000 rand as a one-off payment, after the TRC concluded in 2003. The TRC had recommended annual reparations payments of around 20,000 rand for six years.
“We continued to suffer,” said Mofokeng, who still lives in Sharpeville. “Especially now … I am struggling and my health is not up to standard.”

blocks.caption: Paulina Mathinye, whose father Samson was killed by police in the Sharpeville massacre Photograph: Rachel Savage/The Guardian

blocks.text: The other two test claimants were children when their fathers were killed in the massacre. Paulina Mathinye was five when her father Samson was shot. “Every time he came back from work, I would be so happy to see him that I would run to him, and then he would pick me up,” she said.
Mathinye didn’t initially understand what had happened that day in 1960. “I kept on asking my mum: ‘Mummy, why are you crying?’”

Mathinye’s mother struggled to raise her five children on a domestic worker’s wages and Mathinye, who had wanted to train as a teacher but couldn’t afford the bursary, had to leave education at 17 to find work.

Mathinye, who is now 71, said she hoped for compensation that would make up for some of what she lost when her father died. “Some of my friends are teachers, some of them are nurses, and I’m staying in the same house that my father did,” she said.

Sharpeville’s problems didn’t begin with the massacre in 1960, but with the dispossession of Black South Africans from productive land, their forced removals to townships and their exclusion from the economy, said Vincent Thamae, a PAC member who supports the massacre victims and their families.

“When people talk about compensation now,” he said, “compensation is a concept to them that includes all the land that they lost, the economy that they were taken out of and even how they have been treated in the new democracy.”

articles.title: Barclays faces complaint over backing for power plant near world’s largest mangrove forest
articles.summary:
Bangladeshi complainants allege Rampal power station’s pollution and climate risks threaten the Sunderbans, a world heritage site

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its…

blocks.text: Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.

Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.

The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.

Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.
“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”
Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.

Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.

blocks.caption: The Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and one of the last habitats of Bengal tigers, supports the livelihoods of millions of people.  Photograph: Bengal Picture Library/Alamy

blocks.text: Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources.

The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.

Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank of India between 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.

The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.

The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, including concerns raised by Unesco in a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France, refused to support the project because of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.

Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.

“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”

Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”
The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.
They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.

Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”
The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.
Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.

articles.title: Guinea-Bissau voters approve new constitution expanding presidential powers
articles.summary:
Changes include fewer seats in parliament and new rules on presidential candidates ahead of December elections

Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution significantly expanding…

blocks.text: Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution significantly expanding presidential powers ahead of elections due in December.

According to provisional results, 70% of voters approved sweeping changes in the tiny west African state’s first constitutional amendment since revisions that ended the one-party socialist state more than three decades ago.
The turnout for Sunday’s referendum was reportedly over 55%, amounting to an estimated 544,060 people.

The new constitution will reduce the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65 and cut electoral constituencies from 29 to 12. New provisions will require presidential candidates to have lived continuously in the country for at least five years before the vote, which is believed to target diaspora-based politicians with significant followings.

The referendum’s outcome is expected to pave the way for December’s elections, which many hope will steady the political landscape in Guinea-Bissau, which has been through a series of politically turbulent periods since its declaration of independence from Portugal was globally recognised in 1974. Since then it has had at least 10 coup attempts, half of which have been successful.

The most recent came after last November’s disputed presidential elections. Both candidates declared themselves winners, citing electoral malpractice by the other’s camp. The military forcefully intervened, setting up a transitional ruling council headed by Gen Horta Inta-A Na Man, a former military chief of general staff.
Na Man said: “What we want after this referendum is to allow whoever wins the elections to see out their mandate without hindrance.”
Nelson Moreira, the second vice-president of the transitional council, said the outgoing constitution, which came into effect in 1993, had often been cited as “the cause of instability in Guinea”.

The leading opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), which was barred from fielding a presidential candidate in the 2025 election, had asked its supporters to boycott the referendum, which it called a democratic farce.
“What will happen on 30 August is the continuation of the coup d’état carried out on 26 November,” its leader, Domingos Simões Pereira, had said.

articles.title: Relief as five Australians missing in Nepal-Tibet flood disaster found alive
articles.summary: Several missing Australians have been found since Tuesday morning, bringing the total citizens unaccounted for to 38

blocks.text: A total of five Australians missing after devastating floods ravaged the Nepal-Tibet border last week have been found.
Of the five Australians confirmed safe, one was found in Nepal, one in Tibet, and three outside the crisis-hit area. The total number still missing is 38.
These Australians had not spoken to families and next of kin since the disaster struck seven days ago.
There were “grave concerns” for the dozens of citizens still missing in the disaster, the minister for multicultural affairs, Anne Aly, told the ABC on Wednesday morning.
“There are real logistic issues, including communications to find out where people are,” she said.

“For those families that are still waiting, those 38 individuals unaccounted for, we understand that it’s a really concerning time, and we’ll continue to do what we can to try and locate those people.”
Earlier, the minister for the Pacific, Pat Conroy, told Radio National the government was “focused on establishing their whereabouts and supporting their families”.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Dfat) has received nearly 800 calls in relation to the floods, with 18 Australian personnel having travelled to Nepal to join staff on the ground.
More humanitarian and disaster relief from Australia was due to arrive in Nepal on Wednesday afternoon.
Another Australian, 25-year-old Cara Severino, was safely located last week.
After an Australian in Tibet made contact with family and Dfat yesterday, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said the government was “incredibly thankful”.
“It’s hard to imagine the sense of relief their loved ones must be feeling after what will have been an incredibly harrowing few days.”
The death toll from the ⁠unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud ​and debris on Wednesday last week has risen to 939 people, with 16 more dead reported in Tibet.
More than 4,400 people are missing.
Wong said the government needed to “remain realistic” about the days ahead.
“Communications remain difficult, infrastructure has been destroyed and many areas are still difficult to reach,” she said.
“As each day passes, our grave concerns for those still unaccounted for inevitably grow.
“Our thoughts remain firmly with all those waiting for news of family and friends, and with the search and rescue teams working in extraordinarily difficult circumstances.”
Australia has sent a $8m assistance package for affected communities on the border between Nepal and the Chinese region of Tibet.
Nepal has deployed nearly 20,000 security personnel to support search and rescue, and Chinese state media has reported that 2,141 emergency personnel have been deployed.

articles.title: British aid worker mistakenly identified as a survivor of Nepal-Tibet disaster
articles.summary:
More than 1,000 people confirmed dead and more than 4,000, including 36 British nationals, remain missing

A British aid worker was mistakenly identified by Nepalese authorities as a rescued…

blocks.text: A British aid worker was mistakenly identified by Nepalese authorities as a rescued survivor after returning to Kathmandu on a humanitarian aid flight.
Alastair Chambers, a 45-year-old former Gloucester councillor, said he flew to Nepal last week to distribute sleeping bags, food and essentials to communities cut off by collapsed bridges.
After spending several days in a village near the Trishuli river in central Nepal, Chambers returned by helicopter to the capital, where he was greeted by police officers asking for his details.
“I gave them my details, just abiding by the rules, and they obviously thought that I’d been rescued,” Chambers told the Press Association.
Chambers appeared on a list of 119 names released by local authorities on Tuesday. An army spokesperson then told reporters at a press conference that a British national was among those rescued.

“I was contacted by about 15 different journalists in the last few hours, just asking how I was and how I’m feeling after being rescued, and I had to say: ‘Well sorry, I haven’t been rescued,’” Chambers told PA.
Those rescued included 118 Nepali nationals – 44 women and 74 men.
Thirty-six British nationals are missing, the Foreign Office minister, Stewart Wood, told the House of Lords on Tuesday. The figure had previously been put at 33.

Chambers was fined £49,000 after pleading guilty in June 2022 to breeding and selling dogs without a licence. The 45-year-old, who was the leader of a group of community independents on Gloucester city council until 2024, is due to face trial in November after denying he used homophobic slurs against a bar owner and former council worker.
At least 1,050 people have been confirmed dead in Nepal since Wednesday’s flash floods, while Chinese state media said 66 people had been killed in Tibet. More than 4,000 people are still missing.
Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, said 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region. This included 330 foreign nationals, the Nepalese tourist board said in an update on Tuesday.
Preliminary analysis of satellite imagery suggests the collapse of a glacier high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the disaster.

The collapse – so large it was initially recorded as a magnitude-4.4 earthquake – triggered a deadly torrent of water, mud and ice that tore along the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on Wednesday.
Crews have faced dangerous and difficult conditions while searching unstable terrain and flood debris.
Search efforts are now focused on attempts to reach about 600 workers believed to be trapped inside tunnels at several hydropower stations in the region.
“Massive work has been going on in the tunnel, all the tunnels,” the army spokesperson said on Tuesday.

A rapid deployment rescue team from the UK arrived in Nepal on Saturday to provide support for Britons and their families as part of the government’s £5m commitment to support relief and recovery efforts.
The Red Cross estimates that 93,000 people have been directly affected by the disaster.

articles.title: 'Tapusin na yan!': Prosecution to finish confidential funds article next week, says Chua
articles.summary: Saying they don't want an overly lengthy impeachment trial, members of the House prosecution panel intend to conclude its presentation on the confidential funds misuse article against Vice President…

blocks.text: Saying they don't want an overly lengthy impeachment trial, members of the House prosecution panel intend to conclude its presentation on the confidential funds misuse article against Vice President Sara Duterte next week.
According to solon-prosecutor Manila 3rd district Rep. Joel Chua, the team is already looking to shift to the two remaining articles of impeachment.

“Masasabi natin, baka by next week ay matapos na, hopefully, ang confidential funds, and we will move on to the next article,” Chua said Tuesday afternoon, Sept. 1 during the prosecution's post-hearing press conference.
(We can say that, hopefully, we could finish the confidential funds article by next week, and we will move on to the next article.)

On Tuesday, Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) Colonels Manaros Boransing II and Magtanggol Panopio testified about Army certifications that were used in the Department of Education’s (DepEd) response to state auditors.

In an effort to shorten its witness list, Chua said two other military officers would no longer be presented since their expected testimony would largely repeat the points already placed on the record.
“Iisa lang naman iyong sasabihin nila. To shorten—ayaw naman natin ng protracted hearing. Gusto natin matapos na rin ito.”
(They would only be saying the same thing. To shorten [the proceedings]—we don’t want a protracted hearing. We also want this to be finished.)
Chua said prosecutors already covered the central points involving the Youth Leadership Summits (YLS) and the military certifications.

Respondent Duterte is being accused--among other things--of misuing a total of P612.5 million worth of confidential funds released to the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and Department of Education (DepEd).
On Wednesday, Sept. 2, the prosecution expects to present former DepEd undersecretary and chief-of-staff Michael Wesley Poa, as well as a representative of the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA)

Poa, currently Duterte’s defense lawyer, is expected to address the chain behind the military certifications, while the PSA witness will cover its checks of names appearing in confidential-fund records.

After those witnesses, the Manila solon said the remaining article I lineup would be short. “Ang natitira na lamang si Mr. Edward Fajarda, and probably isa—or at most, dalawa,” he said, referring to DepEd’s former special disbursing officer (SDO).
“The only one remaining is Mr. Edward Fajarda, and probably one—or at most, two [more witnesses].”
He said the prosecution will make its final lineup decision after Wednesday’s hearing. The panel previously finished its presentation of evidence on article IV, or the death threats article.
Defense's turn next
Chua reminded impeachment trial watchers that once the prosecution finishes all four articles of impeachment, the defense must present its own case.
“May target kasi tayo. We have to understand, after us mayroon pang defense; sila naman ang magpe-present. Siyempre ayaw naman natin na umabot pa ito by next year,” he said.
(We have a target. We have to understand that after us, there is still the defense; they will be the ones to present [their case]. Of course, we don’t want this to extend into next year.)

"Sana, hopefully, by November tapos na lahat (Hopefully, everything will be finished by November), so by December we can have the decision of the impeachment court whether or not to convict the Vice President," Chua said.

articles.title: Will impeachment trial prosecutors resign? Not anymore, says Chua
articles.summary: The House prosecution team's core of 11 solon-prosecutors will remain intact in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial. Thus, said prosecutor Manila 3rd district Rep. Joel Chua, with the…

blocks.text: The House prosecution team's core of 11 solon-prosecutors will remain intact in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial.
Thus, said prosecutor Manila 3rd district Rep. Joel Chua, with the revelation shelving a proposal for some of them to resign from the panel so they could speak publicly about the merits of the case.
“We have decided, wala na lang munang mag-resign,” Chua said Tuesday, Sept. 1 following day 20 of the high-stakes proceedings.
The panel considered a reshuffle after the Senate impeachment court reiterated the sub judice rule, or the limits on public comments about matters being tried.

One option was for selected House prosecutors to leave the panel and serve only as spokespersons. “Noong una, isa iyon sa mga naging discussion kung ganoon ang mangyayari. Kasi iyon ang talagang unang option,” Chua said.
(At first, that was one of the discussions, if that was what would happen. Because that was really the first option.)
The idea drew support from lawyers working with the team. “May mga suggestion ang ibang private prosecutor at public prosecutor na may ilan mag-resign para maging spokesperson."
(Some private prosecutors and public prosecutors suggested that some members resign so they could serve as spokespersons.)
But Chua said the prosecution members ultimately chose continuity. He noted that changing the structure of the team at this stage would require finding replacements.
“After considering everything, total isang buwan na lang kung masusunod iyong ating target...Too late na kung magbabawas tayo at magdadagdag pa,” Chua said.
(After considering everything, there’s only about a month left if we follow our target...It’s too late if we start removing and adding members.)
As such, the team will keep public briefings focused on schedules, witness sequencing, and other procedural updates.
More importantly, Chua said the prosectors "will just try to explain things in a way that does not touch on the merits [of the case]".

That was also why Chua, a public prosecutor, appeared at Tuesday’s briefing. He said reporters could still ask about what comes next without forcing prosecutors into a public discussion of the evidence.
“Baka may magtanong tungkol sa procedural aspect outside the merits of the case, so I can answer that,” said the veteran lawmaker from Manila.
(Someone might ask about the procedural aspects outside the merits of the case, so I can answer that.)
The approach allows the public to receive practical updates while the same prosecutors continue their work inside the impeachment court, Chua said.
It also preserves the team’s current assignments as the prosecution tries to finish article I on confidential funds and move to the remaining articles of impeachment against Duterte.
Fifteen private prosecutors are helping the solon-prosecutors gain a conviction from the respondent, free of charge.

articles.title: Philippines prepares for unprecedented 5-million tons rice imports
articles.summary: The Philippines will import a record-high five million metric tons (MT) this year, as it turns to foreign supplies to offset a projected shortfall in domestic production caused by El Niño, according…

blocks.text: The Philippines will import a record-high five million metric tons (MT) this year, as it turns to foreign supplies to offset a projected shortfall in domestic production caused by El Niño, according to the Department of Agriculture (DA).

“As we are facing El Niño, we are projecting that we might need to import up to five million MT for this year,” said Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel during his agency’s budget hearing on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
The projected import volume this year is nearly four percent higher than the current record of 4.81 million MT set in 2024.
Total rice imports as of Aug. 13 reached 3.46 million MT, already higher than the 3.39 million MT recorded last year, according to the Bureau of Plant Industry (BPI).
Tiu Laurel said the additional rice supply will serve as a buffer as the country’s rice production losses are estimated to reach 900,000 MT within the year.
He said the decline represents the “worst-case scenario” of a strong El Niño in the fourth quarter of the year, which is projected to damage several hectares of rice farms.
“What we are all doing this year is precautionary. It is better to be prepared and have enough supply rather than risk having a shortage,” said Tiu Laurel.
Tiu Laurel noted that increased rice imports for the year will also serve as a supply cushion for the first quarter of next year in order to get ahead of a potentially weaker harvest season.
Considering this, the import volume for 2027 may go down to the normal range of between 3.8 million MT and four million MT.
While the country relies on foreign supplies to meet domestic demand, Tiu Laurel said the main objective of the government continues to be increasing local output.
He told lawmakers that the DA is focused on rolling out mechanization measures, expanding irrigation, and developing new rice seeds to further boost productivity.
The agency is also preparing to implement a program requiring traders to first invest in rice mills and processing facilities before they allowed to purchase rice from abroad.
It is estimated that around 80 percent of rice importers in the country are engaged solely in importing and have yet to commit investments in the local rice sector.
“That is one of the plans to make the industry self-sustaining and competitive in the international market,” said Tiu Laurel.
Based on BPI data, Vietnam has maintained its position as the country’s top rice supplier with imports reaching 2.56 million MT, or 74 percent of the total volume, as of Aug. 13.
Other top sources of rice include Thailand with 378,404 MT, Myanmar with 286,052 MT, Pakistan with 107,485 MT, and Cambodia with 87,802 MT.
The DA’s proposed budget for next year is ₱198.45 billion, down eight percent from the allocation of ₱215.69 billion for this year.

Under this budget, the agency wants to prioritize programs that raise farm and fishery productivity, improve infrastructure, reduce post-harvest losses, strengthen logistics and market access, and expand the use of technology.

articles.title: Creamline stays unscathed; EST Cola sweeps Farm Fresh
articles.summary: Creamline routed Ho Chih Minh City, 25-18, 25-16, 25-6, to remain unscathed, while EST Cola swept Farm Fresh, 25-21, 25-16, 25-22, to barge into the win column in the PVL Invitational at the Smart…

blocks.text: Creamline routed Ho Chih Minh City, 25-18, 25-16, 25-6, to remain unscathed, while EST Cola swept Farm Fresh, 25-21, 25-16, 25-22, to barge into the win column in the PVL Invitational at the Smart Araneta Coliseumon Tuesday, Sept. 1.
The Cool Smashers exposed the Vietnamese’s lethargic plays, needing 61 minutes to dominate the guest team for their second straight win in as many outings.
Tots Carlos, Jema Galanza and Jaja Santiago-Minowa paced Creamline with 12 points apiece, including combined 21 kills from Carlos and Galanza, and three blocks from Santiago-Minowa.
So dominant were the Cool Smashers that they overpowered the Vietnamese spikers on attacks, 49-19; blocks, 11-4; and aces, 5-3.
None from Ho Chi Minh City scored in twin figures with skipper Dang Thi Kim Thanh and Le Thi My Xuyen pacing only eight and six points, respectively, as they absorbed their second straight loss.
Earlier, EST Cola made its title bid to improve its record to 1-1 behind the efforts of Papatchaya Phontham.
Phontham blasted 17 points built on 13 kills, three aces and one block to shackle Farm Fresh, which struggled despite the 15-point effort of Trisha Tubu.

articles.title: Yamsuan bent on helping CHEd once travel tax windfall stops
articles.summary: A solon who holds a key position in the House 2027 national budget process has vowed to help find alternative funding for the Commission on Higher Education (CHEd) should the measure abolishing the…

blocks.text: A solon who holds a key position in the House 2027 national budget process has vowed to help find alternative funding for the Commission on Higher Education (CHEd) should the measure abolishing the travel tax becomes a law this year.

Parañaque City 2nd district Rep. Brian Raymund Yamsuan has noted that CHEd, which regulates higher education and administers the government’s financial aid programs for tertiary-level students, gets part of its funding from 40 percent of the total gross collections from the travel tax.

Yamsuan, a member of the House Budget Amendments and Review Subcommittee (BARSc) pointed out that under Malacañang’s National Expenditure Program for Fiscal Year 2027, a portion of the allocation for the CHEd’s Higher Education Development Fund (HEDF) would still be sourced from the travel tax collections of the Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority (TIEZA).

“Kami po ay magtatrabaho sa Kongreso para hanapan kayo ng alternative sources of funding once mangyari po ang pagsasabatas ng abolition ng travel tax,” Yamsuan told CHEd Chairperson Shirley Agrupis during the House Committee on Appropriations’ recent budget deliberations on the agency’s proposed 2027 budget.
(We will work in Congress to look for alternative sources of funding once the travel tax measure is enacted into law.)

Formed during last year's budget cycle as a pro-transparency measure, the BARSc effectively replaced the so-called "small committee", which incorporates individual ammendments to the General Appropriations Bill (GAB) or proposed national budget.

If the bill abolishing the travel tax is passed into law, Agrupis told the House Committee on Tourism last March that without a substitute funding source, the CHEd would lose 85.6 percent of the funding for the HEDF.
She calls this prospect “a structural loss that directly affects scholarships, research and institutional upgrading, and tourism education programs".

The House of Representatives approved on March 16 the measure seeking to abolish the travel tax. Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian earlier said the Senate version of the measure is included in the chamber’s priority list of bills and will be passed this year.

“Kami bilang member ng BARSc, sisiguraduhin ko po na sa susunod na pagpupulong with (Committee on Appropriations) Chair Mika (Suansing) ay gagawa po kami ng paraan upang maibalik ang pondo para hindi maantala ang magagandang programa ng CHEd,” Yamsuan added.

(As member of the BARSc, I would make sure that in the next meeting with Committee on Appropriations Chairperson Mikaela Angela Suansing, we would find ways to restore CHEd’s funding so as not to delay the implementation of CHEd’s good programs)

During the hearing, the Parañaque solon also thanked the CHEd for its efficient implementation of the government’s higher education initiatives and financial assistance to tertiary-level students, particularly the Tulong Dunong Program (TDP).
The TDP provides a financial grant of up to P7,500 per semester or a total of P15,000 per school year to help cover the tuition and other daily expenses of qualified college students.
Yamsuan urged the CHEd to conduct more consultations with Local Universities and Colleges (LUC) to help them institute reforms that would allow them to take part in the TDP.
Out of 170 LUCs, only 116 are CHEd-recognized institutions qualified to accept TDP grants from its enrollees.

articles.title: On the borderline
articles.summary: With these three novels, we use borderline in both a physical sense and in a metaphorical manner, as the trio of books explores what ‘the other side’ can mean. "Sublimation" by Isabel J. Kim Think of…

blocks.text: With these three novels, we use borderline in both a physical sense and in a metaphorical manner, as the trio of books explores what ‘the other side’ can mean.
"Sublimation" by Isabel J. Kim

Think of the immigrant experience, but now seen through a SciFi lens, and you have an idea of what this novel bravely explores. Kim has written short stories that have won Nebula, Locus, and Shirley Jackson Awards, and this is her debut novel. Soyoung Rose Kang is the protagonist here, and at the age of 10, she left Korea with her mother to emigrate to the USA. She left an ‘instance’ in Korea, who would continue to interact with her family and grandfather. And now, with the death of the grandfather, Soyoung (the instance in Korea) gets in touch with Rose (the instance in the USA), to let her know it was their grandfather’s wish that she come to Seoul for the funeral. What Rose isn’t aware of is that Soyoung harbors the desire to reintegrate. This gets complicated by the fact that the grandfather has left his house to Rose - who never tried to establish a relationship with Soyoung, or her ‘lolo’.

Structured initially so that the chapters alternate between Soyoung and Rose’s POVs, Kim pulls off this delicate balancing act with a lot of skill and charm. She endeavors to make both Soyoung and Rose distinct, while also having such similarities so we appreciate how they are, in fact, two versions of the same person. They’re not twins or doppelgangers, but two ‘instances’-and before the grandfather’s death and meeting in Seoul, have not really been in contact with each other. To make our reading more intense, there’s a Yujin in Korea, and his instance, YJ, in New York. Childhood friend of Soyoung, the Yujin pair have their own set of issues, but have been friends since the moment of ‘instance’, communicating regularly. Their story and how it intersects with that of Soyoung Rose take up the last half of this novel, which takes us to some hard decision-making and the facing of consequences. Bold, imaginative writing that speaks of borders and identity.
"The Pinnacle" by Abir Mukhergee

Set in the penthouse of a luxury condominium called The Pinnacle in Mumbai, this new novel from the author of Hunted, which was named 2025 Thriller of the Year, is both a locked-room mystery thriller and a penetrating study of class dynamics in India today. George Abercrombie is an over-the-hill Hollywood actor who’s married to Sweety Sahota, the current queen of Bollywood. Gemma is Sweety’s PA who joined them in India all the way from the US. The premise has to do with George waking up after a quarrel with Sweety and a drinking binge, and finding her murdered on their king-size bed. With no recollection of what he did the night before, one narrative strand has to do with George having to prove he’s innocent. Then there’s Gemma, who’s receiving cryptic text messages. And finally, there’s Amit, George’s shadow and PA, who seems to know too much and goes on the run.

The seedy underbelly of luxury living is exposed in this gripping adventure. We may be on the 68th floor of an upscale skyscraper, but the hypocrisy, filth, and societal evil still reach these heights. The novel revolves around three plots, and the borders of society and social standing are constantly placed as reminders of what our protagonists have to face on a Daily basis.
